chapters.label: Why algorithms?
chapters.text: Module 1 · Introduction to algorithms An algorithm is just a recipe a machine can follow Every business task — brewing tea, running payroll, approving a loan — can be rewritten as a small set of organised steps. This module builds the four working definitions you will use for the rest of the course — then watches how algorithms grow, evolve and never quite finish. 1 Start with chai One cup of tea contains the entire vocabulary of the module. Ingredients 1 cup water 1 cup milk 2–3 tsp loose black tea 2–3 tsp sugar → DATA Equipment Gas / induction stove · strainer do actual work on the data → FUNCTIONS Saucepan · teacups hold the data while steps run → VARIABLES Steps 1 Add water and boil 2 Add tea leaves, boil 1 min 3 Pour milk, add sugar 4 Gentle boil 5 Simmer 2–3 min 6 Strain and serve → ALGORITHM Try the recipe with the milk poured first, or the sugar skipped entirely — the sequence flexes with preference , but the outcome stays the same: a cup of tea. That is the quiet surprise of Lecture 1 — an algorithm is not a sacred order, it is organised steps that work toward an output . Which is exactly why they turn up everywhere: in the kitchen, at the ATM, inside every app you opened today. 2 The working definitions Four words you will meet in every lecture, every exam question. Data The actual values the algorithm works with while it runs — and they change with every situation: more guests at the table means more water and milk. Or marks, salaries, stock counts. Variables Constructs that hold data during computation — think physical vessels: the saucepan holds the tea while it cooks, the teacup holds the serve, S1 holds a mark. Algorithm Organised steps that complete a task — the sequence may flex with preference, but every ordering works toward the same output. Function A subgroup of organised steps inside a larger algorithm — common tasks whose steps are identical wherever they appear: adding numbers, averaging marks, providing heat in cooking. Why business students care A payroll run, a loan approval, an inventory reorder — each one is an algorithm. Data goes in (hours worked, credit score, stock level), organised steps run in between, and a decision comes out. Once you see the shape business process = data + algorithm , you can redesign any of them. 3 Every algorithm is a simplification Start simple, add detail, repeat forever — why nothing ships finished. Lecture 1 · complexity & evolution Here is the sentence that explains half the software industry: every algorithm is a simplification of a real process . Look closely at step 1 of the chai recipe — “add water”. Inside those two words hide a dozen intuitive moves: find the water, find a container, carry both to the stove, fill to the right level. Real life runs on steps that feel too obvious to write down — and an algorithm is exactly the act of writing them down anyway. So algorithms start simple and gain complexity as details are added : one more check, one more condition, one more branch. The tea recipe became a smarter algorithm the moment we asked “is the tea sufficiently brewed?” — and the ATM becomes a smarter machine with every rule the bank adds. Complexity is not a defect. It is the record of every situation the algorithm has learned to handle. Deterministic business systems Payroll, billing, loan approval, the ATM — modern business runs on calculation-based, deterministic rules . Same input, same output, no mood swings. That makes them easy to algorithmize : the logic is already arithmetic waiting to be organised. Physical, real-time systems A warehouse robot, an autonomous car — they decide while the world moves , with sensors and traffic and weather in the loop. Real-time judgement is far harder to codify than arithmetic, which is why these systems remain the hard frontier of algorithm design. …and that is why quality apps update forever Every update you have ever installed adds functions, checks and refined conditions to algorithms that already worked. An app is never “finished” — it is an algorithm still collecting the details life keeps throwing at it. Frequent updates are not churn; they are the simplification catching up with reality. 4 From recipe to flowchart Words describe an algorithm; pictures make it impossible to misread. The six chai steps work as text — but real algorithms branch, loop and join, and words start to lie. The next section draws this exact recipe as a flowchart using all five symbols. First, check yourself: In the tea recipe, the saucepan and teacups are best described as… Lecture 1 · working definitions A Data B Variables C Functions D Output An algorithm is… Lecture 1 · definition A Any programming language B Organised steps that convert data into the desired output C A chart of the company D A type of flowchart Pen-paper drill 3 drills 1 Define data, variable, algorithm and function in one line each — no peeking at the cards above. Hint: Data is the what; variables are the where; the algorithm is the how; functions are the reusable inside. 2 Write the tea algorithm as 6 numbered steps, then label each step INPUT, OUTPUT or PROCESS. Hint: Adding water/milk/tea/sugar are inputs; straining and serving are outputs; boiling and simmering are processing. 3 List the 4 working definitions from memory. Repeat tomorrow until all four come out in order. Hint: D-V-A-F: Data, Variables, Algorithm, Function. Lecture 1 · takeaways Key takeaways An algorithm is a series of organised steps for a specific task — it converts input data into the desired output. Plain English and a flowchart both communicate the same logic — pick whichever your reader follows faster. Algorithms start simple and gain complexity as details, conditions and checks are added. A single execution follows only one path through the decisions — the other branches wait for another run. Every algorithm is a simplification of a real process — “add water” hides a dozen intuitive steps you chose not to codify. Algorithms power everyday situations and business software alike — chai and ATMs obey the same discipline.

chapters.label: Flowcharts
chapters.text: Module 1 · Flowcharts Drawing algorithms — the five symbols A flowchart is the diagram version of an algorithm. Entire company processes are documented with just these shapes — master them once, read any process map forever. 1 The symbol kit Five symbols cover almost every flowchart you will ever draw — four shapes plus the arrows that connect them. Start Rounded rectangle START / END x = x + 1 Rectangle PROCESSING statement INPUT x Parallelogram INPUT / OUTPUT x > 0 ? Diamond DECISION Arrows FLOW Lecture 1 · symbol kit Rounded rectangle START and END — every flowchart opens and closes in one. Rectangle A processing step — something happens: boil, add, compute. Trapezoid Input or output — the lecture’s “slanted rectangle”. Data enters or leaves here. Arrow The flow of logic and data — which step runs next, and in which direction. Diamond A decision requiring branching — a yes/no question with two ways out. One naming note: this course draws the trapezoid as a parallelogram — same slanted shape, same input/output job. Different textbooks pick different names; the meanings above are the lecture’s. And one law the kit hides in plain sight: arrows never branch by themselves — only a diamond may split the flow. A drawing that forks without a diamond is not a flowchart; it is a wish. 2 The tea flowchart The six chai steps, one symbol at a time — watch the flow draw itself. START Add water Boil the water Add tea leaves Boil for 1 minute Add milk and sugar Simmer for 2–3 minutes Strain the tea Serve tea END Read it back symbol by symbol and the grammar explains itself. START and END sit in rounded rectangles — the only two of their kind. Every add step (water, leaves, milk & sugar) and the final serve move data into or out of the pot, so they get the trapezoid . Every boil , simmer and strain transforms what is already inside, so they stay rectangles . Ten nodes, nine arrows, zero branches — the arrows simply carry the flow downward, one direction, no arguments. Input, processing and output each live in their own symbol: that is what makes this a refined flowchart. 3 Adding a decision One diamond turns a straight line into a smart, self-checking process. Lecture 1 · decision loop NO — not ready YES START Add water Boil the water Add tea leaves Boil for 1 minute Add milk and sugar Simmer for 2–3 minutes Sufficiently brewed? Strain the tea Serve tea END The rose edge loops back — “No, keep simmering” — until the tea is sufficiently brewed. The flow revisits its own steps: the mark of a complex flowchart. Decisions make algorithms smart A diamond asks a yes/no question. Yes and No each open a branch — and a branch that loops backwards gives you a loop : repeat until the answer flips. Branching + looping is the entire control vocabulary of every business rule ever written. Trace it Under-brewed pot: the flow passes the diamond — is the tea sufficiently brewed? — three times before Strain; the loop edge (rose) fired twice. The algorithm never “guesses”: it checks, branches, repeats. 4 Simple, refined, complex Flowcharts mature in three stages — and every process map you will ever read sits on this ladder. Lecture 1 · maturity stages Simple processing only — a straight line of rectangles Refined input, processing and output in their own symbols Complex decisions loop the flow back until a condition holds You have already climbed this ladder once today. The first tea chart was refined — ingredients and serving got their own slanted boxes while boiling kept its rectangles. The moment we asked “is the tea sufficiently brewed?” it became complex : a decision diamond sends the flow back to the simmer, and the algorithm revisits its own steps until the answer flips. Simple charts do a task; complex charts handle reality. Which symbol marks where a flowchart begins and ends? Lecture 1 · symbol kit A Rounded rectangle B Diamond C Trapezoid D Arrow Which symbol would you use for 'INPUT the length and width'? Lecture 1 · symbol kit A Rectangle B Diamond C Parallelogram D Oval Flowchart drills 3 drills 1 Draw the tea flowchart from memory — all 10 nodes, correct symbols. Hint: Parallelograms: add water, add leaves, add milk & sugar, serve. Rectangles: boil, boil 1 min, simmer, strain. 2 Mark each step as I/O or processing. Which single step becomes a decision if the taster is picky? Hint: Simmer — split it into “Sufficiently brewed?” with a loop back. 3 A colleague documents a refund process using only rectangles. Which maturity stage is that, and what would you add first? Hint: Simple — processing only. Add trapezoids to separate the input (refund request) from the output (money returned), then a diamond for the approval check.

chapters.label: Decisions
chapters.text: Module 1 · Decisions in flowcharts The ATM machine — branching in action One real machine, two decisions, three possible endings — a successful withdrawal and two polite refusals. Trace it once and every approval workflow you will ever meet — loans, refunds, KYC — becomes obvious. 1 The numbered algorithm Eight steps; steps 6 and 7 each hide a two-way branch. The ATM is Lecture 1’s business application: cash dispensing, stripped to its skeleton. Notice the rhythm before you read a single step — input, input, decision, input, decision, function, end . Machines that handle money are mostly polite questions with hard stops: fail any check and the session ends immediately, no exceptions, no negotiation. Keep this skeleton — you will redraw it for loan approvals, KYC gates and refund flows for the rest of the course. 1 START A customer walks up and the session begins. 2 Check card The machine reads the card details — the session’s first input. 3 Request PIN Screen displays: “Please enter your 4-digit PIN”. 4 Input PIN The customer types it — data enters a variable. 5 Check if PIN correct Verify the PIN against the stored one — a decision. One wrong digit and the session ends right here. 6 Branch on PIN 6a · PIN correct → input amount 6b · Incorrect → end 7 Branch on balance 7a · Balance available → release cash 7b · Insufficient balance → end 8 END Card returns, session closes — every path ends here. 2 The same algorithm as a flowchart Yes edges in olive, No edges in rose — and watch both No edges join. NO NO both join here YES YES START Check card Request PIN Input PIN Pin OK? Input amount Balance available? Release cash END Both rose lanes join at END — a failure anywhere still reaches a clean ending. That shared exit is what makes the machine safe to automate. Branches + joins = every business process A loan application: check credit score (branch), verify income (branch), then join into one approval decision. A refund request, a KYC check, an insurance claim — same skeleton: inputs, checks, branches, a join, one end. If you can draw the ATM, you can draw your company. 3 Two observations the lecture insists on They read like footnotes; they are the whole point of the example. Lecture 1 · one run, one path Not all paths execute in a single run The flowchart shows every route the machine could take — but a decision is a fork, and each run picks exactly one branch. The lucky customer never visits either rose No-lane; the unlucky one never sees “release cash”. Every branch is always possible ; on any given run, most are never executed . Lecture 1 · a function inside “Release cash” is a function of its own One plain box hides a private algorithm: count the notes, verify denominations, update the ledger, confirm pickup. Complex operations get boxed away as functions — subgroups of organised steps, identical wherever they appear — so the main flow stays readable. You will meet the same idea as AVERAGE two chapters from now. The vocabulary, all on duty Run the labels back through the machine: reading the card, requesting the PIN and the amount are inputs — trapezoids. Verifying the PIN and checking the balance are decisions — diamonds. Dispensing the notes is a function — a pre-defined process with an algorithm of its own. One everyday machine; every Lecture 1 term working at once. In the ATM flowchart, the two No branches both lead to… Lecture 1 · ATM example A Request PIN again B Release cash C End D Input amount During one customer’s run, how many branches of each decision actually execute? Lecture 1 · ATM example A Both — every branch runs once B Exactly one — the outcome picks the path C None — decisions are skipped D It alternates between customers Branch drills 3 drills 1 Trace what happens when the PIN is wrong: list every node the flow visits, in order. Hint: Start → Check card → Request PIN → Input PIN → Pin OK? → NO lane → End. Five nodes, never reaching amount. 2 Write the 6a/6b branch pattern for a UPI payment (balance check + limit check). Hint: 6a: within limit → check balance; 6b: over limit → decline. Mirror the ATM diamonds. 3 “Release cash” is a function. Write 4 steps its own algorithm must contain. Hint: Count the notes → verify denominations → update the ledger → confirm pickup and close the session.

chapters.label: Pseudocode
chapters.text: Module 1 · Functions, pseudocode & code From pseudocode to code — and the function in between The same algorithm can be said three ways. Pseudocode keeps the precision of code without the syntax; functions keep the algorithm short by hiding repeated work in reusable boxes. 1 Three levels of saying it Same idea — increasing formality. None of them is “the algorithm”; they all describe it. Algorithm Plain English steps anyone can follow: 1. Input five marks 2. Add them together 3. Divide by 5 4. Output the average Pseudocode “A code-like statement that is understandable in English”: pseudocode.txt read-only 1 IF AVG IS MORE THAN 60 , OUTPUT "FIRST CLASS" Code Implemented in a real language — C/C++, Java, Python — so a machine can execute it. In this course we stop one step before: you trace the pseudocode on paper; the machine never sees a line of it. 2 Functions = reusable boxes Name a common task once, call it everywhere. AVERAGE pre-defined process S1 … S5 in 62 out The double side-bars mark a pre-defined process — a function call. AVERAGE(S1, S2, S3, S4, S5) 62 adds the five marks, divides by 5 square(x) x² multiplies the input by itself UPPERCASE("abc") "ABC" returns the text in capitals 3 Pseudocode with a function The main flow stays six lines — the adding lives inside AVERAGE. average.pseudo read-only 1 DEFINE S1 , S2 , S3 , S4 , S5 AS INTEGER 2 INPUT S1 , S2 , S3 , S4 , S5 3 DEFINE AVG AS FLOAT 4 AVG = AVERAGE ( S1 , S2 , S3 , S4 , S5 ) 5 OUTPUT AVG 6 IF AVG IS MORE THAN 60 , OUTPUT "FIRST CLASS" AVERAGE(S1…S5) is the function call — in the flowchart it appears as a pre-defined process box (rectangle with double side-bars). Why functions simplify algorithms Functions carry out common tasks so the main algorithm never repeats them. Need the average of 5 marks in ten places? Write AVERAGE once. The flowchart shows the call as a single box — readers can trust it without re-reading the internals. Pseudocode is… Lecture 1 · three levels A A programming language B A code-like statement that is understandable in English C Machine code D A flowchart symbol Function drills 2 drills 1 Write AVERAGE as a function: what are its inputs, what does it do, what does it return? Hint: Inputs S1…S5; steps: SUM = S1+…+S5, return SUM/5. 2 Split the tea algorithm into 3 functions — Boil, Add, Serve. Which steps go inside each? Hint: Boil: heat water/tea; Add: milk, sugar, leaves; Serve: strain + pour. The main flow becomes 3 calls.

chapters.label: Average, step-by-step
chapters.text: Module 1 · Worked example Average marks — arithmetic vs algorithm Five marks, one average. The school answer is a number; the algorithmic answer is a machine-followable process — and the difference is exactly what this course is about. 1 The school way Arithmetic gets the answer — but it forgets the method. Average = (60 + 65 + 70 + 55 + 60) / 5 = 310 / 5 = 62 Add the marks 60 + 65 + 70 + 55 + 60 = 310 Divide by the number of subjects 310 ÷ 5 = 62 2 The algorithmic way — memory boxes Step through the pseudocode and watch each variable appear, receive data and compute. Memory-box stepper Step 0 / 15 Pseudocode 1 DEFINE S1 AS INTEGER 2 INPUT S1 3 DEFINE S2 AS INTEGER 4 INPUT S2 5 DEFINE S3 AS INTEGER 6 INPUT S3 7 DEFINE S4 AS INTEGER 8 INPUT S4 9 DEFINE S5 AS INTEGER 10 INPUT S5 11 DEFINE SUM AS INTEGER 12 SUM = S1 + S2 + S3 + S4 + S5 13 DEFINE AVG AS FLOAT 14 AVG = SUM / 5 15 OUTPUT AVG S1 · S2 · S3 · S4 · S5 · SUM · AVG · Press “Next step” and watch memory fill up, one instruction at a time. Next step ▻ Reset 3 Data types matter Every variable is declared with a pre-determined datatype. Type What it holds Business examples Integer Round numbers — no decimal part Number of students, courses, books Float Decimal numbers Temperature, interest rate, CGPA Boolean 0 or 1 — true / false On/off, eligible/ineligible, pass/fail Character Text — letters, words, sentences Name, address, description, role, book title Note: modern languages can infer the type from the first input — assign 8.74 to a fresh variable and it quietly becomes a float. Older languages force you to declare it up front, as our pseudocode does. 4 Level up: FIRST CLASS One IF statement turns the average into a decision. first_class.pseudo read-only 1 DEFINE S1 , S2 , S3 , S4 , S5 , SUM AS INTEGER 2 INPUT S1 , S2 , S3 , S4 , S5 3 SUM = S1 + S2 + S3 + S4 + S5 4 DEFINE AVG AS FLOAT 5 AVG = SUM / 5 6 OUTPUT AVG 7 IF AVG IS MORE THAN 60 , OUTPUT "FIRST CLASS" OUTPUT 62.0 AVG is a FLOAT, so the machine prints 62.0 — and because 62.0 IS MORE THAN 60, the IF fires. SUM 310 AVG 62.0 IF fires FIRST CLASS Same five marks as the lab above — but SUM is reused, AVG is a float, and the output is now a verdict, not just a number. CGPA = 8.74. Best primitive type? Lecture 1 · datatypes A Integer B Float C Boolean D Character AVG is defined as INTEGER but SUM/5 = 62.5. What happens conceptually? Lecture 1 · datatypes A It stays 62.5 — nothing changes B The decimal part is dropped — it becomes 62 C The program always crashes D It becomes the text “62.5” Key takeaways An algorithm is a series of steps to complete a task — chai, payroll or an ATM withdrawal. It can be represented as a flowchart (five symbols — four shapes plus the arrows that join them) or as pseudocode . Algorithms get more complex as details are added — each decision adds a branch. They are finally implemented in languages like C/C++, Java and Python — but the thinking comes first. Variables can have pre-determined datatypes (integer, float, boolean, character); modern languages can infer them. Functions simplify algorithms by carrying out common tasks — shown in flowcharts as pre-defined process boxes.

chapters.label: Course map
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 3 · Course overview The course, the marks, and the bridge between business and machines Before a single data structure: what this course is (no-code, business-first), how it is graded (40/60), who turns business wishes into machine-readable specifications — and why 'looks okay' is the enemy. 1 The course at a glance Logic over syntax: the reference is Codeless Data Structures and Algorithms by Subramanya, and it complements coding courses like Python. The approach No-code: focus on logic and building blocks, never on programming-language syntax Business-relevant applications of data structures and algorithms throughout Complements coding courses (such as Python) by owning the conceptual layer Live sessions on alternate weekends · TA doubt-clearing on the opposite weekends Video recordings available — live sessions add extra examples on top of the deck Four objectives Explain common data structures and their business applications — with no code at all Identify the right data structure for a given business problem Compare algorithmic approaches from managerial and performance perspectives Apply structured logical thinking to real-world business scenarios 2 The assessment scale Forty percent rides on three quizzes — the best two scores are the ones that count. 40% Quizzes 60% Major exam Quizzes · 3 MCQ quizzes · best TWO marks counted · online from home · attend at least two of three Major exam · descriptive · offline · written at the examination centre 3 Data types, chosen for the business Classical languages demand predefined types; Python infers them. Either way, the type is a business decision — not a technical accident. Integer whole numbers only marks (0–100) · number of students Float decimal numbers temperature · interest rates · CGPA Boolean two values only (true/false · 0/1) eligible / not · pass / fail Character / Text text and strings names · addresses · book titles The customer-ID trap A customer ID like B26-SME-001 mixes letters and numbers — so it must be stored as text, not a number . Type selection needs business-domain understanding, end-user consultation, and the business analyst who bridges the two worlds. 4 The business-analyst bridge From domain experts to developers — requirements become an SRS, and the SRS becomes design documents. Domain experts & end-users requirements live here Business analyst collects · prepares the SRS · designs documents Developers technical requirements land here System check vs human check A system validates type and range (a mark must be 0–100 — 63 passes). A human catches logical errors (the employee meant 65, not 63). Both layers are needed. Real-time? It depends UPI shows the confirmation instantly but settles in the backend every two hours; daily summaries run at midnight, not continuously. Business requirements — not technology — set the frequency, and periodic maintenance windows keep heavy jobs off the critical path. Misconceptions, corrected Algorithms cannot be trained by computers — computers run pre-existing algorithms. A precise description guarantees nothing if the precision itself is ambiguous. Algorithms and coding go hand-in-hand, but they are conceptually distinct. Functions are reusable components of algorithms — not replacements for them. Boolean beats integer for true/false values: memory efficiency + error prevention. Multiple conditions need SEQUENTIAL diamonds — one diamond answers only yes/no. Three MCQ quizzes, best two counted — what share of the final marks do the quizzes carry? Lecture 3 · course overview A 20% B 40% C 50% D 60% A discount engine accepts any purchase amount typed as text. Which pairing is the actual failure? Lecture 3 · data types & validation A Data type — amounts must be numeric (integer/float), not text B Finiteness — the engine never ends C Generality — it works for every customer D Feasibility — it cannot be implemented Bridge work 2 drills 1 A university stores course-completion status, student names and CGPA. Assign the correct data type to each and justify in one line. Hint: Boolean (yes/no) · Character/Text · Float (CGPA carries decimals). 2 The registrar says 'process marks in real time', but the exam office only needs totals at midnight. What would you build, and why? Hint: Business requirements set processing frequency — a midnight batch summary, not continuous real-time compute. Key takeaways The course is no-code and business-first — quizzes 40% (best two of three), major exam 60%. Data types are business decisions : Integer, Float, Boolean, Character/Text — chosen with domain experts, not guessed. The business analyst bridges business and technology: requirements → SRS → design documents for developers. Not everything needs real-time execution — UPI settles every two hours ; daily summaries run at midnight. Machines need objective, measurable criteria — "gentle boil" and "looks okay" are where algorithms break.

chapters.label: 9 properties
chapters.text: Module 1 · Properties of algorithms What makes an algorithm a good algorithm? Anything can be called an algorithm; not everything deserves the name. Nine properties — in two families — separate a machine-followable method from a wish written on paper. 1 Two families of characteristics Five core technical properties define an algorithm; four execution & design properties make it a good one. Family 1 · Core technical what the algorithm IS — miss one and it is not an algorithm at all Finiteness must stop after finitely many steps Definiteness every step precisely defined Well-defined inputs clear values given before it runs Well-defined outputs clear result when it ends Effectiveness each step basic enough to actually do Family 2 · Execution & design how it RUNS in the real world — the quality bar for usable algorithms Language independence survives translation into any language Determinism same input → same output, every run Feasibility runnable with available resources Generality works for a whole class of problems 2 The nine properties, each with a twin Every property is easiest to remember by its violation — hover a card and meet the bad example. 1 Finiteness It must end after a finite number of steps. Count the students in a class — stop at the last one. Keep checking whether another customer has entered — it never ends. Infinite. 2 Definiteness Every step is precise and unambiguous. Average = (M1 + M2 + M3 + M4 + M5) / 5 — an exact formula. “Take some tea leaves, add a little milk, boil for a while, add sugar if needed.” 3 Well-defined inputs The values it acts on are exactly specified. Rectangle area: INPUT length L and width W. “INPUT the required values” — which values? how many? 4 Well-defined outputs The result it produces is exactly specified. Loan check → display Approved or Rejected. Display “Processing Complete” — but is the loan approved or not? 5 Effectiveness Every step is basic and actually carryable-out. Stock < 50 → order 200 units. One doable step. “Order more whenever stock looks low” — not basic, not exact. 6 Language independence The logic must not depend on one language’s syntax. Bonus rule written as generic steps — re-express it in C, Java or Python. Hard-wired to one specific Python line — change the language, lose the algorithm. 7 Determinism Same input → same output, every single run. Income ≥ ₹50,000 AND credit ≥ 700 → approve. Identical result every time. The visa officer “feels trustworthy” — a different verdict each run. Indeterminate. 8 Feasibility It must be executable with the resources you have. Payroll: process one employee record at a time. Load ALL records, make multiple copies, process them simultaneously. 9 Generality It works for every member of a class of problems. Bonus by annual sales — works for every employee. “If the employee’s name is Rahul” — built for one specific person. Which is NOT a core technical characteristic? Lecture 1 · properties A Finiteness B Definiteness C Determinism D Effectiveness “Add sugar if needed” violates… Lecture 1 · properties A Generality B Definiteness C Feasibility D Finiteness Property detective 2 drills 1 Classify which property each breaks: (a) “Stir until it feels right”. (b) A bonus rule valid only for the Delhi office. (c) “Compute the average of all sales since the company began” — with no end condition. (d) Output: “Done”. Hint: Think: ambiguity, generality, finiteness, well-defined output. 2 Write the loan algorithm so it satisfies determinism AND a well-defined output: input income and credit score; display exactly Approved or Rejected. Hint: Fix the thresholds: income ≥ 50,000 AND credit ≥ 700 → display Approved; otherwise display Rejected. No “feels”.

chapters.label: Execution properties
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 5 · Properties, second set The execution family, interrogated Five core properties make an algorithm; four execution-and-design properties decide whether it can actually be built, trusted and generalised. This lecture puts each of the four on the stand. 1 Four properties, each with a twin Hover a card: the green twin passes, the red twin fails the property outright. Language independence Express the logic in generic steps that survive translation into any language. A bonus calculation written in plain English re-expresses as C, Java or Python with identical logic. The bonus logic hard-wired into one Python-specific line — change the language, lose the algorithm. Determinism Same input consistently produces the same output, across every execution. Loan approval: income > ₹50,000 AND credit > 700 → the same verdict every single run. Visa approval rides on an officer's subjective judgement of trustworthiness — different verdicts, different runs. Feasibility Implementable realistically within available memory, processing power and time. Payroll reads one employee record at a time: calculate, pay slip, next. Loading ALL employee records into memory simultaneously — very costly and impractical. Generality Handles all valid instances of the problem — no special cases, no favourites. A bonus rule keyed on annual sales applies to every employee equally. Assigning the bonus only to employees named 'Rahul' — specific, unethical, unimplementable. 2 Feasibility is a moving target The same brilliant idea can be infeasible for decades — then inevitable. 1990s Cloud computing the technology existed — slow internet and high costs made it infeasible; cheaper infrastructure brought it to life 1970s Machine learning / AI algorithms existed since the 1970s — feasible only once compute, data and memory got cheap Now Both are everywhere feasibility is a moving target: the same idea is infeasible in one decade and inevitable in the next 3 The property clinic Two review questions from the lecture — diagnose the violation before you peek. An algorithm randomly chooses a discount between 5% and 20% for all customers. Which property does it fail? Lecture 5 · review question 1 A Finiteness B Determinism C Definiteness D Generality Customer submits complaint → determine the customer's true intention → provide solution. Which property fails? Lecture 5 · review question 2 A Effectiveness B Definiteness C Feasibility D Language independence The properties interlock An infinite loop violates finiteness and compromises effectiveness . Missing well-defined outputs usually means the inputs were unclear too. And once definiteness is broken, well-defined outputs become impossible. Fix the first crack — the rest of the wall follows. Key takeaways Execution & design properties: language independence, determinism, feasibility, generality . Determinism = loan approval (fixed criteria) — not visa approval (subjective judgement). Feasibility moves with technology: cloud waited for internet speeds, ML waited for cheap compute. Generality means all valid inputs , never a special case — no bonuses for people named Rahul. Clinic follow-ups 2 drills 1 A payroll algorithm processes one employee per iteration. Rewrite the infeasible twin and say exactly which resource it abuses. Hint: Load-all-at-once abuses memory (and compute); one-at-a-time stays within memory, processing power and time. 2 Give one instruction an algorithm can execute and one it cannot — then name the property each example proves. Hint: 'If stock < 50, order 200' executes (definiteness). 'Stir until it feels right' cannot (definiteness again — subjectivity).

chapters.label: Algorithm types
chapters.text: Module 1 · Types of algorithms Three ways to eat the elephant Every algorithmic strategy you will ever meet is a remix of three instincts: split the problem, grab what looks best now, or remember where you have been. Divide-and-Conquer Split it Take a large problem, split it into many smaller ones — then combine their results. Business story · Auditing a company: each regional office gets its own audit team; the findings merge into one company-wide report. One big problem sub-1 sub-2 sub-3 combine → one report Greedy Grab the best now Take the best decision at the point in time the decision is made — never reconsider. Business story · A cashier returning ₹88 change always hands over the highest denomination note or coin available first: 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1. ₹88 to return 50 20 10 5 2 1 50 + 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = ₹88 — highest first, every time Dynamic Programming Remember the past Make decisions for the future while keeping the past in mind. Business story · Planning 12 months of inventory purchases using previous inventory levels, holding costs and demand forecasts. Jan Mar Jun Sep Dec each order remembers past levels, costs & forecasts Same problem, three lenses Split it when the parts are independent (divide & conquer). Grab the best-now when early choices never need revisiting (greedy). Remember the past when today’s decision changes tomorrow’s costs (dynamic programming). One problem — three perfectly valid attacks; the art is picking the lens that fits. Planning next year’s inventory using last year’s levels and demand forecasts is… Lecture 1 · algorithm classes A Divide-and-conquer B Greedy C Dynamic programming D Binary search Key takeaways An algorithm should fulfil the core technical characteristics and the execution & design characteristics. Core technical: Finiteness, Definiteness, Well-defined inputs, Well-defined outputs, Effectiveness . Execution & design: Language independence, Determinism, Feasibility, Generality . Three major classes: divide & conquer (split & combine), greedy (best at this point in time), dynamic programming (decide for the future with the past in mind). Strategy spotting 2 drills 1 A warehouse chain audits 40 stores. Which of the three classes fits, and how would you divide the work? Hint: Stores are independent → divide-and-conquer; audit teams per region, then merge findings. 2 Why can a greedy change-maker fail for some denomination sets, while it works for Indian currency? Hint: Try ₹60 with notes {50, 30, 20, 10}: greedy takes 50+10 then gets stuck at 0 vs 30+30. Indian denominations are “canonical” — greedy is safe.

chapters.label: Arrays
chapters.text: Module 2 · Linear data structures — arrays Arrays — numbered boxes in a row The first linear structure: one name, one block of memory, positions numbered from 0. Arrays are the structure every other structure is measured against — because of one superpower: direct access. 1 Two addresses, one idea Why structure beats scatter Address 1 · scattered “C/o Shri Jagat Murari, Near Quantum School, Opposite Café Youth, New City” Everything is described by landmarks — nothing predicts its neighbours. Most likely an independent house : the next house could be anything, anywhere. Like loose variables — each one lives on its own. Address 2 · structured “House No. 53, New Friends Colony” A house numbered 53 sits inside a planned colony — houses 52 and 54 must be right beside it . Position predicts neighbours. That is an array : a row of same-type values, numbered, side by side. 51 52 53 54 55 2 Same type, instant access One name — Sub — five numbered cells Same type, instant access Five students' marks live in one array named Sub — every element is the same data type , every element carries an index , and any element is reachable in one direct jump : no scanning, no searching. index → 0 60 1 65 2 70 3 55 4 60 Sub[0] = 60 Sub[3] = 55 read Sub[0] read Sub[1] read Sub[2] read Sub[3] read Sub[4] clear → click a position above — the answer comes back instantly. stores the same data type every element is indexed (0, 1, 2, …) direct access by index sub_array.c — fixed size, declared up front read-only 1 /* C / C ++ — the size is fixed at declaration */ 2 int Sub [ 5 ] = { 60 , 65 , 70 , 55 , 60 }; 3 4 printf ("% d ", Sub[0]); // 60 ← first element 5 printf(" % d ", Sub [ 3 ]); // 55 ← direct access sub_array.py — same idea, friendlier syntax read-only 1 # Python — square brackets instead of braces 2 Sub = [ 60 , 65 , 70 , 55 , 60 ] 3 4 print ( Sub [ 0 ]) # 60 ← indexing starts at 0 5 print ( Sub [ 3 ]) # 55 ← one direct jump 3 Two dimensions Marks for MULTIPLE students, multiple subjects One row of marks served one student . Now imagine every student's marks for every subject: a 2-D array — rows indexed by i (student), columns indexed by j (subject). One pair of numbers addresses any cell: Sub[i, j] . students (i) ↓ subject 0 subject 1 subject 2 subject 3 72 student 0 88 91 67 55 student 1 60 71 80 60 student 2 65 70 55 91 student 3 78 84 90 45 student 4 52 61 58 Sub[2,1] → 65 Sub[4,3] → 58 Sub[2,1] → 65 (student 2, subject 1) · Sub[4,3] → 58 (student 4, subject 3) — still one direct jump each. 4 The five operations + business use cases What you can DO to an array — and what it costs Operation What it does Business use case Speed Read / Access Retrieve the value stored at a position Total the sales of all stores, one by one ✓ instantaneous Search Find a specific item in the array Search a customer ID in the database ≈ depends on position Insert Add a new value at a position Add a new employee to the staff list ≈ depends on position Update Change the value at a position Update stock quantity after every sale ✓ instantaneous Delete Remove a value from a position Remove a discontinued product ✓ instantaneous 5 How insert really works Watch the cells move — the position decides the price Insert at the END 10 20 30 40 99 99 shifts: 0 — just write into the free slot Insert at the BEGINNING 10 20 30 40 99 shifts: n — every element moves right Insert in the MIDDLE (Arr[2]) 10 20 30 40 99 shifts: everything after Arr[2] moves The pattern behind the trio Inserting at the end is free — nothing after it. The further forward you insert, the more elements must shift right to open the gap. That is why the table says insert “depends on position” — while Read and Update never move anything, wherever you aim. 6 Search & update by value The five-step loop the lecture walks through Start index = 0 Compare is Arr[index] the search term? Yes → stop found — return index No → move on index = index + 1 Repeat until found or array ends array_search.pseudo — the loop, written down read-only 1 SEARCH ( Arr , N , term ): 2 index ← 0 3 while index < N : 4 if Arr [ index ] = term : return index // yes → stop 5 index ← index + 1 // no → move on 6 return NOT FOUND // loop ended empty - handed 7 8 UPDATE ( Arr , term , newValue ): // business : stock after a sale 9 pos ← SEARCH ( Arr , N , term ) 10 if pos ≠ NOT FOUND : Arr [ pos ] ← newValue // update is instant once found Benefits vs challenges Benefits Easy to understand — a numbered row of boxes Memory-saving — contiguous allocation, no gaps, no per-item overhead Faster processing — direct access to any position Ideal for predictable datasets — fixed count, same type (30 days of sales) The foundation for other structures — stacks, queues, matrices build on arrays Challenges Fixed length — waste if declared too large, overflow if too small Some operations depend on the element's position (search, insert) Needs contiguous memory — one free block big enough for the whole array Inefficient for frequent modifications — inserts and deletes shift cells Resizing costs time and resources — grow means allocate + copy everything Sub = [60, 65, 70, 55, 60] — what does Sub[3] return? Concept check A 70 B 55 C 60 D 65 Which operation is instantaneous in an array, no matter how big it is? Concept check A Search for a value B Read at a known index C Insert at the beginning D Find the position of a value Pen-and-paper drills — arrays 3 drills 1 Write the search algorithm in exactly five steps: start index = 0 → compare → yes, stop → no, increment → repeat. Hint: Each step must be unambiguous — a computer executes it without guessing. 2 A store keeps its daily sales figure for 30 days. Why is an array the ideal structure for this? Hint: Fixed count, same data type, and any day is read directly by its number. 3 Trace inserting 99 at the beginning of [10, 20, 30]. How many values move, and where does each go? Hint: Every existing element shifts one position to the right — then 99 lands at index 0.

chapters.label: Linked lists
chapters.text: Lecture 7 · Linked lists & linear structures Linked lists — a playlist that never overflows The second major linear data structure after arrays. When the number of items is unknown and changes constantly, contiguity becomes a cage — links beat contiguity: every item carries the address of the next, so data can live anywhere and the chain can reshape itself in cheap pointer moves. 1 Where arrays crack Linear order, the row's three limitations — and when arrays still win Lecture 7 · linear data structures A linear data structure arranges its elements sequentially, in a logical order : the elements are connected so that reaching one item lets you move on to its neighbours. Arrays are the first member of this family — they use indexing for direct access, because the position IS the address. This lecture adds the second member, and it starts from the cracks in the first. Fixed size The size must be defined in advance. Adding elements beyond the initial size means redefining the entire array. Lecture 7 · limitation 1 Inefficient middle modifications Deleting or inserting in the middle forces the other elements to shift — or leaves null spaces behind. Lecture 7 · limitation 2 Static structure Limited flexibility when data requirements change — the row cannot reshape itself. Lecture 7 · limitation 3 When arrays hurt You need elements connected — but you don't know in advance how many there will be. An array forces you to guess a size. You frequently add, delete or rearrange items — every array insert shifts cells and every resize copies the world. A music playlist does both, all day: songs get added at any position, removed, reordered — and nobody knows at breakfast how many songs you will have by midnight. Lecture 7 · best use case — keep the array when… You know the exact number of elements in advance and direct access is a priority — 30 days of sales, a fixed 8×6 programme. Linked lists take over when the count is unknown in advance , items are frequently added, deleted and rearranged , and flexibility with dynamic sizing is essential . 2 The chain in memory Head = the bus stop · node = data + pointer · last node → Null Lecture 7 · head = the bus stop Every linked list starts at a head node — the entry point . The lecture's analogy: the bus stop . Wherever the buses are parked across the city, every journey boards at the same stop — you always enter the list through the head. Each node carries data plus a connection — a pointer, an address — to the next node. The last node points to Null : no next stop, the journey ends. And the nodes themselves? Not contiguous. They can be scattered anywhere in memory — the connections create the logical sequence, not physical proximity. Head Song 1 next Song 2 next Song 3 next Null each node = data + a pointer to the next node — the chain can grow song by song Head holds the first node's address; each node = data + pointer ; the last node's pointer is Null — the chain simply ends. One playlist, two memory maps Lecture 7 · scattered memory The same five songs, stored two ways. Flip between the maps and watch where the data actually sits — and what carries the order. Array — one packed block Linked list — scattered anywhere 0 Song 1 1000 1 Song 2 1048 2 Song 3 1096 3 Song 4 1144 4 Song 5 1192 one contiguous block — addresses run consecutively (stride 48) direct access: Sub[i] jumps straight to 1000 + i × 48 — but no cell can move without moving the block → Array: cells touch, addresses run 1000 · 1048 · 1096 · 1144 · 1192 — position predicts the neighbour. Arrays store elements in consecutive memory locations ; linked lists use pointers — addresses — to link elements regardless of their physical memory locations . Compared with an array, linked-list nodes live… Concept check A in consecutive memory locations B anywhere in memory, connected by pointers C inside the head node D in a fixed 2-D grid 3 Three flavours Play next · play previous · repeat — then walk all three Singly linked list S1 S2 S3 Null Lecture 7 · play next Sequential playback — the chain is walked head → end, one next pointer at a time. Doubly linked list S1 S2 S3 Lecture 7 · play previous Both directions — play next and play previous both work. Circular linked list S1 S2 S3 back to Head Lecture 7 · repeat / shuffle The playlist starts over after the last song — repeat and shuffle live here, and the same loop drives menu systems. Walk the chain — next / prev, three ways Lecture 7 · traversal lab Same three nodes, three navigation personalities. Switch the flavour, then walk: Next follows .next ; Prev needs a prev pointer — only the doubly list has one — and only the circular list can wrap at the ends. Head S1 next S2 next S3 next Null Singly Doubly Circular Next Prev Reset a singly linked list cannot walk backwards — no prev pointers Now playing Song 1 — Head → S1 → S2 → S3 → Null. Use Next / Prev to walk the chain. 4 Surgery — insert & delete Rewire two pointers to insert · redirect one to delete Surgery in two pointer moves 0 cells shifted — an array would move everything after Song 2 To insert Song 2a between Song 2 and Song 3, no element moves. We only rewrite two pointers : Song2.next → 2a, then 2a.next → Song3. Song 1 next Song 2 next Song 3 next Song 2a next move 1 move 2 Rewire in 2 moves Reset Before: Song2.next → Song3 (direct). Delete Song 2 — one pointer rewrite Lecture 7 · delete = redirect Deletion is the mirror of insertion: redirect the previous node's pointer around the victim. Song 2 itself is not erased — it stays in memory but leaves the active list. Head Song 1 next ✗ rewired away Song 2 next still in memory — no longer in the list Song 3 next Null Delete Song 2 Reset Before: Head → Song 1 → Song 2 → Song 3 → Null. The lecture's three facts about deletion: only the pointer connections are adjusted — the previous node is redirected to point at the node after the deleted one; the deleted element remains in memory but is no longer part of the active list; and the operation is extremely efficient compared to array deletion , which must shift every later element to close the gap. 5 Shuffle — pointers, not songs Random playback without moving a single song Shuffle — the songs never move Lecture 7 · reshuffling = pointers Four song nodes at fixed memory locations . Press shuffle and watch the visiting path re-route around them: Head → some new order → … → Null. Head Song 1 next S2 addr 0724 · fixed Song 2 next S3 addr 2044 · fixed Song 3 next S4 addr 1048 · fixed Song 4 next Null addr 1556 · fixed Null Shuffle Reset The original order: Head → Song 1 → Song 2 → Song 3 → Song 4 → Null. ordering #1 of 24 possible orders The data elements stay in their memory locations — every node keeps its address in every ordering. Only the pointer connections are rearranged to create a different order — that is how random / shuffle playback works without physically moving data. 6 Lists of lists — and how to choose Nested chains — then the lecture's choosing checklist User 1 Playlist 1 1A 1B 1C … Playlist 2 2A 2B … Playlist 3 3A 3B 3C … Playlist 4 4A 4B … This is how real apps nest flexible data User → playlists → songs is a linked list whose elements are themselves linked lists . Because every level is a chain, users can own any number of playlists and each playlist can hold any number of songs — nothing was ever pre-declared. Lecture 7 · nested lists in the wild A linked list of linked lists handles complex data with multiple levels of relationships — anywhere a thing owns a varying number of smaller things: University structure A programme → semesters → courses: each semester node owns its own chain of course nodes. Multi-playlist systems A user → playlists → songs — exactly the map above, any count at every level. Hierarchical org data Departments → teams → people — hierarchy with a varying number of sub-elements at each level. Lecture 7 · fixed vs variable The academic programme, both ways Situation 1 · fixed 8 semesters × 6 courses each , same for the whole batch → a 2-D array (Sem[i, j]). Efficient memory usage and fast direct access to any course. Situation 2 · variable Semesters and courses per semester vary student by student — retakes, deferrals → a linked list of linked lists : each semester is a node owning its own course chain, growing and shrinking freely. Lecture 7 · choosing checklist Scenario Best structure Why Fixed number of known elements, direct access needed Array — a 2-D array for multiple dimensions Efficient memory usage and fast direct access Variable number of elements, frequent additions / deletions Linked list Flexibility and ease of modification Hierarchical structure, varying number of sub-elements Nested linked lists Accommodates complexity and variability at multiple levels In a singly linked list, the last node's pointer holds… Concept check A the head's address B Null C its own address D the tail's address Frequent inserts anywhere + unknown final length — which structure fits best? Concept check A Array B Linked list C 2-D array D Stack After deleting Song 2 by rewiring Song1.next → Song 3, Song 2 itself… Concept check A is erased from memory at once B is still in memory but no longer part of the list C moves to the end of the list D becomes the new head When a playlist is shuffled, what actually moves? Concept check A The song files, into a new packed block B Nothing physical — only the pointer connections change order C The head node, to a random song D The nodes are physically re-sorted by name Pen-and-paper drills — linked lists 4 drills 1 Trace deleting the HEAD node of Head → A → B → Null. What exactly must change, and where does A end up? Hint: Head itself holds a pointer — repoint Head to B. Node A still sits in memory; it has simply left the list. 2 Draw four nodes scattered at made-up addresses (0312, 0724, 1556, 2044) and wire TWO different shuffle orders through them. Count how many pointers you rewrote each time. Hint: Every node keeps its address; only the next-cells change — 4 pointer writes per shuffle (the last visited node writes Null). 3 Insert Song 2a between Song 2 and Song 3: write the two pointer moves in order, and say why the order matters. Hint: Song2.next → 2a first, then 2a.next → Song 3. Do it backwards and the rest of the chain is orphaned. 4 The academic programme: the regular batch is a fixed 8 semesters × 6 courses, but retakes and deferrals make real students differ. Which structure fits each situation, and why? Hint: Fixed + known + direct access → 2-D array. Variable at two levels → linked list of linked lists. Lecture 7 · key takeaways Key takeaways Flexibility — dynamic sizing through pointer-based connections : the list grows and shrinks node by node, with no size declared in advance. Memory efficiency — elements need not be contiguous ; scattered nodes can use memory anywhere, because the links carry the order. Directional variants — single, doubly and circular address different navigation requirements: play next, play previous, repeat. Operation efficiency — insertion and deletion are simpler than in arrays : pointer rewiring instead of shifting elements. Hierarchical applications — nested linked lists handle complex multi-level structures: programmes → semesters → courses, users → playlists → songs. Practical implementation — modern languages provide built-in linked list implementations ; understanding the conceptual mechanics is still essential.

chapters.label: LIVE recap · properties & linear DS
chapters.text: Lecture 8 · Live lecture Algorithm properties & linear structures — the live recap A live session compressed three recorded lectures into one sitting: the nine properties that make an algorithm a good one, the three classic approaches, and the two linear structures everything else stands on. Compact by design — the diagrams do the talking. Lecture 8 · live session — what this chapter is This was a live class repeating recorded material , so the chapter is a gallery of comparisons rather than a full walk-through. The full-length versions live in Lecture 3 (properties & types), Lecture 4 (arrays) and Lecture 7 (linked lists) — read those for depth, keep this one for the picture. 1 Nine properties, two families Five technical + four execution & design — each one easiest to remember by its violation Lecture 8 · technical properties Family one asks: does it even deserve the name algorithm? Finiteness Must terminate after a countable number of steps. Counting students in a class ends; waiting forever for the next store customer never does. Definiteness Every step clear and unambiguous. “Add five numbers, divide by five” is definite; “add some tea powder” is not — how much is some? Well-defined input Inputs specified exactly. Rectangle area needs length and width — not “the required values”. Well-defined output The outcome is stated up front. A loan algorithm returns Approved or Rejected — never just “processing complete”. Effectiveness Each step basic enough to finish in finite time. “Stock < 50 → order 200” works; “check stock, order if needed” is vague. Lecture 8 · execution & design Family two asks: does it survive contact with reality? Language independence Plain English or pseudocode first. The idea must survive translation — C, Python or Java comes later. Determinism Same input, same output, every time. A quantitative loan check is deterministic; a visa interview is not — subjectivity leaks in. Feasibility Realistic within memory, money and time. Sequential payroll is feasible; parallel-processing trivial sums is overkill. Generality Handles all situations, not pet cases. No hardcoded employee names, no fixed subject count — accept any number of either. 2 Three ways to attack a problem Divide & conquer · greedy · dynamic programming Divide & conquer Split a large problem into subproblems, solve each separately, combine the results. Regional sales analysis — divide by region, analyse each, total the parts. Lecture 8 · approach 1 Greedy Take the locally best choice at every step — quick and practical, not always globally optimal. The cashier returns change largest-denomination first. Lecture 8 · approach 2 Dynamic programming Let past solutions and decisions inform the current one. Production planning rides the seasonal trends of previous quarters. Lecture 8 · approach 3 3 The flagship Venn — arrays vs linked lists One shared core, two opposite personalities Arrays Linked lists both Arrays only Fixed size — defined at creation — resizing copies the world Contiguous memory — one sequential block of locations O(1) direct access — the index IS the address Shift to insert/delete — middle changes push neighbours around Shared — both Linear — elements arranged one after another Ordered elements — every item has a position in the sequence Foundations — stacks, queues, trees & graphs are built on these two Linked lists only Dynamic size — grows and shrinks — no preset length Scattered nodes + head — data anywhere; the head pointer starts the walk Pointer-hop access — no index — follow links node by node Cheap re-wiring — insert/delete = redirect a pointer, shift nothing Same family, different memory story. The array buys speed with rigidity — fixed size, contiguous, instant indexing. The list buys flexibility with traversal — dynamic size, scattered nodes, pointer hops. The live session's verdict: arrays when the size is known and access is frequent; lists when the size is unknown and the structure changes constantly. 4 Which one, when The ten-second decision — plus the playlist Known size + frequent access → array Thirty days of sales: the count is fixed and any day is read directly by its index. Unknown size + frequent changes → linked list Add, remove and reorder constantly without ever reallocating the world. The foundation duty → both Stacks, queues, trees and graphs are all implemented on arrays or linked lists. The lecture's own example: a music playlist is the classic linked-list citizen — songs are added, removed and reordered all day long without restructuring the entire collection. A visa officer can rule differently on two identical files. Which algorithm property is missing? Lecture 8 · live recap A Finiteness B Determinism C Feasibility D Generality Pen-and-paper drills — the live recap 3 drills 1 Name the broken property: (a) an endless wait for new customers, (b) “stir until it feels right”, (c) the output is just “done”, (d) an algorithm hardcoded to exactly 6 subjects. Hint: finiteness · definiteness · well-defined output · generality 2 A cashier returns ₹88 with denominations {50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1} greedily. Trace the notes — and when could greedy fail? Hint: 88 → 50 + 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1. Odd denomination sets (e.g. {1, 3, 4} for 6) can beat the greedy pick. 3 A 30-day attendance sheet vs a playlist that grows daily: pick a structure for each and defend it with the Venn. Hint: known size + direct access → array; unknown size + constant changes → linked list Lecture 8 · key takeaways Key takeaways Nine properties separate algorithms from wishes — five technical, four execution & design. Every property has a famous violation: the tea-powder ambiguity, the endless customer line, the hardcoded employee list. Divide & conquer splits, greedy grabs the local best, dynamic programming reuses the past. Arrays: fixed, contiguous, O(1) by index. Linked lists: dynamic, scattered, rewired by pointers. Both are the foundation — stacks, queues, trees and graphs all stand on arrays or linked lists.

chapters.label: Stacks
chapters.text: Lecture 9 · Stacks Stacks — the undo machine (LIFO) A stack is a linear structure with one door: everything enters and leaves through the same end — the top. Simple rule, enormous consequences. 1 The undo story You already use a stack every single day Editing a document You are typing and mistakes pile up — a wrong word, a broken sentence, a bad delete. You click Undo : the first click removes the LAST change, the second click removes the second-last , the third removes the one before that… Every editor, every photo app, every Ctrl-Z works this way. This is a Stack. Lecture 9 · every change is stored on the stack removed in reverse-chronological order Physical stacks you already know Lecture 9 · added and removed from the top only Plates at a wedding / buffet Fresh plates land on top; the next guest takes from the top too — the bottom plate waits longest. A stack of newspapers Today's edition goes on top and is read first; older papers sink toward the bottom. Weighing plates in the gym Plates are added to the bar and stripped from it at the same end — the top of the pile. 2 Last-In, First-Out Push, Pop, Peek, Size — press the buttons Last-In, First-Out — try the machine like a pile of plates — last placed, first picked 64 32 53 66 54 top ↑ Push enters here · Pop leaves from here ↑ Push() Pop() Peek() Size() reset Push 64 → 32 → 53 → 66 → 54. Top = 54. The lecture's run: push 64, 32, 53, 66, 54 → top is 54 . Pop() → 54 leaves, Pop() → 66 leaves, Peek() → 53 , Size() → 3 . The last value in is always the first value out — LIFO . stack_ops.pseudo — the four moves read-only 1 Push ( S , x ): Pop ( S ): 2 if Full ( S ): error OVERFLOW if Empty ( S ): error UNDERFLOW 3 Top ← Top + 1 x ← S [ Top ] 4 S [ Top ] ← x Top ← Top − 1 5 return x // the removed value 6 7 Peek ( S ): return S [ Top ] // read the top — remove nothing 8 Size ( S ): return Top + 1 // how many values are stacked 3 Static vs dynamic Two builds of the same abstract idea Static stack — fixed size • Built on an array — capacity chosen in advance • Adobe Photoshop keeps ≈ 50 undo levels — change 51 things and the oldest history is gone • MS Excel keeps ≈ 100 undo steps — same idea, bigger box • Predictable memory, but full is full Dynamic stack — grows as needed • Built on a linked list — a new node for every push • MS Word lets you undo (almost) without a counter — the stack keeps growing • The ultimate limit is the device's memory — not a declared size • Flexible, at the cost of a pointer per element Stacks are ABSTRACT “Stack” is a behaviour (LIFO), not a physical thing — it is implemented through other data structures : arrays for static stacks, linked lists for dynamic ones. Same rules, different foundations. Memory considerations — where the undo history actually lives Lecture 9 · memory considerations • Static stacks (Excel, Photoshop): the stack is cleared when the file is saved — saved work needs no undo history. • Dynamic stacks: limited by the device's physical memory (RAM) — they grow only as far as the hardware allows. • Exhaust that memory and the app crashes — a dynamic stack's only ceiling is the machine itself. • Saving often keeps stacks small — each save wipes the unsaved-changes pile before it can grow toward the limit. 4 When stacks break Two failures with famous names Stack Overflow Pushing onto a FULL stack. Real-life picture: a browser holding a huge number of open tabs — memory is finite; one more push and the structure gives up. (Yes — the website stackoverflow.com is named after exactly this error.) Stack Underflow Popping an EMPTY stack. Real-life picture: clicking Back on a freshly opened browser — there is no history to go back to, so the pop finds nothing and the operation fails. 5 Stack of stacks Each element of the main stack is itself a stack Browser windows, each with its own pile Your browser runs multiple windows — Push and Pop on the main stack adds and removes whole windows . But each window holds multiple tabs — its own LIFO pile. Structures inside structures: that is normal, not exotic. MAIN STACK — each element is a WINDOW Window A Tab 1 Tab 2 Tab — top Window B Tab 1 Tab 2 Tab — top Window C Tab 1 Tab 2 Tab — top each window's element is itself a stack — tabs / history states pile up LIFO, window by window Where stacks earn their keep Lecture 9 · applications undo / redo function-call management expression evaluation & parsing depth-first search browser navigation history Calling Pop() on an empty stack causes… Lecture 9 · concept check A overflow B underflow C reboot D peek Photoshop's fixed 50-step undo is a… Lecture 9 · concept check A dynamic stack on a linked list B static stack on an array C queue D deque Pen-and-paper drills — stacks 3 drills 1 Push J, then A, then N onto an empty stack. Now Pop() twice. Which value remains, and where is it? Hint: Last in, first out — N leaves first, then A. What is left is at the BOTTOM. 2 Name two more places where you meet LIFO behaviour daily, and say what the 'top' element is in each. Hint: Think: plates, a pebble tower, browser Back button, the call stack when functions call functions. 3 Photoshop clears its undo stack the moment you hit Save. Why does saving often keep the stack small? Hint: The stack only holds unsaved changes — each save empties it before it can grow toward the RAM limit.

chapters.label: Queues
chapters.text: Lecture 10 · Queues Queues — first come, first served (FIFO) A queue is a linear structure with two doors: entries at the rear, exits at the front. Fairness by arrival order — the structure behind every waiting line in software. 1 The popcorn line Interval time at the movies Waiting at the movie interval The screen says “Interval” and everyone queues for popcorn. The person who arrived first is served first ; newcomers join at the back . Nobody cares how fast you can wave your money — your order doesn't matter, your PLACE does . That fairness rule has a formal name: FCFS — First-Come-First-Served — also called FIFO (First-In, First-Out). This is a Queue. your PLACE matters, not your pace join at the rear leave from the front 2 Front and rear Enqueue, Dequeue, Peek, Size — press the buttons Front and rear — try the line FCFS · First-Come-First-Served = FIFO Front — Dequeue leaves here Rear — Enqueue enters here Front → 64 · Rear → 54 · Size 5 64 32 53 66 54 Enqueue() Dequeue() Peek / Front · Rear Size() reset Enqueue 64 → 32 → 53 → 66 → 54. Front = 64, Rear = 54. The lecture's run: Enqueue 64, 32, 53, 66, 54 fills left → right. Dequeue() removes 64 (the front — it arrived first), again removes 32 . Then Peek → 53 , Rear → 54 , Size → 3 . Your order doesn't matter — your PLACE does . Pointer choreography — who moves, who stays put Lecture 10 · pointer choreography NQ on an empty queue The very first element occupies BOTH front and rear — one value, two pointers. During Enqueue (NQ) The front pointer stays put; only the rear advances to admit the newcomer. During Dequeue (DQ) The front advances to the next element; rear stays unchanged. DQ takes no parameters — it removes whatever stands at the front. Peek front · Rear · Size Non-destructive reads — they display values and counts without modifying the queue. 3 When queues break Same two failure names, queue flavour Queue Overflow Enqueueing into a FULL queue. Real-life picture: lakhs of people booking Tatkal tickets on IRCTC the second the window opens — the booking queue hits its capacity and further requests are refused. Queue Underflow Dequeueing from an EMPTY queue. Real-life picture: your stream's buffer drains when the internet drops — the player asks the buffer queue for the next chunk, the queue is empty, and the screen freezes. 4 Static vs dynamic + real applications Fixed boxes that drop, flexible lines that grow Static queue — fixed size, built on arrays Wi-Fi router packet buffer A fixed-size circular queue of network packets. When it is full the router intentionally drops new packets instead of crashing — the Tail Drop mechanism. Your video hiccups; the router survives. PC keyboard / mouse buffer A fixed hardware queue (usually 16–64 bytes ). Type faster than the system processes and the extra keystrokes are simply ignored — the queue never grows. Vending machine slots Each drink type sits in a fixed number of slots — a predetermined capacity per column. Sold out means sold out until restocked: the hardware queue never grows. Dynamic queue — grows as needed, built on linked lists Messaging apps' offline buffer Messages sent while offline queue up — the queue expands as long as you stay offline, then drains sequentially (oldest first) when you reconnect, and the memory is freed. Streaming video buffers — Netflix, Spotify, Prime Segments are buffered in dynamic memory queues . When the connection speeds up, the buffer grows to hold more segments — so playback continues stutter-free through dips. Food-delivery order surge The dinner rush fires thousands of orders at once — a dynamic queue swells to absorb the peak, so no order is lost during demand surges. Queue vs stack — the four differences Lecture 10 · queue vs stack Aspect Queue Stack Order FIFO — first in, first out LIFO — last in, first out Insertion at the rear at the top Removal from the front from the top Real-life picture the theater popcorn queue a stack of plates Lecture 10 · important to remember • Elements maintain their order of arrival throughout processing. • The front moves during dequeue — never during enqueue (enqueue is rear business). • Peek examines without modifying — the safe way to inspect queue state. • Static vs dynamic boils down to two questions: is the volume predictable , and is overflow acceptable ? • Real systems fail gracefully when full — dropped packets, ignored keystrokes — rather than crashing. The person served NEXT in a queue is standing at the… Lecture 10 · concept check A rear B front C peek D middle Pen-and-paper drills — queues 3 drills 1 Enqueue A, B, C, then Dequeue twice. Which value is now at the front? Hint: A and B leave in arrival order — C never moved, yet it becomes the front. 2 Find the queue hiding in a printer, a call center, and a ticket window. In each, what is 'enqueue' and what is 'dequeue'? Hint: Documents arrive to be printed in order; callers hold in a line; customers are served by arrival. 3 An empty queue receives NQ(7). Where do front and rear point? Now DQ() — where does rear point? Hint: The first element occupies both front and rear; dequeue advances only the front — rear never moves on its own.

chapters.label: Queue types
chapters.text: Lecture 11 · Queue types Four queues for four situations One FIFO rule, four engineering personalities. Choosing the right queue type is the difference between wasted memory, frozen screens and a smoothly running system. 1 Linear queue The plain version: insert at the rear, remove from the front . Its limitation is memory wastage — in an array implementation, once rear hits the end you cannot insert, even if front spaces have been freed by earlier deletions. free free free 66 54 71 Front Rear — stuck at the end enqueue? ✗ — rear cannot move back, even though 3 spaces are free Lecture 11 · pointer detail front points to the first location where an element is still stored — not to array slot 0. 2 Circular queue The last position connects back to the first — the queue becomes a ring. It reuses the spaces freed by deletions , fixing the linear queue's waste. The rear keeps wrapping into vacated cells , so the ring can serve insertions and deletions indefinitely . Classically implemented via a linked list — and beyond the slides: arrays can do it too, by wrapping indices with modulo . 53 66 54 71 Front Rear wraps to first circular traffic lights multiplayer games circular playlists CPU round-robin scheduling 3 Priority queue Served by priority, not arrival . Equal priorities serve FIFO. The lecture's example: the queue holds (A,8) (T,6) (B,3) ; a new (S,7) arrives and slots before (T,6) — arrival order be damned. A 8 S 7 T 6 B 3 new arrival (S, 7): beats 6 and 3, yields to 8 → slots in before (T, 6) equal priorities? serve FIFO CPU task scheduling hospital emergency room airport traffic control railway disaster management Tatkal quota The lecture's triage, spelled out: accident cases beat recurring headaches · low-fuel long-hauls land before short-hauls · Rajdhani & Shatabdi get green-corridor signals · system tasks run before user apps · rescue goes first to those in immediate danger. 4 Doubly ended queue (Deque) Insert and delete from BOTH ends — so one deque can act as a queue AND a stack at once : front-only use is FIFO, end-only use is LIFO. 10 20 30 40 Insert Front Delete Front Insert Rear Delete Rear Insert Front Insert Rear Delete Front Delete Rear Applications browser forward / back undo + redo in a word processor train coach management doubly linked lists 1 Queue of queues — streaming The Netflix example: playback is queues all the way down The MAIN queue is the browser's master playback line holding the upcoming 5-minute scene segments . Each segment is itself a SUB-QUEUE of thousands of tiny frames / packets . The graphics card rapidly plays the frames inside the current segment — and that is why the video stays smooth while the outer queue quietly refills. SUB-QUEUE — thousands of tiny frames / packets inside ONE 5-minute segment MAIN QUEUE — the browser's master playback line Segment k−1 played Segment k PLAYING now Segment k+1 buffered the graphics card rapidly plays the frames inside the current segment — so the video stays smooth Lecture 11 · reconnection rewind When the connection drops mid-segment, the main queue keeps its progress — but the interrupted sub-queue restarts from its first frame . That is why the video rewinds slightly past the interruption point before playback resumes. Spot the pattern Stacks of stacks (browser windows → tabs), queues of queues (segments → frames), lists of lists (users → playlists → songs). Nesting structures inside structures is how real systems scale simple rules. Which queue type powers a hospital emergency room? Lecture 11 · concept check A Linear queue B Circular queue C Priority queue D Deque Undo AND Redo in one structure suggests a… Lecture 11 · concept check A deque B priority queue C circular queue D linear queue Your stream reconnects and the video rewinds slightly. What happened? Lecture 11 · concept check A the main queue restarted from zero B the interrupted sub-queue restarted — the main queue kept its progress C the whole video was re-downloaded D the circular queue wrapped around Key takeaways A stack is LIFO ; a queue is FIFO — one door vs two. Stack operations: Push · Pop · Peek · Size . Queue operations: Enqueue · Dequeue · Peek(front/rear) · Size . Both can be static (arrays) or dynamic (linked lists) . Underflow = removing from empty · Overflow = adding to full. Lecture 11 four-liner: linear = a regular FIFO line · circular = a ring that reuses freed space · priority = a VIP urgency line · deque = open at both ends.

chapters.label: LIVE recap · stacks & queues
chapters.text: Lecture 13 · Live lecture Stacks & queues — two doors, two disciplines The live session put the last two linear structures side by side: a stack with one open end and a queue with two. Same family, opposite personalities — and between them they run undo, printing, scheduling and buffering. Lecture 13 · live session — what this chapter is A live repeat of the recorded stack & queue material — the full-length versions live in Lectures 9, 10 and 11 . Below: one Venn, one operations strip, the error pair, and the application tour. 1 The flagship Venn — stack vs queue Shared plumbing, opposite doors Stack Queue both Stack only LIFO — last in, first out One open end — everything happens at the top push · pop · peek · size — add, remove, glance, count Undo & Ctrl+Z — the last change is the first reversed Function calls — the call stack remembers where to return Shared — both Linear structures — elements kept in sequence Constrained access — insertion & removal only at designated ends Built on arrays or linked lists — not primitive types — implemented, with rules Overflow & underflow — add to full / remove from empty Logical, not physical — flat memory below; pointers & indices keep the shape Queue only FIFO — first in, first out Two open ends — in at the rear, out at the front NQ · DQ · peek ×2 · size — enqueue, dequeue, glance either end Printing & scheduling — jobs served in arrival order Real fairness — first to arrive is the first served Both are disciplined costumes over structures you already own: the logical order is managed by pointers and indices across flat physical memory — and both fail the same two ways, just at different doors. 2 The operations, side by side Anatomy first, then static vs dynamic builds Lecture 13 · stack ops C B A next slot base — closed end push ↓ pop ↑ top = the only door push — add a new element on top pop — remove and return the top peek — read the top without removing size — count the elements Lecture 13 · queue ops rear — NQ in DQ out — front D C B A FIFO — A entered first (front), A leaves first · D just arrived (rear) NQ — enqueue at the rear DQ — dequeue from the front peek front / peek rear — glance either end size — count the elements Static — array-built Fixed size at creation, memory-efficient when the cap is known. Photoshop keeps ~50 undo steps; Excel keeps 100. Dynamic — linked-list built Grows as needed; RAM is the only ceiling. Word's undo is theoretically unlimited. 3 When they break Overflow = full · underflow = empty Stack overflow Too many browser tabs — the memory stack cannot allocate space for another frame. Queue overflow A ticket-booking rush (IRCTC-style) fills a static queue; the server rejects new requests and appears to hang. Stack underflow The back button clicked with no history — nothing exists to pop. Queue underflow The connection drops mid-stream — the frame buffer empties and the video freezes. 4 Where they run the world Stack duties · queue duties Lecture 13 · stack applications Undo / redo in every editor — Ctrl+Z is a pop Function-call management — return addresses Expression evaluation & parsing Depth-first search Browser navigation history Lecture 13 · queue applications Network printing — jobs in submission order Streaming — client-side frame buffering, a queue of queues CPU scheduling — round-robin slices & shortest-job-first Keyboard buffers — static, typically 16–64 bytes Traffic lights — red → green → yellow, a circular queue Ludo & turn-based games — turn cycles Hospital triage & disaster response — priority queues Clicking the back button on a browser with an empty history is… Lecture 13 · live recap A a stack overflow B a stack underflow C a queue overflow D a successful pop Pen-and-paper drills — stacks & queues 3 drills 1 push A, push B, push C, pop, push D, pop, pop — what does each pop return, and what remains? Hint: Pops return C, then D, then B. Only A remains. 2 Photoshop keeps 50 undos, Word keeps “unlimited”. Which build is which, and what is each implemented on? Hint: static array vs dynamic linked list — RAM is Word's only ceiling. 3 Sort into stack or queue: Ctrl+Z, printer spooler, DFS, keyboard buffer, traffic light cycle, function calls. Hint: stack: Ctrl+Z, DFS, function calls · queue: spooler, keyboard, traffic lights. Lecture 13 · key takeaways Key takeaways A stack has one door (top) and LIFO memory; a queue has two (rear in, front out) and FIFO fairness. Neither is a primitive type — both are arrays or linked lists plus rules. Static builds cap the memory (Photoshop 50, Excel 100); dynamic builds grow to the RAM (Word). Overflow when full, underflow when empty — tab piles and ticket rushes vs empty histories and frozen buffers. Queues quietly run the world: printing, buffering, round-robin CPUs, keyboards, traffic lights, Ludo, triage.

chapters.label: Trees
chapters.text: Lecture 12 · Trees Trees — hierarchy, drawn upside down Arrays, lists, stacks and queues are linear: the path through them is predetermined. Trees are the first nonlinear structure — multiple possible paths, hierarchical relationships.
