Three assumptions run underneath it: Every edge has an associated cost (weight). All costs must be non-negative. Cost is whatever you are optimising — distance, time, tolls. 1 · Initialise source = 0, all others = ∞ 2 · Select smallest unvisited distance 3 · Relax shorter via current? update 4 · Mark visited distance is now final 5 · Repeat until all visited Run Dijkstra on the lecture's graph Lecture 24 · worked example Node A is the source. Edges: A→B 4 · A→C 2 · C→B 1 · C→D 5 · B→D 3 . Press Next to walk the five algorithm steps — watch two direct routes get beaten by detours. Next step Reset step 0 of 5 · Step 1 · initialise 4 2 1 5 3 A start 0 B ∞ C ∞ D ∞ settled = its distance can never improve again · ∞ = not reached yet node A 0 source node B ∞ — node C ∞ — node D ∞ — Initialise: the source A starts at 0; every other node starts at ∞ — unknown. Nothing is visited yet. Lecture 24 · the two discoveries Discovery 1 — B is reachable cheaper Direct A→B = 4 . But A→C→B = 2+1 = 3 — shorter! Dijkstra only trusts a node once no cheaper route can exist. Discovery 2 — D takes the long way round A→C→D = 2+5 = 7 . But A→C→B→D = 3+3 = 6 — shorter! The cheapest road to D runs through B, not straight from C. One source → all nodes Dijkstra answers one question per run: how far is EVERY node from THIS starting point? Lecture 24 · single source Not all pairs It does not give the absolute shortest distance between every pair — that is a different algorithm's job. Lecture 24 · one question per run Start matters Change the starting node and the whole answer sheet changes — results are relative to the source. Lecture 24 · results vary by start 5 Hubs, spokes and the real world Where Dijkstra quietly earns its keep Hubs & spokes — the courier model Lecture 24 · spoke-and-hub Courier firms do not connect every city to every city — that network explodes in complexity. They build hubs (Jaipur, Delhi) with spoke cities hanging off them, and Dijkstra pre-computes the shortest hub-to-hub distances once. hub ⇄ hub · Dijkstra territory Jodhpur Pali Ajmer Agra Kurukshetra Somnath Jaipur · HUB Delhi · HUB 8 cities · all-to-all = 28 direct routes · hub & spoke = 10 routes (and Dijkstra only works the 1 hub-to-hub edge) Ship Jodhpur → Somnath Reset → Ready. A package from Jodhpur to Somnath never takes a Jodhpur→Somnath road — it hops Jodhpur → Jaipur → Delhi → Somnath through the hubs. Lecture 24 · current use cases GPS navigation Route planning computes the cheapest path from you to the destination, live. Food delivery Zomato & Swiggy allocate drivers by shortest reachable path to pickup and drop. Telecommunications Network optimisation routes signals along the lowest-cost links. Courier & logistics Hub-and-spoke networks run on pre-computed hub-to-hub shortest distances. Computer networks Routing protocols pick the least-cost path for every packet through the mesh. 6 The variant family — and how to choose A* and its five cousins Lecture 24 · A* — the GPS standard Plain Dijkstra is direction-blind — it expands in every direction equally. The A* algorithm adds a heuristic : actual cost so far plus a “sense of direction” — if the destination is south, paths heading south get priority. That makes it more optimal than Dijkstra in practice , which is why A* is the engine inside GPS navigation. Lecture 24 · the variant table Algorithm What it does Reach for it when… Uniform Cost Search Expands the lowest-cost paths first Constraints matter — e.g. avoid tolls, minimise spend Bidirectional Search Searches from source AND destination simultaneously, meeting in the middle Both endpoints are known and the space is huge Floyd–Warshall Shortest paths between ALL pairs of nodes You need the whole distance matrix upfront Bellman–Ford Shortest paths tolerating NEGATIVE edge weights Costs can drop below zero Prim's & Kruskal's Minimum spanning tree — connect every node at minimum total cost You are BUILDING the network, not just travelling it Lecture 24 · selection criteria Dijkstra one source → all destinations, positive weights Bellman–Ford negative edge weights exist Prim's / Kruskal's connect ALL nodes at minimum total cost Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths are required A* a directional heuristic is available In practice you SELECT algorithms, you don't write them Real GPS units, delivery platforms and telecom stacks ship variants or combinations of these algorithms, already implemented . The lecture's closing point: understanding which algorithm fits which scenario matters more than implementing one from scratch. In the lecture's graph (A→B 4 · A→C 2 · C→B 1 · C→D 5 · B→D 3), what is the shortest distance from A to B? Lecture 24 · Dijkstra A 4 — the direct edge B 3 — via A→C→B C 2 — via A→C D 6 — via A→C→B→D Your network contains some NEGATIVE edge weights. Which algorithm still works? Lecture 24 · choosing algorithms A Dijkstra's algorithm B Bellman–Ford C Prim's algorithm D Kruskal's algorithm Pen-and-paper drills — network search 4 drills 1 Run Dijkstra by hand on the lecture graph starting from A: write the settled order, each node's final distance, and the path used for D. Hint: Order: A(0) → C(2) → B(3) → D(6). D's path is A→C→B→D — the A→C→D route (7) gets beaten. 2 Re-run the same graph but start from D. Do A, B and C keep the same distances? What does this prove about Dijkstra's output? Hint: Distances are relative to the chosen source — a different start produces a different answer sheet. 3 A delivery app must find the cheapest route for a driver who pays the tolls personally. Which variant fits, and why not plain Dijkstra with time weights? Hint: Uniform Cost Search — expand lowest-COST paths first; the cost variable is rupees, not minutes. 4 A monitoring tool must map a data centre whose connections change weekly. Which traversal do you reach for — DFS or BFS — and what structure powers it? Hint: DFS on a stack: as far as possible per branch, backtracking — ideal for re-discovering topology when new nodes or connections appear. Lecture 24 · key takeaways Key takeaways Network search finds optimal paths between nodes in weighted graphs — the goal shifts from locating an element to routing between two. Dijkstra's algorithm is the fundamental answer to the single-source shortest path problem: one start, distances to all others. It works only on weighted graphs with non-negative weights — the cost is whatever you optimise: distance, time, tolls or a blend. The two lecture discoveries: direct routes can lose to detours (A→C→B beats A→B; A→C→B→D beats A→C→D). Different business scenarios need different variants — Bellman–Ford for negatives, Floyd–Warshall for all pairs, Prim's/Kruskal's to build cheap networks, A* when a sense of direction exists. In practice, selecting the right algorithm beats implementing one — real systems already ship these as library variants and combinations.

chapters.label: Sorting
chapters.text: Lecture 25 · Sorting & bubble sort Sorting & bubble sort The final module opens with the step that makes efficient searching possible: arranging elements by a parameter. Bubble sort is the simplest sorter ever devised — and the clearest demonstration that simplicity has a price. 1 What is sorting? One word, many parameters Lecture 25 · definition Sorting is arranging elements in a specific order — ascending, descending, or by any parameter you choose: numerical value, alphabetical order, relevance, price, quality . It sounds mundane, but hold one fact tight: most search algorithms assume the data is already sorted — which makes sorting the prerequisite for efficient searching . E-commerce Products sorted by relevance, price, quality — every parameter is a different sort. Lecture 25 · e-commerce Flight booking Results ranked by price and travel time; the cheapest flight and the fastest flight rarely coincide. Lecture 25 · travel Academic reporting Marks sorted highest → lowest so grades can be assigned by position. Lecture 25 · academics Multiple parameters, better decisions Platforms never stop at one sort. Sorting the same data several ways — by price, then by rating, then by delivery speed — is what turns a raw list into a decision tool. The parameter is the user experience. 2 Bubble sort — the rising bubble Light values float, heavy values sink Lecture 25 · the name The name comes from air bubbles rising in water : the lighter (smaller) values drift toward the front while heavier (larger) values sink to the end . The machinery is just two moves on loop: compare adjacent elements → swap if out of order . The classic method — largest element to the end, in six rules: 1 Start from the first element and compare it with the next. 2 If the first is larger, swap their positions. 3 Move to the next pair and repeat along the row. 4 After each pass, the largest unsorted element lands in its final position at the end. 5 Repeat — one fewer comparison in each subsequent pass. 6 Total passes needed equals the number of elements. Bubble sort, pass by pass — [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] Lecture 25 · flagship trace The lecture's exact list. Each press of Next performs one adjacent comparison — larger values sink right , smaller ones float left , and after every pass the largest unsettled value locks into its final slot. Next comparison Reset before pass 1 10 idx 0 5 idx 1 8 idx 2 4 idx 3 3 idx 4 2 idx 5 locked cells (olive) are in their final position — never touched again The list as it arrives: [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2]. Pass 1 will make 5 adjacent comparisons — watch the largest value sink. 3 Two directions, one result …and sorting words, not just numbers Lecture 25 · alternative method Smallest element to the front The mirror variant: start from the last element and compare it with the previous one, bubbling the minimum leftward . After each pass, the smallest unsorted element lands in its correct position at the beginning . Same result, opposite direction — the lecture calls it the alternative method. Classic largest sinks to the END each pass Alternative smallest floats to the FRONT each pass Sorting words — not just numbers Lecture 25 · A < Z Bubble sort works on any comparable data . Here is the lecture's name list — the compare step now checks capital letters alphabetically ( A < Z ), and the same swap logic takes over. Sort A → Z Reset Mohan Ram Sham Lakshman Arjun Bheem → [Mohan, Ram, Sham, Lakshman, Arjun, Bheem] as given. Press Sort and watch the same adjacent swaps apply to strings. 4 The price of simplicity — O(n²) From 15 comparisons to 100 million Lecture 25 · the derivation Count the work. Pass 1 makes n comparisons, pass 2 makes n−1 , pass 3 makes n−2 … the final pass makes 1 . Add them up: Sum the passes n + (n−1) + … + 1 Closed form n(n−1)/2 Expand ½n² − ½n Big O rules drop −½n · drop the ½ Verdict O(n²) — quadratic Big O rule 1 · discard lower-order terms −½n is negligible next to ½n² once n grows. Big O rule 2 · remove numerical constants The ½ goes too — ½n² is still O(n²). Grow n — watch n(n−1)/2 explode Lecture 25 · quadratic blow-up 6 elements 10 elements 100 elements 1,000 elements 10,000 elements n(n−1)/2 = 15 comparisons bar on a square-root scale — a linear bar could not fit 10,000 on this screen 15 comparisons — a handful. This is bubble sort's comfort zone: a lecture example, a classroom trace. Lecture 25 · when it's fine Small lists — 5 or 6 elements — are manageable : about 25 operations. For a classroom trace or a tiny array, bubble sort is honest, obvious, and perfectly adequate. Lecture 25 · when it's fatal 10,000 elements ≈ 100 million comparisons — despite its logical simplicity, bubble sort is unsuitable for large datasets or business applications . The next lectures exist to fix exactly this. After Pass 1 of bubble sort on [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2], where does the 10 end up? Lecture 25 · bubble sort A At the front — it floated left B In its final position at the end C Still at index 0 D In the middle of the list The exact comparison count is n(n−1)/2 = ½n² − ½n. Why do we report O(n²)? Lecture 25 · complexity A Because swaps count double B Because Big O discards lower-order terms and constants C Because passes are counted twice D Because n(n−1)/2 simplifies to n² exactly Pen-and-paper drills — bubble sort 4 drills 1 Trace Pass 2 of [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] by hand: list every comparison, every swap, and the final array with two settled values. Hint: Pass 2 makes 4 comparisons: 5,8 stay · 8,4 swap · 8,3 swap · 8,2 swap → [5, 4, 3, 2, 8, 10]. 2 Sort [Mohan, Ram, Sham, Lakshman, Arjun, Bheem] alphabetically using bubble sort's compare-and-swap. How many passes does it take? Hint: Capital letters compare A < Z — same six rules, no arithmetic needed. 3 Compute the total comparisons for n = 6 and n = 20 using n(n−1)/2. Then explain in one sentence why the second number should worry you. Hint: 15 vs 190 — twenty elements already cost 12× more work than six. 4 Write the six rules of the ALTERNATIVE method (smallest to the front). Which end of the row do you walk from, and which end locks first? Hint: Start from the last element, compare with the previous one, bubble the minimum left; position 1 locks first. Lecture 25 · key takeaways Key takeaways Sorting arranges data by a parameter of your choice — numerical, alphabetical, relevance, price — and multiple parameters mean multiple useful orders. Most search algorithms assume sorted data — sorting is the prerequisite for efficient searching. Bubble sort orders data by successive adjacent comparisons and swaps — light values float forward, heavy values sink. Each pass moves one element into its final position ; passes needed equal the list size, with one fewer comparison per pass. Time complexity is O(n²) : n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n−1)/2 → fine for 5–6 elements, unusable at 10,000 (~100 million comparisons). The next algorithms in the module exist to fix this efficiency problem for large datasets.

chapters.label: Selection sort
chapters.text: Module 4 · Lecture 26 · Selection sort Select it, swap it home Selection sort picks one element per pass — the minimum of everything still unsorted — and swaps it into its final position. One element finalised per pass, exactly one swap per pass. 1 The core loop Assume the first unsorted slot holds the minimum. Compare with everything to its right; when something smaller appears, mark it. After the sweep, swap the marked minimum with the slot — then step forward one slot. The selection machine · [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] frame 1/12 10 0 5 1 8 2 4 3 3 4 2 5 Start — nothing sorted yet Reset Step Play green = finalised · red = the minimum being scanned · amber = the slot about to swap 2 The worked example, by hand The lecture's array: [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] — four passes, four swaps, sorted. Pass 1 minimum of all six = 2 swap 2 ↔ 10 [2, 5, 8, 4, 3, 10] Pass 2 minimum from position 2 = 3 swap 3 ↔ 5 [2, 3, 8, 4, 5, 10] Pass 3 minimum from position 3 = 4 swap 4 ↔ 8 [2, 3, 4, 8, 5, 10] Pass 4 minimum from position 4 = 5 swap 5 ↔ 8 [2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10] Final result — the array is sorted after n−1 passes. 3 Three variants, one complexity Minimum, maximum, bidirectional — the direction changes, the O(n²) bill never does. Minimum selection sort classical Searches for the smallest element starting from the beginning — minimum elements land at the front, one per pass. Maximum selection sort backwards Starts from the last position and works backward — maximum elements land at the end, one per pass. Bidirectional selection sort both ends Finds the minimum from the front and the maximum from the back in a single pass — passes halve, comparisons don't. Why bidirectional doesn't improve the complexity Passes drop to half — but every pass still has to compare from both ends toward the middle, so the total number of comparisons stays the same . O(n²) is O(n²), whichever direction you sweep. 4 Selection vs bubble — same O(n²), different swap bill Both are quadratic; the difference is how many swaps each pass performs. Aspect Bubble sort Selection sort Complexity O(n²) O(n²) — all variants Swaps per pass up to n−1 — an element can hop many times exactly ONE — after the minimum is found Guaranteed after a pass largest unsorted element bubbles to the end smallest unsorted element selected to the front Verdict simplest possible idea more swap-efficient — still impractical at scale Alphabetical data works identically — compare letters lexicographically (A < B < C … < Z), select the earliest, swap it home. Selection sort, classical form: what exactly happens in one pass? Lecture 26 · selection sort A Adjacent pairs are compared and swapped wherever the left is larger B The minimum of the unsorted portion is found and swapped with the first unsorted slot C Each element is inserted into its correct position among the sorted ones D The list is split in half and the halves are merged Sorting [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2]: what does the array look like after Pass 2? Lecture 26 · worked example A [2, 5, 8, 4, 3, 10] B [2, 3, 8, 4, 5, 10] C [2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10] D [5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 2] Trace it on paper 2 drills 1 Run maximum selection sort on [4, 9, 1, 7]. Show the array after every pass and count the swaps. Hint: Pass 1: max 9 → end. Pass 2: max 7 → second-from-end. Two swaps, done. 2 Selection sort performs at most n−1 swaps for n elements. Why can bubble sort need far more for the same list? Hint: Bubble hops an element right by one position at a time — up to n−1 hops for a single element in one pass. Key takeaways Selection sort = select one element per pass , place it in its correct position through swapping. Exactly one swap per pass — the swap-efficient sibling of bubble sort. Minimum, maximum and bidirectional variants all keep O(n²) time complexity . Great for education and small datasets ; avoid it for larger lists despite the tidy swap count.

chapters.label: Insertion sort
chapters.text: Module 4 · Lecture 27 · Insertion sort Movement, not swapping Bubble and selection swap; insertion moves. Pick the next key, shove everything larger one slot to the right, drop the key into the gap. The left portion is always sorted — the algorithm only ever extends it. 1 The five steps Start from the second item — the first element is assumed sorted. STEP 1 Take the second item as the KEY; compare it with the items on its left STEP 2 Move every element LARGER than the key one position to the right STEP 3 Keep comparing until something smaller appears — or the list begins STEP 4 INSERT the key at the vacant position STEP 5 Repeat for each subsequent element until the whole list is sorted 2 The machine [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] — watch each key lift, its larger neighbours slide right, and it drop into place. The insertion machine · [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] frame 1/12 10 0 5 1 8 2 4 3 3 4 2 5 Start — the first element is already 'sorted' Reset Step Play red = the key being inserted · green = the sorted portion · grey = still untouched 3 The lecture walkthrough Same array, all five passes, movements counted. Pass 1 key 5 10 moves right [5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 2] Pass 2 key 8 10 moves right [5, 8, 10, 4, 3, 2] Pass 3 key 4 10, 8, 5 move right [4, 5, 8, 10, 3, 2] Pass 4 key 3 all larger elements move right [3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 2] Pass 5 key 2 everything moves right [2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10] 4 Three variants, same O(n²) Direction changes the choreography — never the complexity class. Minimum insertion sort Classical: minimum elements land at the beginning; larger elements move right; starts from the front. Maximum insertion sort Maximum elements land at the end; smaller elements move left; starts from the second item from the end — the mirror image. Bi-directional insertion sort Both ends at once: minimum and maximum found in a single pass, placed at their respective correct positions. 5 Where insertion sort actually wins O(n²) rules out large random lists — but four scenarios make it the right tool. New item in a sorted list A new student joins an alphabetically ordered roster — insertion finds the slot without a full re-sort. E-commerce categories Inventory already sorted by category; new products insert straight into their subcategory position. Partially sorted data When most of the list is already in order and only a few elements are out of place, insertion barely works. Dynamic data arrival Data arrives sequentially and the list must stay sorted in real time — insertion is the natural fit. The disadvantage Inefficient for large, randomly ordered lists — O(n²) means comparisons and movements grow by the square (list of 4 → 9 operations, 5 → 16, 6 → 25…). Multiple comparisons and movements per unsorted element. The name is the algorithm Insertion sort takes an element and inserts it into its proper place within the sorted portion. Small lists: efficient. Nearly-sorted lists: excellent. Sorted lists receiving new arrivals: unbeatable. Sorting [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] by insertion: what does Pass 3 produce? Lecture 27 · walkthrough A [5, 8, 10, 4, 3, 2] B [4, 5, 8, 10, 3, 2] C [3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 2] D [5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 2] A sorted roster receives one new student. Which sort fits best — and why? Lecture 27 · use cases A Bubble sort — it handles any order B Insertion sort — a nearly-sorted list needs only a short leftward comparison for the new key C Selection sort — one swap per pass D Any O(n²) sort works equally well here Key takeaways Insertion sort moves elements to create space — it does not swap them. Every variant — minimum, maximum, bi-directional — stays O(n²) . It shines on small, partially sorted, or dynamically growing lists. New-item insertion into a sorted list is its home turf — no full re-sort needed. Trace it on paper 2 drills 1 Run minimum insertion sort on [7, 3, 9, 1]. List the array after each pass and count total movements. Hint: Pass 1: key 3, 7 moves right. Pass 2: key 9 stays. Pass 3: key 1 — 9, 7, 3 all move right. 2 Why is insertion sort 'significantly useful for inserting new elements into already sorted lists' while bubble sort is not? Hint: Insertion touches only the leftward path of one key; bubble sweeps every adjacent pair of the whole list each pass.

chapters.label: Final recap
chapters.text: Module 4 · Lecture 28 · The final overview The whole module, stitched shut One last sweep: the Big O ladder, the price list of every data structure you met, and the five searches on a single map. Complexity measures the growth rate — never the stopwatch. 1 The Big O ladder From fastest to slowest — the growth pattern is the entire story. O(1) Constant fixed operations regardless of input size — rare in practice O(log n) Logarithmic slow growth, ideal for practical applications (halving) O(n) Linear proportional to input size — manageable O(n log n) Linearithmic slightly faster growth than linear, still acceptable O(n²) Quadratic rapid growth, impractical for large datasets O(2ⁿ) Exponential extremely rapid — avoid at all costs 2 Every structure's price list The operations you can afford — and the ones that quietly cost a full scan. Arrays Read with known index O(1) · direct access Sequential read O(n) · one by one Search O(n) · linear sweep Insert at end O(1) · single operation Insert at begin / middle O(n) · shifting required Update at a location O(1) · direct modify Delete by searching O(n) · search first, then delete Linked lists Insert in middle O(1) · only links update (2–4 ops) Insert with search O(n) · search dominates Search O(n) · traverse one by one Stacks & queues Push / pop (stack) O(1) · fixed position: top Enqueue / dequeue (queue) O(1) · fixed positions: front & rear Search inside either O(n) · must remove elements to see them Trees & graphs General tree traversal O(n) · visit every node Unbalanced binary tree search O(n) · degenerates to a linked list Balanced BST search O(log n) · space halves at each step Graph traversal DFS / BFS O(V + E) · all vertices and edges 3 The five searches, side by side Data size, sorting status, distribution and growth rate — pick the strategy that matches all four. Search Requirement Signature move Linear O(n) works on unsorted data simple but inefficient for large datasets Binary O(log n) sorted data required 10 million records ≈ 24 comparisons Jump O(√n) sorted data required fixed √n jumps, then a linear sweep in the block Exponential O(log n) sorted data required jumps double (1, 2, 4, 8…), then binary in the range Hash O(1) avg well-distributed hash function worst case O(n) when everything collides And the network finale — Dijkstra & friends Dijkstra: single-source shortest path, weighted graphs, non-negative weights , O(V²) basic implementation. A* adds a directional heuristic for GPS. Bellman-Ford survives negative weights. Floyd-Warshall answers all pairs; Prim and Kruskal connect every node at minimum total cost. Then the business layer: database queries, e-commerce filtering, GPS routing, student records, food-delivery optimisation. Binary search needs ~24 comparisons for 10 million records. Linear search on the same data needs… Lecture 28 · final recap A ~24 — both halve the space B ~10,000 — one comparison per thousand records C up to 10 million — every record in the worst case D logarithmically fewer — linear search self-optimises Inserting into the MIDDLE of a linked list is O(1) — but inserting while SEARCHING for the spot is O(n). Why the gap? Lecture 28 · cost tables A Linked lists re-index after every insert B The links update in 2–4 operations, but finding the insertion point still requires a one-by-one traversal C Middle inserts are physically faster in memory D The O(n) comes from shifting elements right Key takeaways Complexity measures the growth rate of work as input grows — never absolute seconds. O(1) and O(log n) are preferable ; exponential O(2ⁿ) must be avoided. Arrays buy O(1) direct access but pay O(n) to shift; linked lists pay O(1) to rewire but O(n) to find. The five searches trade sorted-ness for speed : hash O(1) needs none of it — binary O(log n) needs all of it. Close the module 2 drills 1 Rank these by scalability for 10 million records: linear search on an unsorted register, hash lookup by roll number, binary search on a price-sorted catalog. Hint: Hash O(1) average → binary O(log n) → linear O(n). The register's lack of order is what forces the slow lane. 2 A startup's data doubles every quarter. Which single complexity class should its core lookups target — and which one ruins the roadmap? Hint: Target O(log n) or better (halving scales); anything quadratic or exponential compounds the same way the data does.

chapters.label: Course map
chapters.text: Lecture 1 · Orientation Accounting is the language of business — and this course teaches you to read it. Every organization depends on accounting information: to record transactions, communicate performance, and support decisions. Before any vocabulary arrives, here is the whole journey — five modules, one cycle, three outcomes. 01 The five modules From first concepts to reading annual reports like a manager Module 01 Introduction Concepts, conventions, terminology — and a first look at the balance sheet and income statement. Module 02 Records & Systems The mechanics: journal entries, T-accounts, ledger accounts, trial balances. Module 03 Statement Preparation Balance sheet and P&L structure — accrual accounting, revenue recognition. Module 04 Cash Flow Statement The most honest statement — its preparation, plus inventory valuation and depreciation. Module 05 Assets & Analysis Long-lived assets, depreciation methods — and reading annual reports for managerial insight. No prior background required The course is core for the BS in Management and Technology programme at IIT Jodhpur, taught by Dr. Manisha of the School of Management and Entrepreneurship. It assumes nothing — but it does demand practice: accounting is a skill, and fluency comes from repetition across many transactions. 02 The accounting cycle How raw data becomes a financial statement — click a station The cycle — six stations 01 Transaction source document 02 Journal day book, in time order 03 Ledger T-accounts, by account 04 Trial balance do the columns agree? 05 Adjustments deferrals & accruals 06 Statements P&L · balance sheet · cash flow Transaction. Every story starts with a source document — a cash receipt, an invoice, a salary bill. No document, no entry. 03 Three outcomes What you should be able to do when the course ends Understand the role Grasp the nature of accounting and its critical role in business decision-making. Prepare & comprehend Prepare and comprehend the financial statements of real firms. Analyze & extract Draw useful managerial information for managers, investors and other decision-makers. Key takeaways Accounting is the language of business — recording, communicating and deciding run on it. The course walks the full accounting cycle : journal → ledger → trial balance → adjustments → statements. Specific areas — receivables, inventories, long-lived assets, depreciation, amortization — get dedicated depth. The end goal is financial analysis : reading annual reports and extracting managerial insight.

chapters.label: The four verbs
chapters.text: Lecture 2 · Foundations Four verbs, three branches, one equation that must always balance. The textbook definition: accounting is the process of identifying, recording, measuring and communicating financial information about an economic entity to permit judgments and decisions by its users. Run the pipeline. 01 The four-step pipeline Click a verb — see what passes and what is filtered out Identifying Verb 1 Recording Verb 2 Measuring Verb 3 Communicating Verb 4 Recognize events with a financial impact — and filter out the rest. A machine breakdown that stops production? Financial. A star employee's dedication? Not recordable. Why the filter matters Employee dedication and company reputation matter enormously to a business — but accounting cannot record them, because they cannot be expressed in monetary terms. The measurement step is where accounting's greatest strength (one comparable number-language) and greatest limitation (important things left out) come from the same source. 02 The umbrella — three branches One word, three audiences, three rulebooks External users Financial Accounting Reports overall performance and position to investors, creditors, lenders and regulators. Standardized formats, regulatory rules (Ind AS in India, IFRS globally) — and the information is public. Standardized Public Rules-bound Internal users Management Accounting Detailed, forward-looking information for planning, budgeting and internal decisions. No standardized format — it never leaves the organization. Forward-looking Internal Free format A branch of management Cost Accounting Tracks and analyzes the costs of producing goods or services — pricing decisions, cost control, operational efficiency. Costs Pricing Efficiency 03 The entity concept & the equation The business is a separate unit — and its story always balances The entity concept The business is treated as separate and distinct from its owner. Personal assets, liabilities and expenditures stay out of the books. An owner's investment is recorded as equity — the business's obligation to its owner. Only then can business performance be measured meaningfully on its own. The foundation of everything that follows Assets = Liabilities + Equity Assets — what the business owns (cash, furniture, machinery, vehicles) Liabilities — what the business owes to others Equity — the owner's capital; the residual claim (also called shareholders' equity) Friend lends the business money? Assets ↑ (cash received) Liabilities ↑ (debt owed to the friend) …and the equation stays balanced. A proprietor pays for his family's vacation from his personal account and wants it recorded as a business expense. Which foundation does this break? Lecture 2 · check yourself A Money measurement — a vacation has no monetary value B The entity concept — personal affairs do not belong in the business's books C The dual aspect concept — only one side of the entry exists D The communication step — the information was never published Which branch of accounting is forward-looking, format-free, and never leaves the organization? Lecture 2 · check yourself A Financial accounting B Cost accounting C Management accounting D Tax accounting Key takeaways Accounting = identify → record → measure → communicate — and the filter is money measurement. Three branches: financial (external, standardized, public), management (internal, free format), cost (production focus). The entity concept separates the business from its owner; owner investment is recorded as equity. Assets = Liabilities + Equity must balance after every single transaction — the course's one invariant.

chapters.label: Users & regulators
chapters.text: Lecture 3 · Objectives, users & regulation Who reads the numbers — and who writes the rules . Five objectives give accounting its job description. Two families of users consume its output. And without uniform standards, comparison dies — so three Indian institutions police the language. 01 Five objectives From the first ledger line to the solvency verdict 01 Systematic recording Record all financial aspects of transactions methodically — bookkeeping, the foundation for everything else. 02 Classification & summarization Organize recorded transactions logically to prepare financial statements with meaningful insights. 03 Ascertainment of results Profit if revenues exceed expenses; loss if expenses exceed revenues — determined through the profit & loss account. 04 Financial position The balance sheet presents assets and liabilities at a specific date — the overall health of the organization. 05 Decision-making & solvency Reveal liquidity (short-term obligations) and solvency (long-term obligations) — the raw material of planning and strategy. 02 The two families of users Same statements, completely different questions — toggle the side Internal users External users Managers & directors Budgeting, targets, resource allocation, performance review — open a new factory or shut one down? Employees Company stability, job security, prospects for salary increases. Internal auditors The company's financial watchdogs — verify recording, catch errors, test internal controls. Internal users live inside the organization — they receive detail beyond the published statements. 03 Why standards exist at all Without uniform rules, comparison is impossible Each company could invent its own system — stakeholders could not evaluate or compare performance. Different methods could produce vastly different profits for identical revenues — misleading comparisons. Lenders and investors would lack a reliable basis for comparing loans or opportunities. 04 India's three pillars The author, the legislator and the police ICAI The author Institute of Chartered Accountants of India Apex professional body; drafts standards through its Accounting Standards Board Issues guidance notes and certifies chartered accountants MCA The legislator Ministry of Corporate Affairs Prescribes standards under the Companies Act 2013 Enforces compliance through registrars of companies; monitors firms SEBI The police Securities and Exchange Board of India Regulates listed companies; mandates disclosure norms and quarterly reporting Protects investors through stringent disclosure requirements 05 The global layer — IFRS & Ind AS One language, localized for India IFRS Issued by the International Accounting Standards Board, headquartered in London — adopted by more than 140 countries . The objective: a single set of high-quality global standards, so financial statements are comparable across borders. Ind AS — India's converged IFRS Notified by the MCA under the Companies Act 2013. Mandatory for all listed companies and large unlisted companies with net worth exceeding ₹250 crore . Indian statements become comparable with international ones — while accommodating country-specific deviations. Who drafts India's accounting standards, and who gives them the force of law? Lecture 3 · check yourself A SEBI drafts; ICAI enforces B ICAI drafts; MCA notifies under the Companies Act 2013 C MCA drafts; SEBI notifies for listed companies D The IASB drafts; India adopts directly An unlisted company has a net worth of ₹310 crore. Are Ind AS mandatory for it? Lecture 3 · check yourself A No — Ind AS is only for listed companies B Yes — large unlisted companies above ₹250 crore net worth must follow Ind AS C Only if it borrows from a bank D Only if it exports goods Key takeaways Five objectives: record, summarize, ascertain results, show position, enable liquidity & solvency decisions. Internal users (managers, employees, internal auditors) want detail; external users (investors, lenders, government, suppliers, customers, public) rely on published statements. ICAI drafts → MCA legislates → SEBI polices listed companies. IFRS: 140+ countries. Ind AS : India's converged version — mandatory above ₹250 crore net worth.

chapters.label: Why accounting?
chapters.text: Module 1 · Why accounting exists Five openings — every one ends at the same question No definitions yet. Five rooms, five arguments — and the same ghost in each: what did the business really earn, and who can trust the number? 01 The argument at the dinner table Same transactions, same year — opposite verdicts The case Priya and Rohan jointly inherited their father’s small manufacturing business. At year end they sit down to figure out how it did. Priya says it “barely made anything” and wants to sell. Rohan says it “did great” and wants to expand. Same transactions, same year — but Priya counted the full cost of a new machine as this year’s expense, while Rohan counted no wear-and-tear on the older equipment at all. Why both are wrong “Profit” is not a fact lying around to be picked up — it is a constructed number . Until rules decide how the machine’s cost is spread and how wear-and-tear is recognised every period, two honest people looking at the same year will build two different profits. That is what accounting conventions are for: one agreed way, so the argument ends. 02 The notebook and the investor \u20B915 lakh is waiting — but on whose word? The case Ramesh runs a street-food business that grew from one stall to three. He tracks everything himself — cash in, cash out — in a personal notebook, in his own shorthand. A close friend offers to invest ₹15 lakh so Ramesh can open five more stalls — but asks to see “the financials” first. Ramesh says, “It’s all in my head, and in this notebook — ask me anything, I’ll tell you.” The friend trusts Ramesh personally — and is still hesitant to invest. The gap the course fills Personal trust does not scale into capital. The friend is not doubting Ramesh’s honesty — he is doubting a system where one person’s shorthand decides what counts as income. Financial statements exist to replace “ask me anything” with numbers prepared by agreed rules, so a stranger can check them too. 03 Who reads this, and why One set of statements, three different conversations The case Vasudha runs a small chain of three gyms. One set of statements — a balance sheet and an income statement. On the same afternoon she shows them to a bank (a loan for a fourth location), to Arjun (a friend investing “the company’s profit”). She assumed one set of numbers would mean one conversation. All three meetings went completely differently. The bank Can the business service a loan? Stability, collateral, cash cover for interest. The investor What is my 10% stake worth? Growth, quality of profit, future returns. The managers Will the bonus plan pay out? The profit line they are tied to — and how it is built. So what is financial accounting, really? A common language for the money story of a business — prepared once, but read by lenders, investors, managers, the government. The statements are the same; the question each reader brings decides the conversation. Learning the language is learning all three meetings at once. 04 Would you lend them money? \u20B950 crore of revenue each — very different profits Company X Revenue ₹50 crore, profit ₹8 crore — but the ₹8 crore came almost entirely from selling off a factory : a one-time gain. The core, ongoing operations lost money this year. Company Y Same ₹50 crore revenue, only ₹2 crore profit — but every rupee of it from normal day-to-day business , grown steadily for three years running . Your \u20B910 crore loan application is on the desk of one of these two. Which profit figure would you rather be judged by — and why? The lending decision A Company X's ₹8 crore — bigger is better B Company Y's ₹2 crore — it repeats, X's does not C Neither — profit is irrelevant to lending D Whichever company has more factories 05 Profitable — and out of cash The gap between the income statement and the bank account The case Solaris Furnishings had a great year on paper: sales up 40%, the highest net income in five years. Four months into the next year it could not pay its suppliers and shut down two of its three factories. What happened? Nearly all sales were made to a handful of large retail chains — on credit, 120-day terms — and it bought a mountain of raw material upfront. By year-end, a large share of its “sales” existed only as amounts owed to Solaris — not as cash in the bank. Profit is an opinion about a period — cash is a fact at a moment Accrual accounting recognises revenue when it is earned , not when cash lands. That is what makes profit comparable across periods — and it is also why a “profitable” company can die of thirst. The statement pair exists because of this gap: the income statement tells the story of the period, the cash (and balance-sheet) view tells you what is actually in the vault. Key takeaways Profit is constructed — conventions (not opinions) decide what counts, so the argument ends the same way every time. Statements replace “trust me” with “check me” — that is what turns personal goodwill into investable capital. One set of statements, many readers: lenders, investors, managers — each brings a different question to the same numbers. A one-time gain is not a business model — recurring profit is what repays debt. Profitable companies can still run out of cash — the income statement and the bank account tell different truths. Seminar drills — argue it out 3 drills 1 How can two people looking at the same year of the same business reach opposite conclusions about performance? Hint: Each privately chose a different measurement rule for the machine and the wear-and-tear — the number follows the rule. 2 What would prevent this disagreement in a company with professionally prepared statements? Hint: Agreed conventions + a measurement framework applied by someone other than the winner of the argument. 3 Why does accounting rely on agreed-upon rules at all, instead of everyone calculating profit their own way? Hint: Think of Ramesh's investor and Vasudha's three meetings — numbers only trade value when strangers can trust how they were built.

chapters.label: The eight concepts
chapters.text: Module 1 · The measurement assumptions Four quiet assumptions under every rupee The purpose of accounting is to measure and communicate an enterprise's economic activities. But it only measures events that affect the financial position — and it measures them on four assumptions. 01 What counts as a transaction — and what gets measured Transactions Business transactions are events that result in the transfer or exchange of value between parties — monetary exchanges, non-monetary exchanges, or one-way transfers (a donation given, a theft suffered). If value moved, accounting is interested. The filter Accounting measures events only if they affect the financial position of the enterprise. Signing a promise, hiring a star employee, losing a key customer to a competitor — real events, but until value moves, the books stay silent. 02 The four assumptions Reporting entity · Going concern · Periodicity · Money measurement 1 Reporting Entity Business is distinct from its owners and from other firms — the books draw a boundary around one enterprise. 2 Going Concern The business is assumed to continue operating — no liquidation on the horizon, so cost is meaningful. 3 Periodicity Activities are divided into artificial time periods — usually a year, sometimes a quarter. 4 Money Measurement All transactions are recorded in monetary terms — the rupee is the only common denominator. 03 The full eight — the lecture's complete concept list Four assumptions above, four more concepts, one invariant: Assets = Liabilities + Capital Concept 5 Cost Recorded at acquisition price — land bought for ₹50,000 stays ₹50,000 whether market later reads ₹60,000 or ₹40,000. Objective, auditable — blind to inflation. Concept 6 Dual aspect Every transaction has two equal effects — the foundation of double entry and of the equation itself. Concept 7 Accounting period Business life divided into segments (usually a year) so results can be studied at each stop. Concept 8 Realization Revenue recognized when the sale is made — property in goods passes to the buyer — not when cash arrives. The cost concept, argued both ways Advantages: it removes subjectivity — a standardized measurement brings objectivity to the statements. Limitation: it cannot account for inflation — in high-inflation periods historical cost may not reflect the firm's true financial position. That trade-off is the price of the objectivity every other user relies on. Why the assumptions matter more than they look Every controversy you will meet in this course — the dinner-table argument, the revalued car, the commission paid in the wrong month — is one of these four assumptions being bent. Name the assumption being violated, and you have named the error. That is the violation-spotting skill the lectures keep drilling. Spot the assumption 3 drills 1 A firm values its brand loyalty at ₹5 crore and lists it as an asset. Hint: It is real advantage — but can it be measured in money with reasonable objectivity? 2 A shop records its owner's personal wedding expenses as business promotion. Hint: Whose affairs are these — the entity's, or the owner's? 3 A company about to be liquidated keeps showing its land at ten-year-old purchase cost. Hint: What does going concern justify — and what happens when it no longer holds?

chapters.label: Dual aspect
chapters.text: Module 2 · The dual aspect concept Every rupee tells two stories Every business transaction has a DUAL effect — it touches two aspects simultaneously. One idea, and the whole of double-entry book-keeping falls out of it. 01 A starts with ₹10,000 — and two things happen at once Aspect one — the business has an asset The business now holds cash of “10,000 — a resource it controls. Aspect two — the business owes it The business must repay that sum to the proprietor: “10,000 of proprietor’s capital . Same number, other side of the coin. the same transaction, seen from both sides CAPITAL ₹10,000 CASH ₹10,000 = Equities (claims) Assets (resources) The expression, written as an equation Capital (Equities) = Cash (Assets) ₹10,000 = ₹10,000 02 Three transactions — watch the two columns grow in lock-step Liabilities + Capital = Assets (or) Equities = Assets Step Transaction Equities (claims) Assets (resources) 1 A invests ₹10,000 capital Capital ₹10,000 Cash ₹10,000 2 Buys furniture ₹5,000 Capital ₹10,000 Cash ₹5,000 + Furniture ₹5,000 3 Borrows ₹30,000 from bank Capital ₹10,000 + Bank loan ₹30,000 Cash ₹35,000 + Furniture ₹5,000 The foundation stone “For each debit, there is an equivalent credit” — that sentence is the foundation of double-entry book-keeping . The two columns above move in lock-step not because accountants are careful, but because the arithmetic cannot do otherwise. Two names, one equation Liabilities + Capital = Assets (or) Equities = Assets rearranged with outsiders first: Assets = Liabilities + Equity Under the accounting equation approach, which family of accounts INCREASES with a debit? Debit / credit directions A Liabilities, capital and revenues B Assets, expenses and drawings C Only capital D Only liabilities

chapters.label: Periods & matching
chapters.text: Module 1 · Assumptions, deep-dive Time, cut into periods — and the match that follows Investors cannot wait a lifetime for results. So the business's long story is chopped into artificial years — and every chop creates a question: which period owns which cost? 01 Periodicity — the root of most accounting controversies The chop We assume a long life for a business — but investors, creditors and the government cannot wait indefinitely for information. Periodicity requires activities to be divided into artificial time periods : usually a year, sometimes as short as a quarter. The crack Artificial periods create real difficulties — the equipment bought today must serve for years, so its useful life has to be estimated . Those estimates ride on management’s judgment and are often subjective. This assumption is the root cause of many accounting controversies — including the dinner-table one. 02 Periodic matching of costs and revenue Revenue of December 2010 · cost of the same December — payment date irrelevant REVENUE Sales made in December 2010 earned in this period COST Commission paid to salesman in January 2011 — for December 2010 sales — cost of earning THAT revenue MATCH When payment was received or made is irrelevant — this is why year-end adjustments exist. Where the adjustments come from On account of this one concept, year-end adjustments are made for outstanding expenses, accrued incomes, prepaid expenses and unearned incomes . Module 4 of this course builds every one of them — they are all this diagram wearing different clothes. 03 Realization — revenue waits for delivery, not cash Order in March, goods delivered in April → revenue belongs to April The rule Revenue is recognized when a sale is made — specifically when property in the goods passes to the buyer and the buyer becomes legally liable to pay. The moment of delivery, not the order and not the payment, owns the revenue. The two famous exceptions Hire purchase: ownership passes only at the final installment — yet sellers record revenue progressively as installments fall due, because waiting would misstate every interim period. Long-term construction: profit is recorded yearly on work certified, not only at completion — a bridge billed over five years cannot hide four years of results. Both exceptions exist for one reason: waiting for legal completion gives a misleading picture of the period. 04 Money measurement — the rupee is the only common denominator The rule Under the money measurement assumption, all business transactions are expressed and recorded in terms of money . Money is the only common denominator that lets a factory, a bank loan and a cartage bill sit in one statement — in India, the rupee is the monetary unit. The cost of the rule Anything that cannot be measured monetarily has no place in accounting : a loyal workforce, the owner’s reputation, a perfect location. Real advantages — but not numbers, so not in the books. Every discipline buys its power with a boundary; this is accounting’s. 05 What's wrong with these practices? Identify the assumption or principle violated — the lecture's own violation round (a) Owner's home electricity A business records an expense for the electricity charges of the owner's home. Reporting entity — personal expenses must stay out of the business's books. (b) Car revalued after one week A car bought at auction for ₹40,000 is re-recorded at ₹50,000 a week later. Historical cost — assets stay at original purchase price, not fluctuating market values. (c) Personal smartphone as business asset A smartphone bought for the owner's personal use is recorded as a business asset. Reporting entity again — only business-related items belong in the company's books. Key takeaways Accounting measures only events that affect financial position — value must move. The four assumptions: reporting entity, going concern, periodicity, money measurement . Going concern justifies historical cost ; when it breaks, fair value takes over — say so on time (Kingfisher). Periodicity chops time into years — and every chop creates an estimation question. Periodic matching owns the year-end adjustment family: outstanding / accrued / prepaid / unearned . Money measurement is the price of one common language — the unmeasurable stays out . Commission is paid to a salesman in January 2011 for sales made in December 2010. The commission expense belongs to\u2026 December sales, January commission A January 2011 — that is when cash left B December 2010 — the period whose sales it earned C Split 50/50 across both months D Whichever year the auditor prefers

chapters.label: Four conventions
chapters.text: Lecture 7 · Conventions Not rules — evolved customs that keep statements fair. Concepts are the assumptions accounting stands on. Conventions are the customs and traditions accountants follow when preparing statements — developed over time to ensure consistency and fairness. 01 Convention 1 — conservatism Anticipate no profit; provide for all possible losses The conservatism dial goods costing ₹1,00,000 · drag the market price Current market price ₹1,40,000 Cost ₹1,00,000 Valuation ₹1,00,000 Market ₹1,40,000 Inventory valued at ₹1,00,000. Market above cost — value at COST. The unrealized gain stays out of the books. Anticipate no profit — so a gain is never booked before it is realized. Provide for all possible losses — so the moment market slips below cost, the write-down hits the books. The same logic creates provisions for doubtful debts from this year's profits, without waiting for an actual default. The cost of playing safe Conservatism has critics: it can create secret reserves , understate assets, overstate liabilities and show artificially low net income — so the statements may not reflect the true and fair value of the business. That tension is exactly why the next three conventions exist. 02 Conventions 2, 3, 4 Disclosure · consistency · materiality Full disclosure Statements must fully and fairly disclose what they purport to represent. Born of joint-stock companies: owners separated from managers rely entirely on the statements. The Companies Act legally requires a true and fair view — notes to accounts (contingent liabilities, investment values) are part of the deal. Consistency Practices must stay consistent period to period, or year-on-year comparison collapses. But not rigid inflexibility: better techniques may be adopted — provided the change and its profit impact are explicitly disclosed. Switching depreciation methods? Say so, and quantify it. Materiality Attach importance to significant details; ignore insignificant ones. Highly context-dependent: a debtor's ledger needs exact paise, a board report may round to hundreds. Judgment, permitted under the Companies Act, keeps statements free of useless clutter. 03 The sorting drill The lecture's four scenarios — pick the convention, then reveal A pending lawsuit is reported in the notes to accounts Which convention? Rounded figures for top management; exact paise for individual debtor ledgers Which convention? Switching inventory valuation methods to inflate this year's profit Which convention? Creating excess provisions for bad debts to hide profits for a rainy day Which convention? Goods cost ₹1,00,000; market price has fallen to ₹80,000. At what value does inventory appear — and which convention says so? Lecture 7 · check yourself A ₹1,00,000 — cost, because that is what was paid (consistency) B ₹80,000 — the lower of cost and market (conservatism) C ₹1,40,000 — replacement value (going concern) D ₹90,000 — an average of the two (materiality) A company switches depreciation methods and says nothing. Even if the new method is genuinely better, what has it violated? Lecture 7 · check yourself A Materiality only — the amount is small B Nothing — better techniques are always allowed C Consistency and full disclosure — changes are allowed but must be disclosed with their profit impact D Conservatism — the new method must be more pessimistic Key takeaways Conservatism: value inventory at the lower of cost and market; provide for doubtful debts from current profits. Full disclosure: true and fair view is a legal requirement — contingent liabilities go in the notes. Consistency: same practices year to year; changes allowed, but disclosed and quantified. Materiality: significance is contextual — exact for debtor ledgers, rounded for management reports.

chapters.label: Equation, worked
chapters.text: Module 2 · The equation, worked Three balance sheets, one equation Find the missing figure, close the balance sheet, prove the totals — the equation is not decoration, it is a solving machine. 01 (a) Hot Chocolate — find the equity Assets ₹87,000 · liabilities ₹53,000 Worked (a) — the residual Equity = Assets − Liabilities = ₹87,000 − ₹53,000 = ₹34,000 02 (b) Abraham Company — find the missing liability Six asset figures, one unknown expenses payable Worked (b) — substitute, then solve for x Assets = Liabilities + Equity Cash 5,000 + Trade receivables 17,000 + Supplies 9,000 + Equipment 19,000 + Building 21,800 + Land 21,000 = Loan payable 12,000 + Expenses payable x + Equity 77,300 92,800 = 89,300 + x Expenses payable x = ₹3,500 03 (c) Coffee Corner — close the balance sheet Equity is twice its liabilities · assets ₹81,000 Worked (c) — one unknown, two figures Assets = Liabilities + Equity 81,000 = L + (2 × L) → equity is twice liabilities 81,000 = 3 × L L = ₹27,000 Equity = ₹54,000 Coffee Corner — balance sheet ₹ Assets 81,000 Liabilities 27,000 Equity 54,000 Check — 27,000 + 54,000 81,000 ✓ Complete the missing items — the lecture's six-row drill 6 drills 1 (a) Assets 30,000 · Liabilities 20,000 → Capital? Hint: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = 10,000. 2 (b) Assets 60,000 · Liabilities 25,000 → Capital? Hint: 60,000 − 25,000 = 35,000. 3 (c) Liabilities 25,000 · Capital 30,000 → Assets? Hint: A = L + C = 55,000. 4 (d) Liabilities 10,000 · Capital 80,000 → Assets? Hint: A = 90,000. 5 (e) Assets 25,000 · Capital 15,000 → Liabilities? Hint: L = A − C = 10,000. 6 (f) Assets 40,000 · Capital 30,000 → Liabilities? Hint: L = 10,000. In Abraham's workout, why is it legal to write 'Expenses payable = 92,800 \u2212 89,300'? Equation discipline A Because expenses always equal assets minus equity B Because the equation must balance — the unknown claim is whatever makes both sides equal C Because expenses payable is an asset D Because the lecturer said so

chapters.label: Transaction effects
chapters.text: Module 2 · Transactions in action The four moves — run them yourself Every transaction the course will ever show you is one of a handful of patterns: two sides rise together, or one side reshuffles itself. Meet the patterns, then drive them. 01 Pattern (a) — capital and asset rise together Commenced business with cash ₹1,00,000 Effects (i) Cash comes in → increase in asset (ii) Capital provided by owner → increase in capital Capital = Assets Capital = Cash (+) 1,00,000 = (+) 1,00,000 02 Pattern (b) — one asset in, another out Bought furniture costing ₹5,000 by paying cash Effects (i) Furniture comes in → increase in asset (ii) Cash goes out → decrease in asset Liabilities = Cash + Furniture (−) 5,000 (+) 5,000 ← total unchanged 03 Pattern (d) — liability and asset fall together Paid creditors ₹10,000 Effects (i) Cash goes out → decrease in asset (ii) Creditors are paid → decrease in liability Creditors = Cash (−) 10,000 = (−) 10,000 04 Now drive the machine Rani's automobile business — the lecture's own running example, transaction by transaction The equation machine 1 2 3 4 Reset Transaction Assets ₹ Claims ₹ applied: 0 of 4 Cash Stock Furniture Capital Creditors Press a step number — each transaction lands on both sides at once. Rani deals in automobiles. Four transactions, two sides — watch them stay equal. What the machine is whispering Step 3 changed nothing on the claims side; step 4 shrank both sides by the same 8,000 . Two assets can trade places all day; only capital and liabilities move the size of the business. Exam instinct For every transaction, ask exactly two questions: which two families are touched, and which way does each move? Write the two effects before touching any account — the entries then write themselves. Key takeaways Dual aspect: every transaction has two effects — the equation is book-keeping’s law of gravity. Debits grow the asset / expense / drawings family; credits grow liability / capital / revenue . An asset needs control + future benefit — miss either and it is out. Equity is the residual : investments and profits raise it, distributions and losses lower it. The equation holds after every single transaction — Rani’s four steps prove it. Rani pays ₹8,000 to her creditors. In the machine's language, that transaction is\u2026 Pattern recognition A ↑ Asset · ↑ Liability B ↓ Asset · ↓ Liability — the equation shrinks on both sides equally C ↑ Asset · ↓ Asset D ↓ Asset · ↑ Capital

chapters.label: Entity & concern
chapters.text: Module 1 · Assumptions, deep-dive The boundary — and the promise to continue Two of the four assumptions do the heaviest lifting: one draws the line around the business, the other justifies how everything inside the line is valued. Reporting entity Accountants treat a business as a reporting entity — distinct and separate from its owners and from every other firm. The entity defines the scope of activities included in the financial statements: the owner’s personal affairs stay outside, permanently. Owner's home electricity → not a business expense Owner's personal smartphone → not a business asset Owner's wedding → not business promotion Going concern Unless there is substantial evidence to the contrary, accountants assume the business is a continuing enterprise . This assumption is what justifies recording assets at historical cost — cost only makes sense if the business lives long enough to use the asset. Fair value — “the amount for which an asset could be exchanged, or a liability settled, between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm’s length transaction.” If liquidation were imminent, cost would become irrelevant — assets would move to likely sale prices. 01 When the promise breaks: the Kingfisher file A going-concern case study, 2012–13 The case In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, bank auditors were faulted for not issuing going-concern exceptions for any of the major banks that collapsed or needed bailouts — Lehman Brothers, Citigroup, Bear Stearns, Countrywide. Auditors do not cause corporate collapses, but staying silent at the wrong moment means failing their role as a watchdog . On Kingfisher Airlines’ 2012 and 2013 statements, the auditors observed that although the accounts were prepared on a going-concern basis, there were doubts : equity wiped out by losses, the air-operator permit lapsed, banks recalling loans. Management answered that it was confident of raising capital, renewing the permit and rescheduling debt. The company ceased operations in late 2012 . The lesson that survives the case Going concern is an assumption with a duty attached : when the evidence turns, someone must say so — on time. Timely going-concern warnings are how the statements protect the very readers (investors, lenders, employees) the whole apparatus exists for. A car is bought at auction for \u20B940,000 and re-recorded at \u20B950,000 one week later \u2014 \u201Cbecause that is what it is worth now.\u201D Two assumptions are involved; what is the cleanest one-line verdict? Violation spotting A Money measurement violated — the car cannot be valued B Historical cost violated — assets stay at original purchase price while the entity is a going concern C Periodicity violated — one week is not a period D No violation — fair value is always allowed

chapters.label: The three elements
chapters.text: Module 2 · The three elements Assets, liabilities, equity — the whole cast Every account in every ledger belongs to one of three families. Learn what admits a resource into each family, and you can classify anything a business does. 01 What is an asset? A resource controlled by the entity, from past events, with future benefit expected Two conditions — both must hold Control — the entity can restrict others from using the resource. Future benefit — the resource is expected to generate economic value going forward. If either condition is missing, it is not an asset . Candidate Verdict Why Public park Not an asset You enjoy it — but you cannot control access Broken iPod Not an asset You control it — but no future benefit Cash The ideal asset Controlled — and it buys every other asset 02 Types of assets Same quality — future economic benefit — classified by form and claim Tangible assets Physical form you can see and touch. Land & buildings Plant & equipment Inventories Intangible assets Exclusive rights, no physical substance. Patents Copyrights Trademarks Financial claims Legally enforceable claims on other parties. Accounts receivable Investments in bonds Cash & equivalents 03 What is a liability? A present obligation, from past events, whose settlement is an outflow of resources Contractual liabilities Most liabilities arise from contracts — amounts payable for electricity used, salaries owed to employees, loans payable. Typically precise, known amounts . Statutory liabilities Some obligations arise from law — employer contributions to a provident fund, income tax payable. These may require estimation based on applicable rules. 04 What is equity? The residual interest — what truly belongs to the owners The leftover, defined Equity is the residual interest in the assets after deducting all liabilities — the “leftover” value once every debt is settled. It increases through owner investments and profits from operations ; it decreases through distributions to owners (dividends) and losses . In a company, this is called shareholders’ equity . Share capital The amount contributed by shareholders towards the company’s capital, recorded in the share capital account — the foundational investment made when shares are issued. Retained earnings The cumulative net profit kept in the business rather than distributed as dividends. It grows when the company earns profits and shrinks when it incurs losses or pays dividends. 05 Apply your knowledge The lecture's own classification round — three tasks, no answers given 1 Identify assets List the chief assets of Biocon, Dell, ICICI Bank, Microsoft and Wipro — consider tangible, intangible and financial-claim assets for each. 2 Identify liabilities List the chief liabilities of BHEL, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, SBI and TCS. 3 Revenues & expenses Name the chief revenues and expenses of Google, Jet Airways and SAIL — then judge whether each would report a net profit or a loss. A famous actor endorses a bakery for free for five years. The bakery wants to list 'celebrity goodwill' as an asset. Correct call? Classification A Yes — it has enormous future benefit B No — control over the actor's goodwill cannot be restricted, so it fails the asset test C Yes — if the auditor agrees D Only if it is recorded at fair value

chapters.label: Classification & journal
chapters.text: Lecture 10 · The traditional approach Personal, real, nominal — three families, three rules . The equation approach feels the effect; the traditional approach knows the rule. Accounts split into personal and impersonal, impersonal into real and nominal — and each family carries its own debit-credit law. 01 The classification tree Every account the business will ever open lives somewhere here Accounts Personal — persons Natural persons human beings — Ravi's account Artificial persons firms, companies, banks — Tata, Reliance Representative persons accounts standing for groups — outstanding wages (the workers owed) Rule: debit the receiver, credit the giver Impersonal — everything else Real — assets, tangible & intangible Cash, raw materials, machinery, buildings, furniture · goodwill, trademarks, copyrights, patents Rule: debit what comes in, credit what goes out Nominal (fictitious) — events, not things Expenses & losses: salaries, rent, depreciation, bad debts · Income & gains: sales, interest, discounts Rule: debit expenses & losses, credit incomes & gains — closed to P&L at year-end 02 The three rules, side by side Click a family — see its law in action Personal account Debit the receiver, credit the giver Real account Debit what comes in, credit what goes out Nominal account Debit all expenses and losses; credit all income and gains In action: Sell goods to Ravi on credit → debit Ravi (receiver), credit sales (giver) Natural (Ravi) · Artificial (Tata, banks) · Representative (outstanding wages) 03 The journal — book of original entry Five columns, chronological, straight from the source documents Anatomy of a journal entry Date | Particulars | LF | Debit | Credit ------------------------------------------------------ | Cash A/c Dr. | 50,000 | | To Somu's Capital A/c | | 50,000 | (Being business commenced | with cash — the narration) Debit first, followed by "Dr." Credit indented, preceded by "To" LF = the ledger folio (page) the posting lands on Journalizing — seven steps 1 Analyze the transaction — identify the accounts (minimum two) 2 Classify each account: personal, real or nominal 3 Apply the rule for each type 4 Enter the date 5 Write the debit account first (…Dr.), then the indented credit (To …) 6 Enter the amounts in the debit and credit columns 7 Write the narration 04 Simple entries — the lecture's five Each one names its rule Paid Anbu ₹10,000 by cheque Personal Anbu A/c Dr. 10,000 To Bank A/c 10,000 (Anbu is the receiver — personal; bank is the giver) Purchased furniture for cash ₹5,000 Real Furniture A/c Dr. 5,000 To Cash A/c 5,000 (What comes in is debited — real accounts both) Paid rent ₹5,000 in cash Nominal Rent A/c Dr. 5,000 To Cash A/c 5,000 (Expense debited — nominal; cash goes out — real) Somu commenced a printing business with cash ₹50,000 Mixed Cash A/c Dr. 50,000 To Somu's Capital A/c 50,000 (Cash comes in — real; Somu is the giver — personal) Bought goods for cash ₹4,000 Mixed Purchases A/c Dr. 4,000 To Cash A/c 4,000 (Purchases is an expense — nominal) 05 Compound entries — more than two accounts The settlement and the insolvency Full settlement — Kyrthana Owe Kyrthana ₹5,000; pay ₹4,800 in full settlement (₹200 discount). Kyrthana A/c Dr. 5,000 To Cash A/c 4,800 To Discount Received A/c 200 Kyrthana (personal) debited — the receiver. Cash (real) credited — what goes out. Discount received (nominal) credited — a gain. Insolvency — Dinesh, 40 paise in the rupee Dinesh owes ₹10,000 and is declared insolvent; his estate pays 40 paise/₹. Cash A/c Dr. 4,000 (40% of 10,000) Bad Debts A/c Dr. 6,000 (the loss — 60%) To Dinesh's A/c 10,000 (debtor settled) The unrecoverable 60% is a nominal loss — debited, then closed to the P&L. Outstanding wages account represents the workers a firm owes money to. What kind of account is it? Lecture 10 · check yourself A Real — it will be paid in cash B Nominal — wages are an expense C Personal — a representative personal account standing for a group of people D Impersonal real — it is a liability A customer owing ₹10,000 is declared insolvent and pays 40 paise in the rupee. How is the missing ₹6,000 treated? Lecture 10 · check yourself A Credited to bad debts recovered B Debited to bad debts — a nominal loss, later closed to the P&L C Carried forward as a receivable until the estate pays more D Debited to the cash account at 60% Key takeaways Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver — natural, artificial and representative persons. Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out — tangible and intangible assets. Nominal: debit expenses & losses, credit incomes & gains — closed to P&L at year-end. The journal is the book of original entry: date, particulars with Dr./To, LF, amounts, narration. Compound entries handle three or more accounts — settlements with discounts, insolvencies at paise in the rupee.

chapters.label: Journal
chapters.text: Module 3 · Recording — the journal The pipeline, and the day book Two approaches exist for recording transactions — the accounting equation approach and the traditional approach. Both land in the same place: a journal where every event is written with its two effects, the day it happens. Transactions value moves 01 Journal the day book 02 Ledger T-accounts 03 Trial balance Dr = Cr check 04 Adjusted TB deferrals · accruals 05 Final accounts P&L + balance sheet 06 every rupee travels this pipeline — this module walks steps 2 and 3, chapter 12 checks step 4 01 The Vogue Company A business that supplies new designs for dresses — June, transaction by transaction The set-up Vogue is a business supplying new designs for dresses. The lecture records its June transactions in terms of debits and credits — and warns early: not every item below is an accounting transaction . If an item does not qualify, the correct answer is to say why it does not. 02 The three-line ritual ANALYSIS → RULES → ENTRY — the same three moves, every single time ANALYSIS Which accounts are affected, and which way? RULES Debit assets/expenses to increase — credit liabilities/capital/revenues to increase. ENTRY Write the debits, the credits, and a narration that says why. 03 The journal, ruled like paper Ten entries from Vogue's June — including one compound entry Vogue Company — journal (selected entries) · amounts in ₹ Date Particulars Dr (₹) Cr (₹) Jun 1 Cash A/c Dr 50,000 To Share Capital 50,000 (Being capital invested in cash) Jun 2 Office Supplies A/c Dr 2,000 To Cash 2,000 (Being office supplies bought) Jun 3 Rent Expense A/c Dr 1,500 To Cash 1,500 (Being office rent paid for June) Jun 4 Equipment A/c Dr 3,000 To Cash 3,000 (Being equipment bought from Agrawal Company) Jun 6 Prepaid Insurance A/c Dr 720 To Cash 720 (Being one-year fire policy paid in advance) Jun 7 Cash A/c Dr 2,000 To Revenue from Services 2,000 (Being a design sold for cash) Jun 8 Cash A/c Dr 1,500 To Unearned Revenue 1,500 (Being Kidswear's advance for services to be provided later) Jun 9 Office Supplies A/c Dr 3,500 To Trade Payables 3,500 (Being supplies bought on credit from Mohan Company) Jun 10 Trade Receivables A/c Dr 9,000 To Revenue from Services 9,000 (Being Shah Company billed for designs completed) Jun 25 Cash A/c Dr 1,000 Trade Receivables A/c Dr 2,000 To Revenue from Services 3,000 (Being designs completed for Gupta Company; ₹1,000 received in part payment) June 5 — the agreement that books nothing Vogue signs with EthniWear: a special design, fee ₹2,000 payable on completion . No entry. Signing transfers no value — no asset moves, no obligation is born. Accounting records transactions , not intentions. June 21 — the appointment that books nothing An office manager is appointed on a monthly salary of ₹1,500. No entry. Hiring changes no asset, liability or equity — the salary becomes an expense period by period , as the work is actually received and paid. On June 25, Vogue completes ₹3,000 of designs for Gupta Company and receives ₹1,000 in part payment. The entry touches\u2026 Compound entries A Cash only — revenue is recorded when fully collected B Cash Dr 1,000 + Trade receivables Dr 2,000 / To Revenue 3,000 C Revenue Dr 3,000 / To Cash 3,000 D Nothing until the final ₹2,000 arrives

chapters.label: Ledger
chapters.text: Module 3 · Recording — the ledger Posting — where the journal grows accounts The journal records events in time order; the ledger regroups them by account. Open one page per account, post every debit and every credit to its page, and each page ends with a balance that speaks. 01 One account to rule them all: Cash Every rupee that entered or left Vogue in June, on one T-shaped page Vogue Company — Cash account · for June · amounts in ₹ Dr · money in Jun 1 To Share Capital 50,000 Jun 7 To Revenue from Services 2,000 Jun 8 To Unearned Revenue 1,500 Jun 18 To Trade Receivables 4,000 Jun 25 To Revenue from Services 1,000 Total — 58,500 Cr · money out Jun 2 By Office Supplies 2,000 Jun 3 By Rent Expense 1,500 Jun 4 By Equipment 3,000 Jun 6 By Prepaid Insurance 720 Jun 14 By Trade Payables 1,000 Jun 27 By Telephone Expense 200 Jun 28 By Salaries Expense 800 Jun 29 By Electricity Expense 150 Jun 30 By Dividends 2,200 Total — 11,570 Balance c/d — ₹46,930 Dr 58,500 in − 11,570 out = 46,930 · carried down to July 1 Read the T like a story The debit side is the cash coming in (capital, service revenue, collections, an advance); the credit side is cash going out (supplies, rent, equipment, insurance, settling suppliers, phone, salaries, electricity, dividends). Nine outflows against five inflows — and the account still closes at ₹46,930. The pipeline clicks shut That ₹46,930 debit balance is exactly the Cash line in Vogue’s June 30 trial balance . The ledger balance is not near the trial-balance figure — it is the trial-balance figure. Same numbers, next station. 02 The ledger, grouped Exhibit 3.3 groups Vogue's June accounts into asset, liability and equity categories Asset accounts Cash · Equipment · Office supplies · Trade receivables · Prepaid insurance Liability accounts Trade payables · Unearned revenue Equity accounts Share capital · Dividends · Revenue · all expense accounts Why does Vogue's Cash account end with a DEBIT balance of \u20B946,930? Ledger mechanics A Because cash is revenue, and revenue carries debit balances B Because total debits (58,500) exceed total credits (11,570) — and cash, an asset, keeps its balance on the debit side C Because dividends were paid in cash D Because the ledger always balances at zero

chapters.label: Opening & balancing
chapters.text: Lecture 12 · Ledger mechanics Balances carried down , balances brought down . Ongoing businesses do not start from zero. The opening entry brings forward the accounts that never closed — and at period end every account earns its balance c/d, which becomes the next period's balance b/d. 01 The opening entry Only real accounts carry forward — nominal ones went to the P&L Joy's business — the opening entry balances brought forward Debit — assets come in Cash 45,000 Stock 50,000 Sohan (debtor) 35,000 Furniture 50,000 Total assets 1,80,000 Credit — who has claims Ram (creditor) 20,000 Joy's Capital 1,60,000 Total claims 1,80,000 1,80,000 = 1,80,000 — balanced, as it must be. Narration: “Balances of assets and liabilities brought forward.” Nominal accounts never open here: their old balances went to the P&L — only real accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) carry forward. 02 Balancing an account Total both sides; park the difference on the lower side as Balance c/d Cash account — balanced Dr. | Cr. ---------------------------------+--------------------------------- To Capital A/c 3,00,000 | By Bank A/c 2,00,000 To Sales A/c 5,000 | By Purchases A/c 10,000 | By Balance c/d 95,000 3,05,000 | 3,05,000 Debit total 3,05,000 > Credit total 2,10,000 → the difference ₹95,000 is parked on the CREDIT side as "By Balance c/d" → the account carries a DEBIT balance → next period it opens as "To Balance b/d 95,000" The CD/BD handshake Balance c/d Balance b/d The difference placed to equalize an account (c/d — carried down) becomes the opening figure of that account in the next period (b/d — brought down). The side with the higher total decides the account's nature: debit balance or credit balance.
