Conventions on the page Debit side entries read “To …”; credit side reads “By …” Every opening balance is marked b/d; every closing balance c/d A line rules off the account once both sides total Drawings (cash or goods taken by the owner) sit debited, and move to capital at year-end What each account says when balanced Capital — the proprietor's stake, usually a single credit. Bank — deposits and withdrawals, balanced like cash. Personal accounts — the outstanding owed to or by each person. Purchases & sales — the period's trading volume. Drawings — what the owner took for personal use, on its way to the capital account. Joy's books open with cash ₹45,000, stock ₹50,000, debtor Sohan ₹35,000, furniture ₹50,000 — and creditor Ram ₹20,000. What is the capital? Lecture 12 · check yourself A ₹1,80,000 — the total of all assets B ₹1,60,000 — assets ₹1,80,000 minus creditor Ram ₹20,000 C ₹2,00,000 — assets plus the creditor D ₹1,50,000 — cash and stock only A cash account shows debits of ₹3,05,000 and credits of ₹2,10,000. On which side does the balancing figure go, and what is the account's nature? Lecture 12 · check yourself A ₹95,000 on the debit side — credit balance B ₹95,000 on the credit side as Balance c/d — debit balance C ₹95,000 on the credit side — credit balance D ₹5,15,000 — the two sides added Key takeaways The opening entry brings forward real accounts only — nominal balances died in the P&L. Balancing: total both sides, park the difference on the lower side as Balance c/d . c/d this period = b/d next period — the handshake between periods. Higher side decides nature: assets & expenses carry debit balances; liabilities, capital, incomes carry credit balances.

chapters.label: Trial balance
chapters.text: Module 3 · Checking — the trial balance Do the columns agree? The third phase of the accounting process: after posting the ledger, a statement lists the debit and credit balances of every account at a specific point in time. If double entry has been honoured, the two totals must meet. 01 What the agreement proves — and what it doesn't Why it must balance Under the double entry system, amounts on the debit sides of various accounts are always equal to amounts entered on the credit sides of other accounts — so the totals of the debit sides must equal the totals of the credit sides . An agreeing trial balance gives reasonable confidence the work is free of clerical errors . What can still hide Agreement is not proof of cent-per-cent accuracy . Errors of principle (wrong class of account), compensating errors (two mistakes cancelling out), wholly omitted transactions and postings to the wrong account at the right amount can all survive a perfect trial balance. 02 Accounts keep their favourite side Some accounts carry only debit balances; others only credit Only debit balances Assets (cash, debtors, buildings, furniture) Drawings Purchases Sales returns Expenses Losses Only credit balances Liabilities (creditors, bank overdraft, provisions) Reserves Incomes Sales Purchases returns Gains 03 Pearl's books, balanced From the balances extracted from Pearl, a trader — as on 31st March 2017 S.No Name of account Debit (₹) Credit (₹) 1 Capital 44,000 2 Bills receivable 5,000 3 Wages 800 4 Drawings 4,000 5 Purchases 75,000 6 Interest on investment 2,000 7 Customs duty 3,000 8 Computer 20,000 9 Sales 72,000 10 Opening stock 10,200 Total 1,18,000 1,18,000 Read the totals like an auditor 5,000 + 800 + 4,000 + 75,000 + 3,000 + 20,000 + 10,200 = 1,18,000 of debits; 44,000 + 2,000 + 72,000 = 1,18,000 of credits. The columns agree — Pearl’s postings are arithmetically sound. 04 Two ways to draw it up Vogue's June 30 trial balance, both methods Vogue Company — trial balance, June 30 Balance method Total method (net figure per account) (both gross sides of every account) Cash .................... 46,930 Dr Cash ......... 58,500 Dr | 11,570 Cr Trade payables ........... 2,500 Cr Trade payables 1,000 Dr | 3,500 Cr Revenue from services ... 14,000 Cr Revenue ...... — | 14,000 Cr TOTALS ........... 68,000 = 68,000 TOTALS ... 86,370 = 86,370 Why the total method is bigger — and equally true The total method lists both sides of every account before netting, so the grand total rises (86,370 vs 68,000). The proof is identical: both columns agree. Ledger balances on a specified date — that is all a trial balance is; a basic check on bookkeeping. 05 Now sort it yourself Ten accounts from Pearl's extraction — which column does each belong in? Trial balance sorter Pearl’s books · tap Dr or Cr for each account Reset Capital ₹44,000 DR CR Bills receivable ₹5,000 DR CR Wages ₹800 DR CR Drawings ₹4,000 DR CR Purchases ₹75,000 DR CR Interest on investment ₹2,000 DR CR Customs duty ₹3,000 DR CR Computer ₹20,000 DR CR Sales ₹72,000 DR CR Opening stock ₹10,200 DR CR Check my trial balance Rule of thumb: assets, drawings, purchases, expenses → Dr · liabilities, capital, incomes, sales → Cr Key takeaways The trial balance is the third phase : journal → ledger → trial balance. It proves arithmetic consistency , not accuracy — principle and compensating errors survive. Assets, drawings, purchases, expenses, losses → debit balances; liabilities, capital, reserves, incomes, sales, gains → credit . Balance method nets each account ( 68,000 ); total method lists both gross sides ( 86,370 ) — same proof. The Cash ledger balance is the Cash trial-balance line — the pipeline has no gaps. Pearl's trial balance agrees at \u20B91,18,000. Which error could STILL be sitting in her books? The honesty of the check A A debit of 5,000 posted without a matching credit B A purchase of machinery debited to Purchases (an error of principle) C Debit totals of 1,19,000 against credit totals of 1,18,000 D A cash payment entered twice on the credit side only

chapters.label: Suspense & errors
chapters.text: Lecture 15 · Trial balance, continued A balanced trial balance is not a clean chit . Murali's books totalled ₹1,62,250 on both sides — arithmetic accuracy. But errors of principle, omission and compensation can all hide behind agreeing columns. When the columns refuse to meet, the suspense account buys time. 01 The suspense account A temporary holding bay that lets reporting deadlines survive When the columns disagree Debit total > Credit total by ₹X → Credit the difference: "Suspense A/c Cr. X" Credit total > Debit total by ₹X → Debit the difference: "Suspense A/c Dr. X" The cycle continues. When the errors are found and rectified, suspense closes to zero and leaves the books. Why it exists Reporting cannot wait for a forensic hunt. The suspense account bridges the gap between unequal totals while the errors are being found — a temporary account, never a home. Once the errors are located and rectified, it is closed and removed. The baseline proof Prepared from Murali's ledger balances, both sides agreed at ₹1,62,250 — revenue (credit: sales), expenses (debit: interest paid, office rent, audit fees), assets (debit: land), liabilities (credit: bank overdraft, creditors). Classification is everything. 02 Four errors the columns cannot see Click each — learn whether the trial balance would catch it Error of principle TB still agrees An executive desk (₹40,000) debited to office repairs instead of furniture — capital expenditure treated as revenue expense. Error of omission TB still agrees A ₹25,000 cloud-server invoice paid but never recorded in the journal at all. Error of commission TB breaks A cash sale of ₹85,000 correctly credited to sales — but debited to bank as ₹35,000. Compensating error TB still agrees One account understated by ₹2,000; another overstated by exactly ₹2,000. 03 Case file — ABC Startup A ₹50,000 gap, three errors, one closure The diagnosis Trial balance refuses to agree — a ₹50,000 gap, parked in suspense to meet the deadline. ① Omission ₹25,000 cloud-server invoice paid, never recorded → NO effect on TB (both sides missing) ② Principle ₹40,000 executive desk debited to office repairs → NO effect on TB (debit still recorded) ③ Commission cash sale ₹85,000 credited to sales correctly — but bank debited ₹35,000 → ₹50,000 gap ✓ FOUND The fix: record ①, reclassify ② (debit furniture, credit repairs), and ③ already explains suspense. Suspense closes. Books move on. Capital expenditure recorded as revenue expense — what happens to the trial balance? Lecture 15 · check yourself A It breaks by the amount involved B It still agrees — this error of principle hits both sides equally C It breaks by double the amount D It depends on the depreciation method Debit total ₹X, credit total ₹X − 50,000. Where does suspense go? Lecture 15 · check yourself A Debited with ₹50,000 B Credited with ₹50,000 C Split ₹25,000 each side D Nowhere — omit the difference Key takeaways Trial balance = the third step: journal → ledger → trial balance ; the bridge to final statements. Agreement proves arithmetic accuracy only — principle, omission and compensating errors slip through. The suspense account parks the difference on the shorter side until errors are found, then closes. Error of commission (one side wrong) is the kind the gap actually catches — like ABC's ₹50,000.

chapters.label: Cash vs accrual
chapters.text: Lecture 16 · Basis of accounting Cash received is not profit earned . Two ways to keep books: record cash as it moves, or record what is earned and incurred. One of them is honest about performance — and the matching principle decides which period owns which cost. 01 The opening case A software company, ₹1,000 upfront, twelve months of service The ₹1,000 question cash received Jan 1 · service runs 12 months Months of service delivered 1 / 12 Cash basis says ₹1,000 profit on January 1 — the moment cash arrived. All of it. Accrual basis says ₹83 earned so far — ₹83 of revenue matched against the cost of delivering it. The rest is a liability (unearned). Is this ₹1,000 of profit on January 1? No — the revenue must be matched with the expenses of delivering twelve months of service. That single sentence is the whole lecture. 02 The two bases, face to face Where each one lives and what it costs you Cash basis Record revenue when cash is received; record expenses when cash is paid. Profit = cash revenues − cash payments. Accrued income, prepaid expenses, outstanding costs — none of it exists here. Where it lives Small personal businesses, non-trading entities (clubs, charitable trusts), receipt-and-payment accounts. For Simple, objective, no adjusting entries, suits cash-heavy shops. Against No fair picture of performance; ignores matching; no capital/revenue distinction; profit can be manipulated by timing cash — and reporting turns inconsistent. Accrual basis Record revenues and expenses in the period they become due — irrespective of cash. Credit sales count in the period of sale; expenses count when the service is used. Outstanding costs, prepaid expenses, accrued earnings and advance income are all recorded. Where it lives Commercial institutions everywhere — the most widely accepted basis. For Accurate period profit; true financial position; reflects all relevant transactions. Against Lengthy, complex procedures; many adjustments through the year; quick profit checks are hard. 03 The matching principle When to match, and what to match When — regular intervals, not the end of life Waiting until the business closes would make every number obsolete — and tax demands profit year by year. So business life is chopped into intervals, typically twelve months, and each period must carry its own matched result. Realization: a machine built in December, shipped in March, paid for in May — revenue is recognized in March , when ownership transfers. Not December, not May. What — three buckets of expense Direct (product costs) Raw materials, direct wages, machinery — matched to the specific revenue they create. Indirect (period costs) Rent, administrative salaries — matched to the period in which they are incurred. Losses Warehouse fire, theft — no product, no period, no future revenue. Recognized immediately. Two distinctions worth keeping Expenditure vs expense: expenditure is any disbursement; only the portion consumed this period to generate revenue is an expense. Revenue vs cash: credit sales create receivables, not receipts — and manufacturing creates inventory, not revenue. Exceptions exist where a market is settled (gold is recognized when mined) and where contracts span years (revenue as work is certified). 04 Operating skill vs market luck The replacement-cost lens on the same ₹10 Operating skill vs market luck cost ₹20/kg · replacement ₹25/kg · drag the selling price Selling price per kg ₹30 Traditional lens ₹10 profit ₹30 − ₹20 historical cost. Simple, auditable — all profit treated as operating performance. Replacement lens ₹5 operating + ₹5 holding ₹30 − ₹25 replacement = operating skill; ₹25 − ₹20 = holding gain from inflation. Same total, honest sources. Under the accrual basis, a machine built in December, shipped in March and paid for in May earns revenue in… Lecture 16 · check yourself A December — when production happened B March — when ownership transferred C May — when cash arrived D Split across all three months You buy stock at ₹20/kg, replace it today at ₹25/kg, and sell at ₹30/kg. Under the replacement-cost approach, how much of the ₹10 is holding gain? Lecture 16 · check yourself A ₹10 — all of it B ₹5 — replacement cost minus historical cost C ₹2 — one fifth of the profit D ₹0 — holding gains are never recognized Key takeaways Cash basis: simple but blind to performance — profit moves with cash timing. Accrual basis: record when due , not when paid — the basis commercial institutions use. Matching: revenue is matched with the expenses of the same period — realization decides when. Expense buckets: direct (product), indirect (period), losses (immediately). Replacement-cost thinking splits operating skill from holding gain — both sum to the same profit.

chapters.label: Adjusting entries
chapters.text: Module 4 · Adjusting entries Cash is instant. Recognition is not. Cash transactions don't always happen in the same period as the related revenue or expense. Adjusting entries are how the books catch up with reality — before any statement is allowed to speak. 01 Two families of mismatch Deferral — cash moved first · Accrual — recognition moved first Deferral A lag in recognising an expense already paid or a revenue already received . Relates to past cash movements, apportioned between two or more periods. Prepaid insurance Office supplies Unearned revenue Accrual Recognition of an expense incurred but not paid, or revenue earned but not received. Relates to expected future cash movements — previously unrecorded items. Salaries payable Accrued interest expense Accrued interest income Unbilled revenue DEFERRAL — cash ₹12,000 paid Oct 1 recognition — later ₹3,000 expense by Dec 31 ACCRUAL — recognition salaries earned in December cash — later salaries payable, paid in January cash first or recognition first — the adjustment always forces them into the same period 02 Example 1 — prepaid insurance, split live ₹12,000 for one year, paid October 1 · year ends December 31 The prepaid splitter ₹12,000 · one-year policy · paid October 1 Months of protection consumed 3 / 12 ₹3,000 ₹9,000 Insurance expense — this year Prepaid insurance — an asset The lecture moment — Dec 31 year-end Expense = 12,000 × 3/12 = ₹3,000 Prepaid insurance (asset) = 12,000 − 3,000 = ₹9,000 Oct + Nov + Dec = 3 months — ₹3,000 becomes expense; ₹9,000 waits as a future benefit. Why the whole 12,000 is not an expense on October 1 Because the insurance provides protection for 12 months . On December 31 you have consumed only October + November + December — 3 months. Cash happened first; expense recognition happens gradually afterward. The unused ₹9,000 is a future benefit, so it remains an asset called prepaid insurance. 03 Example 2 — unearned revenue, earned slowly ₹60,000 received in advance for a six-month service contract The two-step recognition Initial receipt: Cash A/c .................. Dr 60,000 To Unearned Revenue ........ 60,000 After 1 month of service: Revenue = 60,000 × 1/6 = ₹10,000 Unearned revenue (liability) falls by ₹10,000 → ₹50,000 left Is your revenue ₹60,000? No. You haven’t provided the service yet. You hold the cash — but the obligation (a liability) is what you owe until the service is delivered. Cash received first → revenue recognised later. 04 The adjustment map Six mismatches, one destination: profit or loss Deferral Unearned revenue Cash received in a past period — work done in the current period Accrual Revenue receivable Cash to be received — work done in the current period Deferral Prepaid expenses Cash paid in a past period — benefit used in the current period Accrual Expenses payable Cash to be paid — benefit used in the current period Revenue (work done) − Expenses (benefit used) = Profit or Loss 05 Deferred revenue in the wild Tech Mahindra's annual report, year ended March 31, 2010 The case A customer paid Tech Mahindra ₹9,682 million for changes to a long-term contract. The company recognised ₹2,005 million as revenue that year for services provided, and treated the balance of ₹7,677 million as deferred revenue. Deferred revenue is a liability — the amount must either be repaid to the customer or the services must be provided; in either case, cash is payable. What happens if prepaid expenses are NOT adjusted Without the adjustment, the used-up portion never becomes an expense: the statements understate expenses and overstate assets and equity — both statements wrong, in opposite directions. The income statement and the balance sheet are both incorrect until the split is made. Vogue received ₹1,500 from Kidswear on June 8 for services to be provided later. At June 30, ₹500 of service has been delivered. The adjusting entry is\u2026 Deferral or accrual? A Dr Cash 500 / Cr Revenue 500 B Dr Unearned revenue 500 / Cr Revenue from services 500 C Dr Revenue 500 / Cr Unearned revenue 500 D No adjustment until all the service is delivered

chapters.label: Trading account
chapters.text: Module 4 · The trading account Did buying and selling pay? The trading account gives the overall result of trading — the purchasing and selling of goods. If the sales value exceeds the cost of goods sold, there is a gross profit; if it is less, a gross loss. 01 Cost of goods sold — the ladder Adjust the cost of goods still on hand at year-end against the purchases The COGS ladder Opening Stock *** Add: Purchases (Net) ** Add: Direct Expenses ** --- Less: Closing Stock (***) --- Cost of Goods Sold *** Direct expenses ride along A trader incurs expenses to purchase goods and bring them to the shop: brokerage or commission paid to agents, cartage or carriage charges for bringing goods in, wages paid for transportation. All such expenses increase the cost of goods sold — they belong inside the ladder. 02 Opening stock, closing stock — and the valuation rule Closing stock Goods unsold at the end of the year. Shown on the credit side of the Trading Account and as an asset in the Balance Sheet. Opening stock Goods unsold at the beginning of the year — last year's closing stock. Shown on the debit side of the Trading Account. Valuation rule Closing stock is valued at cost or at net realisable value, whichever is LOWER — the convention of conservatism: never anticipate profit. 03 The equation, and the T-format Gross profit = (Sales + Closing stock) − (Opening stock + Purchases + Direct expenses) Equation for preparing the trading account Gross Profit = Sales − Cost of Goods Sold Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Purchases + Direct Expenses − Closing Stock Therefore: Gross Profit = Sales − (Opening Stock + Purchases + Direct Expenses − Closing Stock) Or: Gross Profit = (Sales + Closing Stock) − (Opening Stock + Purchases + Direct Expenses) Trading account of … for the year ended … · the T-format Dr — the cost side To Opening Stock To Purchases (less: Returns outwards) To Direct expenses: Freight & Carriage Customs & Insurance Wages Gas, Water & Fuel Factory Expenses Royalty on production To Gross Profit c/d* ← only one of the two appears Cr — the revenue side By Sales (less: Returns inwards) By Closing Stock valued at cost or NRV, lower By Gross Loss c/d* ← only one of the two appears *Gross profit or gross loss — exactly one of them closes the account, balancing the two sides. Quick gross-profit drills 3 drills 1 Net sales 35,000 · net purchases 25,000. Gross profit? Hint: 35,000 − 25,000 = 10,000 — the lecture's Example 1. 2 Same trader, but closing stock of 5,000 remains. Gross profit now? Hint: COGS = 25,000 − 5,000 = 20,000; GP = 35,000 − 20,000 = 15,000. 3 Where does that closing stock of 5,000 reappear? Hint: As an asset in the balance sheet — it does double duty.

chapters.label: The adjusting lab
chapters.text: Lecture 19 · The cycle, in one case Six adjusting entries — the whole cycle in one sitting . Journal → ledger → trial balance → adjusting entries → adjusted trial balance → statements. The Vogue Company case runs the full pipeline: before any statement may speak, six adjustments catch the books up with reality. 01 The pipeline Where adjusting entries sit — between the trial balance and the statements Journal Ledger Trial balance Adjusting entries Adjusted TB Statements 02 Vogue's six adjustments Step through each — story, computation, entry, reason 01 02 03 04 05 06 Adjustment 01 — the story Prepaid insurance consumed On June 6 the company paid ₹720 for twelve months of insurance. 720 ÷ 12 = 60 for one month One month of protection is consumed — shift it from the balance sheet to the income statement. The adjusting entry Insurance Expense A/c Dr. 60 To Prepaid Insurance A/c 60 ← Previous 1 / 6 Next → Why adjusting entries cannot be skipped Three reasons: efficiency — nobody journals a supplies count every day; expiration — prepaid rent, insurance and depreciation burn down quietly over time; the unrecorded — utility bills and earned-but-unbilled fees exist even when the paperwork has not arrived. Skipping the adjustments overstates assets, understates expenses and revenues, and lies to every statement downstream. 03 The real-world scale Tech Mahindra — deferral at ₹9,682 crore A customer paid ₹9,682 million for a long-term contract — but the company recognized only ₹2,005 million as revenue that year, because that was the value of services actually provided. The remaining ₹7,677 million sat as deferred revenue: a liability, waiting to be earned. The same logic as Vogue's ₹900, at industrial scale. Supplies account ₹3,700; the physical count finds ₹2,900. The adjusting entry is… Lecture 19 · check yourself A Debit Office Supplies Expense ₹2,900; credit Office Supplies ₹2,900 B Debit Office Supplies Expense ₹800; credit Office Supplies ₹800 C Debit Office Supplies ₹800; credit Supplies Expense ₹800 D No entry — supplies are only adjusted at year-end An employee hired June 21 works 10 days by June 30 at ₹1,500/month. Why does the company credit Salaries Payable ₹500? Lecture 19 · check yourself A Because the salary will be paid in cash next month B Because services were received but not yet paid — an accrued expense C To reduce next month's salary expense D Because the payroll system requires it Key takeaways Adjusted TB = unadjusted TB + adjusting entries — the direct basis for the final statements. Deferrals (cash first): prepaid expenses , unearned revenues . Accruals (cash later): accrued revenues , accrued expenses . Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset — it keeps the original cost visible. Unbilled revenue is an asset ; unearned revenue is a liability — earned vs received decides. Tech Mahindra: ₹9,682 million in, ₹2,005 million recognized — deferral at industrial scale.

chapters.label: Gross profit lab
chapters.text: Module 4 · Worked examples Six examples — then drive the lab The lecture's own numbers, from the simplest trading result to a full T-format trading account — and a lab that recomputes the ladder as you type. 01 Examples 1 & 2 — returns, then stock Purchases 30,000 · returns 5,000 · sales 40,000 · returns 5,000 02 Examples 3 & 4 — the full ladder OS 10,000 · purchases 40,000 · returns 5,000 · sales 60,000 · SR 10,000 · CS 15,000 Examples 1 → 4, compact EX 1 Net sales 35,000 − Net purchases 25,000 = GP ₹10,000 EX 2 … with closing stock 5,000: COGS = 25,000 − 5,000 = 20,000 GP = 35,000 − 20,000 = GP ₹15,000 EX 3 Net sales 50,000; COGS = 10,000 + 35,000 − 15,000 = 30,000 GP = 50,000 − 30,000 = GP ₹20,000 EX 4 … plus wages/carriage of 5,000 to bring goods in: COGS = 30,000 + 5,000 = 35,000; GP = 50,000 − 35,000 = GP ₹15,000 The 'merchandise' footnote The term “merchandise” is also used for the term “goods” — same thing, older word. And note what Example 4 taught: expenses incurred to bring goods to the shop are not operating expenses — they are part of the cost of goods sold . 03 Example 5 — working backwards to closing stock First year: 15,000 unsold · next year: purchases 1,50,000 · direct expenses 10,000 · COGS 1,45,000 Backward, then the full account Cost of unsold goods at the beginning of the year 15,000 Purchases during the year 1,50,000 Direct Expenses 10,000 —————— 1,75,000 Less: Cost of sold goods during the year 1,45,000 Closing Stock 30,000 Trading account (net sales 2,00,000): Dr: 15,000 + 1,50,000 + 10,000 + GP 55,000 = 2,30,000 Cr: Sales 2,00,000 + Closing stock 30,000 = 2,30,000 ✓ 04 Example 6 — a complete trading account M/s. ABC Traders · for the year ended 31st March 2022 In the books of M/s. ABC Traders · trading account · ₹ Particulars (Dr) ₹ Particulars (Cr) ₹ To Opening inventory 1,00,000 By Sales 11,00,000 To Purchases (6,72,000 − 72,000) 6,00,000 Less: Returns inward (1,00,000) 10,00,000 To Carriage inwards 30,000 By Closing inventory 2,00,000 To Wages 50,000 To Gross profit c/d 4,20,000 Total 12,00,000 Total 12,00,000 Read the account like its author Net sales 10,00,000; the cost side stacks 1,00,000 + 6,00,000 + 30,000 + 50,000 = 7,80,000 minus the closing stock of 2,00,000 → COGS 5,80,000. Gross profit is the balancing figure : 10,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 7,80,000 = 4,20,000. The totals agreeing at 12,00,000 is the double-entry system signing its own work. 05 The gross profit lab Five figures, one ladder — try the lecture's presets or your own Gross profit lab edit any figure — the ladder recomputes Reset Example 3 · stock both ends Example 4 · + carriage in Example 6 · ABC Traders Opening stock Net purchases Direct expenses Closing stock Net sales The ladder, live Opening stock 10,000 + Net purchases 35,000 + Direct expenses 0 − Closing stock (15,000) = Cost of goods sold 30,000 Net sales 50,000 = Gross PROFIT ₹20,000 Key takeaways The trading account answers did trading pay? — its result is gross profit or gross loss. COGS = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses − closing stock. Closing stock: valued at cost or NRV, whichever is lower ; credit side of the trading account AND an asset in the balance sheet. Gross profit is the balancing figure — Example 6’s 4,20,000 closed both sides at 12,00,000. The lab is the exam in miniature: two questions — which figures enter the ladder , and can you close the account ? ABC Traders: carriage inwards ₹30,000 and office rent ₹80,000. Which enters the trading account's cost side? Capstone A Both — all expenses are direct B Only carriage inwards — it brought the goods to the shop; office rent waits for the P&L C Only office rent — carriage is a selling cost D Neither — both go to the balance sheet The course, in one breath Five openings asked what a business really earns. Four assumptions set the rules. The dual aspect gave every rupee two stories. The journal wrote them down, the ledger grouped them, the trial balance checked the arithmetic, the adjustments made the periods honest — and the final accounts turned the whole pipeline into two answers: did we profit, and what do we own and owe? That is Financial Accounting — one equation, kept true from the first ₹10,000 to the last ₹12,00,000.

chapters.label: P&L & closing entries
chapters.text: Lecture 21 · Net result & the chain Everything closes — and the statements hold hands . The P&L account sweeps up every operating expense and income, opens with the trading account's gross profit, and balances into net profit — which closes into capital. Then the statements chain: income statement → retained earnings → balance sheet → cash flow. 01 Inside the P&L account Gross profit arrives; operating items settle; net profit leaves Debit side — expenses & losses Salaries Discounts given Bad debts Depreciation Legal charges Consultancy Audit fees Electricity Telephone Stationery Interest on loans Indirect expenses — the costs of existing as a business, beyond the buying and selling of goods. (A gross loss, if any, also opens on this side.) Credit side — incomes & gains Discounts received Commission received Rent received Interest received Dividend received Bad debts recovered + Gross profit (from trading) Credit bigger than debit → net profit (appears on the debit side, then closes to capital). Debit bigger → net loss. 02 The four closing entries Click through the year-end ritual 01 · Expenses in 02 · Income in 03 · Gross profit in 04 · Net profit out Profit & Loss A/c Dr. … To Salaries / Rent / … A/c … What it does Every expense account hands its balance to the P&L. Narrations follow each entry — “transfer of balances of various expenses to profit and loss account”, and so on. Nominal accounts end the year at zero. 03 The retained earnings statement The bridge between the income statement and the balance sheet The retained earnings statement $ thousands · drag the dividend Dividends paid to shareholders $50 Beginning + net income − dividends = ending Beginning retained earnings $500 Add: Net income for the period +$100 Less: Dividends paid −$50 ───────── Ending retained earnings $550 Also called retained surplus or accumulated earnings. The ending balance walks straight into the equity section of the balance sheet , beside share capital. The lecture's own figures: 500 + 100 − 50 = $550,000 . 04 The chain Each statement hands its bottom line to the next Income statement bottom line: net income Retained earnings net income − dividends Balance sheet ending RE joins equity Cash flow cash must reconcile Each statement provides specific information while building on data from the previous one — the relationship that keeps financial reporting consistent. Where does the trading account's gross profit go at year-end? Lecture 21 · check yourself A Straight to the balance sheet as an asset B Credited to the Profit & Loss account via a closing entry C Debited to the capital account directly D It stays in the trading account forever Beginning retained earnings $500k, net income $100k, dividends paid $50k. The balance sheet's equity section shows retained earnings of… Lecture 21 · check yourself A $500k — beginning balances carry forward B $550k — 500 + 100 − 50 C $600k — 500 + 100, dividends are an expense D $450k — 500 − 50, net income is not included Key takeaways P&L credit side: gross profit + incomes ; debit side: operating expenses ; the balance is net profit/loss. Four closing entries: expenses in, incomes in, gross profit in, net profit to capital . Retained earnings statement: beginning + net income − dividends = ending → joins equity. The chain: income statement → retained earnings → balance sheet → cash flow .

chapters.label: Five statements
chapters.text: Module 3 · Reporting — the five statements One month of transactions, five statements Five major statements work together to give a full picture of an enterprise's financial story. Meet Softomation — one small company, five transactions — and watch them ripple through every statement. 01 Statement of Profit & Loss Reports financial performance over a period. 02 Statement of Retained Earnings Shows how earnings were distributed or retained. 03 Balance Sheet Shows financial position at a point in time. 04 Cash Flow Statement Summarises cash inflows and outflows. 05 Statement of Changes in Equity Explains how equity changed during the period. 01 Meet Softomation One small company, five transactions — March The five transactions 01 — Founders invest ₹50,000 cash as share capital. 02 — ₹20,000 in software services billed and collected in cash. 03 — ₹5,200 paid for salaries (4,000), rent (1,200) and other operating costs. 04 — ₹3,500 distributed to shareholders as a cash dividend. 05 — Net result: profit of ₹14,800; the statements below carry these five events into five different shapes. 02 Statement of Profit & Loss Also called the income statement — performance over the period Softomation · statement of profit and loss · month ended March 31 · ₹ Revenue from services 20,000 Salaries expense 4,000 Rent expense 1,200 Total expenses 5,200 Net profit 14,800 03 Statement of Retained Earnings The bridge between the P&L and the equity section of the balance sheet Softomation · statement of retained earnings · month ended March 31 · ₹ Beginning balance 0 Add — net profit 14,800 Available for distribution 14,800 Deduct — drawings (dividend) (3,500) Ending balance 11,300 Dividends are not expenses Profit distributions appear “below the line” — in this statement, not in the profit and loss. They are a return of the owners’ money , not a cost of operations. Retaining earnings signals the owner is reinvesting in the business. 04 Statement of Changes in Equity Capital and retained earnings, side by side Capital (₹) Retained earnings (₹) Total (₹) Beginning balance 0 0 0 Capital introduced 50,000 — 50,000 Net profit — 14,800 14,800 Withdrawn — (3,500) (3,500) Ending balance 50,000 11,300 61,300 05 The balance sheet — position at a point Softomation closes March at ₹85,300 — claimed by outsiders and owners Assets ₹85,300 = Liabilities ₹24,000 + Equity ₹61,300 Equity ₹61,300 = share capital ₹50,000 + retained earnings ₹11,300 — the two statements above, folded into the balance sheet’s last line. A full balance sheet to keep — Abraham Company · September 30 · ₹ Assets Cash 5,000 Trade receivables 17,000 Supplies 9,000 Equipment 19,000 Building 21,800 Land 21,000 Total assets 92,800 Liabilities & equity Loan payable 12,000 Expenses payable 3,500 Equity — Abraham 77,300 Total claims 92,800 06 Cash flow — the third mirror The same month, told strictly in cash Operating activities Cash from customers (₹20,000 billed & collected) minus cash to suppliers and employees. The engine room of the business. Investing activities Cash spent on long-lived resources — Softomation's equipment purchases live here. Financing activities Capital introduced (₹50,000) and dividends paid (₹3,500) — the owners' channel in and out. Why a profitable company needs this statement The P&L says ₹14,800 of profit; the cash statement tells you what actually landed in the bank — and which bucket each rupee travelled through. Solaris (chapter 1) died in the gap between those two mirrors. Key takeaways Five statements, one story: performance · retention · position · cash · equity . The P&L measures the period ; the balance sheet photographs the point . Dividends are below the line — a return to owners, never an expense. The balance sheet’s equity line is the changes-in-equity statement’s ending balance . The cash flow statement’s three buckets — operating, investing, financing — are the same month, told strictly in cash. Softomation earned ₹14,800 and distributed ₹3,500. Which figure links the P&L to the balance sheet? The bridge statement A ₹20,000 — the revenue line B ₹11,300 — retained earnings, the P&L's profit minus what was distributed C ₹50,000 — the share capital D ₹61,300 — total equity including capital

chapters.label: Balance sheet
chapters.text: Lecture 22 · The photograph What the firm owns and owes — on one date . The balance sheet is a snapshot, valid only for the date it names: a single transaction can change every figure. Prepared after the P&L — together they are the final accounts — and the two sides must always agree, because capital equals assets minus liabilities. The P&L is a video Performance over a period — revenue and expense items, every account closed after transferring to the P&L. The balance sheet is a photograph Position at a point in time — capital-nature items, balances that are not closed but carried forward to the next year. 01 Sort the balance sheet Every item the lecture names — click its family The classification drill 0 / 13 sorted Cash in hand & at bank Current asset Fixed asset Intangible Current liability Test: will it become cash within a year → current asset. Built to last → fixed asset. No physical form but exclusive rights → intangible. Owed within a year → current liability. 02 Two ways to arrange the same sheet Liquidity order or permanency order — toggle liquidity order permanency order Assets — liquidity 1 Cash in hand 2 Cash at bank 3 Trade receivables 4 Inventory 5 Machinery 6 Land & buildings Liabilities & capital — liquidity 1 Bank overdraft 2 Trade creditors 3 Bills payable 4 Long-term loans 5 Capital & reserves Most convertible first: cash leads, land trails. Current liabilities before long-term. Favourite of short-term lenders. 03 The final step of the cycle Journal → ledger → trial balance → statements — and the sheet must agree Why the two sides must always be equal Assets = Liabilities + Capital ↓ always, by construction Total of one side = Total of the other If they do NOT match, it is not a mystery — it is an error in preparation. The sheet is a re-arrangement of double entry itself. P&L vs balance sheet — the audit table Purpose profit or loss for a period position at a date Time an interval — usually one year a point in time Items revenue & expense nature capital nature Accounts all closed to the P&L not closed — carried forward Source trial balance trial balance A firm's trial balance shows assets ₹9,00,000 and liabilities ₹2,00,000. What must capital be — and what happens if the sheet shows otherwise? Lecture 22 · check yourself A ₹7,00,000 — and a mismatch means an error in preparation B ₹11,00,000 — assets plus liabilities C ₹9,00,000 — capital equals assets D It depends on the year's profit Which list is arranged in liquidity order? Lecture 22 · check yourself A Land → machinery → inventory → receivables → cash B Cash → receivables → inventory → machinery → land C Cash → land → machinery → inventory → receivables D Receivables → cash → land → inventory → machinery Key takeaways A point-in-time statement — valid only for the date it names. Current liabilities: payable within a year (creditors, overdraft, outstanding expenses, advances). Fixed: not due within a year. Assets: current (cash, receivables, stock) · fixed (machinery, buildings) · intangible (patents, trade rights). Two arrangements: liquidity order vs permanency order — same items, different lens. The balance sheet completes the accounting cycle — prepared after the P&L, and its sides must always agree.

chapters.label: The fourth pillar
chapters.text: Lecture 23 · The fourth pillar Where did the cash actually come from — and where did it go? The income statement, balance sheet and retained earnings statement each leave the same question unanswered. The cash flow statement exists to answer it — and of all the statements, it is the most honest. 01 What the other three cannot say Each statement has a blind spot Balance sheet Shows that equipment changed — not whether it was bought with cash or credit, nor where the cash came from. Income statement Shows net income — computed on accrual, not cash. The actual cash generated by operations stays invisible. Retained earnings Shows dividends declared — not whether they were actually PAID in cash during the period. Cathay Pacific — the paradox in one sentence The airline purchased assets worth HK$9.2 billion while reporting an HK$8.6 billion loss . Neither the loss nor the balance sheet can explain how such purchases were financed. Only the cash flow statement can. (And remember Soleris from Lecture 4: 40% sales growth, and still unable to pay suppliers.) 02 What counts as 'cash'? Cash in hand + demand deposits — and the equivalents test Cash & cash equivalents Cash in hand and demand deposits are cash. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into cash with minimal risk of value change — think maturities around three months . Firms deploy idle cash into such instruments, staying able to pull it back for operations. Click each candidate — does it pass the test? A fixed deposit with 2-month maturity judge Equity shares of another company judge A 1-year fixed deposit judge A 1-year FD with 2 months remaining judge Preference shares shortly before redemption judge The three activity families Operating — the principal revenue-generating activities: receipts from sales, interest and dividends received; payments to suppliers, employees, government (tax) and lenders (interest), insurers. Investing — acquiring and disposing of long-term assets: fixed assets, shares and debt instruments of other companies, advances and loans given; proceeds from their disposal, repayments, interest and dividends received. Financing — changes in the size and composition of capital: proceeds from issuing shares, debentures, loans; repayments, interest paid, dividends paid. The non-cash trap Converting debt into equity reshapes the balance sheet — and moves no cash at all. Non-cash transactions never appear on the cash flow statement. 03 Sort the flows The lecture's own transactions — click the family The three-activity sorter 0 / 12 classified Cash from selling goods Operating principal revenue-generating activities Investing buying & selling long-term assets Financing raising & repaying capital Industry twist: for a bank, lending is an operating activity — lending is the business. For everyone else, lending is investing. 04 Why net income ≠ operating cash Four reasons the two numbers part ways Different bases Net income is accrual: revenue when earned, expenses when incurred. Operating cash counts only actual cash moving. Non-cash expenses Depreciation and amortization cut profit but spend nothing — added back when converting to cash. Working capital Receivables up: sales booked, cash not collected → cash flow falls. Payables up: expenses booked, cash not paid → cash flow rises. Non-operating items Gains/losses on asset sales sit in profit, but the sale proceeds belong to investing — removed from operating. Who reads it, and why Investors and creditors assess future cash flows and their timing; employees and creditors check whether salaries, debts and declared dividends can actually be paid; every user judges the reliability of reported net income by comparing accrual earnings with cash generation — and investing/financing lines explain why assets, liabilities and equity changed. A company converts ₹50 lakh of debentures into equity shares. How does this appear on the cash flow statement? Lecture 23 · check yourself A As a financing inflow of ₹50 lakh B As both an inflow and an outflow of ₹50 lakh C It does not appear — no cash moved D As an investing outflow Interest RECEIVED on investments and interest PAID on loans — where does each belong? Lecture 23 · check yourself A Both operating B Received → investing; paid → financing C Received → financing; paid → investing D Both financing Key takeaways The fourth pillar answers what the other three cannot: where cash came from, where it went . Cash = in hand + demand deposits; equivalents = short-term, liquid, minimal risk (~3-month maturity, counted from acquisition). Three families: operating (the business), investing (the assets), financing (the capital). NI ≠ operating cash: accrual basis, non-cash items, working capital, non-operating items . Non-cash transactions — like debt-to-equity swaps — never appear.

chapters.label: Final accounts
chapters.text: Module 4 · Final accounts Two questions, two statements Final accounts are prepared at the end of an accounting period to reveal the result of operations and the financial position. Everything the course has built — journal, ledger, trial balance, adjustments — now gets asked its purpose. Question 1 — over the period “Did the business earn a profit or suffer a loss over the period?” Answered by the Trading & Profit and Loss Account — the statement of performance. Question 2 — at a point in time “What is the financial standing of the business at this specific point — what do we own, and what do we owe?” Answered by the Balance Sheet — the statement of position. 01 From adjusted trial balance to final accounts Each adjusted trial balance item moves into one of the two statements Trading & Profit and Loss Account Revenue and expense balances: sales, purchases, stock, wages, rent, interest . Answers: did we earn a profit or suffer a loss this period? Sales Purchases Stock Wages Rent Interest Balance Sheet Asset, liability and capital balances: cash, debtors, machinery, creditors, loans, capital . Answers: what do we own and owe at the year end? Cash Debtors Machinery Creditors Loans Capital The sorting rule is the whole skill Look at an adjusted trial balance item and ask one question: is it a flow (revenue or expense) or a stock (asset, liability or capital) ? Flows go to the Trading & P&L account; stocks go to the balance sheet. Every exam question on “prepare the final accounts” is this sorting test, then arithmetic. From an adjusted trial balance: closing stock ₹15,000. Where does it go? Sorting round A Trading account (credit side) AND balance sheet (current asset) — it does double duty B Only the trading account — it is a flow C Only the balance sheet — stock is an asset D Nowhere — closing stock is never recorded

chapters.label: Direct vs indirect
chapters.text: Lecture 25 · Building the statement Two roads to operating cash . The statement has a fixed skeleton — three activity sections that sum to a net change, which must reconcile with the balance sheet's cash. Operating cash can be built directly from receipts and payments, or indirectly, by walking net income back to cash. 01 The skeleton Header → three sections → net change → the check Operating daily business: receipts from customers, payments to suppliers, employees, tax Investing long-term assets: purchases and sales of PPE and investments Financing capital: shares issued, loans taken, repaid, interest & dividends paid The check beginning cash + net change = ending cash — which must equal the balance sheet's cash & cash equivalents 02 Direct vs indirect Follow the cash — or walk profit back to it Direct method Record every actual cash receipt and payment: cash from customers, less cash to suppliers, employees and operating expenses, less taxes — equals net operating cash. Sourced straight from the accounting records and cash-book analysis. Advantage: the received amounts help estimate FUTURE cash flows. Less common in practice. Indirect method Start with net income and adjust: add back non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortization, goodwill write-offs), deduct non-cash income (gains on disposal), then apply the working-capital rules. The one annual reports actually use — it reconciles profit to cash. 03 The working-capital rules Four moves — current assets and current liabilities Current asset ↑ → deduct cash is locked in (receivables, inventory grew) Current asset ↓ → add assets turned into cash Current liability ↑ → add expenses booked, cash kept (payables grew) Current liability ↓ → deduct old bills were paid down 04 The ladder, run for real Jaws Photo Plus — ₹73,000 of profit becomes ₹69,700 of cash Jaws Photo Plus — the reconciliation ladder reveal the adjustments one by one Net income the accrual starting point ₹73,000 Depreciation expense non-cash — add back ₹7,000 Running total: ₹80,000 Reveal next adjustment → Read the fourth step twice: an increase in receivables means sales were booked but cash never arrived — profit up, cash down. A decrease in payables means old bills were settled — cash left, profit untouched. (Some summaries mislabel the payables line as an addition; the arithmetic that reaches ₹69,700 requires the deduction shown here.) The full format, condensed Cash Flow Statement Jaws Photo Plus · FY… OPERATING Net cash from operating activities 69,700 INVESTING Purchases (PPE) / sales / interest rec. … FINANCING Shares, loans, interest & dividends paid … ───────────────────────────── Net increase / decrease in cash … Beginning cash & equivalents … Ending cash & equivalents … ↳ must match the balance sheet exactly Inventory increased by ₹12,000 during the year. In the indirect method, this is… Lecture 25 · check yourself A Added — inventory is an asset B Deducted — cash was spent buying stock that has not sold yet C Ignored — inventory is not cash D Added only if sales also increased Why is the gain on disposal of plant assets DEDUCTED in the operating section? Lecture 25 · check yourself A Because gains are never real B Because the sale proceeds belong to investing — leaving the gain in operating would double-count C Because gains are taxed separately D Because the asset was bought in an earlier year Key takeaways Ending cash must reconcile exactly with the balance sheet's cash & cash equivalents. Direct = follow actual receipts & payments; indirect = net income walked back to cash (the standard). Adjustments: add non-cash expenses, remove non-operating gains/losses, apply the working-capital rules . Jaws Photo Plus: 73,000 + 7,000 − 2,500 − 4,000 − 3,800 = ₹69,700 . Negative operating cash flow = the core is spending more cash than it generates — investigate.

chapters.label: The indirect build
chapters.text: Lecture 26 · The indirect method at work Three adjustment families — then the numbers land . The indirect method converts accrual profit into cash-based profit. Everything fits three categories: non-cash items, non-operating items, and working-capital changes — then tax paid, computed properly, and the statement is done. 01 The formula ladder Memorize the sequence — every problem is this ladder The indirect method, top to bottom Net Profit (or Profit Before Tax) − non-cash expenditures (depreciation, bad debts) − non-operating gains (added back if losses) − non-operating income (interest income…) − non-cash interest expenses = Operating profit before working-capital changes ± working-capital adjustments = Cash generated from operations − income tax PAID = Net cash flow from operating activities Tax paid = Tax expense + Opening tax payable − Closing tax payable 02 Category by category What moves, and which way 1 · Non-cash items Depreciation — added back Bad debts / provisions — added back Goodwill write-offs — added back They reduced profit without moving cash. 2 · Non-operating items Gain on sale of equipment — subtract Loss on sale — add back Interest income — subtract (investing) Interest expense — add back (financing) Only operating activity belongs here. 3 · Working capital Inventory ↑ subtract · ↓ add Receivables ↑ subtract · ↓ add Prepaids ↑ subtract · ↓ add Payables ↑ add · ↓ subtract Timing gaps between booking and cash. 03 Case study — Compass Company Two years of statements (2004, 2005), all three categories applied Compass Company — the verified result Profit before tax + depreciation & bad debts (non-cash) − gains on asset sales, investment income ± inventory, receivables, payables changes − income tax actually paid ────────────────────────── Net cash flow from operating activities = ₹72,000 The full three-section statement then follows: investing (asset purchases & disposals) and financing (capital raised & returned). 04 Exercise — Ajay Company ₹4,32,000 of profit, adjusted move by move Ajay Company — profit before tax ₹4,32,000 step through the adjustment moves Profit before tax ₹4,32,000 0 / 7 adjustments applied Apply next adjustment → The lecture gives the moves and the verified landing figure — ₹4,32,000 of accrual profit becomes ₹3,48,000 of operating cash. Note how the same profit can fall by ₹84,000 purely on timing, with no change in the business's health. Two traps the lecture warns about Not everything touches cash — equipment bought on credit never appears on the statement. Gains and losses on disposals are adjusted in operating, but the cash itself sits in investing — miss that and you count it twice. Interest income received on advances given to suppliers belongs to… Lecture 26 · check yourself A Operating — it is income B Investing — returns on amounts lent C Financing — it involves cash D It is excluded entirely Tax expense for the year is ₹50,000; opening tax payable ₹30,000; closing ₹50,000. Cash paid for tax is… Lecture 26 · check yourself A ₹50,000 — the expense itself B ₹30,000 — 50,000 + 30,000 − 50,000 C ₹70,000 — 50,000 + 30,000 − 10,000 D ₹20,000 — the increase in the payable Key takeaways Ladder: PBT → non-cash → non-operating → working capital → cash generated → tax paid . Compass lands at ₹72,000 ; Ajay walks ₹4,32,000 down to ₹3,48,000 . Interest/dividends received → investing ; paid → financing . Tax paid = expense + opening payable − closing payable. Credit purchases of assets never touch the statement — no cash, no entry.

chapters.label: Six questions
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · The diagnosis Six questions turn a statement into a verdict . The three sections are the anatomy; analysis is the medicine. Compass Company's statement answers six questions about earnings quality, financing, expansion strain, flexibility — and whether the dividend can survive. 01 The six questions Compass Company, interrogated Question 1 Why did cash fall despite profits? Quality of earnings. Compass shows ₹11,41,000 of net profit but only ₹72,000 of operating cash — the profit never became cash. Inventory tied up ₹58,000, receivables another ₹44,000; sales of ₹8,081,000 out of ₹9,025,000 (≈90%) converted to cash; and equipment purchases of ₹11,73,000 drained the rest. Question 2 How were equipment acquisitions financed? From everywhere at once: operating cash ₹72,000, share capital raised ₹1,00,000, disposal proceeds (equipment ₹22,000 + investments ₹16,000 = ₹45,000), interest received ₹5,000 — and existing cash balances. Equipment bought on credit (₹49,000) never appears: no cash moved. Question 3 How were the equity proceeds used? ₹1,00,000 raised: ₹28,000 repaid existing loans; of the ₹72,000 remaining, ₹25,000 went to dividends and ₹22,000 to interest — leaving ₹25,000, which is why financing cash flow is still positive. The debenture-to-equity conversion, again, moved no cash. Question 4 Is capacity expansion straining cash? Yes — investing shows a net outflow of ₹11,28,000, financed only partly from long-term sources. Rapid supplier payments, loose inventory control (+₹58,000) and rising receivables (+₹44,000) added pressure. Expansion is being paid for out of operations and existing reserves. Question 5 Does the company have financial flexibility? Fair flexibility: current investments could be liquidated without disrupting operations; debt-to-equity of 0.54:1 leaves borrowing capacity; supplier terms and bank lines are open; and operating cash flow of ₹72,000 is a buffer against adverse conditions. Question 6 What about creditors and shareholders? Creditors sleep well: operating cash covers interest 3.3× (72,000 ÷ 22,000). Shareholders should worry: the ₹25,000 dividend is 12.5% of share capital, and after interest only ₹50,000 remains — a 50% payout of available cash. Maintaining 12.5% on the enlarged base would demand ≈₹43,750 a year against thin cash. 3.3× interest cover — 72,000 ÷ 22,000 ₹11,41,000 → ₹72,000 profit vs operating cash — the quality gap 12.5% → 50% dividend rate vs payout of available cash 02 Worked example — Pioneer Limited A full statement, built from working notes The working notes — where the numbers come from Net profit: change in reserves & surplus = 1,70,000 + tax provision +50,000 + proposed dividend +50,000 = Net profit before taxation = 2,70,000 Depreciation: furniture 30,000 + equipment 15,000 = 45,000 Amortization: patent 1,00,000 → 95,000 = 5,000 Equipment: opening 2,00,000 + bought 80,000 − depreciation 15,000 − closing 2,30,000 = 35,000 sold at a 5,000 loss → proceeds = 30,000 Tax: opening provision 30,000 PAID this year; closing 50,000; the 20,000 increase is added back Operating Net profit before taxation +2,70,000 Depreciation (furniture + equipment) +45,000 Patent amortization +5,000 Loss on sale of equipment +5,000 Provision for taxation (increase) +20,000 Working-capital adjustments … Cash generated from operations 1,82,000 Less: tax paid −30,000 Net cash from operating activities +1,52,000 Investing Financing The closing check Operating +1,52,000 Investing −1,50,000 Financing −60,000 ──────── Net change −58,000 Opening cash 2,00,000 − 58,000 = Closing cash 1,42,000 ↳ verified against the balance sheet. The statement closes. Compass earned ₹11,41,000 of profit but generated ₹72,000 of operating cash. The FIRST question an analyst asks is… Lecture 27 · check yourself A Is the auditor independent? B What is the quality of earnings — did profit become cash, or is it trapped in receivables and inventory? C Should the dividend be raised? D Is the depreciation method too aggressive? Pioneer's equipment account: opening ₹2,00,000, purchases ₹80,000, depreciation ₹15,000, closing ₹2,30,000. Sold at a ₹5,000 loss. Sale proceeds were… Lecture 27 · check yourself A ₹35,000 — the book value B ₹30,000 — book value minus the loss C ₹40,000 — book value plus the loss D ₹50,000 — cost minus depreciation Key takeaways Six questions: cash decline, financing sources, equity use, expansion strain, flexibility , creditor & shareholder outlook. Profit of ₹11,41,000 vs cash of ₹72,000 = a quality of earnings flag, not necessarily fraud. Creditors read interest cover (3.3×); shareholders read the dividend's sustainability . Pioneer: 2,70,000 → +1,52,000 / −1,50,000 / −60,000 → net −58,000 → closing cash 1,42,000 , verified. Working notes first, statement second: depreciation, disposal book values and tax paid must be derived.

chapters.label: FS analysis
chapters.text: Lecture 28 · From preparing to interrogating Raw data in — insight out . Financial statement analysis converts statements into decisions: how did the business perform, where is it strong and weak, what are the prospects? It needs standards to compare against and techniques to compare with. 01 Four standards of comparison Against what, exactly, are we judging? Rule of thumb Broad benchmarks applied across firms — the current ratio of 2:1. Quick and easy, but blind to quality: a 2.2:1 firm may hold slow-moving inventory while a 1.6:1 firm turns stock fast and manages liquidity better. Past performance Compare this year with previous years; extrapolate the trend. But regulation, competition and technology can break the trend; policy changes (depreciation, inventory valuation) break comparability; non-operating items distort — and growing 10% while the industry grows 30% is an illusion of growth. Internal standards The company's own benchmarks: profit targets, ROI/ROA expectations, budgets, predetermined costs, material-consumption and labor-efficiency controls. The management-control lens. Industry standards Compare with peers. But firms span multiple businesses — HUL runs soaps, detergents, toothpaste and food, so P&G, ITC and Colgate only partly overlap — and accounting policies differ across companies. No perfect peer exists. Kodak — the past-performance trap Peak sales of $16 billion in 1996 , profits of $2.5 billion in 1999 — and bankruptcy in 2012 . Dominating the camera market meant nothing once digital disruption redrew it. Relying solely on past performance masked the existential threat; the trend was accurate right up to the moment it stopped being the world it described. 02 Four techniques The analytical toolkit 01 Horizontal (Current − Previous) / Previous × 100 Two years side by side — absolute change and percentage change. 02 Trend Base year = 100 → index each year Horizontal extended over 5, 10, 15 years — the long trajectory. 03 Vertical Each line item as % of a base Gross profit as % of sales — composition and proportions. 04 Ratio The relationships themselves The most popular technique — detailed in later sessions. 03 Case study — Dr. Reddy's 2015-16 A profit decline that wasn't a decline Dr. Reddy's Laboratories · FY 2015-16 flip the lens Headline view Operating view +4.49% Revenue from operations +4.38% Total revenue +3.49% Total expenses −7.01% Tax expense −7.92% Net profit Net profit fell 7.92% despite revenue growing faster than expenses. The headline says: core business weakening. The distortion checklist Non-recurring and exceptional items create misleading impressions; accounting policy changes (depreciation, inventory valuation) break year-to-year comparability; different fiscal year-ends block direct comparison; and different policies across an industry complicate peer analysis. Always ask: what is the source of this number? A company's profit grew 10% last year. Its industry grew 30%. What is this called? Lecture 28 · check yourself A Quality of earnings B The illusion of growth C Horizontal analysis D A favorable variance Dr. Reddy's reported a 7.92% profit decline in 2015-16. What did the operating view reveal? Lecture 28 · check yourself A The core business had weakened badly B A one-time ₹4,621 thousand FX loss (Venezuela) explained it all — operating profit actually grew 9.23% C Expenses had grown faster than revenue D Tax had risen sharply Key takeaways Four standards: rule of thumb , past performance (Kodak's trap), internal , industry (no perfect peer). Four techniques: horizontal , trend , vertical , ratio . Watch for exceptional items , policy changes, fiscal-year mismatches. Dr. Reddy's: headline −7.92% vs operating +9.23% — one FX loss, two completely different stories.

chapters.label: Profit is an opinion
chapters.text: Lecture 29 · The closing argument Profit is an opinion . Cash is a fact . A company can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash — because accrual accounting records what is earned, not what arrived. One stationery shop explains the entire lecture series. 01 Mira's stationery shop One credit sale, three months, the whole lesson March April May March — The sale happens Mira's stationery shop sells ₹1,00,000 of stock to a coaching centre on credit. The P&L immediately shows ₹1,00,000 of sales. The cash box shows nothing. 02 The three statements, one line each What each one is for Balance sheet A snapshot: what the company owns and owes at a specific point in time. Profit & loss Performance over a period — revenue and expense, without tracking cash movement. Cash flow The fundamental question: where did cash come from, and where did it go? 03 Why profit ≠ operating cash — three sources The lecture's own numbers Non-cash expenses ₹24,000/yr A ₹1,00,000 photocopier depreciated at ₹24,000 a year cuts profit — but the cash left two years ago. Add it back. Working capital ₹1,00,000 / ₹30,000 Mira's credit sale raises profit but not cash; her ₹30,000 credit purchase of paper cuts profit but keeps cash. Non-operating items ₹5,000 gain An old computer, book value ₹10,000, sold at ₹15,000: the ₹5,000 gain sits in profit, but the full ₹15,000 proceeds belong to investing. 04 The student analogy You already run three cash flows Operating Monthly pocket money in; mess charges and daily living out. Investing Buying a laptop — an asset with lasting value; parking savings in a fixed deposit. Financing Taking an education loan, and repaying it (with interest) for years. The four-company reality check Real statements from four different industries show net income and operating cash flow are never equal : for Lenovo and BP, operating cash ran below profit; for the others, above. The metrics are measured on different bases — accrual vs cash — and that is precisely why lenders scrutinize the cash flow statement first: cash is fact, whatever the accounting policies say . The course, in one balance Concepts & conventions → the equation → journal & ledger → trial balance → adjustments → final accounts → the balance sheet → the cash flow statement → analysis that asks: can I trust this number? Answer the last question with cash first. Mira sells ₹1,00,000 of stock on credit in March; the coaching centre pays in May. In March, Mira's books show… Lecture 29 · check yourself A ₹1,00,000 profit and ₹1,00,000 cash B ₹1,00,000 profit and no cash — a receivable instead C No profit until cash arrives D A ₹1,00,000 liability Why do banks and lenders read the cash flow statement before anything else? Lecture 29 · check yourself A It is the shortest statement B Because profit depends on accounting choices, but cash is objective — unaffected by policies C Because it shows the highest profit D Because tax law requires it Key takeaways Accrual profit and cash move on different clocks — Mira sells in March, gets paid in May. NI ≠ operating cash for three reasons: non-cash expenses, working capital, non-operating items . Cash equivalents: liquid, readily convertible, minimal risk — judged from acquisition date. The student analogy: pocket money = operating, laptop = investing, education loan = financing . Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact — the sentence the whole course was building toward.

chapters.label: The course map
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 1 — the course map Introduction to Economic & Business History Prof. Manu Kanchan, School of Management & Entrepreneurship, IIT Jodhpur. One course, one promise: by the end, the headlines of today's economy will read as history repeating — and you'll know why. 01 What the course covers Three main areas, one continuous story Definition What economics and business mean in a historical context — the foundational terms and concepts. Evolution over time How economic ideas and business practices changed — and how those changes reshaped society's socio-cultural context. Interconnection How economics and business influenced each other: economic developments shaping business practice, business innovations shaping economic thinking. The broad topics on the syllabus Agrarian economies · ancient trade routes · colonialism · the Industrial Revolution · labour movements · business families · entrepreneurship history · modern corporations. Every one of them is a station on the same line — the story of how humans organised production, distribution and consumption. 02 The five modules The course is organised into two halves — a global story, then an Indian one The five modules — tap one to open its brief M1 The Lens M2 Early Systems M3 The Machine Age M4 The Corporation M5 Indian Business M1 · The Lens Lectures 1–9 Economics · business · history — and how each shapes the others (L1–L9) Economic History — global lens How economic systems, rules and logic evolved — from Western Europe outward. The first three modules live here. Business History — Indian focus How business organisations, strategies and structures developed — Indian examples and context from Module 4 onward. (India's own economic story spans 300–400 years.) 03 History is about why, not when Context · time · change — the three critical dimensions The method of the whole course Historical change happens over extended periods , not overnight. LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation — was initiated in the mid-1980s but fully implemented in 1990–1995 and beyond. The Industrial Revolution took centuries to manifest its effects. And the evidence lives in sources: policy documents, parliamentary debates, annual reports, court verdicts, advertisements, personal correspondence. No mandatory textbook — “Global Economic History: A Very Short Introduction” is recommended, nothing more. The why-questions this course answers • Why did the Industrial Revolution happen in the UK, 17–18th century? • Why did LPG policies emerge in India in 1991? • Why did the guild system decline? • Why do economic policies — and economic crashes — repeat in shape? The course has five modules. What is the split between the two halves of the course? Lecture 1 A Five equal modules, all global B First three modules: Western European and global economic development — modules four and five bring in Indian examples and context C All five modules focus only on India D The course has no modules — one continuous timeline Key takeaways The course covers definition, evolution over time, and the economics–business interconnection — across agrarian economies to modern corporations. Five modules: global story first (M1–M3), Indian business history second (M4–M5) . History = context, time and change — argued from evidence, never memorised.

chapters.label: What is economics?
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 1 — the first lens What is economics ? Before we can watch economies change over five centuries, we need to agree on what an economy even is — and why the subject exists at all. The lecture opens not with a definition, but with a student. 01 The first-year student Unlimited wants, limited resources — the birth of the subject The example Imagine a first-year student. The resources she has: Time — 24 hours, Money — limited pocket money and/or income, Energy — limited. What she wants : good grades (books, fees, tuition), entertainment (OTT subscriptions, movie tickets, stand-up shows), sports (equipment, memberships), friends (fun activities). Everything cannot be had at once. Why economics exists The problem: unlimited wants, but resources are limited . Because resources must be allocated, choices become necessary — and that is why economics exists. It holds for a family, for states, for a country/nation: the Government of India has a limited budget — should it spend more on education, defence, healthcare, or infrastructure? Same student, bigger scale. Time 24 hours — the same for everyone, never enough Money Limited pocket money and/or income Energy Limited — attention is a resource too 02 Three definitions, one subject Production · scarcity · decision-making Definition A — The flow The study of the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. Definition B — The gap The study of scarcity — how people use resources and respond to incentives. Definition C — The choice The study of decision-making. 03 Two branches Macro means large — micro means small 1 · Macro economics — Set B “Macro” means large. Studies the economy as a whole. · Why does unemployment rise? · What causes inflation? · Why do economies grow? · What creates economic crises? 2 · Micro economics — Set A “Micro” means small. Studies consumers, households, firms/businesses. · Why does the price of tomatoes increase? · Why & how do firms hire workers? · How do consumers make choices? 04 Economics and business, wired together The circular flow — businesses, households, and the two rivers between them Businesses · produce and sell products · hire inputs from households Households · buy products from firms · provide inputs to firms OUTPUTS — goods and services (products) INPUTS — labour · capital · land · entrepreneurship Why this diagram matters for a history course Economics frames the rules and logic of the economies — how (& why) societies organize economic activity and determine the production and distribution of goods and services. Business is one of the main actors playing a role within those economies. Rules on one side, actors on the other — hold that pairing; the whole course is about how both of them change. The Government of India has a limited budget and must choose between education, defence, healthcare and infrastructure. At the country level, this is the same problem as… Lecture 1 A A firm deciding which factory to shut B The first-year student allocating 24 hours, limited money and limited energy C A guild setting the price of hats D A merchant choosing between sea and land routes Key takeaways Economics = the study of scarcity, incentives and decision-making — production, distribution, consumption. Macro studies the economy as a whole ; micro studies consumers, households, firms . Business is one of the main actors inside economies; economics frames the rules and logic they play by.

chapters.label: What is business?
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 2 — the second lens What is business ? One sentence in the lecture carries the whole definition — and then quietly redefines business as something society does, not just something firms do. 01 The definition, word for word Four parts hiding inside one sentence The lecture's definition Business is defined as an economic activity involving the production and sale of goods and services , undertaken with a motive of earning profit by satisfying human needs . Economic activity It belongs to the economy — not to hobby or charity Production & sale It makes (or arranges) and sells — both halves Profit motive Profit = Revenue − Cost; the engine that keeps it alive Satisfying needs Profit earned by a satisfied customer — needs first 02 Goods and services Tangible products and intangible activities Goods — tangible products Things you can drop on your foot: mobile phones, FMCG — fast-moving consumer goods on a supermarket shelf. Services — intangible activities Things done for you: healthcare, a hair salon — you cannot stack them in a warehouse, but you pay for them all the same. 03 From the corner shop to the multinational Same definition, wildly different scale Small / local shops — retail shops, hair salon shops Big corporations, MNCs — Infosys, Apple 04 Why do businesses exist? Start from the individual — then watch the answer flip The counterfactual Could each individual satisfy their own needs? Grow their own food? Make their own clothes? Build their own houses? Manufacture their own smartphones? Every one of those is possible in principle and impossible in practice — nobody would ever own a smartphone if each of us had to smelt, etch and assemble our own. The answer Businesses exist to satisfy human needs efficiently , and to earn profits . The bridge between the two is specialisation — businesses specialise, and specialised producers are efficient producers. Hence the lecture’s widest sentence: business is a mechanism through which societies organize production and exchange. 05 Studying decision-making in business Forms, domains, and ownership What business studies decide Forms opted → Partnership · Limited Liability · LLP · LLC Domains → Marketing · Finance · HR · Information Systems · Strategy · Entrepreneurship Ownership → Family-owned companies · Big corporations A barber earns ₹800 a day cutting hair; a salon owner earns ₹800 a day in profit from three chair-renters. Which line from the lecture separates the two situations? Lecture 2 A Goods are tangible; services are intangible B Profit = Revenue − Cost — the owner's number is what remains after costs C Businesses must be incorporated to count D Specialisation requires machinery Key takeaways Business = economic activity + production & sale + profit motive + satisfying human needs . Goods are tangible (phones, FMCG); services are intangible (healthcare, salons). Businesses exist to satisfy needs efficiently — through specialisation — and to earn profit; they are society’s mechanism for production and exchange .

chapters.label: What is history?
chapters.text: Module 1 — the third lens What is history ? Not a stack of dates. The lecture defines history as a method: change, over time, through evidence — and then shows you what that method does to real questions. 01 Not just memorizing dates The study of change over time, through evidence The definition History is the study of change over time through evidence . Not just memorizing dates. The real questions are: why (& how) did events happen? And why did some institutions rise or fall? Event Why did the Industrial Revolution happen in the UK? In the 17–18th century — and not elsewhere? The question this course spends Module 3 on. Policy Why did LPG policies emerge in India in 1991? Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation — a rule change with a history. Institution Why (& how) did guilds fall? An institution that ruled medieval cities — gone. Module 2 watches it break. 02 The three habits of the historian Context · time · complex causes How history thinks Context matters → nothing happens in a vacuum Change happens over time → today is someone's tomorrow Cause and effect are complex → one event, many reasons = the Science/Study of Context, Time, and Change 03 The evidence shelf Sources from the period — and analyses written later From the actual time period · Policy documents (Industrial Policies) , parliamentary debates · Annual reports · Court case verdicts · Letters, business ledgers, old advertisements, contracts Written later · Textbooks · Articles · Analyses — scholarship standing back from the period Both piles matter — but the exam question “which is a primary source?” is asking which pile the document sits in. 04 Why bother? To understand the present Patterns above, sectors below Economic Recognize patterns — economic policies and economic crashes rhyme across centuries. Businesses The rise of big corporations — and the rise (& fall) of different sectors . Today’s headlines have ancestors. A researcher compares a 1962 factory licence file with a 2015 journal article about India's License Raj. Which of the two is the primary source — and why does the distinction matter? Module 1 A The 2015 article — it is peer-reviewed and therefore more reliable B The 1962 licence file — it is evidence from the actual period; the article is an analysis written later C Neither — history only uses books D Both are primary because both are old Key takeaways History = the study of change over time through evidence — context matters, causes are complex. Sources split into from the period (ledgers, policies, ads, verdicts) and written later (textbooks, analyses). The payoff is the present : patterns in policies and crashes, the rise of corporations, sectors rising and falling.

chapters.label: Rules & players
chapters.text: Module 1 — the frame of the whole course The rules and the players Economic & Business History is the timeline and analysis of how (& why) the Rules and the Players changed over time. One sentence — four fields hiding inside it. 01 Four fields in two rows Rules or players — snapshot or over time Machine 01 — the two-by-two · tap a cell the rules · snapshot Economics the rules · over time Economic History the players · snapshot Business the players · over time Business History Studies the rules and logic of economies. Its questions: How (& why) do societies organize economic activity — and determine the production and distribution of goods and services? 02 Two histories, one sentence apart Economic history follows the rules; business history follows the players Economic History Explains how (& why) the rules and logic of the economies changed over time — how revolutions (industrial), crises, and government policies rewrite the economic system; how policies changed economic outcomes; why some societies became wealthy while others remained poor.
