Business History Explains how (& why) the players — firms, entrepreneurs, businesses — changed over time — how did the modern corporation emerge; how did management structures evolve; why did some firms grow into multinational enterprises; how have technology and innovation transformed business organizations? 03 The shelf behind the course Three books the lecture puts on your desk Global Economic History: A Very Short Introduction Robert Allen (2011) · Oxford The whole divergence debate — why some countries rich, some poor — in one slim volume. The Shortest History of Economics Andrew Leigh (2024) Economic history at sprint pace — exactly the lens this course trains. The Economic History of India 1857–2010 Tirthankar Roy (2020) · Oxford University Press The India spine — colonial rule to liberalisation, the long arc behind the License Raj. A historian asks: \u201CHow did government policies rewrite the economic system after 1947?\u201D Another asks: \u201CHow did Bajaj Auto grow from a licence-holder into a multinational?\u201D Which fields are these two questions? Module 1 A Both are Business History B Economic History — then Business History C Business History — then Economic History D Both are Economics Key takeaways The course = how (& why) the Rules and the Players changed over time. Economics → rules now · Economic History → rules over time · Business → players now · Business History → players over time. The reading shelf: Allen , Leigh , Roy — global lens, sprint history, India’s long arc.

chapters.label: Economy → business
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 3 — the first current Economy → business: the License Raj How does the economy influence businesses? India's answer for four decades was brutally concrete: almost nothing important could be done without a government licence. 01 What was the License Raj? Extensive government controls, after independence The definition The License Raj refers to the system of extensive government controls — through licences and regulations that governed most economic activities in India after independence. 02 What all did it control? Six levers, every one of them inside the firm Starting companies A licence was required just to start a new company Manufacturing Producing new products — or expanding production capacities — needed approval Prices Government control over prices Hiring & firing Government approval needed for laying off workers — and for shutting down Finance Capital and credit sat inside the controlled zone Import High tariffs, low import quotas — and outright bans on certain products 03 Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 The constitution of the licence system Schedule A — 17 industries The exclusive responsibility of the Government (Central & State): arms and ammunition, atomic energy, railways and air transport, heavy industries, utilities & mining. Schedule B — 12 industries Open to both the private and public sectors — the automobile sector lived here. Schedule C — Everything else All industries not included in the two schedules — open to the private sector. The mood behind the schedules Adoption of the socialist pattern of society/economy · a state-led development mode · expansion of the public sector in core and capital-intensive industries · equitable distribution of income and wealth · balanced regional industrial growth · promotion of small-scale and cottage industries · encouragement of cooperative enterprises and workers’ participation in management. 04 One sector under the lens: automobiles Schedule B, a scooter order, and a foreign-exchange act Scooters (Distribution & Sales) Control Order, 1960 · Distribution (and sales) of scooters by manufacturers; sales by dealers · Procedure to purchase: apply to the dealer → a written guarantee from the bank to pay the dealer ₹250 · Maintenance of a register by the dealer; re-sale of scooters regulated Then the dial turned · 1960–1969 — collaborations with foreign firms were encouraged · 1970 — FERA Act (foreign exchange regulation) · Late 1960s & early 1970s — nationalisation of banks , privy purse abolished You want to launch a new scooter model and double your factory's output in 1970s India. Which items on the licence checklist will you meet? Lecture 3 A Only the import desk B Manufacturing approval for the new product AND for expanding production capacity — with prices, hiring/firing and imports all separately controlled C Nothing — Schedule C left automobiles free D Only a marketing permit Key takeaways License Raj = extensive government controls via licences and regulations over most economic activity. IPR 1956: Schedule A (17, state-exclusive) · Schedule B (12, both) · Schedule C (rest, private) — in a socialist-pattern, state-led frame. Even a scooter purchase was scripted: dealer, ₹250 bank guarantee, register . Economy → business, at the counter.

chapters.label: Case: Bajaj Auto
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 3 — the case Case: Bajaj Auto under the licence system Two tracks run side by side in the lecture's table: what the economy allowed, and what the company did. Read them together and the License Raj stops being an abstraction. 01 The two-track table Economy level on the left rail · company level on the right Year Economy level Company level — Bajaj Auto 1945 — Incorporated 1948 — Started selling imported two- and three-wheelers in India 1959/60 — Obtained licence from the Govt. of India to manufacture two- and three-wheelers — 6,000 a year 1960 — Obtained a licence from Piaggio (Italian company) to manufacture Vespa — the Vespa 150 1960–1969 Collaborations with foreign firms were encouraged Riding the Piaggio collaboration 1970 Policy promoted domestic companies — 1971 — Collaboration with Piaggio ended — began selling the Bajaj 150 and the Bajaj Chetak 02 Read the two tracks together Where policy ends and the firm begins The licence that built the middle-class dream In 1959/60 Bajaj obtained the Government of India licence to manufacture two- and three-wheelers — capped at 6,000 a year . In 1960 it licensed Piaggio’s Vespa 150 design. When policy turned to promoting domestic companies, the Piaggio collaboration ended (1971) — and Bajaj began selling its own Bajaj 150 and the legendary Bajaj Chetak . What the case teaches Every milestone on the company track is enabled, capped or redirected by the economy track: the licence set the volume (6,000/yr), the Scooter Control Order scripted the selling, the foreign-collaboration window (1960–69) shaped the technology partner, and the 1970 pivot ended it. The economy didn’t influence Bajaj Auto — it drew the railway tracks the firm ran on. 6,000 two- and three-wheelers a year — the licensed ceiling. Scarcity by paperwork: waiting lists, not showrooms, were the Indian car market’s native habitat. Bajaj's collaboration with Piaggio ended in 1971 — the same era in which policy began promoting domestic companies. What did Bajaj begin selling afterwards? Lecture 3 A Imported Vespas under a new licence B The Bajaj 150 and the Bajaj Chetak C Only three-wheelers D Nothing — the firm paused production Key takeaways Bajaj timeline: 1945 incorporated → 1948 imports → 1959/60 licence (6,000/yr) → 1960 Piaggio Vespa 150 → 1971 own bikes. Economy track: 1960–69 foreign collaborations encouraged → 1970 domestic promotion (FERA era). Read the tracks together — the firm’s every turn is the economy’s rule made visible.

chapters.label: Society → business
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 4 — the second current Society → business Two lecture questions open this current: why don't all businesses sell the same products across every country? And why do companies change their advertisements, products and services over time? 01 The burger that explains a country McDonald's in India — the McAloo Tikki The case McDonald’s in India: the McAloo Tikki Burger , introduced in 1998 , has become the face of the McDonald’s menu in India. Why? Indian society consumes vegetarian food in a major way — different from the countries where McDonald’s originated and operates. The chain of causation Society → food habits → the business’s product — what they produce and sell. The menu is not a recipe decision; it is a society decision . 02 The chocolate ad that aged into a mirror Cadbury Dairy Milk — mid-1990s vs 2021 Mid-1990s “Kya Swad hai Zindagi mein” The girl sneaking chocolate — indulgence framed for its time. 2021 The same jingle, a different India The ad is remade for a society where women’s position has shifted — the business’s advertisement tracking the socio-cultural environment. The lecture's two-line verdict Businesses are embedded within society. As society changes, businesses change / adapt . Society has strongly influenced businesses — what they produce , how they operate , whom they employ , and what consumers choose to buy . 03 What counts as 'society'? The eight-layer environment the business lives in Culture — food, clothing, language Religion Traditions Values Family structures Education Demographics Social norms Food habits are just one layer — the socio-cultural environment wraps every product, ad and hire. Put the lecture's causation in order for the McAloo Tikki Burger. Lecture 4 A Business's product → society's food habits → vegetarian society B Indian society consumes vegetarian food in a major way → society's food habits → business's product (McAloo Tikki, 1998) C McDonald's global strategy → Indian law → menu change D Supply chain costs → menu change → society adapts Key takeaways Products differ across countries because society differs — McAloo Tikki, 1998, the vegetarian majority. Ads change because society changes — Cadbury mid-1990s vs 2021, women’s position. Businesses are embedded within society : as society changes, businesses change/adapt.

chapters.label: Business → society
chapters.text: Module 1 · Lecture 5 — the current reversed Business → society: the story of the weekend If society influences business, can businesses also change or influence society? The lecture's proof is something you are using right now: Saturday and Sunday. 01 Which society invented the weekend? Industrial — during and after the Industrial Revolution Industrial society During / after the industrial revolution ✓ the weekend is born here Agrarian society Farming-based communities / society Feudal society Related to agrarian society Nomadic society Hunter-gatherers and nomadic cultures 02 Why only industrial society could need one How work was organized — before and after the machine Society How was work organized? Consequence Industrial society Machines, factories, artificial light 24-hour work possible — workers moved into factories Agrarian society Seasons (of the year), daylight Work happened in agricultural fields, depended on rains, etc. The trap, then the fight Industrial society made 24-hour work possible — and delivered long working hours (10–12 hours a day) . Work-life balance — the effective management of time and energy between professional responsibilities and personal life — had to be won , by the working class through the Labor/Working Class Movement (1870s–80s). 03 The weekend, assembled step by step 1886 → 1938 — four moves, one institution 1886 The eight-hour day The Labor Movement wins the eight-hour day 1908 US first five-day workweek So Jewish workers could attend sabbath on Saturday 1926 Ford shuts Sat–Sun Ford stops its factories on Saturday and Sunday 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act 40-hour workweek · overtime pay · national minimum wage · child labor bans The weekend — Saturday and Sunday, off/holidays — is an industrial-society artifact : built by machines, artificial light, and the labor movement that answered them. 04 The full ledger of business on society Positive and negative — both columns are real Positive · Employment · Innovation · Growth · Taxes · Technology · CSR Negative · Pollution · Inequality · Exploitation · Consumerism · Environmental damage Agrarian society had daylight and seasons; industrial society had machines, factories and artificial light. What did that difference make POSSIBLE — and what did workers then have to WIN? Lecture 5 A Possible: 24-hour work and 10–12 hour days; won: the eight-hour day, the five-day week, and finally the 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act B Possible: remote work; won: the weekend by royal decree C Possible: child labor bans immediately; won: nothing further D Possible: unemployment insurance; won: the minimum wage in 1886 Key takeaways The weekend was invented by industrial society — machines and artificial light made 24-hour work possible. Timeline: 1886 eight-hour day → 1908 five-day week → 1926 Ford → 1938 FLSA. Business on society runs both ways: employment, innovation, growth, taxes, technology, CSR vs pollution, inequality, exploitation, consumerism, environmental damage .

chapters.label: Economies & technology
chapters.text: Module 1 · Live Session 2 — the current completes Business → economies, and technology → business Ford's assembly lines lift an economy; bundled mortgages sink one; a DVD-by-mail startup eats Hollywood. The last current of Module 1 is the loudest. 01 Business → economies: the positive ledger Ford and mass production Job creation Rising incomes Growth of industries Faster economic growth 02 …and the negative ledger The financial crisis of 2007–2008 How risky home loans became a global crisis Risky home loans (subprime mortgages) ↓ Bundled into complex financial products and sold to investors globally ↓ Many borrowers could not repay their loans ↓ FINANCIAL CRISIS Falling dominoes: rising unemployment · slower economic growth in many countries · decline in international trade 03 Technology → business: the Netflix story DVD by mail (1997) → streaming (2007) → standalone (2010) → discs retired (2020/2023) 1997 Founded in the US A DVD rental business 2007 Streaming & video-on-demand High-speed internet; consumers watching movies online 2010 Standalone streaming Offered separately from DVD rentals 2020/2023 DVD rentals discontinued The original business retired What the internet actually changed Not just the product — the complete business, and the business model itself . Older technologies became obsolete. The enablers were ordinary: the internet (modem), wireless tech (broadband, WiFi), mobile phones (smartphones), microphones, cameras, laptops/computers, software platforms. 04 The general law of technology Four doors it kicks open in every business Technology changes products It can create new markets and products — streaming created a market that DVDs never could Technology changes production How things get made — the whole of Module 3 is this sentence Technology changes advertising / promotional campaigns Where the Cadbury ads of 1998 met their 2021 remakes Technology changes distribution DVD-by-mail to broadband — the pipe is the business 05 One frame to hold them all PESTLE — the environment a business stands in Economies → business · Society → business · Technology → business — plus Environment → business . The lecture bundles them: P Political E Economic S Social T Technological L Legal E Environment Political · Economic · Social · Technological · Legal · Environment Match the mechanism: (1) subprime mortgages bundled and sold globally, (2) high-speed internet meeting a DVD-by-mail firm. What does each demonstrate? Live Session 2 A Both demonstrate technology changing products B (1) Business → economy: firm behaviour can crash the whole system; (2) Technology → business: the internet rewrote the complete business model C (1) Society → business; (2) Business → society D (1) Political change; (2) Legal change Key takeaways Business → economies: jobs, incomes, industry growth (Ford) — and 2007–08 : subprime → bundled products → default → crisis. Technology → business: Netflix 1997 → 2007 → 2010 → 2020/23; the internet changed the complete business and its model . Technology changes products, production, advertising, distribution — all held in the PESTLE frame.

chapters.label: Agrarian economies
chapters.text: Module 2 · Lecture 7 — pre-industrial economies Agrarian economies Before factories, before corporations — economies where the calendar was agricultural, the family was the factory, and land was the only wealth that mattered. 01 What is an agrarian economy? Seasons controlled the economy — and society The lecture's four marks Seasons controlled the economy and society. Life revolved around agriculture and the seasons — harvest, sowing seasons, the rainfall cycle. Agriculture meant families — the family was the unit of production. And land was the main asset : owning more land meant rich. Land as the core asset Land ownership was not just property — it was the primary source of capital and social stratification . Land functioned as the core asset determining wealth, power, and production capacity . Social stratification: a society’s categorisation of its people into groups based on socioeconomic factors — wealth, income, race, education, ethnicity, gender, occupation, social status, or derived power. 02 Three questions organise the whole module Who owned · who decided · how was it organised Module 2's spine — memorise these three 1. Who owned the land? 2. Who decided what and how much to produce? 3. How was the production, distribution and consumption of agricultural products organized? 03 Answer 1 — the feudal model (Western Europe) The crown, the lords, and the bound peasants The pyramid The Crown/Lords owned the land and provided military protection. The Peasants/Serfs were bound to the land, paying rent via crop shares or manual labour. Serfdom : a legal and economic system where a peasant is bound to a plot of land owned by a lord — they could not leave, move to another town, or marry without the direct permission of their lord . The feudal pyramid of power — obligations flowing both ways King / Crown gives: Grants land (fiefs) · gets: Loyalty of the realm Nobles / Lords gives: Provides estate management · gets: Land from the crown Vassals / Knights gives: Offers military protection · gets: Land & money, knights Peasants / Hereditary Serfs gives: Manual cultivation · gets: Protection & a strip to live from 04 Answer 1 — the zamindari / colonial model The state, the intermediaries, the squeezed ryots The chain The State granted revenue-collection rights to intermediaries ( Zamindars ). The tenant farmers bore the brunt of high fixed tax rates — leading to systemic debt cycles. Under British colonial rule the chain ran: British Colonial Government [demanded tax] → the Zamindars — hereditary, land-owning elites [extracted variable, highly inflated rents] → Cultivators / Tenant Ryots [vulnerable farmers]. 05 Answer 2 — who decided what to produce? Nobody asked the market The feudal model · Production was heavily localised and traditional · The lord mandated how much labour went to his personal fields · Peasants decided what to grow on their subsistence plots based purely on immediate survival needs The zamindari / colonial model · Zamindars demanded heavy cash rents ; the British state required specific revenues · Cultivators were forced away from food crops toward high-value, risky cash crops (like indigo, opium, or cotton) to pay their debts The line to remember Production was not determined by a free market of consumer demand . It was dictated either by the survival needs of the worker or the coercive financial demands of the ruling elite . 06 Answer 3 — how was it organised? Production, distribution, consumption Production Labour-intensive, low-technology farming organised around the family unit — or forced communal labour days. Distribution — feudalism Moving goods was highly inefficient: surplus distributed locally via mandatory tithes to the Church and physical crop deliveries to the Lord's granary. Distribution — zamindari Extractive and global: crops sold into colonial merchant supply chains, shipped to overseas markets — often leaving the local region vulnerable to famine. Consumption realities — a deeply unequal split The vast majority of the population — peasants/tenants — lived on subsistence consumption . Luxury and surplus consumption were entirely restricted to the tiny landlord and merchant elite . 07 The impact — why this world couldn't industrialise Three locks holding the economy shut Immobile labour Workers could not leave the land — preventing the rise of a free labour market. Zero disposable income Surplus crops went to landlords, so the peasant class could not buy external goods — stalling retail consumer markets. Land as wealth Wealth was stored in land rather than reinvested into commercial innovation or banking systems. A colonial ryot switches from rice to indigo — a high-value, risky cash crop. Which mechanism from the lecture forced that choice? Lecture 7 A A free market signal: indigo prices rose B Zamindars demanded heavy cash rents and the British state required specific revenues — debts pushed cultivators toward cash crops C The guild mandated indigo over food D The Church's tithe schedule Key takeaways Seasons ran the economy; land was the core asset — wealth, power and stratification all grew from it. Feudal model: Crown → lords → knights → serfs , bound by permission, paid in crop shares. Zamindari: state → zamindars → ryots , paid in inflated rents and debt. Three locks: immobile labour, zero disposable income, land as wealth — the pre-industrial world could not break its own chains.

chapters.label: Land ownership
chapters.text: Module 2 · Lecture 10 — land ownership zoomed in Feudal Europe & the Zamindari , side by side Lecture 8 asked who owned the land. Lecture 10 puts the two answers on one table — and reads the human cost printed in the margins: low life expectancy, high infant mortality, and a world that could not innovate. 01 The two ladders One grew from inside; one was bolted on from outside Machine 03 — two land systems, side by side Feudal model Zamindari / colonial Feudal model — Western Europe Internal, organic development The Crown / King owns all land — ultimate authority Lords & Nobles granted land — owe military protection & produce Knights (vassals) granted land by lords — owe service Peasants & Serfs bound to the land — cannot leave, marry or move without permission Who decided what to produce: Decentralised and local — lords decide crops and labour; production follows survival needs and tradition. 02 The comparison ledger Six aspects — read them row by row Aspect Feudal model Colonial / zamindari Land ownership King grants land to nobles British government grants to zamindars Decision-making Decentralised — local lords Centralised, externally imposed Production basis Survival needs & tradition Global market demand (for Britain) Distribution Local, limited Extractive, global System origin Internal, organic development Externally imposed Labour status Serfs bound to the land Cultivators & tenants controlled 03 The cost ledger — life inside both systems No incentive, no income, no mobility No incentive to innovate No competition, no need to improve production methods or efficiency — innovation had no buyer. Low life expectancy 30–35 years, the direct arithmetic of harsh working conditions and limited resources. High infant mortality Lack of resources for the majority population — families could not afford to raise children. Labour immobility Workers could not move to pursue better opportunities — industrialisation needs mobile labour. No disposable income All surplus went to elites; peasants had nothing extra to invest or spend. Wealth stored in land only People invested in acquiring more land — not banking, commerce, or business. 04 The six critical insights What to carry into every later lecture Lecture 10 — the six insights 1. LAND AS CORE ASSET — wealth, status and power all grew from it 2. SOCIO-ECONOMIC INTEGRATION — land ownership decided social relationships, freedoms, entire life trajectories 3. LACK OF INNOVATION — no competition, no incentives, no disposable income → no new technologies 4. IMMOBILE LABOUR — bound labour made industrialisation impossible 5. EXTREME INEQUALITY — tiny elite held the surplus; the vast majority lived at subsistence 6. EXTERNAL CONTROL — the colonial system was imposed from outside, restructuring economies to serve distant powers Individual life, and the society it built The individual: lives revolved around agricultural seasons; social relationships were dictated by land ownership; freedom was restricted — movement, marriage and livelihood controlled by lords; survival depended entirely on agricultural success and the lord’s decisions. The society: a self-perpetuating hierarchy with clear class distinctions, social life intertwined with economic obligations, and little opportunity for upward mobility — until the guilds and craftsmen opened the next chapter. One sentence separates the two systems. Which is it? Lecture 10 A The feudal system used money; the zamindari used barter B The feudal system was decentralised, traditional and survival-based; the colonial system was centralised, externally imposed and market-oriented — but for foreign benefit C The feudal system had no hierarchy; the zamindari had kings D Both systems were identical in every respect Key takeaways Feudal = organic and decentralised (King → lords → knights → serfs). Zamindari = imposed and centralised (British state → zamindars → cultivators). The cost ledger: life expectancy 30–35, high infant mortality, no disposable income, immobile labour , wealth buried in land. Six insights — lead with land as core asset and close with external control ; they explain why this world could not industrialise.

chapters.label: Guild systems
chapters.text: Module 2 · Lecture 8 — the city's operating system Guild systems & early trade organizations For three centuries, if you wanted to weave, smith, brew or bake in a European town, you asked the guild first. It was employer, union, quality bureau, court and church all at once. 01 What is a guild? Mutual aid, protection, standards The definition An association of craftsmen or merchants formed for mutual aid and protection , and to maintain standards . Two families: Merchant guilds — the traders — and Craft guilds : blacksmiths, weavers, potters, hatters, goldsmiths, carpenters, and more. 02 History & rise From Rome's collegia to the craft explosion The timeline of the guilds Classical Rome → collegia: associations of merchants & artisans. Vanish in Western Europe after Rome's collapse. 1000–1150 AD → RISE OF MERCHANT GUILDS · innovation in agriculture (food surplus: three-field crop rotation, the heavy plough) · revival of long-distance trade · urbanization (growth of towns) · protection: merchants pooled resources against robbery, high transit tolls, arbitrary seizures by feudal lords 1100–1300 AD → CRAFT GUILDS · urban manufacturing & specialised crafts expand · weavers, blacksmiths, carpenters, goldsmiths… Throughout → guilds provided predictability and a social security net 03 Charters — permission on parchment The Weaver's Guild of London, 1155 Granted by King Henry II Guilds were established by charters from the city or the ruler. The Charter of the Weaver’s Guild of London (1155), granted by King Henry II : “Know ye that I have granted to the weavers of London to have their guild in London with all the liberties and customs which they had in the time of King Henry my grandfather; and so that none shall intermeddle within the city concerning their craft, unless he belong to the guild…” That guild exists to this day — as the Worshipful Company of Weavers . 04 Structure of the guild Apprentice → journeyman → master Machine 02 — the guild ladder · climb it Apprentice Journeyman Master Apprentice step 1 of 3 Pay Paid nothing Rights Learns skills — no ownership The catch Bound to a master; the hatters' rules fixed a term of no less than seven years — and only a freeman could take an apprentice at all Climb to Journeyman → 05 Functions of the guild Economic, social, religious, political Economic · Quality control — wardens searched all hats for sale; defects went before the Mayor of London for punishment · Training — the apprenticeship system itself · Price regulation & production control · Worker welfare · market reputation · regulated competition · Even daylight-only work — night work hid defects from inspection Social · religious · political · Social — care for the sick and elderly; burial and funeral benefits; support for dependents. The Guild of the Tailors (Lincoln, 1328): if a brother falls into poverty, “he shall have a penny every day from the common box” · Religious — patron saints and altars: St. Joseph for carpenters, St. Crispin for shoemakers · Political — guilds operated their own courts, settling commercial disputes; “guild wars”: craft guilds frequently launched political revolts against the merchant guilds A journeyman in 1250 wants to open his own hat workshop in London. Standing in his way, per the lecture, are… Lecture 8 A Nothing — journeymen were free to open shops B A masterpiece to produce, judged by other Masters — plus guild rules on who may take apprentices C A royal licence costing 250 rupees D A seven-year waiting list at the Worshipful Company Key takeaways Guild = craftsmen/merchants organised for mutual aid, protection, standards — merchant guilds 1000–1150 AD , craft guilds 1100–1300 AD . The ladder: apprentice (unpaid, learning) → journeyman (wages, any master) → master (workshop, apprentices — via the masterpiece ). Four function-faces: economic (quality, prices, competition), social (sickness, burial, poverty), religious (patron saints), political (own courts, revolts).

chapters.label: Life before machines
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 9 — the threshold Life before machines The Industrial Revolution arrives around the 1760s, in Great Britain. To feel what it shattered, imagine England around 1700: you want 100 shirts — and there are no factories, no power looms, no steam-powered production lines. 01 The world as it stood Agriculture the mainstay, guilds the rulebook Agriculture The mainstay of the population — most people, most fields, most hours. Hand work on the land, made viable by skill and sweat. Guilds Craftsmen worked in guilds — regulated professions and markets at the city level . Your 100 shirts would be slow, manual, skilled labour — produced under guild rules, workshop by workshop. 02 How did the system break? Two cracks: the agricultural revolution and the putting-out system The lecture's answer, in two lines How did the agriculture and guild system break, allowing the factories to exist? → the AGRICULTURE REVOLUTION → the PUTTING-OUT SYSTEM developed 03 The agricultural revolution Rotation, tools, and enclosure Four-field crop rotation Clover · barley · wheat · turnips — fields never exhausted, animals fed through winter, soil renewed in a cycle. Innovation in tools Jethro Tull's seed drill (1701) — seed sown in neat rows instead of scattered, yields up. …and then enclosure The legal earthquake that redrew the countryside — next step. 04 The enclosure movement Common land becomes private property — by Act of Parliament Before and after Before: the open-field system — a portion of land categorised as “common” , with grazing rights , and life that necessitated co-operation among the residents of the manor/village . Then: Enclosure Acts through Parliament — created legal property rights to land previously held in common; abolished communal rights ; consolidated small strips into massive private farms ; landowners built physical boundaries — fences, hedges, or stone walls . Before — open fields & commons THE COMMON — grazing rights, shared by all After — enclosed private farms MASSIVE PRIVATE FARM FARM II FARM III FARM IV fences · hedges · stone walls Not bloodless — the Midland Revolt, 1607 Enclosure riots. In the Midland Revolt (1607), thousands of peasants in Northamptonshire and Warwickshire — calling themselves “Diggers” and “Levellers” — organised to level enclosure fences . Easier to manage Land became easier to manage as a single economic unit Greater incentive For agricultural improvement — your farm, your profit Higher productivity More food available than ever before Labour released Some labour now available for non-agricultural work 05 The putting-out system Subcontracting around the guild — the first crack The bottleneck Labour was available (enclosure had seen to that). But the guild was the bottleneck: it held a monopoly on manufacturing , strictly limited the number of workers , set prices , and banned new technology . The workaround Merchants developed a method of subcontracting production : the merchant provided distributed raw materials to workers; the workers completed the work in their own homes or small workshops; workers were paid wages . This was the beginning of the breaking of the guild system — and the first sketch of the factory, drawn in cottages. Looming ahead, the lecture’s last word of the day: Machines — the Spinning Jenny, the Steam Engine. Module 3 is their story. Chain the causes: enclosure → food → factories. Which rung is the lecture's explicit link? Lecture 9 A Enclosure made farming romantic, so more people farmed B Enclosure consolidated strips and raised productivity — more food available, and some labour now free for non-agricultural work C Enclosure banned guilds directly D Enclosure created the seed drill Key takeaways Pre-industrial Britain: agriculture the mainstay , guilds regulating trades city by city. Agriculture revolution: four-field rotation , Tull’s seed drill (1701) , and enclosure — commons into private farms, resistance from the Diggers & Levellers (1607). Putting-out: merchants subcontracted raw materials → homes → wages — the guild system begins to break.

chapters.label: Why machines?
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 10 — the demand explosion Why did people begin using machines for production? Nobody woke up one morning and invented the factory out of curiosity. Labour had been freed, demand had exploded — and the old way of making things hit a wall made of human muscle. 01 Engine one — labour becomes available The agricultural revolution's gift From Module 3's opening The Agricultural Revolution (enclosure, rotation, the seed drill) had already done its work: availability of labour . Hands were leaving the countryside — the factories would be waiting for them. 02 Engine two — demand explodes Population and global trade, both compounding Population rise 5–6.5 million → 9–11 million 1700 → 1801. More mouths, and more buyers. Global trade rising £6.5M → £14.7M → £43.2M 1700 → 1760 → 1800. The export market multiplies over six-fold. Textiles accounted for 70% to 90% of all manufactured exports. Whatever transformed cloth-making transformed the economy. 03 Engine three — the old system's ceiling The putting-out system's limits of human muscle Where putting-out broke A de-centralized system : time and money spent moving raw materials to rural households and collecting finished goods. And beneath it all, the limits of human muscle . Productivity had to be increased — in the old system, it took four spinners to keep up with one weaver . 04 The production chain Where the machines would strike first Textile production chain — the machine map Raw cotton / wool the fibre Spinning fibre → yarn Jenny 1764 · Water Frame 1769 Yarn the thread Weaving yarn → cloth Flying Shuttle 1733 Cloth the product Put the lecture's three engines of mechanisation in order: why machines, why then? Lecture 10 A Invention first, then demand, then labour B Labour freed by the agricultural revolution + demand exploding (population 5–6.5M → 9–11M; trade £6.5M → £43.2M; textiles 70–90% of exports) + the putting-out system's muscle ceiling C Government policy alone D Cheap coal replacing expensive wood Key takeaways Three engines: freed labour + exploding demand (population, trade, textiles at 70–90%) + the putting-out ceiling . The chain: raw fibre → spinning → yarn → weaving → cloth — machines struck at spinning and weaving first. The ratio to remember: four spinners kept pace with one weaver — productivity had to rise.

chapters.label: Shuttle & Jenny
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lectures 10–11 — the first wave How machines transformed textile production Three machines, three inventors, three mobs. The shuttle, the jenny and the water frame doubled, then eightfold-ed, then industrialised the making of cloth — and resistance met every step. 01 Weaving — the Flying Shuttle (1730s) John Kay, 1733 — one weaver, twice the cloth The machine and its mathematics John Kay (1733) : one weaver could weave much faster and produce fabrics of any width alone — earlier, two workers were needed. Productivity: a single weaver produced twice as much cloth ; one weaver instead of 2 or 3 . The side-effect: a supply crisis — it took more spinners to supply one weaver. The response — 1753 An angry mob attacked — smashing his furniture and destroying his models. The problem lay with the weavers (whose livelihoods the machine threatened). Meanwhile factory owners quickly pirated his design — the “Shuttle Club” — to avoid paying royalty to John Kay. Kay fled to France. 02 Spinning — the Spinning Jenny (1760s) James Hargreaves, 1764 — eight threads at once The machine and its mathematics James Hargreaves — 1764 : a single worker turned a wheel to rotate multiple spindles at once . The traditional spinning wheel could spin only one single thread of yarn at a time. Productivity: an individual’s yarn production rose eightfold . The response — 1768 Problems with the spinners: a mob of local spinners broke into Hargreaves’ house in Blackburn — smashed his spinning jennies and forced him to flee the town . Machine 04 — the thread race · spinners vs weavers Before 1733 Flying Shuttle · 1733 Spinning Jenny · 1764 The old balance Equilibrium 4 spinners per weaver 1 2 3 4 threads spun in the time one weaver weaves The traditional wheel spins one single thread of yarn at a time. Slow, manual, skilled labour — four spinners keep one weaver fed with yarn. 03 The leap — the Water Frame (1769) Richard Arkwright: barber, wigmaker, and the birth of the factory From muscle to water Spinning had relied strictly on human muscle — limited in strength and speed. Richard Arkwright — 1769 (a barber and wigmaker by trade) patented the water frame : water-powered machinery . The machines were too heavy for homes — sparking the birth of the factory system — and enabled mass production of cloth . Cromford Mill — 1771 In Derbyshire — the world’s first water-powered cotton spinning mill . Presently the centerpiece of the Derwent Valley Mills UNESCO World Heritage Site . Birkacre Mill — 1777 Lancashire — burnt in the 1779 machine-breaking riots , as Lancashire became an epicenter of cotton production. 04 The Arkwright monopoly Patents, courts, and a cascade of mills Arkwright's rise and fall 1769 patents the water frame 1775 GRAND PATENT — second massive patent, covering the preparatory carding process 1785 monopoly BROKE — court invalidated and overturned the patents 1788 Arkwright-style water mills → 143 1800 300 of the 900 factories are massive, centralized "Arkwright-type" complexes → 300–400 workers each The pattern to carry forward Every machine in this chapter repeats one rhythm: productivity leaps → resistance from spinners & weavers → mass production → the factory system → working-class resistance . Hold that rhythm — the next chapter is what it did to geography, and the one after is what it did to people. Three inventors, three escapes: what happened to Kay (1753) and Hargreaves (1768) — and why is Arkwright the exception? Lectures 10–11 A All three fled to France B Mobs attacked Kay (smashing his models) and Hargreaves (smashing his jennies) — but Arkwright became a rich & successful businessman, his patents building a mill empire until courts broke them in 1785 C None faced resistance — the machines were welcomed D Kay and Hargreaves were executed; Arkwright fled Key takeaways Flying Shuttle (Kay, 1733) : 2× cloth, any width, one weaver — and a supply crisis in spinning. Spinning Jenny (Hargreaves, 1764) : multiple spindles, eightfold yarn . Water Frame (Arkwright, 1769) : water power, machines too heavy for homes → factory system ; Cromford 1771; patents broken 1785.

chapters.label: Trade routes
chapters.text: Module 2 · Live Session 3 — the long distance Trade routes & the Commercial Revolution The Silk Road was less a road than a relay of speeds — and the maths of those speeds decided what could be traded, by whom, and which cities got rich. 01 Three ways to move a bale of silk Speed decided the cargo Transport mode Primary engine Average daily speed Economic viability Overland caravan Camels / mules / horses 30–40 km / day High-value luxury only (silk, gems, incense) — due to high feeding costs River barge River currents / human towing 10–20 km / day (upstream) Bulk domestic goods (grain, stone, agricultural tax revenue) Ocean-going ship Monsoon winds / trade winds 100–150 km / day International bulk & luxury (spices, textiles, timber, ceramics) 02 Feel the maths Why the sea beat the camel for everything cheap Machine 03 — the Silk Road speedway · pick a mode, drag the days Overland caravan Camels / mules / horses River barge River currents / human towing Ocean-going ship Monsoon winds / trade winds Days of travel 30 days 3,000 – 4,500 km covered Economic viability: International bulk & luxury — spices, textiles, timber, ceramics. The wind is free; the ocean is a highway. Average daily speeds from the lecture: caravan 30–40 km/day · river barge 10–20 km/day (upstream) · ocean ship 100–150 km/day . 03 What the routes did to the world Power, faith, and ideas moved with the cargo Political power and conflict Strategic control of key mountain passes and desert oases — whoever held the choke points taxed the flow. Cultural and technological exchange Spread of faith — and new ideas . Goods travel with their makers’ gods, scripts and techniques attached. 04 The Commercial Revolution — Europe 11th century to the mid-18th: trade builds a continent Two headlines A European economy develops based on trade — 11th century AD until the mid-18th century. Italy : 1,00,000+ residents in Venice, Florence, and Milan. And beneath it, a new class: the rising urban merchant class — wealth became liquid , measured in money and goods rather than land — and the laws/policies began to be written by that urban merchant class. Connect it back Remember the agrarian world’s third lock — land as wealth ? The Commercial Revolution is where that lock starts to rust: once wealth is measured in money and goods , it can move, split, pool and multiply — land cannot. A merchant in Venice wants to ship 40 tonnes of ordinary grain to a domestic buyer, 600 km upriver. A rival wants to move 2 crates of gems 3,000 km overland. Using the lecture's speeds and viability logic, who has the cheaper per-kg journey? Live Session 3 A The gem merchant — luxury goods travel cheapest B The grain merchant — barges (10–20 km/day) exist precisely for bulk domestic goods; the caravan's feeding costs forbid cheap cargo C Both pay the same per km D Neither — grain never travelled in the pre-industrial world Key takeaways Three engines: caravan 30–40 · barge 10–20 · ship 100–150 km/day — speed sorted luxury from bulk. Routes carried more than goods: power (passes, oases) and culture (faith, ideas). The Commercial Revolution made wealth liquid — money and goods, not land — and merchant classes wrote the laws.

chapters.label: The water frame
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 15 — the factory is born The Water Frame & the birth of the factory The shuttle doubled weaving and the Jenny eightfold-ed spinning — but both still ran on human muscle. Richard Arkwright's water frame moved the power source to nature, and moved the worker out of the home. 01 Where we stand — and why machines were adopted Demand up, resistance loud, muscle still the engine Growing global demand Textile goods and rising populations needed more cloth than human hands could spin. The putting-out ceiling Home-based production depended on human labour with restricted productivity. Worker resistance Spinners and weavers protested against machines — grievances that would later feed the labour movement. 02 1769 — Richard Arkwright patents the water frame Barber and wigmaker by trade; industrialist by instinct The key transformation The water frame shifted the power source from human beings to natural resources — the first water-powered cotton spinning machine. It represented a fundamental change in production organisation : machines could run continuously without fatigue, drive heavier and more numerous machines at once, and hold productivity steady all day — roughly ten metres of cloth per hour , with any drop below that signalling a machine problem to repair. Machine 06 — the power ladder · three phases of energy Human muscle → 1769 Water power 1769 → Steam → next chapter The liberation (with a catch) Phase 2 · Water power Arkwright's water frame shifts the power source to nature: more energy than muscle, machines run continuously without fatigue, heavier and more numerous machines at once — but the mill must sit beside a constant, perennial stream that doesn't freeze in winter. 03 Production concentrates Mills follow the water — and workers follow the mills The location constraint · Mills needed constant, perennial water sources · Streams that didn’t freeze in winter — for year-round, 24/7 operation · Machines too heavy for homes → dedicated industrial spaces The factory, specified · 300–400 workers per facility · 25–40+ machines powered by water · Continuous operation for extended periods — mass production at unprecedented scale 04 Arkwright's business model Patents, mills, courts — and a cascade Machine 07 — the mill cascade · from one patent to 300 factories 1769 1771 1788 1800 143 143 Arkwright-type mills One year after the courts invalidated the patents, the floodgates open. The patent ledger, 1769–1785 1769 Initial patent — the water frame machine 1775 GRAND PATENT — covers the preparatory carding process too ↑ Other mill owners copy the technology; court cases fly both ways 1785 Patents INVALIDATED — the monopoly breaks Removal of restrictions → rapid expansion 1788: 143 large-scale water mills 1800: 300 massive centralised factories Cromford Mill — 1771 Derbyshire — the world’s first water-powered cotton spinning mill, strategically placed in the Derwent Valley . Today a UNESCO World Heritage Site . Birkacre Mill — 1777 Lancashire — and in 1779 the machine-breaking riots arrived: workers burned and destroyed mills (Arkwright’s included), seeing machines as symbols of their exploitation. 05 What the factory made — and what it cost Mass production up; the working class forms Achieved · Energy source moved from human power to renewable natural resources · Factory system development; mass production capabilities · New social divisions — factory owners vs working class ; wealth concentrating among industrialists Endured · Long working hours — 10–14 hours daily ; low wages despite rising productivity · Widespread employment of children in harsh conditions · A distinct working class emerges — demanding shorter hours, higher wages, better conditions Why exactly did the water frame — not the shuttle or the Jenny — give birth to the factory system? Lecture 15 A It wove cloth instead of spinning yarn B Water-powered machines were too heavy for homes — production had to move to dedicated industrial spaces with constant water, concentrating 300–400 workers per mill C The government required all spinners to register D It was cheaper than the Spinning Jenny Key takeaways Arkwright 1769 : power shifts from muscle to water — continuous, tireless, heavier machines; ~10 metres of cloth an hour. Cromford 1771 opens the factory era; patents (1769 + Grand Patent 1775) break in 1785 → 143 mills by 1788, 300 by 1800 . The trade: mass production and a new industrial class gained; 10–14-hour days, child labour, and the working class's birth paid for it.

chapters.label: Steam & Cottonopolis
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 12 — the liberation Steam & Cottonopolis Water power had a catch written into geography: fast-flowing rivers. James Watt's rotary steam engine erased the catch — and Manchester grew from a market town into Cottonopolis. 01 The limitation — geography and nature Water wheels only turn where rivers run fast Before steam Water-powered mills were dependent on geography and nature — they required fast-flowing rivers to turn water wheels . Which meant mills sat in rural / mountainous river valleys — away from consumer markets and ports . 02 Watt's rotary steam engine — 1781 Heat in, motion out — anywhere Heat energy burning fuel Pressurized steam the working fluid Mechanical work rotation, on demand James Watt’s rotary steam engine — patented 1781 — a mechanical device that converts heat energy into mechanical work by using pressurized steam. It broke the limitation. Geographical liberation Factories could now be built anywhere — and they relocated to urban centers closer to ports . Around them grew steam mill towns : towns organized around factories . 03 Manchester — Cottonopolis A town that reorganised itself around the mill Machine 05 — the Cottonopolis counter · Manchester’s mills, year by year 1802 1816 1853 108 108 massive cotton mills Cottonopolis at full roar — the town built around the factory. Population 1771 20,000 Population 1851 3,00,000 04 The inputs — coal and cotton Why here, why then Coal supply Coal was available nearby — the South Lancashire coalfield Bridgewater Canal — 1761 10 miles / 16 km — carried coal to Manchester Liverpool port Cotton arriving from across the seas What steam left behind Geographical liberation · steam mill towns · the rise of the factory system · the rise of the corporation (joint stock company) — and, gathering in the streets, the labor movement: the Luddites, et cetera . Next chapter. A mill owner in 1800 weighs two sites: a fast river in a mountain valley, or a coal-and-canal town near a port. After Watt (1781), what decides it — and what grew around the choice? Lecture 12 A Rivers still win — steam was only for mines B Steam broke the geography limitation: factories could be built anywhere and relocated to urban centers closer to ports — steam mill towns organized around factories C The guilds chose the sites D Parliament assigned each mill a town Key takeaways Water power was captive to geography — fast rivers, far from markets. Watt’s rotary engine (patented 1781) : heat → pressurized steam → mechanical work, anywhere. Manchester — Cottonopolis : 50+ (1802) → 43 (1816) → 108 mills (1853) ; population 20,000 → 3,00,000 ; coal + canal + port.

chapters.label: Phase One
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 13 — the answer from below The labor movement during the Industrial Revolution The factories had created a new class — and the class answered. From secret societies to a massacre to a half-freedom written into law: the working class learning to organise. 01 Why a movement at all? The factory's conditions built its own opposition Dangerous conditions Unguarded machines, dust, injury Long hours 12–16 hours a day Child labor Small hands, smaller wages Secret resistance Unorganized — from the 1760s The labor movement — the collective organisation of the working class to further their shared political and economic interests . Its tool: collective bargaining — the negotiation process between employers and a labor union (representing the workers) to set wages, working hours, and employment conditions . Its form: trade unions . 02 Phase 1 — secret resistance & the Luddite myth (1760s–1820s) Ned Ludd, the Combination Acts, and Peterloo The folklore first Ned Ludd — folklore about a young weaver’s apprentice who broke two knitting frames. His name became the flag for everyone who answered the machine with a hammer. 1760s Unorganized, secret resistance The first murmurs under the factory roof 1799–1800 The Combination Acts Outlaw trade unions and collective bargaining 1811–1816 The Luddite protests Smashing automated knitting frames and power looms — 'collective bargaining by riot' 1812–1813 The state answers in blood Frame Breaking Act 1812 — machine-wrecking a capital crime; 1813: seventeen Luddites executed 1819 The Peterloo Massacre 60,000 peaceful workers in Manchester; cavalry charges; 18 dead, hundreds injured Byron's protest, 1812 The British government prioritized industrial property over human lives — the Frame Breaking Act made machine-wrecking a capital crime, punishable by death. “Is there not blood enough upon your penal code?” — Lord Byron . In 1813, seventeen Luddites were executed under the new law. Peterloo, 1819. A peaceful crowd of 60,000 workers gathered in Manchester — demanding parliamentary reform . The cavalry charged the crowd: 18 people died and hundreds were injured. 03 Phase 2 — legalization and grand alliances (1824–1830s) Repeal, strikes, and the half-freedom of 1825 1824 Repeal of the Combination Act 35 statutes over 520 years — undone; a wave of strikes follows through late 1824 and early 1825 1825 Combinations of Workmen Act 'Statutory unions' legalized — but stripped of effective collective action: wages and hours only Read the 1825 Act like a lawyer Legalized : unions may exist — as “statutory unions”. Permitted : meeting and combining to discuss and agree upon their own wages, prices, or hours of work . Still illegal : combining to strike over machinery use , hiring/firing practices , or the number of apprentices a shop took on. Result: a drive toward underground and alternate methods . Sequence the state's four answers to worker organising: what came first, and what came last? Lecture 13 A Peterloo → Combination Acts → Frame Breaking Act → Repeal B Combination Acts (1799–1800) → Frame Breaking Act (1812) + executions (1813) → Peterloo (1819) → Repeal (1824) and the 1825 Act C Repeal first, then the Combination Acts D The 1825 Act preceded all violence Key takeaways The movement = collective organisation of the working class for shared political & economic interests — via collective bargaining and trade unions . Phase 1: secret societies → Combination Acts (1799/1800) → Luddites (1811–16) → Frame Breaking Act (1812) → Peterloo (1819) . Phase 2: Repeal 1824 → strike wave → 1825 Act : unions legal, but wages & hours only — everything else still illegal.

chapters.label: Phase Two
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 18 — the great repeal Phase Two: Legalization & Grand Alliances (1824–1830) From secret resistance to legal recognition — and then straight back to restriction. The most paradoxical half-decade in labour history, run by a tailor and a radical MP. 01 The repeal architects A tailor's files and an MP's bill Francis Place — the tailor Compiled extensive documentation of working-class conditions — the crucial evidence of workers’ hardships that made the argument for repeal. Joseph Hume — the radical MP Introduced the repeal legislation. Their combined case: the Combination Acts were the primary cause of industrial violence and labour disputes — legalise unions and the artificial tensions dissolve through improved communication. The market-based argument that won Wages, Place and Hume contended, are determined by natural laws of supply and demand — not by factory owners’ decisions alone. Legalising unions wouldn’t break the market; it would merely let the market speak. That economic logic — addressed to a Parliament of political economists — convinced enough members to support the repeal. 02 1824 — what the repeal actually did Not just two acts — thirty-five statutes, five centuries The 1824 repeal — scope Repealed: 35 separate statutes, passed over ~500 years (dating back to the 14th century) Included: the Laborer's Act of 1425 — which had banned collective bargaining among masons Legalised: • the right to form and join labour unions • collective bargaining over wages, hours, and working conditions • protection from conspiracy prosecution for organising or recruiting workers A watershed moment Centuries-old legal barriers to worker organisation — gone in one statute. Workers could no longer be prosecuted simply for combining or organising. The UK labour movement’s legal winter had ended. 03 The strike wave (late 1824 – early 1825) The unexpected consequence Where A massive wave of coordinated strikes swept Britain — shipping, textile mills (particularly Manchester), and the coal mines. Why owners caved An economic boom meant high market demand — factories could not afford idle machinery or closures, so wage demands were accepted. The number Coal miners secured wage increases of up to 80% — concrete proof of what unified action could achieve. 04 1825 — the Combinations of Workmen Act Passed within one year of the repeal: the doors close again What survived · Unions could legally exist — statutory unions, a historic first · Negotiation over wages and working hours remained lawful What was stripped away · No negotiation over machinery use, hiring/firing, or apprentice numbers · No pressure on non-union workers to join strikes or unions · Common law immunity removed — prosecution risk returned · Pressuring others to support labour actions: criminalised 05 The paradox — victory and defeat in one act Three consequences that shaped the next fifty years Machine — the phase-two ledger · tap a year 01 1799–1800 Combination Acts 02 1824 The Repeal Place & Hume strike down 35 statutes spanning ~500 years — including the Laborer's Act of 1425. 03 Late 1824–1825 The strike wave 04 1825 Combinations of Workmen Act 05 1825–1870s Legal stagnation The victory The repeal of 500 years of restrictive legislation, and unions’ first legal recognition — a watershed no amount of 1825 fine print could erase. The defeat The 1825 Act nullified much of the practical benefit — unions existed legally but lacked meaningful bargaining power, pushing organising underground again. The 1824 repeal was a watershed. How many separate statutes did it sweep away — and which medieval law went with them? Lecture 18 A 2 statutes — just the Combination Acts of 1799–1800 B 35 separate statutes over ~500 years, including the Laborer's Act of 1425 which had banned collective bargaining among masons C 500 statutes over 35 years D 12 statutes, none older than 1800 Key takeaways Repeal engineers: Francis Place (evidence) + Joseph Hume (legislation) — the wages-are-supply-and-demand argument carried it. 1824 legalised unions → strike wave (coal miners +80%) → 1825 Act legal-but-toothless: wages and hours only . The paradox: victory (500 years of bans repealed) and defeat (bargaining power stripped) — stagnation until the 1870s.

chapters.label: Empire & mercantilism
chapters.text: Module 3 · Live Session 4 — the global engine Growth of Britain’s empire & mercantilist policies The Industrial Revolution didn't happen in isolation in a single country. Its raw materials came from colonies; its goods sold back to them. The lecture closes the module by wiring Britain to the world. 01 Companies, not crowns How Britain's empire actually began The 1600s — a corporate land-grab Efforts to establish overseas settlements began in the 1500s . Then the 1600s : in America — British colonies in New England, Virginia, and Maryland : the Virginia Company of London established Jamestown in 1607 ; the Massachusetts Bay Company took New England; Maryland was granted to Cecilius Calvert (Lord Baltimore) . In the East, the East India Company began establishing trading posts in India in 1600 — leading, by the 1700s , to the 1757 Battle of Plassey . The kicker: early colonies were efforts of particular companies rather than of the English crown . 02 Mercantilism — the empire's operating system Raw materials in, manufactured goods out, British ships between The mercantilist loop The colonies · A source of necessary raw materials for England · Monopolies on their products — tobacco, cotton, indigo, & sugar — in the British market · Markets for British manufactured goods Britain · Processes raw materials into manufactured goods · All colonial trade conducted by British ships — the Navigation Act (1600s) · Excluded other countries from trading with its colonies — the flow was focused onto Britain 03 The Industrial Revolution, globalised No island industrialises alone The lecture's closing frame The globalization of the Industrial Revolution : it didn’t happen in isolation — not in a single country. The Industrial Revolution and the colonies : colonies supplied raw material and served as markets for manufactured goods . Recall the demand numbers from Lecture 10 — trade climbing to £43.2 million by 1800 — and you can see the empire inside the arithmetic. And so the course closes its first loop Rules and players — you have now watched both move at every scale: a student’s pocket money, a zamindar’s ledger, a guild’s masterpiece, a mill owner’s patent, a Luddite’s hammer, a company’s charter. Module 4 (History of Business, 1850–1950) and Module 5 (Indian Business History, pre-1947) will pick up the players’ thread: division of labour, scientific management, the rise of large corporations — and India’s entrepreneurs between the wars. Jamestown (1607) and the East India Company's trading posts (1600) share one surprising feature, per the lecture. What is it? Live Session 4 A Both were royal expeditions commanded by the crown B Both were efforts of particular companies rather than of the English crown C Both were religious missions D Both were financed by French investors Key takeaways The empire began as company business : Jamestown 1607, Massachusetts Bay, Maryland, EIC posts from 1600, Plassey 1757. Mercantilism: colonies = raw materials + captive markets ; trade on British ships (Navigation Act); rivals excluded . The IR was global from birth — colonies fed it raw material and bought its goods.

chapters.label: Phase Three
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 20 — the phase that changed the law Political action & legislative wins (1830s–1850s) Union power was still capped at wages and hours — so workers went national, went political, and went to Parliament. Some attempts failed spectacularly; some laws changed the world. 01 Where the movement stands Three phases, one arc Machine — the labour movement in three phases Phase One 1760s–1820s Phase Two 1824–1830 Phase Three 1830s–1850s Phase Three (1830s–1850s): Political action & legislation: national unions, the Tolpuddle test, the Factory Acts, and the Chartists. 02 Two attempts at a national union Both failed — both proved the demand NAPL — 1830 · National Association for the Protection of Labor — founded July 1830 by Irish unionist John Doherty · First attempt at a national trade-union centre; 10,000–20,000 members within 6–12 months · Textile workers, mechanics, blacksmiths, potters, miners under one umbrella · Failed by 1832 — internal disagreements and high fees (£1 per society, one shilling a member); published the United Trades Cooperative Journal (later Voice of the People ) GNCTU — 1834 · Grand National Consolidated Trades Union — founded February 1834 by Robert Owen , textile manufacturer & philanthropist · One mega-union for all British workers; core principle: cooperation over competition · Failed within months — internal splits, and workers’ suspicion of a founder who owned factories · Still: it proved national-level organisation was viable and wanted 03 The Tolpuddle Martyrs (1834) Lawful organising, punished anyway The Tolpuddle ledger — six men of Dorset 1833 Six agricultural laborers form the Friendly Society of Agricultural Laborers Wages cut from 9 → 7 shillings/week; they demand 10 shillings Law? Formation + wage talks were LEGAL under the Combinations Act of 1825 Charge Instead: the Unlawful Oaths Act of 1797 (built for naval mutinies!) — members took initiation oaths Verdict Convicted → 7 years' transportation to Australia 1834–35 Massive public protests 1836 Pardoned; sentences rescinded What Tolpuddle proved The government could not suppress lawful union activity using alternative legislation — the public would not stand for it. The pardon raised national awareness of workers’ rights and government overreach. The movement had learned to fight in the courtroom of public opinion. 04 The legislative wins Four laws that rebuilt the industrial world 1833 Factory Act First major workplace regulation. Children under 9 banned from textile mills; ages 9–15 capped at 8–12 hours/day — after parliamentary investigations recorded child workers describing 12–13-hour days. Government becomes responsible for worker protection. 1847 Ten Hours Act 10-hour limit for women and children/teenagers — the fruit of a 15-year movement. Supported, paradoxically, by landowners retaliating against the 1846 Corn Laws repeal (factory owners had pushed the repeal to cut food prices and wage demands; landowners answered by capping factory profits). 1848 Public Health Act Answers the cholera epidemic of 1846–47 and widespread pollution: air and water quality regulated in industrial cities — protecting workers and entire urban populations. 1838–48 The Chartist Movement Political democracy for workers: votes for all men, secret ballots, no property requirements for MPs. Its specific demands failed in its lifetime — but it connected the economic movement to political action and set the precedent for workers organising around democratic rights. 05 The movement divides — and the ceiling holds New Model Unions and the 1871 horizon New Model Unions (1850s) · Skilled workers organise separately — engineers, machinists, carpenters, bricklayers, smiths, millwrights, pattern makers · Amalgamated Society of Engineers (c. 1850s); strategy: negotiation over strikes · A move toward what would later be called “white-collar” — and a new skilled/unskilled divide What remained pending · Unions still limited to wages and working hours — hiring/firing, machine usage, other workplace issues remained out of bounds · Full legal recognition came only in 1871 , with new legislation recognising unions as fully legal entities Six agricultural labourers formed a legal Friendly Society in 1833 — and were transported to Australia for seven years anyway. Under which law were they prosecuted? Lecture 20 A The Combinations Act of 1825 B The Unlawful Oaths Act of 1797 — originally designed to suppress naval mutinies C The Framebreaking Act of 1812 D The Corn Law of 1815 Key takeaways National unions: NAPL 1830 (Doherty) and GNCTU 1834 (Owen) — both collapsed, both proved the demand for national organisation. The Tolpuddle Martyrs tested the state — prosecuted under the 1797 Oaths Act, pardoned by 1836; public opinion became a weapon. Legislative wins: Factory Act 1833 · Ten Hours Act 1847 · Public Health Act 1848 · Chartists 1838–48 — and full union legality only in 1871 .

chapters.label: Economic systems
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 21 — three answers to ownership Economic systems: Capitalism, Socialism, Communism The Industrial Revolution didn't just change how things were made — it forced the question of who should own the making. Three systems answered, in sequence: capitalism first, then socialism and communism as responses to what capitalism did to labour. 01 Capitalism — and why it rose first Ownership, machines, transport, ideology, law Machine — the system switcher · three answers to one question Capitalism Socialism Communism Capitalism Private ownership Who owns? Private individuals and businesses own the means of production — factories, tools, land, service institutions. Who decides? Supply and demand set prices and production; minimal government interference (laissez-faire). Why it rose Expensive industrial technology — steam machinery & boilers priced far beyond any artisan; only wealthy investors (capitalists) could finance industry Transport innovations — canals, Turnpike Trusts (1770s–1830s), railways (1830s–40s) — widened markets and demanded stock-market financing Free-market ideology — Adam Smith (1770s–1790s): unregulated markets maximise efficiency and wealth for society Legal innovations — the company as a legal entity separate from its owners (Companies Acts; 1956 & 2013 in India) The ownership precedent came early: the Agricultural Revolution's enclosures converted common lands into private property 100–150 years before industrialisation. 02 The infrastructure that made capitalism inevitable Canals, turnpikes, railways — and the stock market they demanded 1700s– Canals Cut transport costs; Manchester's coal arrived cheap 1770s–1830s Turnpike Trusts Parliament-chartered toll roads, better surfaces 1830s–1840s Railways Steam replaces horse-drawn boats; global market reach Every link demanded massive capital investment — which is precisely why stock markets and modern financing mechanisms grew alongside them. Raw materials in (coal from Manchester, cotton from America and India), finished goods out, worldwide. 03 The timeline of three systems A century of emergence, 1760s–1890s Systems × Industrial Revolution — the timeline 1760s–1790s Industrial Revolution begins; capitalism & free-market ideology emerge 1770s–1790s Adam Smith writes — laissez-faire economics 1770s–1830s Canal & road revolutions expand transport 1830s–1840s Railway mania; the labour movement gains momentum 1830s–1850s Socialism & utopian socialism answer capitalism 1850s–1890s Communism develops as the theoretical response to capitalist exploitation 04 No pure systems exist The modern economy is a mix Private ownership Capitalism's engine — most production, most innovation Public ownership of sectors Socialism's footprint — healthcare, education, utilities Community-based initiatives Communist elements — local resource management Why the mixing matters for a history course These systems emerged as distinct ideologies during industrialisation — but real-world economies require combinations of their principles to function: government regulation and safety nets, democratic participation alongside market mechanisms. That pragmatism is itself a historical outcome of the Industrial Revolution. Why did capitalism rise first, rather than socialism or communism? Lecture 21 A Because kings ordered it B Industrial technology was prohibitively expensive — only wealthy investors could finance it; transport revolutions demanded stock markets; Adam Smith's laissez-faire provided the ideology; and company law made ownership scalable C Because workers voted for it in 1776 D Because the guilds supported it Key takeaways Capitalism = private ownership , born from expensive technology, transport revolutions, Smith's ideology and company law — with the enclosures as precedent. Socialism = collective ownership via democratic pressure (Owen, Factory Acts, Chartists); Communism = Marx & Engels' stateless, classless society after class struggle. Timeline: capitalism 1760s–90s → socialism 1830s–50s → communism 1850s–90s — and no pure system survives in practice.

chapters.label: Systems & society
chapters.text: Module 3 · Lecture 22 — the human ledger Systems compared & the social-cultural impact Module 3's finale: weigh each economic system honestly, match it to the right sectors — then watch what industrialisation did to cities, families, classes, science, women and time itself. 01 Part 1 — the honest scorecard Every system buys its strengths with real costs Machine — the pros & cons board · pick a system Capitalism Socialism Communism Private ownership of businesses, corporations and means of production; prices and production controlled by supply and demand. Pros · Drives innovation — individual incentives create products and services · Economic freedom — consumer choice; anyone can start a business · High growth potential — 7–8%+ GDP growth in developing economies Cons · Wealth inequality — growth benefits are not distributed equally · Market failure — assumes consumers have information & negotiating power they often lack (healthcare, education) · Environmental degradation — air, water and industrial pollution Sector–system fit (Part 2 of the lecture) Capitalist systems fit sectors where consumers hold power and information · socialist systems fit essential services with information asymmetry (healthcare, education) · communist systems fit local resource management and environmental protection. 02 Part 3 — cities swelled beyond recognition Urbanisation, in two numbers Manchester 20,000 → 300,000+ 1760s → 1850s — a 13–14 fold increase in roughly 80 years London 1.1M → 4.7M 1801 → mid-19th century — overcrowding, poor sanitation, inadequate housing Work and family pulled apart Industrial work became divorced from household activities — employment moved to factories, not homes. Two distinct life spheres emerged: working life and family life . Family arrangements shifted as members worked different shifts in different places — and 10–12-hour workdays left minimal time for either. 03 Three new classes The pyramid the factories built Machine — the class pyramid · three classes, one revolution Bourgeoisie (industrial owners) Owners of factories, tools, land and services — they controlled the means of production. Middle class (the new class) Small factory owners & merchants · professionals (engineers, managers, carpenters) · skilled laborers · the educated with purchasing power and cultural preferences. Proletariat (working class) Factory workers earning minimal wages, working long hours under poor conditions. Why the middle class mattered: it demanded new cultural products and experiences — different leisure, theater choices and artistic interests from the working class — stimulating new literature, theater, fashion and the arts. Education and literacy let it engage with emerging cultural forms. 04 Science, awareness and the rise of the individual Reason takes the throne Science applied Discoveries went straight to work: the spinning jenny, flying shuttle, steam engine. Knowledge from observation and experiment replaced tradition. Kant: “Have courage to use your own understanding.” Darwin's observations of species variation became the theory of evolution. Social awareness Poverty, overcrowded housing, sanitation, exploitative conditions, women and child labour — addressed through novels (Dickens' Hard Times: “It was a town of red brick, or of brick that would have been red if the smoke and ashes had allowed it”), newspapers, and theater — feeding the Factory Acts (1833) and Ten Hours Act (1847). Individualism & women Self-reliance, personal ambition, individual freedom, the individual as consumer. Women moved into factory work — conditions worse than men's, but the shift led to 20th-century voting-rights and equality movements. 05 Standardisation of time Railways forced the clocks to agree Railways span regions every city keeps its own time — chaos Time standardised national, then global standards “Time is Money” society re-values temporal resources Transportation technology — especially railways — required uniform timekeeping across regions. Different cities had kept different times; standardisation enabled efficient transport and communication networks — the connective tissue of modernity . The lecture's sector–system fit: where do socialist principles belong? Lecture 22 A Everywhere — socialism always outperforms B Essential services like healthcare and education — where consumer power is limited and information asymmetry exists C Luxury goods — where brands matter most D Nowhere — markets handle everything Key takeaways Every system pays: capitalism buys growth with inequality and market failure ; socialism buys safety nets with taxes and slow growth ; communism buys equality with shortages . The social ledger: Manchester ×15, London ×4 , work and family split apart, three new classes , and a middle class that demanded culture. Science, social awareness, individualism — and “Time is Money” : the railways forced clocks, and clocks changed how society valued life itself.

chapters.label: Taylorism
chapters.text: Module 4 · Lecture 23 — management becomes a science Division of labour & Taylor’s scientific management Factories with thousands of unskilled workers needed methods that small workshops never had. Adam Smith split the task; Frederick Taylor timed it — and both raised a human cost. 01 Before the science — rule of thumb Intuition in a workshop of five to ten Pre-industrial management · Skilled artisans in small workshops — 5–10 workers · Management ran on “rule of thumb” — intuition and personal experience · No standardized rules for hiring, firing, or measuring productivity · Metrics subjective and inconsistent across workplaces The post-Industrial challenge · Factories packed thousands of unskilled workers into single facilities — one company employed 17,000 across sites · Managing 400–500 workers at a single site was unprecedented · Owners lacked any standard for a “fair day’s work” — the minimum acceptable output under proper conditions 02 Division of labour — Adam Smith, 1776 Break the job into eighteen pieces Machine — the pin factory · Adam Smith, 1776 One artisan, every step 18 distinct operations 1 worker 18 steps 1 pin / day One worker producing an entire pin alone could make only one pin per day. Specialization Workers focused on single tasks become skilled at them — learning each machine's peculiarities. Unskilled workers become task-specific skilled workers. Efficiency No more wasted time switching between tools, machines or workstations — time saved, focus on task completion increased. Mass production Combined with machinery, division of labour lets factories produce goods far faster and significantly cheaper. 03 Frederick Taylor — the stopwatch era “Father of Scientific Management” Taylor's core principles 1. RULE OF SCIENCE FOR EACH TASK — develop scientific rules for every job aspect from objective data, not intuition: which tools, how performed, time required, body motions needed 2. SCIENTIFIC WORKER SELECTION — hire on job requirements and abilities, not favoritism or nepotism; fitness and skills must match job demands 3. TIME & MOTION STUDIES — stopwatches break movements into seconds and minutes; unnecessary motions eliminated; time benchmarks set; objective performance standards based on research, not manager judgment Machine — the pig-iron gauge · Bethlehem Steel, 1898–1901 Before — the average worker 12.5 tons/day Schmidt, after time & motion direction 47.5 tons/day Taylor selected a physically fit, highly motivated worker — Schmidt — and directed him through precise movements and rest periods: “pick up the pig, walk, sit down and rest, walk.” Result: 12.5 → 47.5 tons loaded — roughly a 400% increase . 04 The critical limitations What the stopwatch couldn't measure Mechanistic view of humans Workers treated as extensions of machines; social needs, workplace relationships and emotional well-being ignored; motivation assumed to be money alone (piece-rate incentives). Monotony & alienation Repeating one standardized task across an 8–10-hour day created psychological boredom; workers lost engagement. Worker exploitation Time studies raised production quotas without proportionally raising wages — more output, lower relative compensation. Loss of autonomy Workers could not innovate or modify methods; planning separated from doing — managers decided, workers executed. No control over how to improve their own work. The labour-management fallout Scientific management increased efficiency and productivity — and deteriorated relationships between management and workers.
