The descriptive read — n = 50 mean x̄ = 73,340 miles median = 72,700 miles (25 fail before, 25 after) s = 24,849 miles ← huge spread mode = none — failures scattered, not clustered skewness ≈ 0+ — nearly symmetric 95% CI (σ unknown → t): x̄ ± E = 73,340 ± 7,076 = [66,264 , 80,416] miles Planning the follow-up study Target: ±5,000 miles at 95% confidence, planning σ = 24,849 (from this sample): n = (z·σ/E)² = (1.96 × 24,849 / 5,000)² = 95.26 → round up → ≈ 100 vehicles Cost per mile of precision: the mean cost of the s = 24,849 spread is width — the only cure is more data. The red-flag arithmetic 19 vehicles failed below 66,264 — earlier than the lower confidence bound — and 18 failed above 80,416 . The mean of ~73,000 hides a heavy tail of early failures , and those are the warranty-killer: averages comfort, distributions decide. Where the analysis goes next Supply side: production batches, material quality, plants, suppliers . Demand side: driver behaviour, terrain, climate, maintenance . Layer those variables on with regression or ML models and correlate against failure mileage — the univariate answer here is exactly where the next statistics course begins. 02 Check yourself One case, two instincts Metropolitan's interval is [66,264, 80,416] and 19 of 50 cars failed below 66,264. The managerial lesson is… Case file II · check A averages hide the early-failure tail — distributions drive warranty risk B the sample mean should be replaced by the mode C the confidence interval proves no quality problem exists D the sample size of 50 is already sufficient — no follow-up needed To promise ±5,000 miles at 95% confidence with planning σ = 24,849, Metropolitan needs… Case file II · check A n = (1.96 × 24,849 / 5,000)² ≈ 95.3 → 100 vehicles B n = 24,849 / 5,000 ≈ 5 vehicles C n = 1.96 × 24,849 ≈ 48,700 vehicles D n = 50 — the current sample suffices Key takeaways The descriptive read : x̄ = 73,340, median = 72,700, s = 24,849, no mode, skew ≈ 0 — spread is the headline, not the mean. The interval : x̄ ± 7,076 → [66,264, 80,416] ; 19 early failures below the bound are the warranty story. The follow-up : n = (1.96 × 24,849/5,000)² ≈ 95.3 → 100 vehicles for a ±5,000 promise — then supply- and demand-side variables explain the tail.

chapters.label: Hypothesis testing framework
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Hypothesis Testing — the framework Two claims, one verdict Interval estimates describe; hypothesis testing decides. Put a claim about μ on trial: the null hypothesis holds the status quo with its equality, the alternate carries what you hope to show — and the sample data delivers the only two verdicts statistics allows. 01 The two competing statements H₀ always carries the equality — =, ≥, or ≤ Null hypothesis — H₀ · A tentative assumption about a population parameter · The status quo, the current belief, the “nothing changed” · Always contains =, ≥, or ≤ · The statement we attempt to reject with sample evidence Alternate hypothesis — Hₐ · The opposite of the null — what the researcher hopes to prove · Carries the inequality: <, >, or ≠ · Becomes the conclusion only if H₀ is rejected · Sets the tail — and therefore where the evidence must land 02 Two ways to set the stage Research objective focus — or challenge an assumption Approach 1 — prove something new Put what you want to demonstrate in Hₐ . A new battery claims more life? Hₐ: μ > the old life , so the burden of proof sits on the new product — the data must actively contradict the status quo before the claim wins. Approach 2 — challenge a belief Put the existing belief in H₀ and let the sample try to knock it down. Quality control lives here: H₀: the process meets spec , and only strong evidence shuts the line. Common in verification and audit scenarios. 03 The three forms — and where the region lives Left · right · two-tailed — set by Hₐ's inequality The three forms — where does the rejection region live? tap a form Left-tailed test Right-tailed test Two-tailed test μ₀ — the claimed value rejection region · α H₀ μ ≥ μ₀ Hₐ μ < μ₀ Lecture example Emergency response: H₀: μ ≥ 12 min vs Hₐ: μ < 12 — meet the 12-minute goal? 04 The courtroom of errors Type I is priced (α) · Type II is the silent one The decision courtroom — tap a verdict presumption: H₀ is “innocent until proven guilty” Reject H₀ — but H₀ is true Type I error · P = α Reject H₀ — and H₀ is false Correct · power Fail to reject — H₀ is true Correct decision Fail to reject — but H₀ is false Type II error Type I error — the false positive You rejected H₀ when it was actually true: the innocent person goes to jail, a good batch is scrapped. Its probability is exactly α — the level of significance, and the error statisticians control directly. The court can only convict or acquit — never declare innocence. Same in statistics: we reject or fail to reject H₀; “accepting” the null is how Type II errors sneak into reports. A hypothesis is a testable statement, never a conclusion. 05 Check yourself Read the claim, name the test An online platform claims average test scores of 70; a researcher suspects the true average is lower. The hypotheses are… Lecture 27 · check A H₀: μ ≥ 70 vs Hₐ: μ < 70 B H₀: μ < 70 vs Hₐ: μ ≥ 70 C H₀: μ = 70 vs Hₐ: μ ≠ 70 D H₀: x̄ ≥ 70 vs Hₐ: x̄ < 70 A quality inspector concludes a process is out of control when it was actually meeting spec. This is… Lecture 27 · check A a Type I error — probability α B a Type II error — probability α C a correct decision D a Type I error with probability β Key takeaways H₀ holds the equality (=, ≥, ≤) and the status quo; Hₐ carries the inequality and the research hope. The tail follows Hₐ. Three forms: μ ≥ μ₀ vs μ < μ₀ (left) · μ ≤ μ₀ vs μ > μ₀ (right) · μ = μ₀ vs μ ≠ μ₀ (two-tailed). Type I = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α, controlled). Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ — the silent error. The only verdicts are reject and fail to reject — “accept” is not a statistical word.

chapters.label: Why marketing?
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 1 Why marketing? You're already inside it Marketing is a comprehensive business discipline that extends far beyond selling products or creating advertisements — it is understanding customer needs, analyzing how people make purchasing decisions, exploring brand preferences, and enabling businesses to create meaningful value. Before this course asks you to define marketing, it asks you to notice it. Every phone you chose, every dish you ordered, every brand you keep coming back to — each is the visible end of a discipline that studies needs, decisions, preference and value . This opening chapter sets the frame: what marketing really means, where it already touches your day, and what you will be able to do by the end. 1 What marketing really means Four beats — and none of them is 'selling' What marketing really means — four beats Lecture 1 · the definition surface 1 Beyond selling 2 Reading decisions 3 Brand preference 4 Creating value Beyond selling Marketing is not limited to selling or product promotion. Play Next Reset Beat 1 of 4 · Beyond selling — Marketing is not limited to selling or product promotion. Lecture 1 · the shift The discipline moves from transacting sales to creating value : understanding consumer behavior and decision-making, and explaining why customers prefer certain brands over competitors. Selling is one visible slice; understanding is the whole base. 2 Marketing in everyday life You were a consumer long before you were a student of consumers Marketing permeates all aspects of daily consumer experience. The lecture names five surfaces — check which ones you have already touched today: Mobile devices and technology Clothing and fashion choices Food and dining preferences Mobile applications and digital platforms Brand trust and loyalty decisions 3 Where this course takes you Six learning objectives 1 How companies identify and analyze customer needs 2 Product and service design strategies 3 Pricing strategies and value determination 4 Brand building and development 5 Effective communication and marketing messaging 6 Methods for establishing and maintaining long-term customer relationships Course significance The aim is to equip you to recognize and analyze marketing in your everyday life , while building a comprehensive understanding of marketing as a critical business discipline within the BAS program in management and technology . Key takeaways Marketing is not limited to selling or product promotion — that is the first and most repeated correction of Lecture 1. Its real work: understanding consumer behavior and decision-making , and why customers prefer certain brands over competitors. The destination is creating value , not just transacting sales. Marketing already permeates your devices, clothes, food, apps and brand loyalties — this course trains you to see it . Six objectives ahead: needs analysis, product & service design, pricing & value, brand building, communication, and long-term relationships.

chapters.label: Anticipation
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 2 Anticipation — see the turn before it comes Three giants — BlackBerry, Hertz, Blockbuster — had customers, revenue and reputation. What they lacked was marketing's core function: anticipating consumer needs and market evolution before the market moved. The lecture opens with its fundamental concept: anticipation . Each case below is the same story in a different industry — a dominant player reading today perfectly, and tomorrow not at all. Run each machine and watch the same pattern draw itself. 1 Three declines, one pattern BlackBerry · Hertz · Blockbuster — trace each fall event by event Three giants, one missing skill Lecture 2 · anticipation BlackBerry Hertz Blockbuster BlackBerry the keyboard everyone trusted share price · schematic time → 2007 2008 2010 End 2007 · Apple launches the iPhone. The stock price begins a gradual decline. Play Next Reset BlackBerry · event 1 of 4 — The stock price begins a gradual decline. 2 The pattern of organizational decline Gradual drop, then the cliff — unless someone pivots first The decline curve Lecture 2 · pattern sudden collapse initial gradual performance drop anticipators pivot before the cliff unable to anticipate → rapid market exit 1 · The gradual drop Performance erodes slowly at first — easy to explain away, easy to miss. 2 · The pivot window Organizations that anticipate market changes pivot successfully before the sudden decline. 3 · The sudden collapse Those unable to anticipate face a rapid market exit — the cliff always arrives faster than the slope. 3 The definition that follows Marketing's core function, stated plainly Marketing is the function that enables organizations to anticipate consumer needs and market evolution . Success requires understanding not only current consumer requirements but also predicting future needs and demands. Anticipation allows companies to create products consumers will value — before competitors do . Key takeaways BlackBerry: the stock declined after the iPhone (2007), hit bottom in 2010, deepened with Android (2008) — bankrupt for failing to anticipate the shift . Hertz: Uber ($17 billion valuation) brought an asset-light model — outsourced drivers and vehicles — against an owned fleet's capital and maintenance costs; Hertz exited the global market by 2018 but remains operational in southern India. Blockbuster: Netflix moved from DVD rentals to personalized recommendations (2002) and streaming (2012); the CEO dismissed Netflix as non-competitive — bankruptcy followed as OTT disrupted the industry. The decline pattern: gradual drop → sudden collapse ; anticipators pivot before the cliff, non-anticipators exit fast. Marketing's core function is to enable organizations to anticipate consumer needs and market evolution — and to build what consumers will value before competitors do.

chapters.label: Top line & bottom line
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 2 The top line & the bottom line Marketing's financial argument in two numbers: revenue generated through sales, and the profit that remains after cost. The lecture grounds both in a café selling cold coffee. Every organization lives on two metrics. The top line is revenue — the total money earned through sales. The bottom line is profit — sales minus cost. And the lecture's fundamental principle links them in one direction only: Top line Revenue generated through sales — the total money earned by the organization. Bottom line Profit, calculated as Sales minus Cost. The principle There must be a top line (revenue) for there to be a bottom line (profit). 1 The café's cold coffee, priced and counted ₹120 a glass · 80 glasses a day · ₹70 a glass to make The cold-coffee P&L — run the café yourself Lecture 2 · price ₹120 · 80 glasses · cost ₹70 Price per glass ₹120 Glasses a day ₹80 Cost per glass ₹70 Top line · revenue ₹9,600 price × volume Total cost ₹5,600 cost × volume Bottom line · profit ₹4,000 revenue − cost ■ cost share · ■ profit share of the top line ₹120 × 80 − ₹70 × 80 = revenue ₹9,600 − cost ₹5,600 = profit ₹4,000. Back to the lecture's café The lecture's run: ₹120 × 80 − ₹70 × 80 → revenue ₹9,600 , cost ₹5,600 , profit ₹4,000 . Why marketing sits upstream of profit Marketing ensures steady revenue streams , directly enabling profit generation and organizational financial success. No marketing, no customers; no customers, no top line; no top line — and the bottom line never arrives. ₹120 × 80 glasses = ₹9,600. In the lecture's language, that number is the café's… Lecture 2 · concept check A bottom line B top line C profit D cost Key takeaways Top line = revenue from sales; bottom line = sales − cost. The café: ₹120 × 80 = ₹9,600 revenue; ₹70 × 80 = ₹5,600 cost; ₹4,000 profit. There is no bottom line without a top line — the dependency runs one way. Marketing's financial job is to keep the top line steady — profit generation follows.

chapters.label: Marketing vs selling
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 2 Selling the pen vs understanding the hand Selling pushes a finished product and its attributes. Marketing begins by understanding consumer needs before the product is even presented. The lecture's humble prop — a pen — carries the whole distinction. 1 The pen test One pen, two completely different postures One pen, two postures Lecture 2 · the pen test Sales-dominant Marketing — ask first Push the product's attributes Selling focuses on pushing products to consumers after creation — so the pitch is all product: writes flawlessly black color good grip improves exam marks Now ask the four questions instead Sales-dominant: push the pen's attributes — after the product already exists. Lecture 2 · why asking wins Understanding customer needs before presenting the product ensures better fit — and more successful sales outcomes . The pen never changed; the sequence did. 2 The definition Understand → create → communicate → deliver Understand consumer needs and preferences Create value through product or service development Communicate value to consumers Deliver value through satisfactory transactions What happens when value lands When value is successfully delivered, customers become advocates — they speak positively about the brand and generate repeat business and revenue . Advocacy is delivered value, amplified. 3 Marketing in the wild — or is it sales? Five marketing moves and one sales move, straight from the notes Spot the marketing Lecture 2 · six moments from the notes ₹1 shampoo sachets Smaller sachets, for one rupee, targeting value-conscious consumers. 20% off at a restaurant A restaurant runs a 20% discount. Iced-coffee study A brand studies student preferences for iced coffee. Zomato's timed notifications Time-targeted, humorous notifications about food deals. Chocolates at the billing counter Chocolates kept near the billing counter. The laptop pitch A salesperson convinces a customer to buy a laptop. Marketing Sales Reset answered 0/6 · correct 0 Pick an activity, then call it Marketing or Sales. 4 Marketing → sales The relationship, stated precisely Sales is the transaction that results from successful marketing. Marketing does creates awareness, builds desire, communicates value — then sales completes the transaction. Together both are essential — but marketing precedes and enables sales. The order customer-centric understanding comes first; product development follows. 5 Where the course goes next Keep a repository of notes as you go Upcoming lectures take up the evolution of marketing — how concepts and practices developed over time — and the fundamental consumer-behavior triad of need vs want vs demand : distinguishing customer requirements from desires, and desires from actual purchasing behavior. You are encouraged to maintain a repository of notes on brands, organizations and marketing concepts encountered throughout the course, for practical application and future reference. “Do you prefer ballpoint, pilot, or ink pens?” · “What is your budget?” · “Fine or broad nib?” — this opening is… Lecture 2 · concept check A selling B marketing C promotion D distribution Key takeaways Selling pushes products after creation and leans on attributes; marketing starts with understanding consumer needs before the product exists. The pen: sales says writes flawlessly, black, good grip, improves exam marks ; marketing asks ballpoint or ink? budget? fine or broad nib? which color? Marketing = understand → create → communicate → deliver value — and delivered value turns customers into advocates. The lecture's marketing sightings: ₹1 shampoo sachets, 20% discounts, iced-coffee research, Zomato's notifications, chocolates at the billing counter — the laptop persuasion alone is sales. Sales is the transaction that results from successful marketing — marketing precedes and enables it.

chapters.label: Definitions
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 3 What marketing is — definitions & perspectives An outside-in approach that starts with understanding customer needs rather than simply selling products: creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers, clients, partners, and society. American Marketing Association · the theoretical definition “Marketing is the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating value, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large .” The business perspective translates the AMA definition into daily work. Marketing is identifying and meeting human and social needs ; it is making lives better by making better things ; it is connecting with consumers — the Apple CEO's perspective. The stories below are that definition, wearing different logos: Google Products and services that are relevant and required by consumers — effectively connecting with target audiences. IKEA Revolutionized furniture through DIY — quality, aesthetically pleasing furniture you assemble yourself, solving the problem of tedious furniture installation. Urban Ladder & PepperFry Captured an untapped Indian market by recognizing that modern consumers move frequently between cities and don't want furniture for generations — convenient, economical solutions. Uber & Ola Replicated the traditional agency model in digital format — drivers now receive 25–30 bookings daily instead of 1–2 through traditional channels. Apple iPod · Steve Jobs “Marketing is about meeting needs profitably” — great products combined with business viability. Seth Godin Marketing is not about selling more products but making better things that create genuine value for consumers. 1 Outside-in vs inside-out The distinction that separates marketing from selling — again, with arrows Two directions, two disciplines Lecture 3 · outside-in vs inside-out Outside-in · marketing Inside-out · selling MARKET consumers · needs · wants ORGANIZATION research · strategy · product needs · wants · market dynamics → Outside-in — gather information from the market about consumer needs, wants and market dynamics, then bring this knowledge into the organization. Both are essential and interconnected — marketing cannot succeed without sales, and sales cannot succeed without marketing insights. Key takeaways AMA: marketing is the activity, set of institutions and processes for creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value — for customers, clients, partners, and society at large. Business view: identify and meet human and social needs · make lives better by making better things · connect with consumers. Outside-in (marketing): gather market information — needs, wants, dynamics — and bring it into the organization. Inside-out (selling): push a finished product out through retailers, distribution, online. The stories: Google (relevance), IKEA (DIY), Urban Ladder & PepperFry (frequent movers), Uber & Ola (25–30 bookings vs 1–2), Jobs (“meeting needs profitably”), Godin (“better things”). Marketing cannot succeed without sales, and sales cannot succeed without marketing insights — interconnected, both essential .

chapters.label: The marketing system
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 3 Industry ↔ market — a system of four flows Zoom out from definitions and marketing becomes a system: sellers on one side, buyers on the other, and four flows constantly crossing the gap between them. The framework has two core components. The industry is a collection of sellers ; the market is a collection of buyers . Between them run four key flows — two going out, two coming back: Communication From industry to market — about products, offers, and promotions. Goods & services Tangible offerings from industry to market. Money Payment from consumers back to sellers. Information Market feedback that helps organizations redesign and refine products. 1 Run the exchange Highlight each flow, or let the machine cycle all four The marketing system, alive Lecture 3 · four key flows INDUSTRY a collection of sellers MARKET a collection of buyers communication ↑ goods & services money · information Communication Goods & services Money Information Play Next Reset Flow 1 of 4 · Communication (industry → market) — products, offers and promotions flow from industry to market. Why the return flows matter The money flow pays for everything — but the information flow is what keeps the system alive: market feedback is how organizations redesign and refine products. A system with only outbound flows is a broadcast, not a market. Key takeaways Industry = collection of sellers ; market = collection of buyers . Outbound: communication (products, offers, promotions) and goods & services . Inbound: money (payment from consumers) and information (feedback for redesign and refinement). The four flows make marketing a system , not a megaphone — value travels both ways.

chapters.label: What can be marketed
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 3 Ten things you can market Marketing extends far beyond tangible products — from goods and services all the way to persons, places, properties, organizations, information and ideas. The lecture's list is deliberately surprising. Goods are only the first of ten marketable entities — and the further down the list you go, the less the offering looks like a “product” at all. Explore each entity; the examples are all from the notes. 1 The entity explorer Goods → ideas: click through all ten The ten marketable entities Lecture 3 · Kotler's shelf Goods physical products Services deeds & expertise Experiences memories, not features Financial services the card as gateway Persons trust precedes product Places destinations as brands Properties real estate & status Organizations institutions market themselves Information rankings as credentials Ideas concepts that connect Goods physical products Apple iWatch — tangible products with specific features. explored 1 of 10 entities Reset Why this list matters When American Express markets an experience rather than a card, when Rajasthan Tourism markets a place through people, when HBS markets an organization through legacy — each proves the same point: marketing is the discipline of creating and exchanging value, whatever form the offering takes. Key takeaways The ten entities: goods, services, experiences, financial services, persons, places, properties, organizations, information, ideas . Experiences: Imagica sells happiness and memories; Sunburn sells the festival, not the setlist; Coca-Cola's “Make a Friend” connected India–Pakistan vending machines. Persons: The Rock's Papatui, Oprah's skincare, Hrithik's HRX, Virat Kohli, Kriti Sanon's Hyphen — trust in the person precedes the product . Properties: World Towers (name, location, facilities), Trump Towers (legacy), The Camellias (₹85–100 crore; ambience, views, amenities, status). Information & ideas: NIRF rankings and ACSB accreditation as credentials; Zomato's “Hungry” New Year idea and Blinkit's “Food mangoge, do minute mein dunga” vs “Kheer mangoge, kheer dengunge” .

chapters.label: Need · Want · Demand
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 3 Need → want → demand Three interconnected concepts that explain every purchase: the requirement that pre-exists, the object it attaches to, and the purchasing power that turns desire into behavior. Need A basic human requirement — biological or fundamental (food, shelter, clothing). It pre-exists naturally; marketers do not create needs. Want A need directed toward a specific object — shaped by marketing, culture and personal preferences. Hunger becomes a want for pizza, tandoori chicken, or vada pao. Demand A want backed by the ability to pay — the conversion of desire into actual purchasing behavior. 1 Hunger, ₹20, and the making of demand The lecture's food triad, played out step by step Hunger, ₹20, and the making of demand Lecture 3 · the triad in motion NEED · hunger wallet · empty Pizza hidden Tandoori chicken hidden Vada pao hidden The need. Hunger strikes. Needs are basic human requirements — food, shelter, clothing. They pre-exist naturally, and marketers do not create them. Play Next Reset Step 1 of 4 · The need — Hunger strikes. Needs are basic human requirements — food, shelter, clothing. They pre-exist naturally, and marketers do not create them. 2 The Starbucks check Same want, different cities — only one becomes demand Tier 1 vs Tier 3 Lecture 3 · ability to pay Consumers in a Tier 3 city may want Starbucks coffee exactly as much as consumers in a Tier 1 city. But only in Tier 1 cities do they have the ability to pay ₹300 for a coffee — and that is what creates demand . The want is universal; the demand is economic. 3 What the marketer controls Three honest lines of authority Cannot create Needs — they pre-exist; marketers recognize rather than create them. Can create & shape Wants — attaching needs to specific objects and solutions. Can influence Demand — through pricing, availability, and promotion. Key takeaways Need : basic human requirement — food, shelter, clothing. Pre-exists naturally; marketers do not create it. Want : a need attached to a specific object — pizza, tandoori chicken or vada pao — shaped by marketing, culture, personal preference. Demand : want + ability to pay. With ₹20, demand is limited to vada pao; with more money, all three become possible. Starbucks: the want exists in Tier 1 and Tier 3 cities alike — ₹300 of purchasing power is what turns it into demand. The marketer's authority: recognize needs, shape wants, influence demand through pricing, availability and promotion.

chapters.label: Needs & demand states
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 3 Five needs, eight demand states Under every stated request lie four deeper layers of need — and every market sits somewhere on a spectrum from negative demand to unwholesome demand. Reading both correctly is the marketer's diagnostic skill. 1 The five types of consumer needs A car purchase, dissected layer by layer Five needs under one car Lecture 3 · types of consumer needs Stated Real Unstated Delight Secret Stated need “I want a car” What the customer explicitly asks for. The deeper the layer, the less the customer says it out loud. Stated need — “I want a car”. What the customer explicitly asks for. 2 The eight demand states From actively-avoided to socially-unwanted — click each state The eight demand states Lecture 3 · click a state 01 Negative 02 Non-existent 03 Latent 04 Declining 05 Irregular 06 Full 07 Overfull 08 Unwholesome Negative demand Consumers actively avoid the product — and may even pay to prevent it. dentist appointments purchasing ad-free music subscriptions Negative demand — Consumers actively avoid the product — and may even pay to prevent it. Examples: dentist appointments, purchasing ad-free music subscriptions. Lecture 3 · key principles • Needs are pre-existing ; marketers recognize rather than create them. • Wants and demands are malleable — they can be shaped through marketing strategies. • Successful marketing requires understanding all types of needs and demand states . • Marketing must address customer needs profitably to be sustainable. • The most effective marketing connects consumers with products through meaningful ideas, experiences, or emotional connections — not direct product promotion. Paying extra for an ad-free music subscription is the lecture's example of… Lecture 3 · concept check A negative demand B latent demand C full demand D irregular demand Key takeaways Five need types: stated (“I want a car”), real (low operating costs), unstated (service & warranty), delight (built-in GPS), secret (status symbol). Eight demand states: negative → non-existent → latent → declining → irregular → full → overfull → unwholesome . Signature examples: dentist appointments (negative), BlackBerry Key2 (non-existent), better cameras (latent), floppy disks & CDs (declining), ACs & seasonal fruits (irregular), OTC drugs (full), bread & milk (overfull), cigarettes (unwholesome). Needs pre-exist — marketers recognize them; wants and demands are malleable . Marketing must address needs profitably , and connect through ideas, experiences and emotion rather than direct product promotion.

chapters.label: The closed system
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 4 The consumer mind is a closed system By default the mind recycles familiar options, known brands and established habits. Drowning in information overload, it opens only when something triggers genuine interest — and marketing is the discipline of engineering that trigger. Consumers are exposed to countless advertisements and brands daily . To survive the noise, the mind selectively opens only when something creates a compelling reason to consider alternatives. Lecture 4 turns this into one clean, measurable relationship: 1 The linear law of interest and openness X-axis: openness to receive information · Y-axis: interest in the product Open the closed system Lecture 4 · interest × openness Slide the consumer's interest 0 Play Reset openness to receive information → interest ↑ the linear law — interest and openness rise together CLOSED Interrupts Promotional offer Celebrity endorsement Limited-time deal Exclusive collection The mind recycles familiar options, known brands, established habits. Interest 0 — the system is closed. Interest 0 · Openness 0 — the linear law holds. Mind: CLOSED. The key principle, verbatim “If a consumer is interested in something, they will be open to learning more about it. Conversely, openness to information indicates underlying interest.” This relationship remains consistently linear across different consumer segments — and both conditions (interest generation + information receptivity) must be met simultaneously to move from a closed system to an open one. 2 Breaking the loop Every consumer has a unique breaking point Every consumer has a breaking point — a threshold at which they become willing to explore beyond established preferences. Marketing efforts serve as interrupts that break the habitual loop and create openness to new possibilities. The lecture names four: promotional offers, celebrity endorsements, limited-time deals, and exclusive collections . You fired all four in the machine above. The critical distinction Marketing always starts with the customer, not the product . Products are essential for business operations — but understanding and opening the consumer's closed system is the prerequisite for successful marketing efforts. Key takeaways The mind is a closed system by default : familiar options, known brands, established habits — with resistance driven by information overload. Openness (X) and interest (Y) rise linearly and together ; both conditions must be met simultaneously. Every consumer has a unique breaking point ; marketing's interrupts — offers, celebrities, limited drops, exclusives — crack the loop. Interested → open; open → interested. The law holds across consumer segments . Marketing starts with the customer, not the product .

chapters.label: The business value
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 4 The business value of marketing Organizations run on two financial metrics — and marketing is the engine of the first one. Every organization, regardless of its nature, needs revenue to keep functioning. Top line (revenue/sales) The total income generated from selling products or services — the number of products sold multiplied by their selling price. Bottom line (profit) The net income remaining after deducting costs from revenue — Revenue minus Total Costs. The critical relationship Without a top line (revenue), there cannot be a bottom line (profit). Every organization — including NGOs and social enterprises — requires revenue to sustain operations, pay employees, and continue functioning. 1 The four levers Pricing, product, promotion, distribution — working together The marketer's four levers Lecture 4 · the role of marketing Pricing · price the offering Product · develop the product Promotion · communicate the value Distribution · put it within reach Consumer demand created by marketing Top line products sold × selling price Bottom line revenue − total costs schematic — the point is the dependency chain, not the decimals Play all four Reset No levers pulled — without a top line there is no bottom line. 2 Two fundamental approaches The same inside-out / outside-in distinction, from the business side Inside-out · sales • Focuses on what the organization has produced or created. • Pushes existing products to consumers. • Centers on transaction completion. Outside-in · marketing • Begins with understanding consumer needs, desires, and preferences. • Conducts market research to gather consumer insights. • Focuses on relationship building rather than immediate transactions. Key takeaways Top line = products sold × selling price ; bottom line = revenue − total costs . No revenue → no profit — true for every organization, NGOs included : revenue sustains operations and pays employees. Financial success depends on marketing's ability to generate revenue across pricing, product development, promotion, and distribution — together creating consumer demand and driving sales. Inside-out pushes what was already made; outside-in begins with the customer's needs, desires and preferences.

chapters.label: The chai example
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 5 One chai, three prices , three values Customer perceived value is not merely the price printed on a product — it is a calculation made in the consumer's mind. The lecture's opening proof is a cup of tea sold at three very different prices. The same tea. Three contexts. The roadside cup costs ₹20 , the café cup ₹250 , the airport cup ₹500 — and no one is being cheated at any of the three counters. What changed is not the product; it is the consumer's situation, and therefore the value computed in their mind . 1 The three cups Pick a context — the cup never changes Same cup, three contexts Lecture 5 · the chai example Roadside tea ₹20 Café tea ₹250 Airport tea ₹500 the product never changes perceived value · context 1 of 3 ₹20 Roadside tea Economical option, suitable for casual consumption. Play Next Reset Roadside tea, ₹20 — Economical option, suitable for casual consumption. Same product, different perceived value. The lecture's point, stated exactly Customer perceived value is a calculation made in the consumer's mind based on the benefits received minus the costs incurred . The value is highly subjective and contextual , varying based on individual situations and circumstances. The same product carries different perceived values depending on the consumer's context and needs. Key takeaways Roadside tea ( ₹20 ): economical, casual. Café tea ( ₹250 ): business meetings, ambiance, impression management. Airport tea ( ₹500 ): no other options, or traveling. CPV is computed in the mind — benefits received minus costs incurred — not read off a price tag. Value is subjective and contextual : it varies person to person, situation to situation. Context matters even when the product is identical — this cup is Lecture 5's anchor example for everything that follows.

chapters.label: The value formula
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 5 CPV = Benefits − Costs The theoretical framework behind the chai: customer perceived value is a mental ledger of four kinds of benefits against direct and abstract costs — and organizations can move either side of the equation. The formula Customer Perceived Value = Benefits − Costs. The insight Value is calculated in the consumer's mind — benefits extend beyond the physical product, and costs extend beyond the price. 1 The balance machine Toggle benefits and costs; watch value tip The CPV balance Lecture 5 · benefits − costs Benefits — toggle on/off ✓ Psychological ✓ Functional ✓ Economic ✓ Extended psychological Costs — toggle on/off ✓ Direct price ✓ Time Effort Psychological stress Disposal B 4 C 2 CPV = B − C = +2 Ice cream: walk to the store Ice cream: order by app Reset Benefits 4 − Costs 2 = CPV +2. Value tips toward the customer. Four benefits on the left pan, price and time on the right — CPV starts positive. Toggle chips to move the scale. 2 The four benefits — and their ceilings Three benefits hit limits; one never does Psychological benefit Limited by the maximum warmth a jacket can provide. Functional benefit Constrained by practical design limits — and too many features risk cognitive overload. Economic benefit Cannot be reduced indefinitely without causing business losses. Extended psychological benefit the uncapped one No inherent limitation — organizations can continuously enhance perception through branding and marketing. The extended psychological benefit is particularly powerful in modern marketing — it shapes how consumers feel about social acceptability and personal image, and it is the only benefit with no built-in ceiling. 3 The abstract costs What you pay beyond money Costs are not limited to the direct price. The lecture lists four abstract costs : the time required to purchase and obtain the product, the effort and energy expended, the psychological stress (worrying about parking, traffic), and disposal costs with after-sales service considerations. The ice-cream test Ordering ice cream from a delivery app may cost more money — but its abstract costs are lower: no travel time, no parking concerns, the convenience of home delivery. Against the store visit, the app can win on perceived value while losing on price. Run both scenarios in the balance machine above. 4 How organizations move the equation Two directions: raise the benefits, or cut the costs Increase benefits Improve the product quality, features, or emotional appeal. Reduce costs Lower prices, simplify processes, reduce friction in purchase and usage. Denim: same jeans, different ledger Generic jeans ₹1,000–1,500 the fabric does its job Levi's jeans ₹3,900–5,900 the brand adds its layer Armani jeans ₹25,000–50,000 the label speaks before you do The product remains physically similar — the brand creates the extended psychological benefit through brand equity, moving perceived value by orders of magnitude. Friction is a cost Amazon Prime integrates shopping within entertainment — the “Add to Cart” button appearing during OTT advertisements makes purchasing easier, reducing the abstract cost of obtaining products. Application A Better playlists — but frequent ads and a complex six-step login. Free, and still worth less. Application B A simpler one-step login with minimal friction — superior perceived value . A mattress ad leads with 'memory foam core'. In the lecture's language, that is a… Lecture 5 · concept check A benefit B feature C cost D demand state Key takeaways CPV = Benefits − Costs — a calculation in the consumer's mind, not the price on the tag. Four benefits: psychological (warmth), functional (pockets, hoodie, wind resistance), economic (savings), extended psychological (status) — only the last one has no ceiling. Costs beyond price: time, effort, psychological stress, disposal — the abstract ledger. Denim: generic ₹1,000–1,500 · Levi's ₹3,900–5,900 · Armani ₹25,000–50,000 — brand equity as extended psychological benefit. More features ≠ more value — excess features cause cognitive overload ; communicate benefits (better sleep), not features (memory foam). Organizations create value by increasing benefits or reducing costs — and friction reduction (Amazon Prime, one-step logins) is often the cheapest win.

chapters.label: The environment
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 6 The environment around every sale No organisation sells into a vacuum. Around every transaction sits a task environment the firm touches daily — suppliers, customers, competitors — wrapped in a broad macro environment that shifts underneath it: demographics, law, the economy, culture, climate and technology. The environment ring tap a layer — or let it tour Demographic Political Legal Economic Socio Cultural Physical Technological Suppliers task · micro Customers task · micro Competitors task · micro the organisation Suppliers Customers Competitors Demographic Political-Legal Economic Socio-Cultural Physical Technological Play tour Reset Pick any layer — the inner three touch the firm daily; the outer six shift slowly and indirectly. 9 layers loaded · 3 task + 6 macro. Nothing sells in a vacuum. 1 The task environment — the entities you actually touch Immediate, direct, daily The task (micro) environment consists of the immediate entities with which marketing directly interacts. Three of them matter most. Suppliers provide the resources needed for operations. Customers are the target market for products and services. And competitors are the other organizations offering similar products or services. These are the players a marketer negotiates with, prices against and pitches to — today, this week, this quarter. Why the ring matters Marketing operates within two distinct environments at once. The task environment reacts to you; the broad environment simply moves — and every player inside the inner ring stands on the same shifting macro ground. 2 The broad (macro) environment — six forces you navigate, not control Indirect factors every organisation must consider Demographic Age groups, socio-economic status, income levels, and population characteristics. Political-Legal Government policies, regulations, minimum wage laws, and food safety standards. Economic GST reforms, recessions, inflation, and market conditions. Socio-Cultural Consumption patterns, dietary preferences, and cultural backgrounds that influence consumer behavior. Physical Climate, environmental conditions, and natural factors affecting operations. Technological Innovations such as the transitions from floppy disks to cloud storage, UPI payments, and digital platforms. Notice how concrete each force is. A minimum wage law (political-legal) changes what a delivery platform pays. GST reforms and recessions (economic) change what a family spends. Dietary preferences (socio-cultural) decide whether a new snack lands at all. The floppy-disk-to-cloud and UPI stories (technological) show entire industries rebuilt from the outside in. Climate and natural factors (physical) reshape logistics and demand by season. Task / micro Immediate entities marketing directly interacts with: suppliers, customers, competitors. Broad / macro Indirect forces to consider: demographic, political-legal, economic, socio-cultural, physical, technological. Key takeaways Marketing operates within two distinct environments : the task (micro) and the broad (macro). The task environment is the set of immediate entities — suppliers, customers, competitors — that marketing directly interacts with. The broad environment is indirect but decisive : demographic, political-legal, economic, socio-cultural, physical and technological elements. Macro forces are navigated, not controlled — GST reforms, minimum wage laws, dietary shifts and UPI arrive whether or not the firm is ready.

chapters.label: Exchange systems
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 6 Marketing is an exchange system A food order looks like money for a meal. It isn't. Every Zomato order trades information, time, attention and trust — and returns convenience, choices and transparency. Exchange is far bigger than the transaction. 1 Beyond money-for-product Multiple elements move in every marketing transaction Marketing exchanges involve far more than the simple transfer of money for a product. Every transaction also moves benefits and convenience , costs and efforts , information and personal data , time and attention , and risk and trust . Watch a single Zomato order run through all of them: What a Zomato order really trades 9 flows, 1 tap each You (consumer) Zomato (platform) GIVE → ← GET Money ↑ Money ↑ Personal information ↑ Time ↑ Ratings & reviews ↓ The meal itself ↓ Convenience ↓ Information ↓ Multiple choices ↓ Transparency Play Next Reset Step 1 of 9 · You give: Money — payment for the meal. 2 The modern exchange economy Interconnected markets with continuous exchanges and transactions Resource market Manufacturing market Intermediary market Consumer market resources ↔ money finished goods ↔ money products & services ↔ money money flows back consumer market → resource market: money exchanged for resources and labor Government market — taxes ↔ services exchanges with all markets Resource → Manufacturing Resources exchanged for money. Manufacturing → Intermediary Finished goods exchanged for money. Intermediary → Consumer Products and services exchanged for money. Consumer → Resource Money exchanged for resources and labor. The government market sits centrally, exchanging taxes and services with all other markets. 3 Exchange · transaction · relationship Three concepts, three scopes Exchange Offering and receiving something of value in return. Not limited to money — can involve information, convenience, effort, time, or any element of value. Broader than buying and selling; the foundation of all marketing systems. Transaction An agreed-upon exchange where terms are clearly defined and performance is expected. Always involves money or monetary value, between two parties, on agreed terms — capturing value at a particular moment in time. Relationship An ongoing series of exchanges and transactions that build value over time. Built on mutual satisfaction; when both parties consistently receive value it leads to loyalty, repeat business, and advocacy. Exchange All types of value → Foundation of marketing Transaction Money, one moment in time → Completed sale or service delivery Relationship Series over an extended period → Customer loyalty and advocacy Simple marketing system Industry (set of sellers/producers) + market (set of buyers/consumers), connected by four flows. The four flows Communication (information, both ways), goods & services (industry → market), money (market → industry), information/feedback (market → industry). The system is dynamic and continuous , with all elements constantly interacting. 4 Customer journey mapping — four parties, eight ledgers The food delivery exercise, mapped Student Gives · Payment · Time · Attention · Personal data · Trust Receives · Meal · Convenience · Tracking information Restaurant Gives · Food · Menu information · Packaging Receives · Orders · Revenue · Visibility Delivery Partner Gives · Pickup · Delivery · Reliability Receives · Earnings · Access to orders Platform Gives · App interface · Restaurant matching · Payment processing · Tracking Receives · Commission · Data · Loyalty · Ratings Spotting exchanges inside the journey Most activities throughout the customer journey are exchanges of various values — information, convenience, trust. The specific moment when payment is processed and confirmed is the transaction . And relationships develop when repeat orders occur and customers become advocates for the platform. Key takeaways Marketing functions fundamentally as an exchange system — money is only one of many things traded. A Zomato order exchanges money, personal information, time and ratings for the meal, convenience, information, choices and transparency . The modern exchange economy links resource → manufacturing → intermediary → consumer markets, with the government market exchanging taxes and services with all. Exchange is any value offered and received; a transaction is a money-based moment in time; a relationship is the series that builds loyalty and advocacy. In the journey map, every party — student, restaurant, delivery partner, platform — runs its own gives-and-receives ledger .

chapters.label: Value · price · features
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 7 Value, price & the feature trap A ₹5 pen and a ₹5,000 pen can write the same exam. This session untangles the three distinctions most marketers blur: value vs price, features vs benefits, and benefits vs value. 1 Value is not price An expensive product does not necessarily provide higher value Value is subjective — it depends on the individual consumer's perception. A low-priced item can be more valuable than a high-priced item depending on the context and the benefits derived. The lecture's example: a ₹5 pen for exam writing provides the same functional value as a ₹5,000 pen — but the expensive pen gains additional value from extended psychological benefits when signing important documents. Switch the scene in the machine above and watch which pen wins. 2 Features are not benefits Product characteristics vs the value derived from them Features are product characteristics; benefits are the value derived from those features. Not every feature generates a benefit for every consumer, and features do not directly translate to benefits. A pen with a fine nib (feature) may provide smooth writing without ink spillage (benefit) — but that benefit is not universal to all users. A spec sheet is not a value proposition. 3 Benefits become value only against sacrifices Value = Benefits − Sacrifices The pen machine — value ≠ price same ink, different value Scene: Writing an exam Signing important documents ₹5 pen Provides the same functional value as the ₹5,000 pen — the answers on paper are identical. ₹5,000 pen Writes the same exam. Its higher price buys nothing functional here — value depends on context. Value = Benefits − Sacrifices · toggle the chips + Functional + Psychological + Economic + Personal + Image − Money paid − Time searching − Effort comparing − Travel to stores − Psychological & opportunity +0 Borderline — benefits merely match sacrifices. The consumer is unconvinced. A consumer perceives value when they believe the benefits they gain outweigh the sacrifices they make. And sacrifices extend well beyond the price tag. Buying a laptop involves not just the purchase price but also time invested in research , effort to visit physical stores , and the opportunity to use that money elsewhere . Direct costs The monetary amount paid for the product. Abstract / indirect costs Time spent searching, effort to compare products, physical travel to stores, psychological costs, and opportunity costs. 4 The benefit dimensions Components of customer perceived benefit Functional Direct utility and performance of the product Psychological Emotional satisfaction and confidence Economic Price-related advantages and discounts Personal Individual satisfaction Image How the product affects one's social perception Extended psychological uncapped → next chapter Social status, social acceptability, and how others perceive the consumer using the product — the uncapped one. Key takeaways Never confuse value with price — lower-priced items can be more valuable depending on context. Features and benefits are distinct — a fine nib is a feature; smooth writing without spillage is a benefit, and not for every user. Benefits become value only when compared against sacrifices — Value = Benefits − Sacrifices. Sacrifices include both direct monetary costs and abstract costs — search time, comparison effort, travel, psychology, opportunity.

chapters.label: The luxury lever
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 7 The luxury lever Functional, psychological and economic benefits all have caps. Extended psychological benefits — status, acceptability, how others see you — have none. That single fact explains a ₹100 pen selling at ₹5,000 and a ₹100 crore apartment. 1 Ordinary benefits have limits Upper and lower caps on the capped dimensions Functional, psychological, and economic benefits have upper and lower caps — they cannot be increased indefinitely without increasing costs. Every extra unit of function, comfort or discount costs the firm more to deliver, so the value curve flattens. Push as hard as you like: the ceiling holds. The uncapped dimension Extended psychological benefits have no limitations — these are entirely subjective and can create significant value differences. The same ₹100 pen can be sold for ₹5,000 or even higher based solely on the extended psychological benefit created through branding and perception. The cap machine 3 benefits hit ceilings · 1 never does Press “invest” to pour money into branding and perception. Watch the three ordinary benefit bars slam into their caps — and the extended psychological bar keep climbing, taking the pen's price from ₹100 toward ₹5,000 and beyond . Functional benefit growing… Psychological benefit growing… Economic benefit growing… Extended psychological benefit NO LIMITATIONS — entirely subjective Invest in branding & perception Reset the ₹100 pen now sells for ₹100 A plain ₹100 pen. Every benefit dimension starts near the floor. 2 How the luxury sector operates Manipulating extended psychological benefits Luxury brands primarily operate by manipulating extended psychological benefits . They emphasize exclusivity, premiumness, social status, and belonging to elite circles. The “overcharging” in luxury sectors is justified through enhanced psychological benefits rather than superior functional attributes. Camellias — a ₹100 crore apartment A ₹100 crore apartment in an exclusive society like Camellias derives its value from social status and association with prominent individuals — not from superior functional features. The walls are walls; the address is the product. 3 Marketing without physical products Information, attention, data and concepts Marketing can exist without physical products or services. Marketing involves the exchange of information, attention, data, and concepts — not solely monetary transactions. Concepts are marketed for social causes and religious beliefs , and the attention-based economy runs on it — free apps that collect user data are marketing without a price tag at all. 4 The consumer's perspective Value is subjective — and aspiration counts Subjective Value assessment is entirely subjective and individual-driven — different consumers derive different values from the same product. Target audience Comprises individuals with similar value perceptions — not necessarily those with the most purchasing power. Aspirational consumers Also constitute target audiences — people who don't own it yet but perceive its value. Key takeaways Functional, psychological and economic benefits have caps — they cannot grow indefinitely without growing costs. Extended psychological benefits are uncapped — the most powerful lever for increasing perceived value. Luxury brands live on this lever: exclusivity, premiumness, social status, elite belonging — a ₹100 crore Camellias apartment sells status, not function. Marketing works without physical products — information, attention, data and concepts are marketable. A target audience is a group with similar value perceptions — aspirational consumers included.

chapters.label: Existing & desired state
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 8 Existing & desired state — manufacturing the gap Every consumer lives in two states: the one they're in and the one they believe they deserve. When the two align, minds close. Marketing's oldest lever is pulling them apart. 1 Two states drive every purchase ES — where I am · DS — where I believe I deserve to be Existing State (ES) The current situation or condition a consumer is in. Desired State (DS) The ideal situation a consumer wants to achieve — or the state they believe they deserve. Organizations create value in consumers' minds by manipulating these states . When ES and DS sit at the same level, consumers are satisfied and have no need for a new product — the mind stays closed because there is no gap to fill. 2 Three ways to open the gap Lower ES · raise DS · or both at once Manufacture the gap three strategies, one lever each Itch Guard · lower ES Kohler · raise DS Clean & Clear · dual No campaign DS · Desired State where they believe they deserve to be ES · Existing State where the consumer is now gap = 0 pts no gap · no felt need · mind stays closed ES = DS. The consumer is satisfied and perceives no need for a new product — the mind remains closed because there is no gap to fill. 3 The expectation gap and inertia Why the gap must exist before any purchase The gap between existing and desired states creates an “inertia” that motivates consumers to take action . When ES and DS are aligned, consumers perceive no need for a product. By creating a gap between these states, marketers instigate the desire to purchase — and the larger the gap, the stronger the motivation to bridge it through product consumption. Breaking this inertia is essential for marketers to demonstrate product value. The dual approach is the strongest Pulling down the existing state and pulling up the desired state simultaneously generates stronger consumer desperation to purchase and restore balance — that is why Clean & Clear's dual play works, and why it raises an ethical eyebrow (more on that in Lecture 10). Kohler keeps the existing state positive but pulls the desired state significantly higher — 'your current state is great, but you deserve something better'. Which strategy is that? Lecture 8 · ES/DS strategies A Reducing the existing state (Itch Guard style) B Elevating the desired state C The dual approach D No-gap positioning Key takeaways Every consumer holds an Existing State (current condition) and a Desired State (the state they believe they deserve). ES = DS means no need — satisfied consumers keep their minds closed; there is no gap to fill. Marketers manufacture the gap by lowering ES (Itch Guard) , raising DS (Kohler) , or both (Clean & Clear) . The larger the gap, the stronger the motivation to bridge it — breaking the inertia is essential to demonstrating product value.

chapters.label: The purchase chain
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 8 The value purchase chain Value creation → purchase intention → actual purchase → experience → satisfaction → loyalty. Six links, one asymmetric rule: falling short hurts far more than exceeding delights. 1 Six links from gap to loyalty The journey from consumer awareness to loyalty Walk the value purchase chain 6 links · gap → loyalty Value creation 1 Purchase intention 2 Actual purchase 3 Experience · 4 Satisfaction · 5 Loyalty · 6 Play Next Reset Stage 1 · Value creation Emerges from the gap between existing and desired states. Stage 1 of 6 · Value creation — Emerges from the gap between existing and desired states. 2 The satisfaction formula Transaction-based — expectation vs perceived performance Customer satisfaction is transaction-based and depends on comparing expectation with perceived performance . Satisfaction is high when perceived performance closely matches or exceeds expectations; the expectation gap — the difference between what consumers expect and what they actually receive — determines satisfaction levels. exceeded expectations — a small, pleasant lift fell short of expectations — a heavy, lasting drop the negative effect is significantly stronger Critical threshold — both directions There is an upper and lower limit to expectations. Delivering far below them fails — but delivering unexpectedly above them backfires too: pizza arriving in 10 minutes creates doubt about the product's authenticity . Asymmetric impact The negative effect of failing to meet expectations is significantly stronger than the positive effect of exceeding them. One bad delivery outweighs three good ones. 3 Loyalty ≠ satisfaction Repeated satisfaction over multiple transactions Satisfaction Based on a single transaction or experience. Loyalty Built on repeated positive experiences over an extended period. Loyalty is built on consistent satisfaction across multiple purchases over time . Loyal consumers keep purchasing because they consistently derive value. And the direction matters: loyalty cannot be created through rewards alone — it requires consistent product performance that meets or exceeds expectations. If consumers are not satisfied, they will not become loyal, regardless of reward programs. 4 Case: Apple AirPods vs Bose Superior audio quality lost to superior expectation management Ecosystem integration Seamless pairing with Apple devices created higher perceived value. Design Sleek, modern design appealed to consumers and communicated status. Functionality Using a single earbud provided flexibility Bose couldn't match. Value perception Greater perceived value from integration and design — despite Bose's technical superiority. The verdict Apple exceeded consumer expectations ; Bose failed to deliver on perceived performance. Satisfied Apple consumers became loyal — purchasing successive generations at higher prices — while Bose consumers switched to competitors. Satisfaction depends on meeting expectations relative to perceived performance, not solely on product quality . Key takeaways The chain runs value → intention → purchase → experience → satisfaction → loyalty — and impulse purchases may skip the intention phase. Satisfaction is transaction-based : perceived performance compared against expectations. Impact is asymmetric — failing expectations hurts significantly more than exceeding them delights. There are upper and lower thresholds — pizza in 10 minutes triggers doubt, not delight. Loyalty cannot be bought with rewards alone — it is repeated satisfaction over time; AirPods beat Bose on expectation management, not audio quality.

chapters.label: Context matters
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 9 One delivery, two ratings Two students. Same restaurant, same meal, same 34-minute delivery — warm food, intact packaging, missing cutlery. One gives 2 stars, the other 5. The difference was never the service; it was the anchor. 1 The food delivery example Identical conditions, opposite verdicts Two students ordered the same meal from the same restaurant through a food delivery app with identical delivery conditions: estimated time 30–35 minutes , actual delivery 34 minutes for both , food warm with intact packaging , and cutlery missing for both . Yet one rated 2 stars and the other 5. Run the machine — the delivery is the same; the anchors are not. One delivery, two ratings the anchor decides same meal, same restaurant estimate 30–35 min · actual 34 min warm food · intact packaging cutlery missing for both the identical 34-minute delivery Student A anchor · 25 min expectation set by previous fast deliveries 0 15 30 45 60 anchor 25 min Waiting for the delivery… Student B anchor · 45–50 min expectation set by heavy rain outside 0 15 30 45 60 anchor 45–50 min Waiting for the delivery… Deliver the order Reset Two students. Identical order conditions. Only their anchors differ — 25 minutes of fast history vs 45–50 minutes of rain. 2 Expectations and context Customers evaluate performance against an internal standard Student A — fast history Previous fast deliveries created an expectation of a 25-minute delivery . At 34 minutes the service felt disappointing — and the missing cutlery became evidence for the prosecution. Likely to switch to another app. Student B — rainy evening Heavy rain set realistic expectations of 45–50 minutes . The order arrived in 34 minutes with warm food and reliable tracking — ahead of the anchor. Highly satisfied, likely loyal. Key insight Satisfaction is not determined by objective performance alone, but by how performance compares to customer expectations and contextual factors . The gap between expected service and perceived service determines satisfaction — same 34 minutes, two completely different satisfaction levels. 3 Satisfaction vs loyalty — again, sharper A satisfied customer may not be loyal Satisfaction Transaction-specific — an evaluation of a single purchase or service interaction. A satisfied customer may not be loyal. Loyalty Willingness to continue choosing, preferring, and supporting a brand when alternatives are available — developed across multiple transactions over time. The Swiggy switch A customer highly satisfied with Zomato might still switch to Swiggy for a 50% discount offer . True loyalty means continuing to choose a brand despite better alternatives being available . A customer rates their Zomato order 5 stars — then switches to Swiggy next week for a 50% discount. What does this prove? Lecture 9 · satisfaction vs loyalty A They were never actually satisfied B Satisfaction and loyalty are the same thing C Satisfaction is transaction-specific; loyalty means staying despite alternatives D Discounts create loyalty better than satisfaction does Key takeaways Context shapes perception — expectations and contextual factors matter as much as objective performance metrics. Customers judge service against an internal anchor : 25 minutes of fast history vs 45–50 minutes of rain produced 2★ and 5★ from the same 34-minute delivery. Satisfaction is transaction-based ; each interaction is evaluated independently. Loyalty develops over time — and is proven only when a customer keeps choosing you despite alternatives (the Swiggy 50% test).

chapters.label: Loyalty economics
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 9 The economics of coming back Loyalty isn't a soft metric. 5% more retention lifts profit 20–90%. A new customer costs $100 to acquire; a loyal one costs about $20 to keep. And the chain from expected service to repeat purchase runs in both directions. 1 The numbers that make retention the strategy Why organizations prioritize loyalty programs The retention scoreboard press play — every number counts up Play the numbers Reset Retention +5% → profit 0% – 0% Increasing the retention rate by just 5% can increase business profit by 20–90% . Acquire vs retain 0 vs 0 Acquiring a new customer costs 5 times more than retaining a loyal one — $100 to acquire vs ≈ $20 to retain . Conversion rates loyal 0% new 0% Loyal customers convert at 60–70% ; new customers at only 5–8% — conversion being the percentage of items in a shopping cart that are actually purchased. Repeat spending 1×+ within 2 years Repeat customers spend more than twice their original expenditure within two years post-purchase — order values rise over time. Press play — watch why organizations prioritize loyalty programs: loyalty directly impacts profitability. 2 The value purchase chain — as a process Expected service vs perceived service, looping The gap between what customers expect and what they perceive determines the value delivered. If perceived service meets or exceeds expected service, value is recognized — which drives intention to purchase, then actual purchase, then satisfaction. Satisfied customers place higher value on the brand, product, or platform ; higher perceived value raises the chances of loyalty; and loyal customers make more frequent and larger purchases — which feeds the loop again. 1 Expected vs perceived service 2 Value recognized 3 Intention to purchase 4 Actual purchase 5 Satisfaction 6 Increased brand value 7 Loyalty development 8 Increased purchases the up-cycle each link feeds the next 1 Gap is negative 2 Value not recognized 3 Low intention 4 Low purchase 5 Low satisfaction 6 Minimal loyalty 7 Purchases fall the reverse cycle each link drains the next If the gap between expected and perceived service is negative , value is not recognized → low intention → low actual purchase → low satisfaction → minimal loyalty → which further reduces purchase frequency. The same loop, running backwards. The indirect relationship There is also an indirect relationship between satisfaction and loyalty — higher satisfaction increases the likelihood of loyalty development. Satisfaction is the seed; repeated satisfaction over time is the soil. Key takeaways Retention pays: +5% retention → +20–90% profit; $100 acquisition vs ≈$20 retention (5×). Loyal customers convert at 60–70% vs 5–8% for new customers — and spend more than 2× their original expenditure within two years. The chain process loops: expected vs perceived service → value → intention → purchase → satisfaction → brand value → loyalty → increased purchases . The reverse cycle is just as systematic: a negative gap drains every link that follows. Customer retention is cost-effective — the value purchase chain is cyclical, and positive experiences reinforce it.

chapters.label: Campaigns in ES/DS
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 10 The gap, in the wild Itch Guard pulls the existing state down. Kohler pulls the desired state up. Clean & Clear does both — and Samsung and Sony split a television market between volume and premium value. First, the recap that makes it all work. 1 Recap: closed by default, opened by interest The open vs closed system, and ES = DS By design, the human mind is naturally closed and resistant to new information — the closed system is the default. It becomes open when consumers develop curiosity and interest in a product. The relationship is linear : the more interested you are, the more open you become to learning about that product. The marketer's job is to open this closed system — through advertisements, celebrity endorsements, packaging, color combinations, pricing, and discounts. interest in the product → openness no interest mind closed curious & interested system opens ES = DS Consumers are satisfied and have no need for a new product — the mind remains closed because there is no gap to fill. Creating the gap Pull down the existing state (current situation feels inadequate), pull up the desired state (you deserve better), or do both simultaneously — the most effective strategy. 2 The campaign bench Itch Guard · Kohler · Clean & Clear · Samsung · Sony The campaign bench five brands, five gap strategies Itch Guard Kohler Clean & Clear Samsung Sony DS · Desired State desired state ES · Existing State existing state gap = 32 pts gap open · inertia breaks Itch Guard · lower ES Highlighting the negative aspects of the current situation — embarrassment from scratching in public. Itch Guard: gap = 32 pts. The gap is the campaign. 3 When the direct cost is zero Free apps and gifts — the abstract cost does the charging Direct vs abstract cost where the real price hides Free mobile applications Gifts (pets) Direct cost Negligible — the app is free to download. Abstract cost High — personal data collection, notifications, advertisements, difficulty in uninstalling. Free mobile applications — Users open themselves to the app despite the low direct cost because they accept the abstract costs — the closed system opens. Free mobile applications Direct cost: negligible (free to download). Abstract cost: high — personal data collection, notifications, advertisements, difficulty in uninstalling. Gifts (e.g., pets) Direct cost: zero (received as a gift). Abstract cost: very high — feeding, care, eventual disposal. The ES–DS gap widens as the responsibility becomes clear. 4 The ethical consideration Shades of gray Marketing operates in “shades of gray” Clean & Clear's dual strategy — lowering the existing state by highlighting acne and blackheads — makes consumers vulnerable by highlighting insecurities . Nothing in marketing is purely black or white; a full ethical examination of marketing practices is essential, and the lecture reserves it for a dedicated ethics module. Key takeaways The mind is closed by default ; interest opens it — and interest↔openness is linear. Samsung plays volume (masses, ₹17,000–₹5,00,000, dual gap strategy); Sony plays premium value (select audiences, raise DS for aspirational consumers). Free apps and gift pets prove the point: direct cost ~0, abstract cost huge — data, notifications, care, responsibility. Dual campaigns (Clean & Clear) create the strongest desperation — and the sharpest ethical questions : highlighting insecurities makes consumers vulnerable.

chapters.label: Beyond purchase
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 10 Decisions beyond the receipt Purchase is only one decision consumers make. They avoid, they advocate, they dissuade, they stay loyal without repeat purchases — and most of what marketers actually measure is a proxy. 1 Impulse buying Unplanned — but not triggerless Impulse buying is the unplanned purchase made intuitively, without deliberate thinking about need or want. But even impulse buying has triggers — advertisements, discounts, limited-time offers — and involves some unconscious rational assessment . Its ES/DS connection: impulse purchases may not involve traditional changes in existing and desired states, but are driven by immediate situational factors . 2 Decisions beyond purchase Purchase decisions aren't limited to buying Avoiding a product The decision to stay away — a decision the marketer loses silently. Positive word of mouth Speaking positively about a product without buying it. Negative word of mouth Speaking negatively about a product — advocacy in reverse. Loyalty without repeat Building loyalty without repeated purchases — supporting a brand you rarely buy. Satisfaction Being happy with a product you purchased. Loyalty Continuing to choose a brand even when competitors are available — the same brand, chosen repeatedly. 3 Attribute-based consumer decisions Priorities differ; principles don't close deals alone The attribute weights lab same products, different pain points Every product has multiple attributes. Move the sliders to prioritize what this consumer cares about — and watch which product wins. A product may follow all marketing principles and still fail if it doesn't address the specific pain point that matters most to a particular consumer segment. Price 3 Design 3 Quality 3 Social status 3 Utility 3 Product A 3.2 budget-strong: price + utility Product B 4.0 premium-strong: design, quality, status With these priorities, Product B wins. Same market, different weights — different winner. That is why attribute fit beats principle-following. 4 Measuring purchase behavior Actual is expensive — so most marketers proxy How purchase behavior gets measured actual vs proxy vs neurometrics Actual purchase Intention to purchase (proxy) Neurometric tools Signal realism how close to the real purchase Practicality how usable at scale Intention to purchase (proxy) Used by most marketers as a reasonable indicator of purchase behavior. Intention to purchase (proxy): realism 45 / practicality 92. Most marketers live on the proxy; Nielsen, Coca-Cola and Google can afford neurometrics. 5 The shades of gray Ethics, again — because the tools are powerful Strategies like lowering the existing state can be seen as making consumers vulnerable by highlighting insecurities . Marketing operates in “shades of gray” — nothing is purely black or white — and a full ethical examination of marketing practices is essential (the lecture defers it to a dedicated ethics module). Key takeaways Impulse buying is unplanned but not uncaused — ads, discounts and limited-time offers trigger it, with unconscious rational assessment inside. Purchase decisions include avoiding, positive talk without buying, negative talk, and loyalty without repeat purchases . Consumers prioritize different attributes (price, design, quality, social status, utility) — a principle-perfect product can still lose to a pain-point fit. Actual purchase is difficult and expensive to measure ; intention is the everyday proxy; neurometrics (Nielsen, Coca-Cola, Google) read real responses.

chapters.label: Heterogeneity
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 11 Zoom in and the market splits 100 Netflix users look identical from a distance. Zoom in and six content tribes appear. That zoom — from a homogeneous blob to meaningful segments — is where STP begins. 1 Market heterogeneity The reality that creates the need for segmentation The zoom machine 100 users · 6 audiences 100 Netflix users may seem similar. Zoom in and the diversity appears: vastly different viewing preferences — K-dramas, true crime, anime, documentaries and more. 100 users — homogeneous from a distance Zoom in K-drama True crime Anime Sitcoms Documentaries Scrollers From a distance the market looks homogeneous. Press zoom in — this is market heterogeneity. Consumers differ in meaningful ways that affect their purchase and consumption decisions. A market appears homogeneous from a distance but reveals significant diversity when examined closely. Consumers differ in who they are, what they want, why they buy, and how they buy — and different consumer groups value different product attributes. Understanding this diversity is what lets marketers identify meaningful differences worth addressing. 2 Defining segmentation Meaningful groups — not just any groups Segmentation is the process of finding meaningful groups within a market whose members are similar enough to be marketed to differently . The key distinction: segmentation is not simply dividing consumers into groups — divisions must be meaningful and usable to create differentiated marketing strategies, and the differences must be actionable and relevant for marketing purposes. Within vs between Members within a segment share similar characteristics, needs, and desires; segments are distinctly different from each other — so different that each justifies its own marketing strategy, messaging, and product positioning. 3 The face serum market Four segments, four formulations Without segmentation, a generic “daily serum for all skin types” may be acceptable to many but relevant to few . With segmentation, companies create targeted solutions — and each segment requires different product formulations, ingredient focus, and messaging strategies. SEGMENT 1 Acne control Different formulation · different ingredient focus · different messaging. SEGMENT 2 Barrier repair Different formulation · different ingredient focus · different messaging.
