SEGMENT 3 Hydration and glow Different formulation · different ingredient focus · different messaging. SEGMENT 4 Pigmentation and marks Different formulation · different ingredient focus · different messaging. 4 The problem with no segmentation One-size-fits-all fails heterogeneity ✗ Products become acceptable but not relevant to most consumers ✗ Marketing messages lack resonance with specific audiences ✗ Consumer problems remain incompletely solved ✗ Competitive disadvantage in heterogeneous markets Key takeaways Market heterogeneity is the fundamental reality: consumers differ in who they are, what they want, why and how they buy. Segmentation = meaningful groups marketed to differently — not arbitrary divisions; differences must be actionable. The face serum market splits into acne control, barrier repair, hydration & glow, pigmentation — each with its own formulation, ingredients and messaging. Without segmentation: acceptable but not relevant , no resonance, incompletely solved problems, competitive disadvantage.

chapters.label: Bases of segmentation
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 11 Three classic bases Where you are (Zudio's city-by-city racks), who you are (Pulsar's 'Definitely Male', L'Oréal's age ladder), and how you think (Nike's four tribes) — the geographic, demographic and psychographic bases of segmentation. 1 The bases lab Three windows into the same market The bases lab geographic · demographic · psychographic Geographic Demographic Psychographic Geographic segmentation divides consumers by location and climate conditions. Zudio (Tata) stocks the same fashion chain city by city: Delhi Heavy focus on winter jackets and layers cold weather, October–December Mumbai Lightweight, monsoon-friendly clothing rainy season Bangalore Casual streetwear mild, consistent weather year-round Application areas: climate and weather patterns · regional consumption preferences (rice vs wheat across India) · geographic-specific campaigns and product availability. One Zudio rack, three climates: Delhi layers, Mumbai monsoon, Bangalore streetwear. 2 Netflix's messaging map Same platform, six segment scripts 100 students watching Netflix appear homogeneous from a distance; zooming in reveals six distinct content preference segments — and each requires different marketing messaging: K-drama fans get emotional messaging ; true crime fans get mystery, twists and investigation focus ; sitcom fans get newer-episodes, feel-good, familiar-content messaging . 3 Common questions, straight answers The three questions every segmenter asks What creates the need for segmentation? Market heterogeneity — the fundamental reality that consumers are different from one another. Why isn't age (18–25) automatically useful? Age alone is insufficient. Within an age group, consumers have vastly different needs and preferences — 18–25 year-old Netflix users have completely different content tastes. Age works only combined with other variables: gender, benefits sought, psychographic profiles. Can two firms segment the same market differently? Yes, absolutely. Different organizations can segment identical markets using different criteria — the strategy depends on company objectives, resources, and positioning goals. 4 Why segmentation matters — and when it didn't Strategic importance + the mass-era exception ✓ Targeted product development addressing specific needs ✓ Relevant marketing communications ✓ Justifies differentiated strategies across segments ✓ Improves marketing efficiency and ROI ✓ Competitive advantage through relevance, not just acceptance Historical context — the Pond's era In the mass production eras ( 1980s–1990s ), one-size-fits-all products were viable — think Pond's cold cream . With increasing competition and product variety, segmentation became essential; modern markets require targeted approaches to succeed. Key takeaways Geographic: Zudio sells winter layers in Delhi, monsoon-weight clothing in Mumbai, streetwear in Bangalore. Demographic: Pulsar's “Definitely Male” owns 17–24 males; L'Oréal runs 20+/30+/40+ variants on a 70–80% shared base with age-matched ambassadors. Psychographic: Nike serves Fitness Focused, Sport Aspirers, Style & Status Seekers, and the Sustainability Conscious — inside 15 major psychographic segments. Age alone fails — it must be linked to benefits and aspirations; two firms can legitimately segment the same market differently. Mass eras made one-size-fits-all viable (Pond's); competition made segmentation essential.

chapters.label: Behavior & benefits
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 12 How they act, what they seek Behavioral segmentation reads what consumers do — usage rate, mode, frequency, pack size, promotional sensitivity. Benefit segmentation reads what they want. Surf Excel turned 25% penetration into 75% by doing both. 1 The five behavioral metrics Dividing consumers by how they act and consume Usage rate How frequently and intensively consumers use a product — heavy users who wash clothes frequently need products offering more washes and value for money. Mode of usage How consumers use the product — machine-wash users prefer convenience and need better stain removal, making liquid detergents ideal for them. Frequency of purchase How often consumers buy — distinct from usage rate; helps identify occasional users who may prefer smaller pack sizes. Pack size Occasional users prefer small sachets, while heavy users benefit from larger, value-oriented bulk packs. Promotional sensitivity Responsiveness to offers and discounts — value seekers actively switch brands based on promotional incentives and special offers. 2 Surf Excel: four behaviors, four products 25% → 75% market penetration The 25 → 75 machine Surf Excel's behavioral segments market penetration 25% no segmentation Segment the market → 75% Heavy Users Machine-Wash Users Occasional Users Value Seekers Heavy Users Require value packs offering more washes at economical prices. Without this segmentation, only 25% of potential consumers would purchase the detergent. By segmenting their market behaviorally, Surf Excel created different products for each segment , significantly increasing market penetration. Without this segmentation, only 25% of potential consumers would purchase ; behavioral segmentation enables the company to effectively target up to 75% of the market . 3 Colgate: benefit-based segmentation The final method — what consumers seek from products The benefit shelf Colgate's five variants Strong Teeth Max Fresh Visible White Sensitive Total Colgate Strong Teeth · with Amino Shakti Stronger teeth and better enamel protection. All five are toothpastes — each communicates a distinct benefit to a different consumer segment. That is how Colgate captures broader market share in one category. The benefit-based principle Within each segment, consumers are similar; between segments, distinctly different. That lets organizations communicate specific product benefits to targeted audiences, address diverse consumer needs within the same product category, and expand market coverage by serving multiple benefit-seeking segments. 4 Exercise: segmenting a fitness app Four segments emerge from one user base Convenience Seekers Rea, Mohit Need: Easy and short workouts Busy professionals and easily-bored users Performance Seekers Neha, Karan Need: Metrics and improvement tracking Serious fitness enthusiasts monitoring progress Supported Fitness Seekers Mr. Mehta Need: Guidance and safety Older or health-conscious users requiring expert direction Social Exercisers Simran Need: Interaction and motivation Users seeking community engagement and social validation 5 Why segmentation matters — and where it leads Organizing chaos, feeding STP Organizing chaos Converting a large, complex consumer base into meaningful, manageable groups. Simplifying strategy Enabling marketers to cater specifically to each segment's unique requirements. Reducing complexity Transforming a 10-lakh consumer base into smaller, focused segments with specific characteristics. Segmentation is not merely a classification tool — it is the marketer's systematic approach to organizing and managing market heterogeneity. Without it, organizations risk appealing to no one effectively , wasting resources on misaligned products, and missing significant market opportunities. S · Segmentation Divide the market — geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioral, or benefit-based T · Targeting Select which segments to prioritize and pursue (subsequent lectures) P · Positioning Communicate distinct value propositions to target segments Surf Excel segmented its detergent market behaviorally. What did that do to its market penetration? Lecture 12 · Surf Excel case A From 75% down to 25% — focus costs reach B From 25% of potential consumers up to 75% of the market C No change — penetration is set by pack size D From 50% to 100% of Indian households Key takeaways Behavioral metrics: usage rate, mode of usage, frequency of purchase, pack size, promotional sensitivity. Surf Excel: heavy users → value packs; machine-wash users → liquids; occasional users → sachets; value seekers → BOGO mega packs. Penetration 25% → 75%. Colgate's five benefit variants — Strong Teeth, Max Fresh, Visible White, Sensitive, Total — each speaks one benefit language to one segment. The fitness app exercise shows segmentation in action: Rea & Mohit, Neha & Karan, Mr. Mehta, Simran want four different apps. Segmentation organizes chaos — a 10-lakh consumer base becomes focused groups — and is the “S” that feeds Targeting and Positioning.

chapters.label: Tupo
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 13 Tupo and the 3–15 gap nobody served Segmentation and targeting in the real world: a personal-care brand for growing children — too old for baby products, too young for adult products — and the parents who still control the wallet. 1 A market with only two shelves Homogeneous division, heterogeneous reality Market segmentation divides a homogeneous market into heterogeneous groups with similar characteristics. Traditional personal care was divided into just two categories — baby products (0–2 years) and adult & family products (16+ years) . Tupo identified and filled the previously overlooked gap in between: children aged 3–15 who were “too old for baby products but too young for adult products.” The age map — find the hole Lecture 13 · segmentation in the wild 0–2 · baby 16+ · adult & family 3–15 · the gap Tupo claimed “too old for baby products but too young for adult products” nobody's products — a market served by no one 0 2 3 15 16 20 age → Before Tupo Reveal the 3–15 gap Traditional personal care markets had only two shelves: baby (0–2) and adult & family (16+). Press reveal to see what Tupo saw. 2 Segmentation, then dual targeting Demographic + psychographic; preference-makers + purchasers Demographic Age 3–15 years (growing children) · life stage: early childhood through adolescence Psychographic Age-appropriate product beliefs · natural & organic preference · gentle, non-harsh formulations that prevent skin irritation and infections The key insight — quoted “Children are old enough to have preferences, but young enough that parents still control the wallet and strongly care about their safety.” Children become the preference-makers ; parents remain the purchasers — safety and well-being outrank price. The Tupo case player six beats of a niche, end to end Baby products · 0–2 years 3–15 · nobody home Adult & family · 16+ years Play Next Reset beat 1/6 1. The overlooked middle. Traditional personal care split into baby products (0–2) and adult & family products (16+). Children aged 3–15 fell between the shelves — too old for baby products, too young for adult products. 3 Behaviour shifts the decision pattern Children advocate; parents fund • Children now have distinct preferences rather than simply using parental products. • They actively advocate for specific brands — the lecture's example: daughters requesting Tupo shampoo with shikakai . • Parents value age-appropriate formulations over cost savings. 4 Lessons & the company it keeps What the case teaches — and who else plays this game Cetaphil Bioderma Plum Juicy Chemistry Mama Earth Brands employing similar niche-segmentation strategies — each identified an underserved segment and created a specialised product category. Real-world marketing lessons Live through the problem to identify genuine market gaps · understand evolving preferences and generational differences · create authentic value propositions from genuine needs · balance consumer preference with purchasing-power dynamics · and charge premium prices when clear value differentiation exists. Tupo charges ₹450 for a 300ML shampoo against a market standard of ₹150. The lecture justifies this premium by… Lecture 13 · concept check A mass-production economies of scale B age-appropriate formulation and ingredient quality parents value for safety C heavy discounting to build trial D spending more on celebrity advertising alone Key takeaways A gap between two served shelves — 0–2 and 16+ — left 3–15 unserved ; niches hide in plain sight. Segment on two lenses : demographic (age, life stage) and psychographic (age-appropriate, natural, gentle). Target twice : children choose, parents pay — dual targeting of preference-makers and purchasers. Position on dadi-nani trust (turmeric, hibiscus, amla, shikakai) rather than the “organic” label. ₹150 → ₹450 for 300ML: clear differentiation lets you price premium — and expand (face wash, makeup, Farah Khan).

chapters.label: SAFE targeting
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 14 Targeting and the SAFE framework Segmentation hands you many groups; limited budgets and resources force a choice. Targeting evaluates the segments and decides which to focus upon — because if everyone is your priority, then nobody is your priority. 1 The constraint that creates targeting You cannot market to all segments equally Targeting is the process of evaluating market segments and deciding which segment or segments the organisation will focus upon. Organisations have limited budgets and resources, which makes it impossible to market to all identified segments equally — hence the lecture's fundamental principle: “if everyone is your priority, then nobody is your priority.” 2 Four gates before you commit Size · Accessibility · Fitment · Economics The SAFE four-gate scan four segments · one new running shoe S Size scanning… A Accessibility waiting F Fitment waiting E Economics waiting Gate 1 of 4 · Size Is market demand inside the segment large enough to justify the marketing investment and generate revenue? Sneakerheads First-time runners Marathon runners Comfort walkers Play Next Reset step 1/5 Gate 1 · Size — assess demand inside each segment; it must be large enough to justify the investment and generate revenue. 3 Two dangerous assumptions The traps hiding inside 'obvious' choices The largest-segment assumption The largest market segment is not automatically the best target. Volume matters, but so do value and profit margin — a smaller, more profitable segment may generate greater revenue than a larger one with lower willingness to pay or higher competition. The fastest-growing assumption The fastest-growing segment may not align with the organisation's product fit or capabilities. Growth rate alone should not decide — brand capability and product–segment alignment matter equally. 4 The framework in the wild Netflix, Spotify and the sneaker company Netflix A crime-thriller launch with a limited promotional budget of 10 crores concentrates on the “true crime” segment rather than spreading equally across all six consumer segments — focus maximises return on investment Spotify Students were not the largest segment in Europe & India, yet Premium for Students at a subsidised price delivered higher overall revenue — large volume × price elasticity Sneaker company Four segments (sneakerheads, first-time runners, marathon runners, comfort walkers) scanned with SAFE for one new product line → first-time runners: high market size, medium competition, high brand capability, medium willingness to pay In the sneaker-company SAFE scan, which segment is the optimal target for the single new running-shoe line? Lecture 14 · concept check A Sneakerheads B First-time runners C Marathon runners D Comfort walkers Key takeaways Targeting = evaluating and choosing — limited budgets make “everyone” impossible. SAFE : Size, Accessibility, Fitment, Economics — all four gates must open. Largest ≠ best (volume vs value & margin ); fastest-growing ≠ best (growth vs fit & capability ). Netflix puts a 10-crore budget on true crime ; Spotify wins big with students via volume and price elasticity. If everyone is your priority, nobody is your priority .

chapters.label: Positioning's 3 questions
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 14 Positioning: the three questions Positioning designs an offering and its image so it occupies a distinctive and valued place in the target consumer's mind relative to competitors. How do we differentiate ourselves in the minds of our target audience? 1 The mind already has shelves Mental associations are manufactured Positioning creates immediate mental associations . Dettol is safety and germ protection; adrenaline and action brands are thrill and adventure; Coca-Cola dominates the cola category; Bisleri is the first brand that comes to mind for mineral water. None of this is accidental — each association results from a deliberate positioning strategy. Mental associations — flip to check not accidental; deliberately built Dettol tap to flip the mind holds… Safety & germ protection Coca-Cola tap to flip the mind holds… Dominates the cola category Bisleri tap to flip the mind holds… The first brand for mineral water Positioning creates immediate mental associations when consumers encounter a brand — adrenaline/action brands own thrill and adventure. These are results of deliberate positioning strategies, not accidents. 2 Three fundamental questions Every positioning strategy must answer them — Sensodyne does Three questions, one brand — Sensodyne who · what · why Q1 Who is the target audience? Q2 What category are we competing in? Q3 Why should this target choose us? Sensodyne's answer Consumers experiencing tooth sensitivity — not those seeking whiteness, freshness or general oral hygiene. the sensitive-teeth consumer Play Next Reset who — the audience Why the three questions work Answering who / what / why lets Sensodyne occupy a distinct space focused specifically on sensitivity relief — differentiation from broader competitors like Colgate or Close-Up, without abandoning the toothpaste category. 3 The complete STP framework Three moves, one integrated strategy Segmentation divide the heterogeneous market into homogeneous groups Targeting prioritise by size, accessibility, fitment, economics Positioning create a distinctive image that resonates and differentiates The cost of skipping it Appealing to everyone results in diluted messaging and wasted resources. STP keeps new product launches and campaigns strategically focused. Key takeaways Positioning = a distinctive and valued place in the target consumer's mind, relative to competitors. Associations — Dettol = safety, Coca-Cola = cola, Bisleri = water — are built, not born . Three questions: Who is the target, what category are we in, why choose us? Sensodyne: sensitive-teeth consumers · toothpaste category · specialised sensitivity relief & protection. STP is one integrated strategy — skip a step and the messaging dilutes .

chapters.label: The Accor map
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 15 The Accor map : many positions, one parent Positioning creates a distinct space in consumers' minds — beyond product features, into perception and psychology. Perceptual maps show how one group serves many segments at once. 1 Why positioning earns its own lecture Mental space · dual time · competitive advantage Mental space Positioning is not only what you do with a product — equally important is what you do to the minds of consumers. Coca-Cola and Bisleri created brand perceptions beyond just being beverages Dual-time perspective Effective positioning puts “one foot in the present and one foot in the future” — anticipating market changes and consumer needs Competitive advantage Positioning correctly to multiple segments simultaneously increases revenue and profitability without one segment negatively influencing the parent company's brand image 2 Accor's three-tier map Ibis · Novotel & Mercure · Pullman & Sofitel Legend The perceptual map — price × experience one parent, three positions price per night → room design · amenities · service → ₹3,000+ ₹5,000+ ₹7,000+ ₹9,000+ ₹15,000+ Ibis Novotel Mercure Pullman Sofitel Legend ₹3,000–4,000 / night ₹5,000–7,000 / night ₹9,000–15,000+ / night Ibis Novotel & Mercure Pullman & Sofitel Legend Clear Same parent company — Accor — yet each chain targets a different consumer segment with distinct positioning. Tap a tier to isolate it. 3 The parallel at home ITC runs the same play ITC — five stars above, boutique below Similarly, ITC maintains five-star properties while launching boutique hotel chains to reach price-sensitive consumers — preserving the luxury brand image while capturing segments that would never book the flagship. Multi-segment positioning without brand dilution. Key takeaways Positioning happens in the mind — perception and psychology, not just features. Keep one foot in the present, one in the future — anticipate the market you will serve next. Accor: ₹3,000–4,000 Ibis · ₹5,000–7,000 Novotel & Mercure · ₹9,000–15,000+ Pullman & Sofitel Legend. Multiple segments at once is an advantage only if the positions stay distinct — no dilution. ITC's boutique chains prove the same move works across industries.

chapters.label: Frames · POPs · PODs
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 15 Frames of reference, POPs & PODs Positioning strategy, step by step: first choose the arena you compete in — natural and extended — then defend the points of parity and build the points of differentiation. 1 Step 1 — the frame of reference Natural competitors vs extended substitutes Natural frame Direct competitors offering similar products — for cooking oil: Safola, Dhara, Fortune Extended frame Indirect competitors that may substitute your product — olive oil, pure ghee, mustard oil, as health consciousness increases The frame-of-reference switch who are you actually fighting? Cooking oil Safola Dhara Fortune natural frame — direct competitors Olive oil Pure ghee Mustard oil extended frame — substitutes Natural frame Extended frame Natural frame: direct competitors offering similar products — for cooking oil, that is Safola, Dhara and Fortune. 2 The Gypsy King lesson An empty natural frame is not a strategy The Gypsy King case — a share story launched 1985 1985 competitors enter after market share → Tata Sumo · Mahindra Scorpio AC · power steering · power windows · mileage · ride · seating India's first SUV — no direct competitors share declines — emotional attachment notwithstanding Play Next Reset step 1/4 1985 — Maruti launches the Gypsy, India's first SUV. It has no direct competitors: the natural frame of reference is empty. Key takeaway — the long game Understanding both natural and extended frames of reference is essential for long-term positioning success rather than short-lived market dominance. 3 Step 2 — POPs and PODs Parity earns you a seat; differentiation wins the game POPs Attributes shared with competitors — the bare minimum standards required to be competitive. Uber, Ola and Meru all provide cab services; without POPs a brand loses competitive credibility and consumer trust PODs Unique attributes that distinguish your brand — Uber and Ola run outsourced driver models with personal vehicles, while Meru owns its fleet Lysol vs Gainda Phenyl — pull the POP what happens if parity goes? Germ-killing POP Cleaning POP Lime fragrance POD Shine POD Freshness POD consumer choice Lysol Gainda Phenyl POPs intact Remove germ-killing Lysol's PODs — lime fragrance, shine, freshness — sit on top of the shared POPs (germ-killing, cleaning). Keep the parity; sell the difference. If Lysol removed germ-killing — a POP shared with traditional phenyl — the lecture predicts that… Lecture 15 · concept check A its lime fragrance would carry the brand B consumers would revert to Gainda Phenyl C nothing would change — PODs are enough D removing POPs strengthens positioning Key takeaways Frame of reference first: natural (Safola · Dhara · Fortune) and extended (olive oil · ghee · mustard oil). Gypsy (1985) owned an empty natural frame — then Tata Sumo & Mahindra Scorpio arrived with AC, power steering, power windows, better mileage, ride and seating. POPs are the entry ticket ; PODs are the reason to choose (Uber/Ola's outsourced drivers vs Meru's owned fleet). Lysol: fragrance (lime), shine, freshness = PODs on top of germ-killing & cleaning POPs. Never trade away a POP — parity removed is positioning weakened .

chapters.label: The four levels
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 16 From mass market to market of one The STP framework evolved into micro-marketing — four levels of approach, from serving everyone to serving a single customer by name. 1 Segments are found, not invented The ground rules before the zoom Identify, don't create Marketers do not create segments; they identify existing segments in the market based on shared needs and wants Homogeneity / heterogeneity Within a segment customers are very similar to each other; across different segments they are distinctly different 2 The zoom spectrum Mass → segment → niche → individual The zoom spectrum crowd → group → few → single 1. Mass market 2. Market segment 3. Niche market 4. Individual · market of one 1. Mass market Production-centric: mass production, mass distribution, mass promotion. Target: Everyone — the entire market Coca-Cola Pepsi Amul butter Dettol Advantages: Cost-effective · high volume sales · wide market reach Challenges: Inventory costs if products don't sell · one-size-fits-all alienates specific preferences · waste and storage costs 3 The industrial middle ground Mass customisation & customerisation Mass customisation Combining mass-production efficiency with customised personalisation at the individual level Customerisation A blend of mass marketing with customised messaging and product modifications — broad reach, individual relevance Flexibility is a strategy Organisations can operate at multiple levels simultaneously with different product lines — and large groups may own multiple distinct brands serving different segments (L'Oréal and Body Shop). Key takeaways Mass (Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Amul butter, Dettol): cheapest per unit, but inventory risk and one-size-fits-all alienation. Segment : Dove Men Care, Myntra Forward (Gen Z) — better product–market fit with targeted efficiency. Niche : Nomatic, Lush, Beeswrap — limited competition, loyalty, premium pricing; small size and deep expertise required. Market of one : NIKEiD, Share a Coke with Rahul, Raymond Made-to-Measure, Shaadi.com — maximum personalisation, premium willingness. Mass customisation & customerisation blend scale with individual relevance .

chapters.label: POD → POP evolution
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 16 The POD → POP treadmill Points of parity are the minimum requirements to compete; points of differentiation are the reasons to choose. The catch: differentiation decays into parity the moment competitors copy it. 1 POP and POD, defined Category entry ticket vs reason to choose Point of parity Attributes shared by competing brands in the same category — industry-standard features and the minimum requirements to be considered. All disinfectants must kill germs; without POP a brand cannot be competitive Point of differentiation Unique attributes that distinguish one brand from competitors — reasons to choose one over another, creating competitive advantage Lysol vs Genda-Final: better fragrance, plastic bottle, superior packaging Oral-B blue indicator bristles that fade to white when it's time to replace the toothbrush Gillette Mark 3 three-blade design vs two-blade competitors — originally a POD 2 Watch a POD die Three blades → parity → five blades 🪒 The razor ladder — POD → POP → POD Gillette's endless climb Gillette POP 2 blades Competitors POP 2 blades Play Next Reset step 1/5 The baseline: two-blade razors are the category norm — the POP every competitor must match to be considered. 3 Strategic implications What the treadmill demands Flexibility Operate at multiple levels simultaneously with different product lines Brand portfolio Large organisations may own multiple distinct brands for different segments — L'Oréal and Body Shop Market research Niche and individual-level success requires deep consumer insights into specific needs Positioning Effective STP needs clear understanding of competitors, frame of reference and meaningful differentiation The one-line summary Continuous innovation is necessary to maintain a POD and prevent commoditisation — balance cost efficiency with customisation, because the appropriate strategy depends on resources, market conditions and consumer preferences. Key takeaways POP = industry-standard attributes required to compete (all disinfectants kill germs). POD = unique attributes that create preference (Oral-B's fading bristles, Lysol's fragrance & packaging). Copied PODs become POPs: three blades → parity → five-blade Fusion as the new POD. Run multiple levels and brands at once — flexibility is part of the design (L'Oréal / Body Shop). Innovate continuously or be commoditised .

chapters.label: The three circles
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 17 The three circles of positioning POPs and PODs, located on a map: consumer desires × competitor features × your organisation's features. Where the circles overlap decides what you must have, what wins, and what is wasted. 1 Why the model exists Two elements, balanced POPs represent features and benefits common across all competing brands — basic consumer expectations and category requirements (a toothbrush maintaining oral hygiene; an antiseptic having antiseptic properties). PODs are unique features or benefits competitors do not offer — valued by consumers, genuinely different, and able to fulfil desires in ways competitors cannot. Establish parity to compete; create differentiation to win. 2 The map itself Light the zones The three-circles locator desires × competitors × you Consumer desires Competitor features Your features POP POD invalid Light POP Light POD Light invalid zone Clear Press a button to light a zone — every positioning idea lives in one of these three places. POP location Intersection of all three circles — consumer need overlaps both your and competitor offerings POD location Intersection of consumer desire and your features, excluding competitor features — the unique value proposition Invalid zone Features you offer that competitors also offer, without matching consumer desires 3 PODs expire The Dettol motion-sensor lesson Motion-sensor hand wash — a POD that didn't travel Dettol's motion-sensor hand-wash dispenser was initially a POD — but it became expensive and impractical for home use due to the high frequency of use, never achieved universal adoption, and remained primarily in commercial establishments . PODs have a finite lifespan; once competitors copy a differentiation, it automatically becomes a POP. 4 The two-step strategy, revisited Frame first, then differentiation Determine frame of reference natural + extended competitors → the required POPs Identify points of differentiation find gaps between competitor offerings and consumer desires 5 Critical success factors for a POD Five tests before you ship • Valued by consumers — addresses a genuine need or desire. • Defensible — ideally built on sustainable advantages: technology, patents, brand equity. • Addresses a market opportunity — a gap between what competitors offer and what consumers want. • Not easily replicated — if easily copied, it becomes a POP. • Clearly communicated — the target audience must understand and appreciate the differentiation. In the three-circles model, a POD lives… Lecture 17 · concept check A at the triple intersection of all three circles B where consumer desires meet your features, excluding competitors C where you and competitors overlap without consumer desire D outside all three circles Key takeaways POPs ensure viability in the category; PODs create preference and justify premium pricing or share gains. POP = triple intersection ; POD = desires ∩ you, minus competitors . The you∩competitor overlap without desire is the invalid zone — effort nobody asked for. PODs have a finite lifespan — Dettol's motion-sensor dispenser stayed commercial for a reason. Great positioning fulfils consumer desires in ways competitors cannot .

chapters.label: Case files
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 17 Case files: POPs and PODs at work Three stories that make the framework tangible: a bristle that fades, a sofa that changes clothes, and an antiseptic war fought over a sting. 1 Open a case file Oral-B · House of Quirk · Dettol vs Savlon Case files — open one three brands, one pattern Oral-B toothbrush House of Quirk Dettol vs Savlon POP Maintaining oral hygiene — common across every brand in the crowded toothbrush market POD Colour-changing bristles that indicate replacement — blue dye fades to white, signalling a new brush bristle indicator New brush Weeks pass Fresh brush — indicator fully saturated. The move focused on consumer benefit rather than product feature and differentiated Oral-B overnight without changing the underlying technology . Once competitors copied it, the feature transitioned from POD to POP. 2 The pattern underneath Every case runs the same play Find the POP The shared expectation: oral hygiene · quality furniture · antiseptic properties Add a valued POD Fading bristles · a new look every 10 days · a no-sting formula Defend or reframe When copied, the POD becomes POP — Dettol reframed its sting as proof of working Key takeaways Oral-B: a colour-changing bristle (blue → white) differentiated the brand overnight — benefit, not feature. House of Quirk: furniture covers created a niche between furniture sales and cushion covers — a makeover every 10 days . Savlon attacked the sting Dettol ignored; Dettol came back with “Sting means it's working.” Every case: hold the POP, own the POD , and reframe when attacked. Copied PODs decay into POPs — the pattern repeats across categories.

chapters.label: Why people buy
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 18 Why do people buy ? The fundamental question of consumer behaviour: purchases driven by needs, desires, impulses and emotional states — in minds that are never empty. 1 Every purchase closes a gap Reach · restore · maintain · protect Consumers purchase to reach, restore, maintain, or protect a desired state — the gap between their current state and where they wish to be. And marketing never lands on a blank page: it engages with existing memories, experiences, expectations, desires, identities, biases and goals. Minds are never empty. The desired-state machine reach · restore · maintain · protect desired state current state reach restore maintain protect Clear Purchases are driven by needs, desires, impulses and emotional states — and context matters (the same consumer buys coffee differently at different times of day). Pick a verb. Stimulus and imagination Consumers respond to imagined consumption almost as strongly as to actual product information. Visual representations and storytelling create experiences that make products feel real and desirable. 2 Three case studies — the story beyond the product Swiggy mangoes · TRIA · Forest Essentials Swiggy mangoes Water droplets, fresh appearance — sensory appeal through visual representation. Consumers feel they are looking at real mangoes: imagined consumption that sells an experience and freshness, not just a product. TRIA hair treatment Targets people experiencing hair loss or thinning; before-and-after narratives attempt to reduce the distance between actual self and desired self , connecting with self-esteem. Relevance varies by audience — it matters only to those with the problem. Forest Essentials serum ₹5,500–7,000 for 30ml. Statistics — 100%, 97%, 94% — build credibility; luxury minimalistic upmarket packaging; visual appeal plus scientific claims create desirability. Sample size: 36. Forest Essentials — the evidence machine ₹5,500–7,000 for 30ml clinically claimed result 1 clinically claimed result 2 clinically claimed result 3 Play Next Reset the stats 3 Story over product The insight that ties the cases together • Marketing creates narratives and storylines, not just product features. • The emotional narrative helps consumers achieve their desired state more than the product itself. • Consumers frequently use the appearance of evidence — how data is presented — rather than the actual quality of evidence. • Successful marketing combines product benefits with storytelling that addresses aspirations and self-esteem. Key takeaways People buy to reach, restore, maintain or protect a desired state. Marketing works on minds that are never empty — memories, biases, identities, goals already live there. Imagined consumption is nearly as strong as the real thing — Swiggy's droplets sell freshness . TRIA sells the distance between actual self and desired self — relevance varies by audience. ₹5,500–7,000 serum: 100% · 97% · 94% stats on a sample of 36 — appearance of evidence beats quality of evidence.

chapters.label: Eras & nudges
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 18 Rational → irrational → nudged How the study of the consumer evolved: classical economics trusted the rational buyer, Kahneman and Tversky broke the assumption, and Thaler's nudges now design the choice environment itself. 1 The evolution, era by era Play through seventy years Three eras of the consumer rational → irrational → nudged 1 2 3 1950s–60s 1970s–90s present Classical era · 1950s–60s Dominated by classical economics: consumers are rational beings making predictable choices. People buy only what they need; demand and supply balance naturally; behaviour is easy to forecast. Play Next Reset classical era 2 Evidence for irrationality The breakfast menu experiment Idly, biryani, desserts — in the morning Presented with food menu options in the morning, people choose varied items — idly, biryani, desserts — despite it being early morning. Rational behaviour would suggest everyone picks light breakfast options; the varied choices reflect individual experiences, memories, beliefs and preferences . Heuristics at work — Nutella's Amazon listing 800 ratings 4.5 stars ₹311 discount free delivery cash back offers stock availability Mental shortcuts that help consumers move from one decision stage to the next — and choose right options efficiently. 3 The nudge toolkit Choice architecture in the wild European trash disposal Adding an interactive ramp near trash cans transformed waste disposal into a fun activity — proper disposal behaviour increased. Staircase placement Positioning stairs before elevators encourages physical activity; design influences behaviour positively. Bestseller labels Marking products as bestsellers creates choice architecture without demeaning other products — guiding selection toward popular options. Product recommendations Suggesting products based on consumption patterns guides consumers toward suitable choices. 4 Heuristics vs nudges — the distinction Shortcuts in the mind vs design of the environment Heuristics Mental shortcuts that help compare options — ratings, prices, discounts Nudges Environmental design that guides behavior toward naturally better choices without direct persuasion A 'bestseller' label on a menu is best described as… Lecture 18 · concept check A a heuristic, because it is a mental shortcut B a nudge, because it redesigns the choice environment without restricting choice C a discount, because it changes the price D irrational behaviour with no logical basis Key takeaways Classical era (1950s–60s): rational, predictable consumers who buy only what they need. Cognitive revolution (1970s–90s): Kahneman & Tversky , “Judgment under Uncertainty” — consumers are irrational. Contemporary era: Thaler's nudges — the mother-elephant philosophy of gentle environmental design. Heuristics are mental shortcuts (800 ratings · 4.5 stars · ₹311 discount); nudges are designed environments . Ethical marketing nudges consumers toward decisions beneficial to both parties .

chapters.label: The five stages
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 19 The five stages of buying Problem recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase decision → post-purchase behavior — the theoretical framework every marketer learns first. 1 Walk the stages Play, or step through manually 🧭 The five-stage step player the textbook spine of a decision 1. Problem recognition 2. Information search 3. Evaluation of alternatives 4. Purchase decision 5. Post-purchase behavior Stage 1 · Problem recognition A need or gap between desired and existing state is identified — as simple as feeling hungry, as complex as needing new electronics. The triggering point for all subsequent purchasing decisions. Play Next Reset step 1/5 The theory assumes a linear, sequential process — consumers follow all five stages in order. (Reality is messier; see the next chapter.) 2 Heuristics speed every stage up Mental shortcuts without extensive analysis Ratings & reviews High ratings — like 4.5 stars — provide assurance of product quality. Brand name Established brands like JBL or Samsung serve as quality indicators. Price discounts Percentage off or reduced prices influence purchase decisions. Scarcity “Only 6 rooms left” creates urgency to purchase immediately. Free delivery Adds perceived value to the offering. Warranty & returns Warranty and return policies reduce perceived risk. Visual elements Product images and property photos influence decision-making. H&M's nudge Items labelled “Few pieces left” create urgency to buy before stock-outs. Weighted scoring — assigning importance to attributes like memory, graphics and price — belongs to which stage? Lecture 19 · concept check A Problem recognition B Information search C Evaluation of alternatives D Post-purchase behavior Key takeaways Problem recognition is the trigger — a gap between desired and existing state. Search happens across Amazon, Swiggy Instamart, stores, social media, peers, experts . Evaluation = a consideration set + weighted scoring on key attributes. Purchase is the transaction point , accelerated by heuristics. Post-purchase feelings (satisfaction ↔ regret) decide retention and loyalty — often overlooked, always essential.

chapters.label: The messy middle
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 19 The messy middle Linear vs non-linear: real decisions skip stages, backtrack, and loop between exploration and evaluation — an infinity that only closes when the gap between desired and existing state is satisfied. 1 Theory vs reality The same five stages, two very different shapes Theory vs reality — the same five stages toggle the lens Theory: linear Reality: messy 1 Recognition 2 Search 3 Evaluation 4 Purchase 5 Post-purchase Play Next Reset step 1/5 Theory perspective: a linear, sequential process — Recognition → Search → Evaluation → Purchase → Post-purchase, all five stages in order. 2 The loop, live Exploration and evaluation trade places The infinity loop exploration × evaluation, forever until the gap closes explore evaluate the messy middle Pause Restart The consumer explores options and evaluates alternatives in an infinity-loop pattern — the loop continues until the gap between desired and existing state is satisfied. Non-linear, iterative — never a straight line. 3 What makes the middle messy Involvement and time High-involvement products Cars, laptops, properties — all five stages methodically; extensive evaluation; multiple sources; test drives, physical visits, detailed comparisons. Low-involvement products Everyday items, routine purchases — stages compressed or skipped; reduced evaluation; habit or convenience; heuristics play a more significant role. Time constraints Limited time encourages skipping or compressing stages; speed over thorough evaluation; heuristics become more critical in expedited decisions. 4 Real purchases from class Five journeys, five shapes Novel Online research (Amazon) → reviews → physical store comparison → final online purchase Clothing Quality check → price comparison → fitting → purchase with positive feeling Keyboard Online platform search → review analysis → offer evaluation → purchase Coffee Brand-preference decision — Davidoff, despite cheaper options Jewelry Multiple store visits → selection → price negotiation → satisfied purchase Cart abandonment Add items but don't complete purchase — reconsidering, re-evaluating; a stage of the loop, not a failure of it Cart abandonment is proof, not failure Significant in e-commerce: consumers add items but don't complete purchase — a stage where they reconsider or re-evaluate. Organisations deploy heuristics (scarcity, limited-stock notifications) to reduce abandonment rates. It demonstrates the non-linear nature of modern consumer behaviour. Key takeaways Consumers cannot be assumed to follow linear decision paths. Leverage heuristics strategically at various touchpoints — ratings, scarcity, discounts, visuals. Facilitate easy movement between stages — especially revisiting information and evaluation . Address post-purchase satisfaction to build loyalty. Understanding consumer segments helps predict which heuristics will be most effective .

chapters.label: Journey variations
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 20 Journey variations Schiffman and Professor Jain define consumer behavior; the stimulus–choice frame and the five-stage model give it a skeleton — and then real buyers skip, reverse and loop right through it. Consumer behavior is a multidisciplinary field — psychology, marketing, anthropology, behavioral economics and neurology — that explains why, when, how and where purchases are made. It covers not just the purchase decision itself but the emotions, psychology and behaviors that accompany it. Schiffman Consumer behavior is the study of consumers' choices during searching, evaluating, purchasing, and using products and services that satisfy their needs. Professor Jain Consumer behavior is the study of people and activities associated with purchases — how products are chosen, distributed, and used, considering the emotions, psychology, and behaviors these processes create. 1 Stimulus → choice the whole phenomenon in between is the field STIMULUS — any external element that grabs attention momentarily: advertisements, celebrities, colour combinations. CHOICE — the consumer's preference and decision to purchase a product, brand or service. understanding what stimulus triggered a purchase — and how it influenced the mind — is the heart of the field 2 The five-stage model, summarized the theoretical spine every journey is measured against Need recognition gap between current & desired state — internal or external trigger Information search online, stores, platforms, recommendations Evaluation of alternatives specs, price, availability, discounts, benefits Purchase decision the transaction Post-purchase satisfaction → regret — it decides loyalty 3 …and then reality happens run the five real-world shapes of the same journey The journey-path machine one model · five real-world shapes linear Skip · impulse (70% off) Skip · direct (ketchup) reverse loop stimulus 1 Need recognition 2 Information search 3 Evaluation of alternatives 4 Purchase decision 5 Post- purchase the entire phenomenon between the stimulus and the choice is consumer behavior Play Prev Next Reset Mode: linear · step 1/6 — A stimulus grabs attention — an ad, a celebrity, a colour combination. stage skipping Impulse: jump straight from stimulus to purchase — a 70%-off item bought with no prior need or planning. Direct purchases: a parent's clear instruction ("buy ketchup") skips the first three stages entirely. stage reversal After evaluation, new information can send the consumer back to search . Post-purchase experiences or external feedback may even revisit need recognition — questioning whether the purchase was necessary at all. circular patterns The journey is not always a forward progression — it can loop , with consumers revisiting earlier stages based on new information, changing circumstances, or unexpected feedback from others. Key takeaways Consumer decision-making theoretically follows a linear path but often deviates in practice. Consumers may skip stages, reverse directions, or loop back based on new information and circumstances. Both the framework and its real-world variations matter — that is what makes the behavior influencable. Post-purchase behavior is as important as the pre-purchase process in shaping future decisions and brand loyalty. Discounts, time constraints, recommendations and availability decide which stages get prioritized or skipped .

chapters.label: Autopsy of a purchase
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 20 Autopsy of a purchase A classroom exercise takes one real, ordinary purchase and dissects it stage by stage — revealing the actual path a consumer walks, and the exact nudge that closes the deal. The autopsy of purchase is a practical application of everything above: analyze a recent purchase and surface the stages you actually went through — including the ones theory says should be there but weren't. The specimen on the table: Moroccan oil shampoo . 1 Lay the stages on the table trigger → search → alternatives → the closing nudge → purchase → post-purchase The autopsy table — step through it Moroccan oil shampoo · classroom exercise 1 Trigger 2 Search 3 Alternatives 4 Final factor 5 Purchase 6 Post-purchase Play Prev Next Reset Step 1 of 6 · Need recognition Trigger Internal need — the existing shampoo was running out. The gap opened on its own; no advertisement required. Autopsy status — step 1/6: Trigger · Need recognition Why the autopsy matters The textbook says every stage runs in order. The autopsy found search across Nyka, Amazon and retail stores , four serious alternatives — L'Oreal, Kerastase, Nat Habit, Flam — and then a single 15% discount settling the whole evaluation. Real journeys are shorter than models, and one heuristic can carry the final weight. The stage that outlives the receipt Post-purchase here was satisfaction and confidence in nourishing hair — happiness and positive feelings. That emotional residue is not the end of the journey; it is the trigger waiting for the next repurchase , which lets the consumer skip exploration entirely next time. Key takeaways An autopsy maps the actual stages of a real purchase — not the theoretical checklist. Search spanned platforms and stores ; evaluation produced four alternatives with similar benefits. The final decision factor was a 15% discount on Nyka — one heuristic, one closed deal. Post-purchase satisfaction feeds the next journey — as important as everything before the receipt.

chapters.label: Touchpoints & framework
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 21 Touchpoints & the integrated framework The journey is non-linear; involvement sets its depth; marketing acts far beyond the point of sale — and underneath it all runs a six-part cycle from unfulfilled need to tension reduction. low involvement Pizza at 11:30 PM — triggered by immediate need or a notification. Minimal search or evaluation; a quick decision without extensive comparison; driven by convenience and impulse. high involvement Laptop purchase — extensive search and evaluation; specifications, brands, configurations and price ranges; detailed comparison with assigned weightage; significant emotional response post-purchase. No generalized pattern applies Decision-making is highly subjective and varies from individual to individual — the same person sails through a pizza order and spends weeks inside the messy middle for a laptop. 1 Marketing lives at every touchpoint not just at the point of sale trigger Discounts, celebrity endorsements, events — influence at the trigger phase itself. search Discovering product popularity or best sellers while exploring options. evaluation Product quality comparisons — the evaluation stage is a marketing surface too. post-purchase Reviews, ratings, recall — and past positive experiences become future triggers, letting consumers skip exploration and go straight to purchase. 2 The integrated consumer behavior framework unfulfilled need → fear/tension → drive → behavior → consumption → goal fulfillment & tension reduction The framework-cycle machine unfulfilled need → tension reduced tension ↓ at goal fulfillment 1 2 3 4 5 6 unfulfilled need goal fulfillment & tension reduction Play Prev Next Reset Stage 1 of 6 Unfulfilled need A gap between the current state and the desired state — the lecture's example: hunger. It can be a need, a want or a desire. Cycle status — stage 1/6: Unfulfilled need Individual variability The drive → behavior transition depends on individual perceptions, personality traits, ability to learn, and personal attitudes. The messy middle Once triggered, consumers enter an infinity zone of continuous exploration and evaluation — comparing across Amazon, Flipkart and physical stores, filling carts and wish lists — until a strong enough stimulus converts it into an actual purchase. Key takeaways Decision-making is a continuous, non-linear process of exploration and evaluation. The journey differs sharply by involvement level — pizza at 11:30 PM vs a laptop. Marketing influences multiple touchpoints across the entire journey , not just at purchase. Behavior is fundamentally driven by the need to reduce tension from unfulfilled needs, wants or desires . Outcomes are individually specific — explaining them requires perception, personality, learning and attitudes .

chapters.label: Recap · the journey
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 22 Recap · the decision-journey arc Session notes not captured — this lecture's page in the source PDF is blank. What follows is an honest recap of the Lectures 19–21 arc, plus a short self-test drawn only from that arc. Session notes not captured — recap of the decision-journey arc Lecture 22 arrived as a blank page in the source PDF. Rather than invent notes, this chapter replays the arc the previous three lectures built: the five stages , the infinity loop , and the integrated framework cycle . Everything below comes strictly from Lectures 19–21. 1 Replay the arc three panels, one continuous story — from the linear model to the engine underneath it The arc, one machine three panels · Lectures 19–21 19 · The 19–20 · The 21 · The 1 Need 2 Search 3 Evaluation 4 Purchase 5 Post- theory drew a straight line — Lecture 20 showed every way reality bends it Panel 1 of 3 · Lecture 19 The five stages Need recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase decision → post-purchase behavior. Plus the heuristics — ratings, discounts, scarcity — that shortcut it, and the cart abandonment that proves decisions are non-linear. Play Prev Next Reset Recap status — panel 1/3: Lecture 19 · The five stages 2 Self-test three questions, drawn only from Lectures 19–21 In the integrated framework, what does an unfulfilled need create first? Recap · Lectures 19–21 A An impulse purchase B Fear or tension C A price comparison D Post-purchase regret The “messy middle” describes… Recap · Lectures 19–21 A a linear five-stage checklist B an exploration–evaluation loop that a strong stimulus eventually breaks C the post-purchase warranty window D a pricing heuristic Buying a 70%-off item with no prior need or planning skips… Recap · Lectures 19–21 A only the information search B the purchase decision C need recognition, information search and evaluation D nothing — all five stages still run Key takeaways Five stages — recognition, search, evaluation, purchase, post-purchase: the spine of every journey. The messy middle — exploration and evaluation loop until a strong stimulus breaks it. The framework cycle — need → tension → drive → behavior → consumption → goal fulfillment; tension reduced. Real journeys skip, reverse and loop — the model is a map, not the territory.

chapters.label: Three theories
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 23 Three theories of motivation Freud, Maslow and Herzberg answer the same question — why do we do what we do? — from three directions: the subconscious, the hierarchy of needs, and the two factors of satisfaction. These theories explain what initiates the five-stage decision-making process — need recognition, search, evaluation, purchase, post-purchase. All three remain fundamentally relevant; consumers may not climb the ladder linearly and might skip stages, but knowing which theory is operating helps predict and influence behavior. 1 Freudian theory — the iceberg behavior is guided by subconscious, not conscious, motivations Conscious — thoughts and beliefs you are fully aware of 10% 90% Subconscious & pre-conscious — where most decisions originate pre-conscious — memories recalled when triggered unconscious — deep desires, accessible through dreams ID Basic instincts and immediate desires — wanting that samosa right now. Ego Rationality and reality — eating only the cover of the samosa, balancing desire with health. Super Ego Morality and what is considered correct — refusing the samosa for health reasons. Application Consumer decisions are motivated by which of the three dominates — instinct, reality, or moral consideration. Only 10% of decision-making comes from the conscious mind; 90% originates from the subconscious and pre-conscious. 2 Maslow's hierarchy — the pyramid behavior is driven by the lowest unmet need Maslow's pyramid — climb it the lowest unmet need drives behavior SELF-ACTUALIZATION ESTEEM SOCIAL SAFETY PHYSIOLOGICAL click a level, or let the climber run Play Prev Next Reset Level 5 of 5 · climbing from the base Self-actualization Self-development, personal fulfillment and realization — becoming what one is capable of becoming. Life journey: Later in life, the climb turns to personal meaning. Pyramid status — level 5/5: Self-actualization. Consumers do not progress until the current level is satisfied. The hungry-person test A hungry person would prioritize buying food over purchasing luxury items — the lowest unmet level runs the show. Life journey: students secure physiological and safety needs through education; young professionals build security through employment; mid-career, social and esteem needs dominate; later in life, the pursuit turns to self-actualization and personal meaning. 3 Herzberg's two-factor theory hygiene prevents dissatisfaction; motivating factors create satisfaction The two-factor dials hygiene prevents · motivating propels Hygiene factors — job dissatisfiers Salary & compensation · working conditions · company policies · supervisor relationships Dissatisfaction meter hygiene present Present → dissatisfaction is prevented. But note: no satisfaction is created — hygiene only defends. Motivating factors — job satisfiers Achievement & accomplishment · recognition & appreciation · responsibility · growth & development Satisfaction meter motivators absent Absent → not dissatisfaction — just neutrality. Nothing to be unhappy about, nothing to be excited by. Dual approach: reduce dissatisfaction by improving hygiene (on) · increase satisfaction by enhancing motivators (off). The Free Chai Rule Free chai at work will not make employees love their jobs — but removing it creates discontent . Salary, working conditions and basic amenities are expected : they prevent dissatisfaction without inspiring motivation. True motivation comes from meaningful work, recognition, and opportunities for growth. Key takeaways Freud: 90% of decision-making is subconscious — ID (instinct), Ego (reality), Super Ego (morality). Maslow: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualization; the lowest unmet need leads. Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivating factors create satisfaction — fix both, inspire with the second. All three remain relevant; consumers may skip stages and rarely climb in a straight line. These theories are the ignition system for the five-stage decision process.

chapters.label: Theory match
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 23 Theory match Six confessions from the classroom. Each one is a motivation theory in miniature — pick the theory that explains it, and the reasoning behind the match. Six confessions, three theories 0 / 6 “Salary is fine, but my work is boring and I nap at my desk.” Confession 1 of 6 — whose theory explains it? Freudian Maslow Herzberg Next confession Reset Confession 1/6 on the table — pick Freudian, Maslow or Herzberg. Key takeaways Snooze vs boss and crying at the ad — Freudian: subconscious conflict between ID, Ego and Super Ego. Dead Wi-Fi and the novel — Maslow: unmet lower needs block the climb; satisfied ones release self-actualization. Boring-but-paid and raise-without-thanks — Herzberg: hygiene is present, motivators are not. Diagnosing the theory is the first step to predicting and influencing the behavior.

chapters.label: Perception & brands
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 24 Perception & the brand flip Perception is the lens through which consumers view products and brands — and it is not built on objective reality. Marketers shape it with cues, illusions and brand associations. Perception is the process of how individuals see and interpret the world around them. It is not based solely on objective reality — it is heavily influenced by the external cues and stimuli marketers provide. Selective Consumers only absorb information that aligns with their needs, requirements and background. Subjective The same product or image can mean completely different things to different individuals. Constructive Given partial information, consumers fill in the gaps from existing knowledge and beliefs. Abstract Perception varies significantly from person to person — it is not universally standardized. 1 How marketers influence perception illusions prove the flip is possible — cues decide what you see Cue check — duck, or rabbit? Duck cue Rabbit cue · add carrots no carrot → the beak wins: it's a duck The duck–rabbit exercise: same lines, different perception. Adding elements (like carrots) dramatically shifts how the object is read. The classic illusions The lecture uses two famous ambiguous images — the young lady / elderly lady and the duck / rabbit . Same image, two readings: adding elements — like carrots in the rabbit-duck exercise — dramatically shifts how consumers perceive the object. The marketer's cue kit • Adding visual elements — packaging design, colours, imagery • Introducing price points and discounts • Creating brand associations through endorsements and advertising • Attaching meaning and messaging to physical products 2 The brand flip the same model, three brands, three completely different expectations The brand-flip switcher same model · three different expectations the model — identical in all three ads Nykaa Fab India Label Life Cosmetics brand Nykaa The viewer now expects to see: Makeup Skincare Personal care products Same model, same pose — the brand name alone re-categorizes the entire ad. Brand: Nykaa (Cosmetics brand) → perception shifts to makeup, skincare, personal care products. Simply changing the brand name changes the product category the consumer expects. Key takeaways Perception is selective, subjective, constructive and abstract — never a neutral camera. Illusions (young lady / elderly lady, duck–rabbit) prove that cues decide what is seen . Nykaa flips the same model to makeup and skincare; Fab India to clothing and accessories; Label Life to fashion and lifestyle. The brand name alone re-categorizes the ad — that is the power of brand perception in decision-making.

chapters.label: The almonds experiment
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 24 The almonds experiment Four packs of essentially the same almonds. The class prefers one — until the prices are revealed. Then meet perceptual product categories: the shelf trick that ends pure price wars. The almonds experiment same almonds · four meanings Marketing rarely changes the physical product — it changes the meaning attached to it. Rate the packs on looks first; the prices stay hidden until you reveal them. A price hidden Option A · basic Acceptable, but unremarkable. no strong rating — acceptable this is my pick B price hidden Option B · unimpressive Least preferred packaging. ~4/10 class rating this is my pick C price hidden Option C · transparent You can see the product — moderately preferred. ~6/10 class rating this is my pick D price hidden Option D · premium Most preferred — same almonds, better meaning. ~9/10 class rating this is my pick Reveal prices Reset Rating phase — judge the packaging only. Click "Reveal prices" when ready. 1 Product categories vs perceptual product categories how consumers file products by default — and how marketers want them filed By default, consumers store information as broad product categories — "toothpaste", "cars", "ketchup". The marketing goal is to create perceptual product categories built on specific needs and benefits. That lets marketers cater to different needs, reduce direct price competition, increase overall market sales, and build loyalty on benefits rather than product type. Toothpaste Sensitive teeth (Sensodyne) · overall protection (Colgate Total) · freshness (Close-Up) · whitening (Colgate Visible White) — four perceptual categories, one basic category. Cars Hatchbacks, sedans, trucks, ambulances, fire trucks — same basic category, very different perceived jobs. Ketchup Fresh tomato, premium, chef special — the condiment aisle, split into meanings. 2 The Horlicks case one brand, five perceptual categories — each a life stage Horlicks Growth Plus children's growth & development Horlicks Light health-conscious, reduced sugar Horlicks Jr. children aged 8–14 Horlicks Mother's pregnant women's nutrition Horlicks Women's 30+ age-specific needs for women 30+ Key takeaways Consumers chose Option D (~9/10) for perceived benefits — California almonds, gluten-free, high fiber, antioxidants, reusable zip-lock — not better almonds. The price reveal (₹1,000 / ₹800 / ₹550 / ₹2,700) reshuffled preferences toward C and B — but premium buyers stayed with D. Price is a perceptual cue : expensive reads as better quality. Perceptual product categories (Sensodyne = sensitivity, Colgate Total = 24-7 protection, Close-Up = freshness, Visible White = whitening) end pure price competition — and Horlicks multiplied itself into five life-stage variants.

chapters.label: Sensory thresholds
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 25 Sensory thresholds & the four stages Perception is what people think in their minds — subjective and changeable. It starts at the senses: absolute, subliminal and differential thresholds decide what gets in; four stages decide what it becomes. "First impression is the last impression" — first impressions significantly shape consumer perception. Marketers can mold it strategically by understanding how the brain processes information, and perception's inherent biases can be leveraged for marketing advantage. Sensory stimuli Any information received through the senses — sight, touch, smell, sound. Absolute threshold The minimum level of stimulus needed to capture attention — a lit candle in a dark room. Subliminal perception Ads that appeal to multiple senses and create emotional connections — a beverage ad with pouring liquid and ice cubes appears more appealing than just a bottle. Differential threshold The point at which a noticeable difference between two stimuli is detected — adding grains of rice until the weight becomes perceptible. 1 From stimulus to purchase intent exposure → attention → interpretation → organization → outcome The four-stage flow machine exposure → attention → interpretation → organization → outcome 1 Exposure 2 Attention 3 Interpretation 4 Organi- zation ₹? Outcome sensory receptors register the stimulus — then four stages build the perception Play Prev Next Reset Stage 1 of 4 Exposure Encountering the advertisement or product — the stimulus first reaches the senses. Stage machine — step 1/5: Exposure. Final outcome: purchase or intent to purchase. Key takeaways Perception is subjective and can change over time — and it can be strategically molded. Absolute threshold : the minimum stimulus that captures attention (the lit candle in a dark room). Subliminal perception : multi-sensory ads — pouring liquid, ice cubes — create emotional connection. Differential threshold : the just-noticeable difference, grain by grain of rice. Exposure → attention → interpretation → organization — and the outcome is a purchase or the intent to purchase .

chapters.label: The Gestalt lab
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 25 The Gestalt lab The brain does not process images like a camera — it organizes elements into patterns and predicts from past experience. Five principles, five live demos, and the marketing that rides on each. The Gestalt principle: humans organize visual elements into meaningful patterns rather than processing them separately. The brain predicts what it expects to see from past experience — and when predictions don't match reality, it finds the closest matching interpretation. Aesthetic, organized interfaces (like Pinterest) work precisely because of this: navigation becomes easy to understand. The Gestalt lab — five live demos the brain organizes; it doesn't photograph 1. Figure & ground 2. Continuity 3. Grouping & similarity 4. Proximity 5. Closure Invert figure & ground black ground, white figure — the iPod trick Principle 1 of 5 · Figure & ground The foreground object grabs attention; the background (negative space) provides the contrast that makes it stand out. Clever negative space creates visual impressions without explicitly drawing elements. In marketing Apple's iPod ads — black background, white cords Sensodyne — white teeth against black Wine bottle & fork — both in one negative space Peter and the Wolf cover — the child in silhouette Gestalt lab — demo 1/5: Figure & ground. The brain organizes visual objects into coherent patterns and predicts what it expects to see. Key takeaways Figure & ground — distinguish object from background to create the focal point (iPod, Sensodyne). Continuity — guide viewers through sequences and natural decision flows (road arrows, Cars24). Grouping & similarity — organize related information for easier comprehension (uniforms, menus). Proximity — create logical relationships and facilitate comparison (notice boards, price displays). Closure — engage consumers by letting them mentally complete incomplete information .

chapters.label: Attitude & the buckets
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 26 Attitude & the two buckets Attitude is the bridge between perception and decision — Attitude = f(Object, Attributes). And brands that connect attributes to human traits escape the transactional bucket entirely. Motivation drives individuals to act on needs and desires; perception is how consumers interpret and categorize products — which differs from objective reality. Consumers naturally file products into broad categories ("cars", "toothpaste"), but organizations win by shaping the perceptual categories: Sensodyne = sensitivity relief, Colgate Total = 24/7 protection, Close-Up = fresh breath — and Horlicks splitting into variants for children, adults and diabetics. 1 Attitude as the bridge perception ⇄ attitude, formed from past + fresh experiences Perception Attitude Attitude = f(Object, Attributes) A favorable or unfavorable response toward something. The relationship is bidirectional — perception leads to attitude, and attitude influences perception. Formation depends on past experiences and fresh experiences . The decision is never based solely on the product itself, but on the product's attributes as perceived by the consumer . The attribute war — Borges Olive Leaf Infusion Tea vs green tea Antioxidants vs green tea: 2× Vitamin C vs green tea: 4× oleuropin — helps regulate blood pressure zero caffeine zero added flavors These attributes were perception-driven — organizations have far more flexibility manipulating attributes than the core product itself, and that is what positioned Borges as superior. 2 Humanizing brands — the two buckets Epicurus, 340–270 BC: almost everything is transactional. Almost. The bucket sorter Epicurus · 340–270 BC Employer – employee Buyer – seller Siblings Spouses Parent – child Tire ad · father & daughter Utilitarian / transactional bucket You give something, I give something in return. empty — file something Love bucket Pure affection — no expectation of return. empty — who belongs here? Reset Click a relationship — it lands in the bucket Epicurus filed it under (340–270 BC). Case study — why father-daughter in a tire ad? Because a tire is the most utilitarian product imaginable — so the ad humanizes it. Daughters feel protected and safe with their fathers; that emotional connection (safety, protection) maps to tire quality — a quality tire provides vehicle stability and safety. The tire becomes associated with protecting loved ones , not just a transactional purchase — the brand lands in the love bucket , and loyalty follows. Key takeaways Attitude = f(Object, Attributes) — bidirectional with perception, built from past + fresh experiences. Attributes are the marketer's flexible lever — the Borges tea won on 2× antioxidants, 4× vitamin C, oleuropin, zero caffeine. Epicurus: everything is transactional except parent → child — the only true love-bucket relationship. Humanized brands shift the relationship from transactional to relational — the tire ad's father-daughter safety story is the template.

chapters.label: Retention vs acquisition
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 26 Retention vs acquisition Acquisition is expensive and the market is overcrowded; churn keeps draining the funnel. Retention costs roughly a seventh to a tenth as much — the ROI case is not subtle. The cost-comparison machine acquire 1 vs retain 1 Acquire a new customer — CAC 10 units High investment — especially in an overcrowded market where every competitor is bidding for attention. Retain an existing one 1 unit — 1/7th of CAC Retention costs approximately one-seventh to one-tenth of acquisition costs. 1/7th 1/10th Churn — the leak in the bucket Customer churn : consumers leave for competitors despite every rupee of acquisition effort spent on them. Every churned customer must be re-acquired — at 7–10× the cost of simply keeping them. Focus on retention and the ROI beats constant acquisition — the same effort compounds instead of leaking. Comparison — acquire: 10 units · retain: 1.4 units (1/7th of CAC). Switch the dial to see the bar move; either way, retention wins. The takeaway that outlives the spreadsheet Organizations succeed by understanding that consumers don't purchase products — they purchase solutions to their needs and emotional satisfaction . Recognize perceptual product categories, leverage attributes, humanize the brand — and retention follows. Key takeaways CAC is high in an overcrowded market — attention is the scarce resource. Retention costs about 1/7th to 1/10th of acquisition — the cheapest growth lever available. Churn — customers leaving for competitors — is the major organizational challenge. Focus on retention: better ROI than constant acquisition . Consumers purchase solutions and emotional satisfaction, not products .

chapters.label: The ABC model
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 27 The ABC model of brand humanization Attribute → Benefit → Characteristic: physical features, the advantages they buy, and the human values they carry. CEAT, Asian Paints and a pug show how brands stop selling products and start selling meaning. 1 Walk the chain two brands, the same three steps from spec sheet to human value The A → B → C chain machine CEAT Asian Paints A Attribute B Benefit C Characteristic connect all three and the brand stops selling a product — it sells emotions and values Play Prev Next Reset CEAT · step 1 of 3 Attribute Groove technology in the tire — the physical feature on the spec sheet. Chain status — CEAT: A · Attribute 2 Love bucket vs utilitarian bucket why the humanized approach compounds loyalty utilitarian — transactional • Focuses on product quality, performance, value for money • Every competitor can offer similar features • Easily replaceable — subject to consumer churn love bucket — relational • Incorporates emotional and human elements • Creates deeper consumer connections • Positive word-of-mouth and favorable attitudes • Reduces churn — loyalty beyond functional benefits Anthropomorphism — the Hutch pug Humanizing a brand — anthropomorphism — means relating human-like traits to products and using living elements (humans, animals) to create emotional connection. The Hutch pug advertisement outperformed many celebrity-endorsed campaigns: the dog followed the boy everywhere, and the network "followed you too" — no superstar required. 3 The full sequence where humanization plugs into consumer behavior Motivation the drive that initiates the purchase decision Perception interpretation of product attributes and features Attitude favorable / unfavorable — f(object, attributes) Decision the final choice, influenced by attitude toward the brand Key takeaways A → B → C : attributes (tire grooves, paint colors) → benefits (anti-skid traction, personalized spaces) → characteristics (safety, belongingness, self-expression). CEAT : groove tech → anti-skid → a father protecting his family → the love bucket. Asian Paints : "Har Ghar Kuch Kehta Hai" — belongingness, self-expression, memories, identity; relatable families, not celebrities. Anthropomorphism works: Hutch's pug beat celebrity campaigns. Humanization influences motivation → perception → attitude → decision — and builds long-term preference.

chapters.label: The bias lab
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 28 The bias lab Cognitive biases are systematic errors in judgment that run at an unconscious level — mental shortcuts that help consumers navigate complex choices, and the exact levers marketers build on. 1 Conscious vs unconscious two very different kinds of bias Conscious biases Stereotypes developed through social conditioning, environmental influences, and how the people around us think. Unconscious biases Cognitive biases operating at a subconscious level — unintentional judgment errors that misinterpret information and shape consumer behavior.
