The Benetton controversy — conscious bias on display The lecture's example of conscious stereotyping: in the Benetton advertisement controversy, consumers stereotypically associated darker-skinned individuals with criminals and lighter-skinned individuals with authority figures — bias shaped by social conditioning, not by the ad's intent. 2 Four biases, four live demos anchoring · bandwagon · scarcity · endowment — poke each one Anchoring Attention anchors on one element — and everything else is excluded. In smartphone comparisons consumers anchor on price, ratings or delivery speed . Price Ratings Delivery Phone A Price Ratings Delivery Phone B Price Ratings Delivery Phone C Price Ratings Delivery Pick an anchor — price, ratings or delivery — and watch the rest of the comparison fade. Zoom highlights “Save 16%” when switching from monthly to annual billing — anchoring you to the longer commitment. Bandwagon effect If others are doing it, it must be valuable — the more people use something, the more credible it appears. Course platforms show “15,000 people learning on edX today.” Hotel A 1,157 reviews · 8.5 credibility reads high Hotel B 281 reviews · 8.1 fewer voices, less proof Herd lens Exclusivity lens Theory view: 1,157 reviews at 8.5 look more credible than 281 reviews at 8.1 — the herd validates. Scarcity effect A product about to run out is valued more than one in abundance. The same room, the same price — the message changes the willingness to purchase. Hotel booking — same property, same price “Only 6 rooms left at this price” willingness to book now Scarcity communicated → higher willingness to purchase — the decision accelerates. Scarcity message Abundance message H&M shows “Few pieces left” in checkout carts to prompt immediate purchase — and the inventory often quietly replenishes after 24 hours. The effect diminishes once alternatives exist (a different travel destination works just as well). Endowment effect Ownership creates emotional attachment. The same ₹20,000 phone is priced differently depending on whose hands it is in — a ~50% gap showed up in classroom activities. One phone. ₹20,000 new. You own it. You would SELL it for ₹15,000–18,000 You would BUY one for ₹7,000–10,000 ≈ 50% gap between selling and buying prices — for the identical phone. Put it down — just browsing Owning it: you demand 15,000–18,000 to sell, but would only offer 7,000–10,000 to buy the same phone. Ownership inflates value. Starbucks writes your name on the cup and calls it out — a tiny act of ownership that raises perceived value and loyalty. Key takeaways Cognitive biases are subconscious errors in thinking that lead to judgment errors in decisions. They function as mental shortcuts (heuristics) — useful, but they often produce irrational purchases. Marketers deliberately use them: anchoring (Save 16%), bandwagon (15,000 learning), scarcity (only 6 rooms left), personalization (your name on the cup). Scarcity messaging nudges low-involvement purchases — and the stock often replenishes after 24 hours. Biases are not always bad — but recognizing them makes consumers more deliberate .

Data → information → knowledge → wisdom. data Pillar 1 · The raw material grad-text Without data there is nothing to process, nothing to store, nothing to output. Understanding what data is — and how a raw number climbs the ladder into meaning — is the first step in understanding computing. grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-7 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-xl font-bold mt-4 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-3 rounded-xl bg-[#fdf1e0] p-4 text-center text-[.95rem] font-bold text-[#7c4a12] card-warm h-full p-7 text-xl font-bold mt-3 raw Any unprocessed fact or observation that can be recorded and stored meaning By itself, data has no meaning — 42 is just a number, ‘Mumbai’ is just a word context Only when we give data context — process and interpret it — does it become information mt-12 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] text-muted-warm mt-6 mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] text-muted-warm mt-5 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 xl:grid-cols-4 rounded-xl bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 1px dashed #e5c79d inline-flex items-center rounded-full px-3 py-1 text-[.7rem] font-black text-white mt-2 text-[.86rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 text-center text-[.8rem] text-muted-warm mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-3 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 rounded-xl bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 1px dashed #e5c79d font-bold text-[#7c4a12] mt-1 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] rounded-xl p-4 #fbe9e4 1px solid #e6a08c font-bold #9c3a3a mt-1 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-10 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Course quiz A nurse writes 38.5 on a chart. The ward screen later shows “Temperature: 38.5 °C — above the fever threshold”. At what exact moment did the data become information? When the nurse wrote the number down When the number was given context — a reading, a scale and a fever threshold When the doctor prescribed treatment Never — 38.5 is always information 38.5 alone is raw data. It becomes information the moment context and structure give it meaning — a temperature reading, on a scale, compared against a threshold. The prescription comes later, at the wisdom rung. Course quiz Which sequence shows the correct DIKW ladder? Data → Knowledge → Information → Wisdom Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom Information → Data → Knowledge → Wisdom Data → Wisdom → Knowledge → Information Data gains context to become information; information is synthesized into knowledge; knowledge plus judgement becomes wisdom. Each rung adds what the one below lacks. Course quiz “The doctor prescribes a specific treatment based on patterns recognized from thousands of similar cases.” Which DIKW level is this? Data Information Knowledge Wisdom Acting on patterns with judgement — applying what was learned to make the right call — is the top of the pyramid: wisdom. The recognized pattern itself was knowledge; the number was data. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Data — the raw material of computing } lead= /> “38.5” — is that data? 38.5 is data. But{ } “The patient’s temperature is 38.5 °C, which means the patient has a mild fever” is information . Computing transforms data into information. What data actually is The ladder of meaning Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom Each rung adds something the rung below lacks — structure, then synthesis, then judgement. Case study · a clinic ward One temperature reading, four rungs of the ladder The same 38.5 climbs the whole pyramid — watch what each rung adds. {CLINICAL_STEPS.map((s) => ( {s.k} · {s.name} {s.body} ))} Raw number → trend → diagnosis → prescription. That is the whole ladder — and computing builds every rung below wisdom. Data in modern AI systems Data is the lifeblood of AI . Advanced models require significantly larger datasets than traditional machine learning — the principles never change: {AI_PRINCIPLES.map((p) => ( {p.k} {p.v} ))} The hard limit Without data, even the most sophisticated algorithms are completely useless — no model outlearns what it was fed. <Takeaways items={[ Data is raw and meaningless alone — computing transforms data into information . 38.5 is data; “the patient has a fever” is information. , Context is everything: the same number becomes information only once a scale, a threshold and a purpose surround it. , The DIKW ladder — Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom — adds structure, then synthesis, then judgement, one rung at a time, from a fever chart to a prescription. , Data is the lifeblood of AI : more advanced models need more training data, and better quality plus quantity means better predictions — without data, even the most sophisticated algorithms are completely useless. , ]} />

Which subtype — and why can't you take a strict mean of 'experiences'? Nominal — no order exists Ordinal — order is meaningful but the gaps between stars are unequal Discrete quantitative Continuous quantitative Stars rank (order is meaningful) but the distance between 3★ and 4★ isn't a fixed quantity — that's ordinal. It's still qualitative: no true measurement scale. Concept check Monthly marks of the SAME 500 students tracked over six months is… Cross-sectional data Time-series data Panel (longitudinal) data Unstructured data Panel data tracks multiple subjects over multiple time periods — combining cross-sectional breadth with trend analysis. Time series would follow ONE subject only. mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Data, classified — the taxonomy that decides everything } lead= /> You cannot compute a mean of blood groups, and averaging a "city of birth" yields nothing meaningful. Type of data determines which operations are meaningful and valid — proper classification ensures appropriate analysis methods and reliable conclusions. The 80% problem text images audio video sensor streams ≈80% of all data generated globally is UNSTRUCTURED Quantitative — quant Numerical and measurable. You can count it or measure it. Discrete Countable whole numbers — 30 students, 3 goals, 47 apps Continuous Any value in a range, decimals allowed — height 172.4 cm, temperature 36.8°C, time 9.5 s Operations: mean, median, standard deviation, correlation. Collected via surveys; answers{ } what · how often · how many · how much . Quick to analyze, generalizable with representative samples. Qualitative — qual Categorical and non-numerical — labels, qualities, opinions. Nominal — no natural order Blood group A/B/AB/O, city of birth, phone brand. Operations: mode, frequency count, chi-square Ordinal — meaningful order, unequal gaps Amazon stars 1–5, education level, satisfaction: poor/fair/good/excellent Deep contextual insight, collected via interviews; answers how · why . Costs: prone to researcher bias, needs thematic/content analysis, interpretation is subjective. The taxonomy, in runnable Python <Takeaways items={[ By format : structured (rows/columns), semi-structured (JSON/XML), unstructured — ≈80% of global data . , By time : cross-sectional (one moment), panel (many subjects × many periods), time series (one subject over time). , By nature : quantitative (discrete/continuous — means and medians are legal) vs qualitative (nominal/ordinal — mode only). , The type of data determines the valid operations — classify first, analyze second. , ]} />

The downloaded material is: Primary data Secondary data Metadata Quantitative data Collected by someone else for a different purpose and reused for new analysis — that is secondary data. SEBI, IRDAI, NSSO, WHO statistics, census tables and Wikipedia structured data are all classic secondary sources. Concept check Which of the following is metadata — data about data — rather than the data itself? The pixels of a photo — what you actually see The photo's file size, creation date and GPS location The patients a hospital treated last year A WHO health-statistics spreadsheet Metadata describes the characteristics and context of data without being the data: file name, size, creation date, GPS location, camera model and resolution all describe the photo — the pixels themselves are the data. mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Data classification: origin —{ } primary, secondary & metadata } lead= /> When the question is yours — a screen-time survey of your school, an experiment you designed, sensors you deployed. You pay with time, money and human resources, but you get data that fits exactly and methods you can defend. When the question is big — national income, insurance trends, global health. NSSO surveys, SEBI filings and WHO statistics were built by organizations with resources no individual can match. The catch: someone else decided{ } what to measure, and sometimes a subscription stands between you and the data. Metadata: data about data A photo file holds the actual data — the image pixels, what we see — plus metadata that describes it: file name, file size, creation date, GPS location, camera model, resolution. The pixels are the data; everything that describes them is metadata. Four everyday examples: {META_EXAMPLES.map((m, i) => ( {m.icon} {m.name} {m.fields.map((f) => ( {f} ))} ))} Why metadata matters • Critical for organizing, finding and governing large datasets • Reveals information without exposing the actual content • Essential for data management and system organization <Takeaways items={[ Primary data is collected firsthand for your exact question — tailored, reliable and controlled, but slow, expensive and often limited to small samples. , Secondary data is someone else's collection, reused — large-scale, often free and authoritative; but it may not match your question, and quality depends on the original collector. , Metadata is data about data — photo EXIF, database schemas, library catalogs, WhatsApp message logs — revealing information without exposing content. , Metadata is what makes large datasets organizable, findable and governable — the index-card system of the digital world. , ]} />

The recipe is ordered and repeatable; now make the idea precise. Formal definition An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous, step-by-step procedure { } for solving a well-defined problem. It takes an input , processes it through a series of defined steps , and produces a correct output every time it is executed. • Algorithms exist independent of computers — a recipe, a dance routine, a long-division method. • A computer just executes them fast — billions of steps per second. • The quality of computing depends on the quality of the algorithm . • A bad algorithm gives a wrong or slow result no matter how powerful the hardware . A 9th-century Persian word on your Instagram feed The word algorithm derives from{ } Muhammad ibn Musa Al-Qarizmi , a 9th-century Persian mathematician whose work on arithmetic and algebra introduced systematic problem-solving methods to the world. The word algebra also originates from the title of his book. His methods are the reason your feed is sorted at all. Algorithms existed long before modern computers — during World War II, women “computers” calculated artillery trajectories by hand. And quality has always mattered more than muscle: a well-optimized algorithm works even with less computing power — exactly how 1990s AI researchers made progress on limited hardware. ROM is read-only RAM is volatile — contents vanish without power SSDs are too slow The CPU lacks cores RAM is volatile: it holds your program, variables and open files only while powered. Save to secondary storage and the data persists in non-volatile memory. Concept check Why do modern AI systems depend so heavily on GPUs? GPUs have better marketing Training neural networks means doing the same math on billions of numbers simultaneously — GPU parallelism fits perfectly CPUs cannot do multiplication GPUs use less electricity overall A GPU’s thousands of small cores apply one operation to many data points at once — exactly the shape of neural-network training. CPUs have few powerful cores better suited to complex sequential logic. <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Hardware — silicon that makes ideas run } lead= /> Why hardware decided the AI revolution The explosion of AI over the last decade wasn’t just a breakthrough in software — it was a triumph of hardware . At the absolute center sits the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) : designed for mass parallel processing , it breaks a complex task into thousands of smaller, simpler tasks and solves them all{ } simultaneously . That raw parallel horsepower is what built the foundations of modern AI. The turnaround: AI research had been crawling along since the 1990s , starved of compute — researchers compensated by optimizing algorithms, not hardware. Then in 2012 , scientists built AlexNet , a computer-vision model trained on GPUs, and demonstrated to the world what parallel hardware could do. Today every frontier model trains the same way: large language models like ChatGPT , image generators like DALL-E ,{ } Midjourney and Stable Diffusion , and video AI — all of them

Real-time messaging Asynchronous communication Live video streaming Peer-to-peer file sharing Email clients like Gmail and Outlook enable asynchronous communication — the message waits for the recipient — using SMTP to send and IMAP to receive. Concept check Which of the following is a job of a web browser? Compiling source code to machine code Parsing and rendering HTML, CSS and JavaScript Defragmenting the disk Allocating RAM to other programs A browser parses and renders HTML, CSS and JavaScript, manages multiple simultaneous network connections, and provides developer tools — Chrome, Firefox and Safari all do this. Concept check A C program contains a syntax error. What happens when you compile and run it? It runs and shows partial output The error is found at compile time — no output is produced It runs, just slower than usual The error appears line by line as the program executes Compilers translate the entire source code before execution — errors surface at compile time and nothing runs until they are fixed. That all-or-nothing model is why compiled programs produce no output when errors exist. Concept check An IDE combines four tools in one. Which set is correct? Browser, firewall, antivirus, VPN Editor, code runner, debugger, version control Spreadsheet, presentation, database, word processor Disk cleanup, partitioning, encryption, compression An IDE is the all-in-one: a code editor for writing, a runner for executing, a debugger that pinpoints errors, and version control — PyCharm, VS Code and Google Colab all qualify. mt-8 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Application software — the programs you actually touch } lead= /> {APP_GROUPS.map((a) => ( {a.icon} {a.k} {a.points.map((p) => ( • {p} ))} ))} Specialized / professional software Where domains meet algorithms meet Python Domain Software examples Key algorithms used Python connection {PRO_TABLE.map((r) => ( {r.domain} {r.sw} {r.alg} {r.py} ))} Notice the last column: whatever field you enter, Python follows you in . Arithmetic · BODMAS · floats · str() · lists intro. # The arithmetic five print(2 + 3) # addition → 5 print(3 - 2) # subtraction → 1 print(2 * 3) # multiplication → 6 (asterisk) print(3 / 2) # division → 1.5 print(3 ** 2) # exponentiation → 9 (double asterisk) # Order of operations — Python follows PEMDAS/BODMAS; # parentheses override the default order print(2 + 3 * 4) # 14 print((2 + 3) * 4) # 20 # Integers vs floats — whole numbers vs a decimal point print(16 / 2) # 8.0 — division always returns a float print(1_000_000) # underscores make big numbers readable print(0.2 + 0.1) # expect 0.3? print(0.2 + 0.1 == 0.3) # False! # Every language has this quirk: computers store # decimals in BINARY, and 0.1 has no exact binary # form. Harmless for most apps — and fixable for # display: result = 0.2 + 0.1 print(f"{result:.2f}") # two decimal places age = 23 # message = "happy " + age + "rd birthday" # TypeError! # Python refuses: + joins strings OR adds numbers, # never both. message = "happy " + str(age) + "rd birthday" print(message) # The number stays a number for maths elsewhere: print(age + 1, "next year") favorite_number = 7 message = f"My favorite number is {favorite_number}." print(message) # Say hello to everyone. print("Hello Python people!") # The hash (#) starts a comment — Python ignores the rest of the line. # Write comments for the WHY, not the what: the code already says what it does. bicycles = ['trek', 'cannondale', 'redline', 'specialized'] print(bicycles) # a whole set of information, one variable print(bicycles[0]) # one item out of the set numbers Lecture 10 · numbers, strings & comments grad-text This lecture builds progressively from basic string manipulation to working with numbers and handling mixed data types — the arithmetic five, order of operations, the float precision surprise, str() conversion and comments, before lists enter the story. 1 String operations — the recap Everything strings can do so far, in one compact card card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-2.5 Series of characters Strings are series of characters written between single or double quotes — anything inside quotes is a string. Lecture 11 · Lists. Ordered collections, indexing, add & remove. bicycles = ['trek', 'cannondale', 'redline', 'specialized'] print(bicycles) # the whole list print(bicycles[0]) # first element print(bicycles[0].title()) # Index positions START AT 0, not 1! print(bicycles[1]) # 2nd item print(bicycles[3]) # 4th item print(bicycles[-1]) # last item — negative indexes count backwards motorcycles = ['honda', 'yamaha', 'suzuki'] # MODIFY — assign by index motorcycles[0] = 'ducati' # ADD motorcycles.append('honda') # to the end motorcycles.insert(0, 'ducati') # at any index # REMOVE — three ways del motorcycles[0] # by index popped = motorcycles.pop() # removes & RETURNS last first = motorcycles.pop(0) # pops any index too_expensive = 'yamaha' motorcycles.remove(too_expensive) # by VALUE (first match only) guests = ['ida', 'leo', 'asma'] for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, please come to dinner.") print("
Sadly, asma can't make it.") guests[guests.index('asma')] = 'amir' # replace by index for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, please come to dinner.") print("
Bigger table found!") guests.insert(1, 'kabir') # middle guests.append('tara') # end for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, please come to dinner.") print("
Only two seats now.") while len(guests) > 2: sorry = guests.pop() print(f"Sorry, {sorry.title()} — no room this time.") for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, you're still invited.") lists Lecture 11 · lists grad-text A list is a collection of items arranged in a particular order — letters, numbers or names, related or not — stored in one variable between square brackets. You’ll access, modify, add, remove and loop like a pro; ordering, slicing and tuples live in their own lectures — 12, 15 and 16. grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 bicycles.py ['trek', 'cannondale', 'redline', 'specialized'] trek Trek cannondale specialized specialized My first bicycle was a {bicycles[0].title()}. motorcycles.py — modify · add · remove remove() deletes only the first occurrence — loop it to remove all. pop() is perfect when you want to use the removed value (like popping the most recent player from a roster). mt-6 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold text-[#f5e6cd] mt-5 grid gap-3 flex flex-col gap-1.5 rounded-xl px-4 py-3 sm:flex-row sm:items-baseline sm:gap-4 rgba(255,236,210,.06) 1px solid rgba(255,214,160,.16) shrink-0 font-mono-warm text-[.84rem] font-bold #f5c889 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-4 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#b99a75] mt-8 mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-2 max-w-4xl text-[.9rem] text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 guest_list.py Ida, please come to dinner. 'trek' 'cannondale' 'redline' IndexError Index positions start at 0, so index 1 is the SECOND element: 'cannondale'. Index -1 would give the last item. Concept check Which removal method returns the removed value so you can keep using it? del motorcycles[0] motorcycles.remove('ducati') popped = motorcycles.pop() None of them pop() removes AND returns — perfect when the removed value still matters (a popped player, a printed design). del is gone forever; remove() drops by value with nothing returned. mt-6 Try It Yourself — the guest list (Lecture 11) one list, one loop, one f-string per invitation index assignment replaces a name in place insert(index, guest) shifts everything after it one seat right pop() returns the name you just removed — use it in the apology mt-6 Using individual values: f <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Lists — and working with them like a pro } lead= /> Choosing the right deletion method Three ways out — pick by intent {DELETION_GUIDE.map((d) => ( {d.m} {d.when} ))} del needs an index; pop() hands the value back; remove() hunts by value — three different questions, three different tools. The deck's dinner-party drill guest_list.py — invitations, edits and apologies The classic exercise that touches every operation: invite three guests, one declines — replace them, find a bigger table — insert a guest mid-list, append one to the end, then cut the list down with pop. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Make a guest list with at least three people you would invite — living or deceased — and use it to print a personalized invitation to each person. , hint: }, { q: Add a statement announcing which guest cannot make it; replace that guest’s name with a new invitee and print a new set of invitation messages. , hint: }, { q: Announce a bigger table: use insert() to add one guest to the middle of the list, append() to add one to the end, and print updated invitations for all guests. , hint: }, { q: Only two guests can come: announce it, pop() guests one by one, then del the remaining two — print messages confirming who is still invited. , hint: }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ Lists are ordered and mutable ; indexes start at 0 ; -1 is the last item. , Grow with append()/insert() ; shrink with del/pop()/remove() — pop returns the value. , remove() deletes only the first occurrence ; loop it to purge them all (Lecture 26 does exactly that). , Ordering, slicing and tuples live in their own lectures — ordering in Lecture 12 , numeric lists and slices in Lecture 15 , tuples in Lecture 16 . , ]} />

chapters.label: Organize
chapters.text: Lecture 12 · Organize. sort · sorted · reverse · len · index errors. cars = ['bmw', 'audi', 'toyota', 'subaru'] # sorted() — a temporary look, the list survives print("sorted copy :", sorted(cars)) print("original :", cars) print("reverse copy:", sorted(cars, reverse=True)) # sort() — permanent, the original order is GONE cars.sort() print("after sort :", cars) cars.sort(reverse=True) print("after sort R:", cars) # reverse() — flips the CURRENT order, not alphabetical cars.reverse() print("after flip :", cars) motorcycles = ['honda', 'yamaha', 'suzuki'] print("len() =", len(motorcycles)) # 3 items print("valid indices: 0 …", len(motorcycles) - 1) print("last item, safely:", motorcycles[len(motorcycles) - 1]) print("shortcut to last :", motorcycles[-1]) # THE CLASSIC CRASH — uncomment to meet it: # print(motorcycles[3]) # IndexError: list index out of range list-organize Lecture 12 · organizing a list grad-text Data rarely arrives sorted. Python gives you four tools — two that rearrange forever, two that only look. The difference between them is the difference between a tidy program and a mysterious bug. 1 The four calls, side by side sort() · sorted() · reverse() · len() — two rearrange forever, two only look card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-5 overflow-x-auto warm-table min-w-[640px] font-mono-warm font-bold text-[#8a4508] mt-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 cars.py — permanent vs temporary sorted copy : ['audi', 'bmw', 'subaru', 'toyota'] original : ['bmw', 'audi', 'toyota', 'subaru'] reverse copy: ['toyota', 'subaru', 'bmw', 'audi'] after sort : ['audi', 'bmw', 'subaru', 'toyota'] after sort R: ['toyota', 'subaru', 'bmw', 'audi'] after flip : ['audi', 'bmw', 'subaru', 'toyota'] Run it and watch: sorted() always prints the same answer from the same list — until sort() permanently rewrites the original. Editing the code to add your own cars is encouraged. grid content-start gap-4 insight Which one do I want? warn reverse() is not sort(reverse=True) 2 len() — and the off-by-one trap A list of length 4 has indices 0, 1, 2, 3 — never 4 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 index_bounds.py — the length/index handshake len() = 3 valid indices: 0 … 2 last item, safely: suzuki shortcut to last : suzuki The error message 'list index out of range' is Python telling you the index you asked for doesn't exist. An EMPTY list errors on any index at all. grid content-start gap-4 story Why 'off-by-one' is a rite of passage mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What is the key difference between cars.sort() and sorted(cars)? No difference sort() sorts permanently; sorted() returns a sorted copy sorted() is only for numbers sort() is faster but wrong sort() mutates the list permanently; sorted(cars) leaves the original untouched and hands you a new sorted list. Same for reverse=True on both. Concept check A list holds 4 items. Which index crashes? cars[0] cars[3] cars[-1] cars[4] Valid indices run 0–3 (length − 1). cars[4] is one past the end → IndexError: list index out of range. cars[-1] is always safe for the last item. mt-6 Try It Yourself — organizing drills mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Putting lists in order } lead= /> The four calls, side by side sort() · sorted() · reverse() · len() Call Effect Variation {SORTED_TABLE.map((r) => ( {r.call} {r.effect} {r.alt} ))} Need a one-off view of the data in order — for display, for a report — while the program keeps its own order? Use sorted() . Want every later line of the program to see the new order? Use sort() . Choose deliberately, never accidentally. reverse() simply flips whatever order the list is currently in — no alphabetical arrangement at all. Flip it again and you are back where you started. Humans count from 1; Python counts from 0. The third item lives at index 2 . Every programmer has asked a list for the item one past its end — the error is harmless, and now you can read it like a native. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Store at least five travel destinations in a list, deliberately unsorted. Print the original order. }, { q: Show the list in alphabetical order with sorted() — then print the original to prove it survived. }, { q: Show reverse-alphabetical order with sorted(reverse=True) — original still untouched? }, { q: Use reverse() to flip the real list, print it, then reverse() again to restore the original order. }, { q: Now commit: sort() the list alphabetically and print. There is no going back — that is the point. }, { q: Apply all four tools (sort, sorted, reverse, len) to a list of mountains, rivers, countries or languages. }, { q: Intentionally cause an index error (motorcycles[5] on a three-item list). Read the error, fix it with len()-1 or a negative index. }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ sort() changes the list forever; sorted() hands back a sorted copy — reverse=True works on both. , reverse() flips the current order permanently (call twice to undo) — it is not alphabetical sorting. , len() counts items; valid indices run 0 … len−1 , and −1 is always the last. , Requesting an index that does not exist raises IndexError: list index out of range — empty lists error on everything. , ]} />

chapters.label: For loops
chapters.text: Lecture 13 · For loops. Loop a list · the indentation law. magicians = ['alice', 'david', 'carolina'] for magician in magicians: print(magician) # Doing more work inside the loop for magician in magicians: print(f"{magician.title()}, that was a great trick!") print(f"I can't wait to see your next trick, {magician.title()}.\\n") print("Thank you, everyone. That was a great magic show!") # runs once, after the loop {mode} for-loops Lecture 13 · working with lists grad-text Printing 250 values means 250 print statements — until the for loop. One line walks the whole list for you, and whitespace stops being a style choice: in Python, indentation IS the grammar. 1 Looping through an entire list The for loop walks every item — one line replaces 250 print statements card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 magicians.py alice david carolina Alice, that was a great trick! ... text-[.8rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.16em] text-[#d9b88c] mt-2 grid gap-1.5 text-[.88rem] text-[#e9d7bf] font-mono-warm font-mono-warm font-mono-warm font-mono-warm insight Why this beats copy-paste 2 The indentation law Four classic errors — click through each one and learn to read the traceback mt-6 why The key principle font-mono-warm mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check for magician in magicians\ print(magician) — what happens? It prints all three names IndentationError: expected an indented block It prints only the last name NameError: magician is not defined The body after the colon MUST be indented. With no indentation Python cannot even start — SyntaxError: expected an indented block. Concept check In a for loop, the LAST print line is accidentally NOT indented. What happens? SyntaxError — program won't run It runs once, after the loop, using the final loop value It runs once per item, like the rest The loop is skipped entirely The nastiest of the four: no syntax error is raised, the program runs — but the unindented line executes only once, after the loop, holding the last value. A logical error in disguise. mt-6 Try It Yourself — loop drills mt-6 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Loops & the indentation law } lead= /> The for loop takes the first value from the list, stores it in your loop variable, runs every indented line, then moves to the next value — and stops automatically when the list is exhausted. Code adapts to the list's length with zero changes: Reading the syntax, piece by piece • for — keyword that opens the loop • magician — a fresh variable that holds one item per pass • in magicians — the list to walk through • : — the colon that opens the body • the indented block — runs once PER item • unindented lines after — run ONCE, after the loop finishes Loop code adapts automatically if the list length changes — add a fourth magician and every line still works. That is the difference between code and paperwork. The scope of a for loop is determined entirely by indentation levels . Any indented line after the for statement is part of the loop; non-indented lines that follow are outside it. Before running: verify colons, verify indentation. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Store three friends' names; print a personalized message to each with a for loop. }, { q: Loop a list of transport modes (motorcycle, car, bicycle…) printing "I would like to own a { }!" }, { q: Write a loop with the body deliberately unindented — meet the error, then fix it. }, { q: Write a loop whose second statement escapes the body by accident — predict the output BEFORE running, then verify. }, { q: Break a loop with a missing colon, read the SyntaxError, repair it. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ for item in list: runs the indented body once per item — the loop ends automatically. , Indentation (4 spaces) is syntax, not style : it decides what is inside the loop and what is not. , Four classic errors: missing indent · escaped body line · unexpected indent · missing colon — three crash, one misbehaves. , Unindented lines after the loop run exactly once , when the loop completes. , ]} />

This is the deck's own consolidation lecture: the syllabus for Quiz One, the exam format, and a predict-the-output drill that is exactly the kind of question the paper asks. 1 The format & the stakes 60 MCQs · 20 minutes · the whole foundations lap so far grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-3 card-warm p-5 h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-2 text-2xl font-black text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.85rem] text-muted-warm card-warm p-5 h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-2 text-2xl font-black text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.85rem] text-muted-warm card-warm p-5 h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-2 text-2xl font-black text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.85rem] text-muted-warm mt-6 insight Syllabus & stakes mt-3 text-[.72rem] font-semibold leading-relaxed text-[#a08568] 2 The lap — everything so far in ten cards Skim each station; if one feels foggy, jump back to that lecture before Saturday mt-6 card-warm p-6 eyebrow mt-4 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm font-mono-warm font-mono-warm 3 Predict the output — the quiz, rehearsed Cover the output panel, write your prediction on paper, then run the block quiz_rehearsal.py [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] 7 6 28 ['chennai', 'delhi', 'mumbai'] chennai True ① [1..7] — range stops before 8 · ② seven items · ③ 7−1=6 · ④ 1+2+…+7=28 · ⑤ sort() is permanent, 'chennai' is first · ⑥ False or True → True. Every one of these is a Quiz-One-style question. mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Checkpoint — Quiz One } lead= /> 60 MCQs ≈ 20 seconds per question — pace is part of the test 20 minutes next Saturday, 8:00 AM sharp Best of three the best quiz score counts — one bad day never defines you Everything recorded up to September 20th — including "Working with Lists Part 2" . The evaluation scheme at this point in the course: class participation 10% · quizzes 30% (best of three recorded, 15% each) · final exam 60%, held offline, pen and paper — with real Python code writing, so practise writing code by hand, not just reading it. Note: Lecture 34 later finalizes the assessment — 40% quizzes with the best score of the two actually conducted, 60% final exam, and no participation weightage. See the final word before the end term. The details Quiz One loves Quant vs qual — context decides Discrete counts (number of students = 102); continuous ranges (height 100–190 cm, temperature). Square feet of a house and its price are continuous quantitative because they fall within specific ranges — classification depends on context, not just the numbers. Primary vs secondary — credibility decides Primary: collected by you or your team for the analysis (surveys, Google Forms, sensors, interviews). Secondary: World Bank, IMF, NSSO, Wikipedia, stock-exchange data — World Bank data is more reliable than unknown private sources. Metadata is data about data (the library catalog, not the books). Interpreter vs compiler Interpreter (Python): translates line by line at runtime, errors appear progressively. Compiler (C, C++): translates the whole program before execution — no output until every error is fixed. Methods, nested Dot notation runs the method on the variable: name.title() . Functions nest inside functions — print(name.title()) converts first, prints second. Variables are case-sensitive; spelling matters. <Takeaways items={[ Quiz One: 60 MCQs · 20 minutes · the best quiz score counts toward the final evaluation (the deck's initial scheme was best of three at 15% each; Lecture 34 finalizes it). , Syllabus: all recorded lectures up to September 20th , including Working with Lists Part 2. , The final exam is offline pen-and-paper with code writing — practise writing code by hand. , The evaluation rewards interpretation, not memorization : trace the code, predict the output, explain the logic. , ]} />

chapters.text: Lecture 15 · Numeric lists. range · comprehensions · statistics · slices. for value in range(1, 5): # 1,2,3,4 — stops BEFORE 5 print(value) even = list(range(2, 11, 2)) # start, stop, step print(even) # [2,4,6,8,10] odds = list(range(1, 21, 2)) # odd numbers 1..20 threes = list(range(3, 31, 3)) # multiples of 3 digits = list(range(1, 10)) print(min(digits), max(digits), sum(digits)) # 1 9 45 cubes = [n**3 for n in range(1, 11)] # 2**3 means 2 cubed print(cubes) # The traditional way — 3 lines: squares = [] for value in range(1, 11): squares.append(value ** 2) print(squares) # The comprehension — 1 line, same result: squares = [value ** 2 for value in range(1, 11)] print(squares) digits = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0] print("min:", min(digits)) # 0 print("max:", max(digits)) # 9 print("sum:", sum(digits)) # 45 players = ['charles', 'martina', 'michael', 'florence', 'eli'] print(players[0:3]) # first three print(players[1:4]) # middle three print(players[-3:]) # last three print(players[:3]) # from start print(players[3:]) # to the end players = ['charles', 'martina', 'michael', 'florence', 'eli'] print("Here are the first three players on my roster:") for player in players[:3]: print(player.title()) numeric-lists Lecture 15 · numerical lists grad-text Half of all programming is generating numbers and looking at parts of them. range() is the number factory, list comprehensions fold four lines into one, min/max/sum do the maths, and slices cut lists without wounding them. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 range_basics.py 1 2 3 4 [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] 1 9 45 [1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000] insight Off-by-one, memorized once font-mono-warm font-mono-warm why Million-element lists are fine font-mono-warm 2 List comprehensions — four lines into one The for loop and the list birth, fused into a single readable line grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 squares.py — the same list, two ways [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100] [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100] Read a comprehension out loud: 'give me value squared, for each value in range 1 to 10.' The expression comes FIRST — and note: no colon at the end. That's the grammar. grid content-start gap-4 insight Why Pythonists love these warn Two grammar traps mt-6 3 Simple statistics — min, max, sum Three functions that answer three questions every dataset gets asked digits.py — the one-liner statistics kit min: 0 max: 9 sum: 45 These scale from ten digits to ten million — the million-element list from the checkpoint drill? min, max and sum still answer instantly. 4 Slices — working with part of a list [start:stop] includes start, excludes stop — the same off-by-one rule as range() grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 players.py — slicing ['charles', 'martina', 'michael'] ['martina', 'michael', 'florence'] ['michael', 'florence', 'eli'] ['charles', 'martina', 'michael'] ['florence', 'eli'] A slice [start:stop] includes start, excludes stop — same off-by-one rule as range(). chunks.py — looping a slice Here are the first three players on my roster: Charles Martina Michael Looping through a slice processes a PORTION of a list — chunks of a dataset, one page of results at a time — without ever touching the original. mt-6 mt-6 why Where this pays off mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What does list(range(2, 11, 2)) produce? [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 11] [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] [2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11] [4, 6, 8, 10] Start 2, stop 11 (excluded), step 2 → [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]. The step skips between values; the stop is never included. Concept check Which one line replaces the loop form: squares = []; for v in range(1, 6): squares.append(v**2)? squares = [v**2 for v in range(1, 6):] squares = [v**2 for v in range(1, 6)] squares = for v**2 in range(1, 6) squares = (v**2 for v in range(1, 6):) Expression first, then for, then the range — and NO colon inside a comprehension. [v**2 for v in range(1, 6)] → [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. mt-6 Try It Yourself — numeric-list drills range(1, 21) range(1, 21, 2) range(3, 31, 3) [n**3 for n in range(1,11)] cars[:3], cars[3:6], cars[-3:] mt-6 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Numeric lists, ranges & slices } lead= /> Making numerical lists range() — Python's number factory range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 — it stops before the second number . To reach 5, write{ } range(1, 6) . This habit will save you a hundred bugs. list(range(1, 1_000_001)) is a million numbers — Python builds it in a blink. Printing them takes a while; press Ctrl-C (or stop the cell) if the output floods. Comprehensions are the signature "Pythonic" move: concise, readable, and faster to write than the loop they replace. You will use them in the data-visualization and sentiment-analysis chapters constantly. No colon after the for inside a comprehension, and the expression sits before the for — the reverse of the loop order. Both feel wrong for exactly one day, then forever natural. Chunks of a specific size = batch processing . Controlled amounts per view ={ } pagination . Subsets without modifying the original = safe analysis . In machine learning you will slice datasets into training and testing sets exactly this way. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Use a for loop to print numbers 1 to 20, inclusive. , hint: }, { q: Make a list of 1 → 1,000,000 and verify it with min() (1), max() (1,000,000) and sum(). }, { q: Use range()'s third argument to list the odd numbers 1–20; print each. , hint: }, { q: Make a list of multiples of 3 from 3 to 30; loop and print. , hint: }, { q: Build the first ten cubes — once with a loop, once with a comprehension. (2**3 is 2 cubed.) , hint: }, { q: With a 9-car list, slice and print the first three, middle three and last three — with a message before each. , hint: }, { q: Loop through a slice of your favourite players and print them in title case — the original list must not change. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ range(start, stop, step) stops BEFORE stop; wrap in list() to materialize it. , List comprehensions fuse the loop and the append into one line — expression first, no c

chapters.label: Copies & tuples
chapters.text: Lecture 16 · Copies & tuples. Copy vs reference · immutable tuples. my_foods = ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake'] # CORRECT — a real, independent copy: friend_foods = my_foods[:] my_foods.append('cannoli') friend_foods.append('ice cream') print(my_foods) # both lists grow independently print(friend_foods) # THE TRAP — this is NOT a copy: alias = my_foods # two names, ONE list alias.append('sprouts') print(my_foods) # sprouts appears here too! my_foods = ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake'] friend_foods = my_foods # no slice — a REFERENCE my_foods.append('cannoli') # via my_foods… print(friend_foods) # …cannoli is HERE too friend_foods.append('ice cream') print(my_foods) # …and ice cream lands here print(my_foods is friend_foods) # True: same object! is dimensions = (200, 50) # parentheses, not brackets print(dimensions[0]) print(dimensions[1]) dimensions[0] = 250 # try to change one item menu = ('rice', 'dal', 'paneer', 'salad', 'curd') for food in menu: print(food) # The restaurant changes its menu: # you can't edit an item, but you CAN # redefine the whole tuple: menu = ('rice', 'dal', 'biryani', 'halwa', 'lassi') print("\\nRevised menu:") for food in menu: print(food) copies-tuples Lecture 16 · working with lists & tuples grad-text Sometimes you want a real second list — and sometimes Python quietly gives you the same list wearing a second name tag. Then meet the tuple: the immutable list whose TypeError is a feature, not a bug. 1 The slice that copies — and the assignment that doesn't Same words, nearly: my_foods[:] versus my_foods — two utterly different universes mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 foods.py — copying lists ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli'] ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'ice cream'] ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli', 'sprouts'] Omitting the slice (my_foods[:] vs my_foods) is one of the most common beginner bugs. Always copy with [:]. reference_problem.py — the bug, staged ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli'] ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli', 'ice cream'] True The check proves it: both names point to ONE list object in memory. This is why the deck says the two variables are aliases, not copies. 2 Tuples — the immutable list Parentheses instead of brackets; Python enforces the promise card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mt-2 max-w-4xl text-[.9rem] text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 dimensions.py 200 50 Traceback (most recent call last): TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment Python rejects the change — exactly what we wanted: protection. buffet.py — rewriting a tuple rice dal paneer salad curd Revised menu: rice dal biryani halwa lassi Assigning a NEW tuple to the same variable is legal — mutating the existing one is not. mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-3 List [ ] mutable — users, scores, carts: anything that grows and shrinks Tuple ( ) immutable — rectangle dimensions, config values: data that must not drift Looping identical syntax for both — for item in structure: works the same mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check friend_foods = my_foods (no slice). You append 'cannoli' to my_foods. What does friend_foods hold? The original three items only The original plus cannoli — same underlying list An empty list A TypeError is raised Without the slice you created a second NAME, not a second list — both variables are aliases for the same object, so the append shows through both names. Conditional tests, comparisons, logic. age = 19 if age >= 18: print("You are old enough to vote!") print("Have you registered yet?") print("(this line is not indented — it always runs)") cars = ['audi', 'bmw', 'ferrari', 'jaguar', 'tesla'] for car in cars: if car == 'bmw': print(car.upper()) # test is True → this indented block runs else: print(car.title()) # test is False → this indented block runs # Single = assigns a value; double == compares two values car = 'BMW' # assignment print(car == 'BMW') # comparison → True (values match) print(car == 'Audi') # comparison → False # The exercise pattern: print a prediction, then the test car = 'subaru' print("Is car == 'subaru'? I predict True.") print(car == 'subaru') # True print("\\nIs car == 'audi'? I predict False.") print(car == 'audi') # False # Case matters — Python treats upper and lower as different: 'Audi' != 'audi' car = 'Audi' print(car == 'audi') # False print(car.lower() == 'audi') # True — lower() affects only the comparison print(car) # Audi — the stored value is NOT changed # Real world: websites lower() both sides when checking sign-ups, so # 'John', 'JOHN' and 'john' are ONE username — never three accounts. # != checks inequality — the exclamation point means "not" requested_topping = 'mushrooms' if requested_topping != 'anchovies': print("Hold the anchovies!") # Numerical comparisons — age = 19 from the deck age = 19 print(age < 21) # True print(age >= 21) # False print(age == 19) # True # and / or — parentheses around each test = readability best practice age_0, age_1 = 22, 18 print((age_0 >= 21) and (age_1 >= 21)) # False — BOTH tests must pass print((age_0 >= 21) or (age_1 >= 21)) # True — at least one passes # in — does the value exist in the list? requested_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'onions', 'pineapple'] print('mushrooms' in requested_toppings) # True print('pepperoni' in requested_toppings) # False # not in — is the value absent? (forum banned-users check) banned_users = ['Andrew', 'Carolina', 'David'] user = 'Mary' if user not in banned_users: print("Mary, you can post a response") # Boolean expressions — another name for a conditional test. # True and False are Python keywords (capital first letter). game_active = True can_edit = False if game_active: print("Game is running") # runs — the flag is True if can_edit: print("You can edit") # ignored — the flag is False if Python · chapter 3 grad-text Programs feel smart because they make choices: show this if the user is logged in, charge full price unless you're a student. chapters.label: Branches
chapters.text: Lecture 18 · Branches. if-else · elif ladders · independent ifs. age = 17 if age >= 18: print("Old enough to vote.") else: print("Sorry, you are too young to vote.") # else needs NO condition — it is the # catch-all path when everything above failed alien_color = 'yellow' # try 'green' and 'red' too if alien_color == 'green': points = 5 elif alien_color == 'yellow': points = 10 elif alien_color == 'red': points = 15 else: points = 0 print(f"You just earned {points} points!") age = 12 if age < 4: price = 0 elif age < 18: price = 5 elif age < 65: price = 10 else: price = 3 print(f"Your admission cost is ${price}.") requested_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'extra cheese'] if 'mushrooms' in requested_toppings: print("Adding mushrooms.") if 'pepperoni' in requested_toppings: print("Adding pepperoni.") if 'extra cheese' in requested_toppings: print("Adding extra cheese.") print("\\nFinished making your pizza!") branches Lecture 18 · if statements grad-text Lecture 17 taught you to ASK yes/no questions; this lecture builds the roads the answers choose. Simple if, if-else, the elif ladder — and the design decision every programmer makes: exclusive chain, or independent checks? 1 The chain, walked Python tests conditions in order — the first door that opens wins, the rest are never looked at card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] font-mono-warm font-bold rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 voting.py — if-else: two paths, always exactly one Sorry, you are too young to vote. if-else guarantees exactly one of the two blocks runs. The else block never gets its own test — it is simply 'everything else'. alien_points.py — if-elif-else You just earned 10 points! Python runs ONLY the first branch whose condition is True — the chain is a series of exclusive doors. You can use as many elif blocks as needed, and you may omit the else entirely when a specific final condition is more precise than a catch-all. mt-6 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-2 text-center text-[.8rem] text-[#7a5b39] 2 The amusement park — one price ladder Under 4 free · 4–18 $5 · 18+ $10 · 65+ $3 — the deck's if-elif-else in the wild grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 amusement_park.py — the admission ladder Your admission cost is $5. age = 12: the first test (12 < 4) fails, the second (12 < 18) passes — price becomes 5 and Python skips the rest of the chain. Try age = 4, 18, 70 and run each. grid content-start gap-4 insight Many elifs, one print why Omitting the else 3 Independent ifs — when EVERY answer matters Exclusive chains stop at the first True; separate if statements check them all grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 toppings.py — testing MULTIPLE conditions Adding mushrooms. Adding extra cheese. Finished making your pizza! An if-elif chain stops at the first match — it would have skipped the cheese! Use SEPARATE if statements when every relevant condition must run. Choosing between a chain and independent ifs is a real design decision. grid content-start gap-4 insight Independent vs exclusive why Stage of life — the classic chain mt-6 mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why use separate if statements instead of an if-elif chain for pizza toppings? It looks cleaner An elif chain stops at the first True — other valid toppings would be skipped elif cannot be used with lists Separate ifs run faster An if-elif chain is exclusive — only the first True branch runs. For independent conditions that may all be true (multiple toppings), use a series of independent if statements. Concept check age = 12 in the amusement-park ladder. Which price sticks? $0 — first branch $5 — second branch, then Python skips the rest $10 — the 18+ branch $3 — the senior discount Python tests top to bottom; 12 < 4 fails, 12 < 18 passes → price = 5, and NO later test in the chain is even evaluated. mt-6 Try It Yourself — branch drills mt-6 <2 baby, <4 toddler, <13 kid, <20 teenager, <65 adult, 65+ elder <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ if , elif, else — building the branch } lead= /> if-else covers two paths. The moment you need three or more, add elif (= "else-if") blocks between them. Watch how Python walks the chain for age = 15 — every test is a door; the first one that opens wins: The age bands as full-life mapping — notice each elif needs only one bound, because reaching it means every band above has already been ruled out. Instead of a separate print in every block, each branch just assigns a variable; a single print after the chain does the talking. Change the wording once — not four times. The deck's own optimization tip. Python does not require a final else. For age validation you might test only specific ranges and let invalid data fall through untouched — no accidental catch-all { } executing for data no branch expected. if-elif-else = exactly one path runs (mutually exclusive: alien colors, life stages). Separate ifs = any number of paths may run (independent features: pizza toppings). <2 baby · 2–3 toddler · 4–12 kid · 13–19 teenager · 20–64 adult · 65+ elder. Order matters: test from youngest to oldest, and each elif only needs one bound because earlier branches already failed. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Alien color, simple if: green → print 5 points. Write one version that passes and one that fails silently. }, { q: Alien if-else: green → 5 points, else → 10 points. One version runs the if block, another the else. }, { q: Turn it into if-elif-else: green 5, yellow 10, red 15 — three versions, one per color. }, { q: Stage of life: { } — one assignment per branch, one print at the end. }, { q: favorite_fruits: five independent if statements checking membership — "You really like bananas!" }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ if-else guarantees exactly one of two paths; elif extends it to any number — tested top to bottom, first True wins. , Assign a price variable per branch and print once — the chain stays easy to maintain. , Omitting else is legal and sometimes safer — no catch-all for unexpected data. , Independent ifs check every condition — use t

Recap · the 8-step shipment challenge. starting_inventory = ["router", "switch", "firewall", "server", "cable"] print("start :", starting_inventory) starting_inventory.remove("server") # 2 — by value starting_inventory.insert(0, "fiber_optic") # 3 — to the front starting_inventory[-1] = "USB_hub" # 4 — replace last allocated_device = starting_inventory.pop(1) # 5 — pop & store starting_inventory.append("rack_mount") # 6 — grow at the end del starting_inventory[2] # 7 — delete by index print("final :", starting_inventory) print("allocated :", allocated_device) skills-lab Lecture 19 · the skills lab grad-text The deck's consolidation lecture: why fundamentals still matter in the age of LLMs, the tools you own so far, and one challenge that uses all of them — the shipment inventory. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold mt-3 max-w-4xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 grid gap-3 sm:grid-cols-2 why What you can do after this lap story How the exam will test it 2 The shipment inventory challenge Eight moves on one list — every removal method you own, in one program card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 overflow-x-auto warm-table min-w-[680px] font-black text-[#c2410c] font-mono-warm text-[.8rem] mt-5 shipment_inventory.py — the full challenge start : ['router', 'switch', 'firewall', 'server', 'cable'] final : ['fiber_optic', 'switch', 'USB_hub', 'rack_mount'] allocated : router Trace it by hand first: remove 'server' → [router, switch, firewall, cable] → insert 'fiber_optic' at 0 → [fiber_optic, router, switch, firewall, cable] → replace last: 'cable' becomes 'USB_hub' → pop(1) takes 'router' → [fiber_optic, switch, firewall, USB_hub] → append 'rack_mount' → del index 2 (the 'firewall') → final: [fiber_optic, switch, USB_hub, rack_mount], allocated: router. If your prediction matches the run, you OWN this chapter. mt-6 shipment mt-6 warn The three removal tools, one last time mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check In the shipment challenge, why pop(1) instead of del starting_inventory[1]? They are identical pop() returns the removed value so it can be stored in allocated_device del only works on the last item pop() removes ALL occurrences of index 1 Both remove the item, but pop() hands the value back — and the task says 'store it in allocated_device'. When you need the removed value, pop; when you don't, del. Concept check After insert(0, 'fiber_optic'), where do 'router' and the rest sit? Overwritten — insert replaces index 0 Shifted one position to the right Deleted Moved to the end of the list insert() adds WITHOUT replacing — every element at and after the target index shifts right by one. That's why the final inventory still holds 'router' after the pop. mt-6 Lab extensions — remix the shipment font-mono no index = the LAST item font-mono mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ The skills lab — everything, applied } lead= /> Why fundamentals, when AI can write code?
