chapters.label: If × lists
chapters.text: Lecture 20 · If × lists. Special items · empty checks · multiple lists. # Special items inside a loop requested_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese'] for topping in requested_toppings: if topping == 'green peppers': print("Sorry, we are out of green peppers right now.") else: print(f"Adding {topping}.") # Checking that a list is NOT empty requested_toppings = [] if requested_toppings: # empty list is False! for topping in requested_toppings: print(f"Adding {topping}.") else: print("Are you sure you want a plain pizza?") available_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'olives', 'green peppers', 'pepperoni', 'pineapple', 'extra cheese'] requested_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'french fries', 'extra cheese'] for requested in requested_toppings: if requested in available_toppings: print(f"Adding {requested}.") else: print(f"Sorry, we don't have {requested}.") current_users = ['john', 'admin', 'maria', 'priya', 'sam'] new_users = ['MARIA', 'rahul', 'SAM', 'zoe', 'kiran'] for new_user in new_users: if new_user.lower() in [u.lower() for u in current_users]: print(f"Sorry, {new_user} — that name is taken.") else: print(f"Good news, {new_user} — the name is available.") if-lists Lecture 20 · if statements with lists grad-text The third act of the if chapter: conditional statements wrapped around lists. Special items that need apologies, the empty list that is secretly False, and two lists checked against each other before the kitchen fires up. 1 Special items & the empty-list guard An if INSIDE the loop treats one topping differently; the list name itself IS the emptiness test card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 special_items_and_empty.py Adding mushrooms. Sorry, we are out of green peppers right now. Adding extra cheese. Are you sure you want a plain pizza? grid content-start gap-4 insight A list name is a truth test font-mono-warm why Why guard at all? 2 Multiple lists — validate before you cook Compare what was REQUESTED against what is AVAILABLE before committing grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 available_toppings.py — the availability check Adding mushrooms. Sorry, we don't have french fries. Adding extra cheese. Nested loop + membership test: every requested item is checked against the available list. The 'in' operator you met in Lecture 17, doing real kitchen management. unique_usernames.py — multiple lists Sorry, MARIA — that name is taken. Good news, rahul — the name is available. Sorry, SAM — that name is taken. Good news, zoe — the name is available. Good news, kiran — the name is available. Real systems compare case-insensitively: if 'John' exists, 'JOHN' must be rejected too — that's why we lower() both sides before comparing. mt-6 mt-6 story Chapter closed — where the course goes next mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check if requested_toppings: — what does this test when the list is empty? True — an empty list is truthy False — an empty list is falsy SyntaxError It depends on the toppings An empty list evaluates to False. That one line is the idiomatic Python guard for 'does the list actually contain anything?' Concept check requested = ['french fries']; available has no french fries. What prints? Adding french fries. Nothing — the loop skips it Sorry, we don't have french fries. IndexError 'french fries' in available_toppings is False, so the else branch runs and apologizes. This is data validation: requests checked against reality before processing. mt-6 Try It Yourself — if × lists drills mt-6 font-mono-warm <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ If × lists — filtering the real world } lead= /> if requested_toppings: — Python returns{ } True if the list holds at least one item , False if it is empty. That one line is the idiomatic guard before any "process the list" loop. User input arrives empty more often than anyone expects. Without the guard, an empty order would loop zero times and print nothing — a silent failure. With it, the program asks: plain pizza, really? Conditional tests evaluate to true or false; simple if, if-else and if-elif-else chains handle the roads; combined with loops they filter real data. Up next in the deck:{ } dictionaries — a structure that connects related pieces of information, loops through pairs, and nests into the real world. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Loop usernames: special greeting for 'admin' ("Hello admin, would you like a status report?"), generic for everyone else. }, { q: Add an if test for an empty user list → "We need to find some users!"; empty the list and verify. }, { q: Ordinal numbers: loop 1–9 printing 1st, 2nd, 3rd, then 4th…9th via an if-elif-else inside the loop. }, { q: Build the available/requested kitchen check with YOUR two lists — including one item nobody stocks. }, { q: Case-insensitive username checks for three new sign-ups, one of them a capitalized duplicate. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ If inside a for loop gives special items special treatment — apologies included. , An empty list is falsy : if list: guards every processing loop. , Two lists + in = validation — requests checked against availability (kitchen, usernames, permissions). , Case-insensitive compares ( lower() both sides) are how real systems treat names. , ]} />

chapters.label: Dictionaries
chapters.text: Lecture 21 · Dictionaries. Key–value pairs, add/modify/delete. alien_0 = {'color': 'green', 'points': 5} print(alien_0['color']) # green print(alien_0['points']) # 5 # ADD new key-value pairs at any time alien_0['x_position'] = 0 alien_0['y_position'] = 25 # Start with an empty dictionary and fill it alien = {} alien['color'] = 'green' alien['points'] = 5 # MODIFY a value alien_0['color'] = 'yellow' # DELETE a pair del alien_0['points'] # A dictionary of similar objects (one key → one value per person) favorite_languages = { 'jen': 'python', 'sarah': 'c', 'edward': 'rust', 'phil': 'python', } language = favorite_languages['sarah'].title() print(f"Sarah's favorite language is {language}.") alien_0 = {'color': 'green', 'speed': 'slow'} # This CRASHES if the key is missing: # print(alien_0['points']) → KeyError # get() returns a default instead: point_value = alien_0.get('points', 'No point value assigned.') print(point_value) # get() with no default returns None # (None means "the absence of a value") speed = alien_0.get('speed') print(speed) dicts Python · chapter 4 grad-text You already know lists — but list[0] forces you to memorise what position 0 means. A dictionary replaces positions with labels: alien_0['color'] reads like English. One structure that models users, games, glossaries, entire databases. Four steps and it clicks. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d 2 Build it — create · read · add · modify · delete A dictionary starts empty or full, and every pair can be added, changed or removed at any time mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 alien.py — add · modify · delete green 5 Sarah's favorite language is C. get() — the safe lookup No point value assigned. slow get() is the difference between a program that crashes on missing data and one that handles it gracefully. story Where dictionaries go next mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What does alien_0.get('points', 0) do if 'points' is missing? Crashes with KeyError Returns None Returns 0 instead of crashing Adds the key with value 0 get() looks up the key and returns your provided default (0) when it’s absent — graceful handling instead of a KeyError. Concept check del alien_0['points'] — what happens to the pair? It is hidden until needed It is permanently removed — unrecoverable Its value becomes None A KeyError is raised del permanently removes the key-value pair; a later lookup of 'points' would raise KeyError (that's what get() protects against). mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What does alien_0.get('points', 0) do if 'points' is missing? Crashes with KeyError Returns None Returns 0 instead of crashing Adds the key with value 0 get() looks up the key and returns your provided default (0) when it’s absent — graceful handling instead of a KeyError. mt-6 Try It Yourself — dictionary drills mt-6 {} <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Dictionaries — connecting pieces of information } lead= /> The one idea before any syntax: a list finds things by position, a dictionary finds things by label . Same data, two very different shapes — and the shape on the right is the one that scales to real programs, because “which label?” is a question you can actually answer while writing code: You can build, read, modify and delete pairs. Next: loop through them three ways (.items() / .keys() / .values()) in Lecture 22 — and then{ } nest dictionaries inside lists inside dictionaries in Lecture 23, where fleets of aliens and user databases get built. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Person: store first_name, last_name, age, city in a dictionary; print each piece of information. }, { q: Favorite numbers: five people as keys, a number each as values; print each pair (poll real friends!). }, { q: Glossary: five programming words as keys, meanings as values; print each word and meaning neatly separated with \\n. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ Dictionaries store key-value pairs ; access by key, add/modify anytime, delete with del , build from empty { } . , get(key, default) avoids KeyError; dictionaries of similar objects map one value per key (favorite languages, favorite numbers). , ]} />

chapters.label: Dict loops
chapters.text: Lecture 22 · Dict loops. items · keys · sorted · values · sets. user_0 = { 'username': 'efermi', 'first': 'enrico', 'last': 'fermi', } # ALL key-value pairs — .items() for key, value in user_0.items(): print(f"\\nKey: {key}") print(f"Value: {value}") # ALL keys — .keys() (default!) for name in favorite_languages.keys(): print(name.title()) # Keys in order — sorted() for name in sorted(favorite_languages.keys()): print(f"{name.title()}, thank you for taking the poll.") # ALL values — .values() print("Languages chosen:") for language in favorite_languages.values(): print(language.title()) # Repetition is natural ('python' appears twice). # Use set() when each item should appear ONCE: print("\\nThe following languages have been chosen:") for language in set(favorite_languages.values()): print(language.title()) # Polling: who already responded vs who to invite if 'erin' not in favorite_languages.keys(): print("Erin, please take our poll!") dict-loops Lecture 22 · looping dictionaries grad-text A dictionary can hold a few pairs or a few million. Python gives you three lenses — pairs, keys, values — and one deduplicator. Pick the lens that matches the question you're asking. rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 loop_all_pairs.py Key: username Value: efermi ... Two variables in the loop header — .items() hands you the key AND its value each pass. Name them for meaning (name, language) rather than key, value. And note: for name in dictionary: is identical to .keys() — the keys ARE the default. loop_values_and_set.py Languages chosen: Python C Rust Python The following languages have been chosen: C Python Rust Erin, please take our poll! A set is a collection in which each item must be unique — a list wrapped in set() loses duplicates. One honest caveat: the order of a set's output is the machine's choice, not yours — the values above could print in any order from run to run. Sets guarantee uniqueness, never sequence. mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-3 insight .items() — the pair lens insight sorted(.keys()) — the order lens insight set(.values()) — the dedupe lens mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why wrap favorite_languages.values() in set() before looping? To sort alphabetically To make each language appear only once To speed up the loop To convert values to keys A set keeps only unique items — so 'python' appearing for both jen and phil prints once. Use sorted(keys) when you want order instead. Concept check for name in favorite_languages: — what does this loop over? Key-value pairs The keys — .keys() is the default The values Nothing — it needs .items() Looping a dictionary directly loops its KEYS — writing .keys() explicitly is optional (though it can read more clearly). mt-6 Try It Yourself — dict-loop drills if name in favorite_languages.keys() mt-6 {’nile’: ’egypt’, ’amazon’: ’brazil’, …} <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Looping through dictionaries } lead= /> For greeting every user BY their answer: "Jen's favorite language is Python." The dictionary stores pairs in insertion order; sorted() loops a sorted COPY — the original dict is untouched. Thousands of respondents, four languages: set() answers "which languages exist?" without repetition. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Glossary: five programming terms as keys, definitions as values — loop with .items() and print each neatly. Then expand to ten: the loop picks them up automatically. }, { q: Rivers: { } — print “The Nile runs through Egypt.”, then all river names, then all countries. }, { q: Polling: loop a list of people; thank those already in favorite_languages, invite the rest. , hint: }, { q: Loop the glossary keys in ALPHABETICAL order with sorted() — prove the dictionary itself kept its order. }, { q: Print the distinct languages with set() — then add a fifth person favouring python and confirm the set does not change. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ .items() walks key-value pairs into two loop variables. , .keys() is the default lens — looping the dict directly is the same; sorted() imposes order on a copy. , .values() reads just the answers; wrap in set() to dedupe. , Combine loops + membership ( in .keys() ) for poll invitations and filters. , ]} />

chapters.label: Nesting
chapters.text: Lecture 23 · Nesting. List of dicts · dict of lists · dict of dicts. aliens = [] for n in range(3): aliens.append({ 'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow', }) for alien in aliens[:3]: print(alien) pizza = { 'crust': 'thick', 'toppings': ['mushrooms', 'extra cheese'], } print(pizza['crust']) for topping in pizza['toppings']: print(topping) users = { 'aeinstein': { 'first': 'albert', 'last': 'einstein', }, 'mcurie': { 'first': 'marie', 'last': 'curie', }, } for username, info in users.items(): print(f"\\n{username}") print(info['first'].title(), info['last'].title()) aliens = [] for alien_number in range(30): aliens.append({'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow'}) print("created:", len(aliens), "aliens") # The first three speed up and turn yellow: for alien in aliens[:3]: if alien['color'] == 'green': alien['color'] = 'yellow' alien['speed'] = 'medium' alien['points'] = 10 for alien in aliens[:5]: print(alien) nesting Lecture 23 · nesting grad-text Python lets you nest lists inside dictionaries, dictionaries inside lists, and dictionaries inside dictionaries. The moment real data shows up, structures combine — this is how you model fleets, orders and user bases. 2 The three patterns, runnable Same ideas you saw in Lecture 21 — now with room to breathe and edit grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-3 a list of dictionaries a list in a dictionary a dictionary in a dictionary 3 Generating a fleet — 30 aliens from one loop The deck's video-game pattern: create thousands of objects, then steer them by condition grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 aliens_30.py — generate, then modify created: 30 aliens {'color': 'yellow', 'points': 10, 'speed': 'medium'} {'color': 'yellow', 'points': 10, 'speed': 'medium'} {'color': 'yellow', 'points': 10, 'speed': 'medium'} {'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow'} {'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow'} range(30) iterates the loop 30 times, creating one dictionary per pass. Then a for + if combo modifies only the aliens that meet the criterion — game engines are built on exactly this beat. grid content-start gap-4 insight Why fleets, not variables why Slices + loops + conditions = management font-mono-warm mt-6 warn Nesting has a depth cost mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check aliens holds 30 dictionaries. What does aliens[:3] give you? The last three aliens The first three aliens — as a slice of the list Three random aliens An error — you can't slice a list of dicts Lists of anything slice identically: [:3] is the first three ITEMS — here, three whole dictionaries, which you can then modify key by key. Concept check In users = {'aeinstein': {'first': 'albert', ...}}, how do you reach 'albert'? users.first users['first'] users['aeinstein']['first'] users['aeinstein.first'] Two lookups in sequence: the outer key 'aeinstein' returns the INNER dictionary, then ['first'] reads from it — that's dictionary-in-dictionary access. mt-6 Try It Yourself — nesting drills sum(1 for a in aliens if a['color'] == 'green') mt-6 { } <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Nesting — structures inside structures } lead= /> Thirty dictionaries hand-typed is bureaucracy; thirty generated by one loop is{ } data engineering . Change the blueprint once and every alien in the fleet changes with it. aliens[:3] picks the front of the fleet, the if filters by colour, the assignments steer. The same trio later powers the records-lab in Lecture 24. Two levels (a dict of dicts, a list of dicts) models most of reality cleanly. Three-plus levels get hard to read — when you feel that pain, that's your cue for{ } classes , waiting at the end of the course. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Pets: several dictionaries (kind of animal + owner's name) inside a list called pets; loop and print everything about each. }, { q: favorite_places: three people as keys, one to three favorite places each as lists; loop and print. }, { q: Cities: three cities as keys, each mapping to a nested dictionary { }country, population, fact{ }; print each city with all its information. }, { q: Scale the fleet: generate 50 aliens, promote the first 5 to yellow, the next 5 to red — then count how many remain green. , hint: }, { q: Pizza orders: a list of pizza dictionaries (crust + toppings list) — loop the orders, then loop each order's toppings. }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ List of dicts — fleets and rosters: many objects, one shape, generated by a loop. , Dict with a list value — one key, many values: pizza toppings, favourite languages. , Dict of dicts — hierarchical records: username → profile. , Access nests the same way the data does: outer[key][innerKey] ; loops nest to match. , ]} />

chapters.label: Records lab
chapters.text: Lecture 24 · Records lab. Filter · reward · insert · sort. student_records = [ ['Alice', [75, 88, 92]], ['Bob', [65, 70, 72]], ['Charlie', [88, 90, 95]], ['David', [78, 82, 85]], ['Eve', [45, 50, 55]], ] # 1 — FILTER: keep students whose average is at least 60 eligible = [] for name, scores in student_records: avg = sum(scores) / len(scores) if avg >= 60: eligible.append([name, scores]) student_records = eligible # reassign, don't mutate while looping print("after filter :", student_records) # 2 — REWARD: any paper at 90+ earns 'distinction' for name, scores in student_records: if max(scores) >= 90: scores.append('distinction') # 3 — INSERT: a new student joins at the FRONT student_records.insert(0, ['Zoya', [91, 84, 88]]) # 4 — SORT: alphabetically by name (the lambda picks the key) student_records.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) for record in student_records: print(record) names = ['charlie', 'alice', 'bob'] names.sort() # permanent sort print(names) print(sorted(names, reverse=True)) # temporary, reversed print(names[:2]) # slice — first two copied = names[:] # deep copy copied.append('zoya') print(names, "|", copied) point = (200, 50) # tuple: immutable print(point[0]) eligible records-lab Lecture 24 · the records lab grad-text Five students, three scores each, four operations. This is the deck's interpretation-over-syntax finale: read the nested structure, run the pipeline, and understand every line — not memorize it. grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 card-warm p-4 mt-2 font-bold leading-tight text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-8 student_records.py — the full pipeline after filter : [['Alice', [75, 88, 92]], ['Bob', [65, 70, 72]], ['Charlie', [88, 90, 95]], ['David', [78, 82, 85]]] ['Alice', [75, 88, 92, 'distinction']] ['Bob', [65, 70, 72]] ['Charlie', [88, 90, 95, 'distinction']] ['David', [78, 82, 85]] ['Zoya', [91, 84, 88]] Trace it: Eve averages 50 → filtered out. Alice (92) and Charlie (95) hit 90+ → distinction. Zoya lands at the front via insert(0, …). The sort's lambda x: x[0] says 'rank by element 0 of each record' — the name. mt-6 records mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 why Why build a new list instead of removing while looping? insight Reading vs writing code mt-4 story Course logistics straight from the deck mt-6 eyebrow mb-3 toolbox_recap.py ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie'] ['charlie', 'bob', 'alice'] ['alice', 'bob'] ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie'] | ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie', 'zoya'] 200 Sort, sorted-reverse, slicing, deep copy, tuple indexing — every Lecture 11–16 tool, one screen. If any line surprises you, that lecture is your revision spot. mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why does the lab build and reassign, instead of removing entries from student_records during the loop? It looks tidier Removing items while iterating skips elements — the loop's ground shifts del cannot be used inside loops It is faster Python iterates by index; removing items mid-loop shifts positions and skips elements. Collect survivors into a new list, then reassign — the deck's explicit rule. Concept check What does sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) rank by, for records like ['Alice', [75, 88, 92]]? The scores list The first score (75) Element 0 of each record — the name The record's length The lambda receives each record and returns x[0] — the name — so the sort is alphabetical by name. Without the key, Python would try comparing lists against strings and fail. mt-6 Lab extensions — own the pipeline f-string with :.1f key=lambda x: max(x[1]), reverse=True mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ The records lab — a complete data pipeline } lead= /> {LAB_OPS.map((o, i) => ( {o.icon} {o.title} {o.detail} ))} Modifying a list while iterating it shifts the ground under Python's feet — items get skipped. The safe pattern: collect survivors into a new list, then{ } reassign . The deck calls this out explicitly; the exam will too. The final exam cares more about interpretation than syntax memory: given this pipeline, explain what each operation does, spot the indentation and logical errors, and write small programs with the logic right — pen and paper, flexible syntax. One more quiz is scheduled for the end of October — and{ } no third quiz , so every assessment counts double. Assignments will ask for both code and a detailed explanation ; the descriptive questions come primarily from the foundational topics, while the coding sections test how well you interpret and trace programs like this one. The toolbox this lab leaned on — all re-run, one page <Practice title= items={[ { q: Add operation 5: print each student's average next to their name, rounded to one decimal. , hint: }, { q: Change the filter to 65 and predict WHO leaves before running. Eve goes — anyone else? }, { q: Insert TWO new students at the front, in reverse priority order — then sort and explain why the order they were inserted doesn't matter. }, { q: Reward differently: distinction only if the AVERAGE is 90+ (not any single paper). Who keeps it? }, { q: Sort by best score instead of name — rewrite the lambda. , hint: }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ Filter with sum/len + a new list ; never mutate while iterating. , max(scores) ≥ 90 → append the distinction marker to the record itself. , insert(0, …) puts arrivals first; append() would bury them last. , sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) — lambdas tell sort() what to rank by; here, the name. , The exam rewards interpretation and explanation — trace the pipeline on paper. , ]} />

chapters.label: While loops
chapters.text: Lecture 25 · While loops. input() · int() · modulo · repeat until done. name = input("Please enter your name: ") print(f"\\nHello, {name}!") # Multi-line prompt with += prompt = "If you share your name, we can personalize it. " prompt += "\\nWhat is your first name? " name = input(prompt) # input() ALWAYS returns a string! age = input("How old are you? ") # "21" not 21 # age >= 18 would crash — str vs int # Convert with int(): age = int(input("How old are you? ")) if age >= 18: print("You are old enough to vote!") # The modulo operator % — the remainder number = int(input("Enter a number: ")) if number % 10 == 0: print(f"{number} is a multiple of 10.") else: print(f"{number} is not a multiple of 10.") print(4 % 3) # 1 (odd/even check uses % 2) current_number = 1 while current_number <= 5: print(current_number) current_number += 1 # the update is ESSENTIAL # 1) where the variable starts runs = 0 # 2) the condition that decides to keep going while runs < 3: print(f"lap {runs + 1}") # 3) the change that moves toward False runs += 1 print("done — the condition finally failed") while Python · chapter 5 grad-text Until now your programs ran top to bottom and finished. input() makes them listen; while makes them persist. This chapter is one conversation: ask the user something, keep responding until they say stop. Two steps here — the exits live in Lecture 26. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 greeter.py — clear prompts Please enter your name: Eric Hello, Eric! rollercoaster.py — int() for numbers How old are you? 21 You are old enough to vote! Enter a number: 40 40 is a multiple of 10. 1 2 while — repeat until the job is done A for loop counts items; a while loop keeps going as long as its condition stays True card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 max-w-4xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 counting.py — the while loop in action 1 2 3 4 5 Forget current_number += 1 and the condition stays True forever — an infinite loop. (In a terminal: Ctrl-C to stop; in Colab: interrupt the cell.) the three moving parts — name them in every while you write lap 1 lap 2 lap 3 done — the condition finally failed Every correct while loop answers three questions: where does the variable start, what must stay True, and what changes it each pass? Miss the third and you loop forever. warn Avoiding infinite loops story Four ways out — next lecture mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why does age = input('How old are you? ') followed by age >= 18 crash? input() cannot store numbers input() returns a string; comparing str >= int raises TypeError The prompt must not contain a question mark It doesn’t crash input() always returns a string ('21', not 21). Wrap with int() to convert before numerical comparison — and remember the modulo % for remainder tests like multiples of 10. mt-6 Try It Yourself — input & while drills number % 10 == 0 mt-6 quit <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ User input & while loops — interactive programs } lead= /> input() takes one argument — the prompt — prints it, then freezes the whole program until the user presses Enter. Whatever they typed comes back as a string , and you store it in a variable. Follow the value on its journey — and watch the trap at the bottom of the diagram: Use a while loop when you don’t know in advance how many times to repeat — how many users will log in? how many toppings will they ask for? Python tests the condition, runs the body, tests again… The diagram is the whole story: Every while loop needs something that can make its condition False: a counter that increments, a flag that flips, a break. If the loop never ends, trace the variable the condition depends on — is anything changing it? The exit toolkit — flags, break, continue — and while loops that drain lists and fill dictionaries are the whole of Lecture 26, "Flags, Break & Continue". First, make the counting loop below second nature. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Ask what kind of rental car the user would like; print “Let me see if I can find you a Subaru.” }, { q: Ask how many people are in their dinner group: more than eight → wait for a table; otherwise → table is ready. }, { q: Ask for a number and report whether it is a multiple of 10. , hint: }, { q: While loop for pizza toppings until ; confirm each topping: “I’ll add that topping to their pizza.” }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ input() shows a prompt and returns a string ; convert with int() for math; % modulo gives remainders. , while condition: repeats while True — the counter, flag or break must guarantee eventual False, or you have an infinite loop. , ]} />

chapters.label: Loop control
chapters.text: Lecture 26 · Loop control. Flags · break · continue · while with data. # 1) Let the user choose when to quit prompt = "\\nTell me something, and I will repeat it back. " prompt += "\\nEnter 'quit' to end. " message = "" while message != 'quit': message = input(prompt) if message != 'quit': print(message) # 2) Using a FLAG — one variable governs the loop active = True while active: message = input(prompt) if message == 'quit': active = False # flips the flag else: print(message) # 3) break — exit the loop immediately while True: city = input("\\nWhich city? ('quit' to stop) ") if city == 'quit': break print(f"{city.title()} — great choice!") current = 0 while current < 10: current += 1 if current % 2 == 0: continue # skip the print for evens print(current) sandwich_orders = ['tuna', 'pastrami', 'pastrami', 'veg', 'pastrami', 'grilled cheese'] finished_sandwiches = [] # The deli ran out of pastrami — remove ALL of them: while 'pastrami' in sandwich_orders: sandwich_orders.remove('pastrami') while sandwich_orders: # while list not empty sandwich = sandwich_orders.pop() print(f"I made your {sandwich} sandwich.") finished_sandwiches.append(sandwich) print("\\nAll sandwiches made:") for s in finished_sandwiches: print(f" · {s}") responses = {} polling_active = True # the flag again while polling_active: name = input("\\nWhat is your name? ") response = input("Which mountain would you like to climb someday? ") responses[name] = response # store key → value repeat = input("Another responder? (yes/ no) ") if repeat == 'no': polling_active = False print("\\n--- Poll Results ---") for name, mountain in responses.items(): print(f"{name} would like to climb {mountain}.") pets = ['dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'goldfish', 'cat', 'rabbit', 'cat'] print(pets) while 'cat' in pets: pets.remove('cat') print(pets) # cats: gone. All of them. loop-control Lecture 26 · loop control grad-text Lecture 25 taught the while loop; this lecture hands you the steering wheel. One Boolean to rule the loop, break to leave mid-stride, continue to skip a beat — then while loops that safely drain lists and fill dictionaries. mt-6 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 quit_flag_break_continue.py — three ways to stop All three produce the same conversation — the difference is WHO decides to stop: the while test itself, a variable you flip, or an emergency exit. Pick whichever reads clearest. continue — skip one, keep the loop 1 3 5 7 9 continue never exits — it only abandons the rest of THIS pass and jumps back to the test. break exits; continue skips. That pair is all you need to remember. 2 while + lists — where it beats the for loop Drain a list, purge an item — while loops can safely modify the list they're watching card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 sandwich_shop.py — moving between lists I made your grilled cheese sandwich. I made your veg sandwich. I made your tuna sandwich. All sandwiches made: · grilled cheese · veg · tuna Two idioms to memorize: while x in list: list.remove(x) purges every occurrence; while list: pop() drains it. mountain_poll.py — filling a dictionary --- Poll Results --- Eric would like to climb Denali. Lynn would like to climb Devil's Thumb. A while loop + a dictionary = a program that collects data until you tell it to stop. This tiny pattern is the seed of every survey app. mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 pet_purge.py — remove ALL instances ['dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'goldfish', 'cat', 'rabbit', 'cat'] ['dog', 'dog', 'goldfish', 'rabbit'] remove() alone kills only the FIRST occurrence — the deck flagged that in Lecture 11. Wrap it in while x in list: and every instance falls. When remove() finds nothing, the condition goes False and the loop ends. grid content-start gap-4 insight Why while, not for, here? warn Infinite loops & the stop button mt-6 mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What is the difference between break and continue inside a while loop? They are identical break exits the loop entirely; continue jumps back to the condition test continue exits; break skips one iteration Only for-loops can use break break abandons the loop and moves to the code after it; continue abandons only the current iteration and returns to the while test. Concept check pets = ['dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'cat'] — after while 'cat' in pets: pets.remove('cat'), pets holds… ['dog', 'cat', 'dog'] ['dog', 'dog'] ['dog', 'dog', 'cat'] An infinite loop runs Each pass removes ONE 'cat' and re-tests. When the last 'cat' is gone, 'cat' in pets is False and the loop ends — leaving ['dog', 'dog']. mt-6 Try It Yourself — control drills mt-6 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Flags, break & continue } lead= /> All four exits, side by side in runnable code — read them in order and the escalation makes sense: sentinel → flag → break, with continue as the "skip one" companion: A for loop iterates by position — remove items mid-loop and elements get skipped. A while loop re-tests its condition each pass : pop from the list, append to the new one, and Python never loses track. That is why unverified→verified user pipelines are written with while. No exit condition, no counter update, no flag flip — the loop never ends. In Colab, press the pause/interrupt button ; in a terminal, Ctrl-C. Then re-read the three moving parts from Lecture 25: initialize, condition, update. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Pizza toppings until 'quit'; confirm each: "I'll add that topping." }, { q: Movie tickets: while loop asking age — under 3 free, 3–12 $10, over 12 $15. }, { q: Three versions of one exit: a conditional test in the while statement · an active flag · a break. }, { q: Write a loop that never ends — run it, stop it (Ctrl-C / interrupt), then explain exactly why it never stopped. }, { q: Dream-vacation poll: name → place into a dictionary while polling; print the results block. }, { q: Unconfirmed → confirmed users: while unconfirmed_users: pop from one list, append to the other — then print both. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ A flag is one Boolea

chapters.label: Functions
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Functions. Define, call, reuse — first steps. def greet_user(username): """Display a simple greeting.""" print(f"Hello, {username.title()}!") greet_user('jesse') # call it — reuse forever greet_user('arpit') functions Python · functions · chapter 6 grad-text You have already felt the pain of repetition: the same greeting logic, the same printing pattern, again and again. A function lets you write a job ONCE, give it a name, and summon it by that name forever after. Three steps — the machine, the shape, the call — and it clicks. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d 2 See the shape — anatomy of a definition Two lines of vocabulary — def, parameter, docstring, call — carry the entire chapter rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 greeter.py — your first function Hello, Jesse! Hello, Arpit! def names the function · the string is a docstring describing what it does · parentheses pass information in. 3 What a call actually does — four beats Follow the jump: call → bind → run → return. This rhythm never changes, no matter how big the function You call greet_user('jesse') — Python pauses this line h-5 w-5 #c2410c Python jumps to the def; 'jesse' is copied into username h-5 w-5 #c2410c The body runs the indented steps do their job h-5 w-5 #c2410c Back you go to the line after the call, as if nothing happened h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 card-warm p-6 flex items-center gap-2 h-5 w-5 #f5c889 text-lg font-bold mt-3 grid gap-2 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] grid content-start gap-4 insight Connect it back to Pillar 2 story Where the story goes next <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Functions — named blocks that do one job } lead= /> The mental model first: a function is a machine with a name . You feed it inputs ( arguments ), it does its job (the body ), and it hands a result back. Define the machine once — then call it a hundred times with different inputs: <StepsFlow steps={[ { label: , sub: , icon: , }, { label: , sub: , icon: , }, { label: , sub: , icon: , }, { label: , sub: , icon: , }, ]} /> Why functions matter • They break programs into small parts , each doing one specific job • You can call a function as many times as you want , and store functions in separate files • The result: more efficient code that is easier to troubleshoot and maintain — and reusable across many different programs A function is an algorithm with a name — it has input (parameters), defined steps (the body) and output (return values). All five properties still apply. You’ve been training for this since the flowchart. This page is the shape of the idea. The next two chapters go deeper: arguments & return values (positional vs keyword, defaults, what return really does), then functions at scale (passing lists, *args/**kwargs, modules). Master the machine here and they’ll feel easy.

chapters.label: Arguments
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Arguments. Positional, keyword, defaults & errors. def greet_user(): # defining a function """Display a simple greeting.""" print("Hello!") # the body of the function greet_user() # a function call def greet_user(username): # parameter """Display a simple greeting.""" print("Hello, " + username.title() + "!") greet_user('Arun') # calling the function — 'Arun' is the argument def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name): # defining with arguments """Display information about a pet.""" print("\\nI have a " + animal_type + ".") # the body print("My " + animal_type + "'s name is " + pet_name.title() + ".") describe_pet('hamster', 'harry') # function call describe_pet('Brad', 'Cow') # same order: type first, name second def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name): # same definition """Display information about a pet.""" print("\\nI have a " + animal_type + ".") print("My " + animal_type + "'s name is " + pet_name.title() + ".") describe_pet(pet_name='Kyle', animal_type='Parrot') describe_pet(pet_name='Sachin', animal_type='Goat') def describe_BSMT(course_name, instructor_name='aman'): """Display information.""" print("\\nI am enrolled in the " + course_name + " course.") print("The instructor for the " + course_name + " is " + instructor_name.title() + ".") describe_BSMT(course_name='Foundations of Computing') # default used describe_BSMT(course_name='AI in Business', instructor_name='hari') # default ignored def describe_student(student_name, course_name, instructor_name='aman'): """Display information.""" print("\\nMy name is " + student_name + " .") print("I am enrolled in the " + course_name + " course.") print("The instructor for the " + course_name + " is " + instructor_name.title() + ".") describe_student(student_name='Hardavi', course_name='Foundations of Computing') describe_pet() describe_pet('harry', 'hamster', 'good') args Python · functions · the full chapter — part 1 grad-text grad-text You've seen a function defined and called. The argument toolkit: passing information in three styles, letting defaults do quiet work, and catching argument errors. The return keyword that sends answers back lives in Lecture 28. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 greet.py — no information needed Hello! greet_user() illustrates the simplest possible structure — definition, body, call. grid content-start gap-3 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 greet.py — greeting by name Hello, Arun! chapters.text: Lecture 28 · Return values. return · optional args · dicts · lists in & out. def get_formatted_name(first_name, last_name): """Return a full name, neatly formatted.""" full_name = first_name + ' ' + last_name return full_name.title() # not print() here developer = get_formatted_name('agastya', 'gupta') print(developer) # print happens at the call site def get_formatted_name(first_name, middle_name, last_name): """Return a full name, neatly formatted.""" full_name = first_name + ' ' + middle_name + ' ' + last_name return full_name.title() musician = get_formatted_name('Lana', 'Del', 'Rey') print(musician) # ✅ works musician = get_formatted_name('Arijit', 'Singh') # 💥 middle names aren't always needed def get_formatted_name(first_name, last_name, middle_name=''): """Return a full name, neatly formatted.""" if middle_name: full_name = first_name + ' ' + middle_name + ' ' + last_name else: full_name = first_name + ' ' + last_name return full_name.title() musician = get_formatted_name('Arijit', 'Singh') # no middle name print(musician) musician = get_formatted_name('Lana', 'Rey', 'Del') # middle name supplied print(musician) def build_person(first_name, last_name): """Return a dictionary of information about a person.""" person = {'first': first_name, 'last': last_name} return person student = build_person('aryan', 'manhas') print(student) def build_person(first_name, last_name, age=''): """Return a dictionary of information about a person.""" person = {'first': first_name, 'last': last_name} if age: person['age'] = age return person student = build_person('daksh', 'parashar', age=18) print(student) def get_formatted_name(first_name, last_name): """Return a full name, neatly formatted.""" full_name = first_name + ' ' + last_name return full_name.title() # This is an infinite loop! while True: # condition is always True print("\\nPlease tell me your name:") f_name = input("First name: ") l_name = input("Last name: ") def get_formatted_name(first_name, last_name): """Return a full name, neatly formatted.""" full_name = first_name + ' ' + last_name return full_name.title() while True: print("\\nPlease tell me your name:") print("(enter 'q' at any time to quit)") f_name = input("First name: ") if f_name == 'q': break l_name = input("Last name: ") if l_name == 'q': break formatted_name = get_formatted_name('aman', 'pathak') print("\\nHello, " + formatted_name + "!") def greet_users(names): """Print a simple greeting to each user in the list.""" # docstring for name in names: msg = "Hello, " + name.title() + "!" print(msg) usernames = ['priyanka', 'unnati', 'anaaya'] # function call greet_users(usernames) # Start with some designs that need to be printed. unprinted_designs = ['iphone case', 'robot pendant', 'dodecahedron'] completed_models = [] # Simulate printing each design, until none are left. # Move each design to completed_models after printing. while unprinted_designs: current_design = unprinted_designs.pop() # Simulate creating a 3D print from the design. print("Printing model: " + current_design) completed_models.append(current_design) # Display all completed models. print("\\nThe following models have been printed:") for completed_model in completed_models: print(completed_model) def print_models(unprinted_designs, completed_models): """ Simulate printing each design, until none are left. Move each design to completed_models after printing. """ while unprinted_designs: current_design = unprinted_designs.pop() # Simulate creating a 3D print from the design. print("Printing model: " + current_design) completed_models.append(current_design) def show_completed_models(completed_models): """Show all the models that were printed.""" print("\\nThe following models have been printed:") for completed_model in completed_models: print(completed_model) unprinted_designs = ['iphone case', 'robot pendant', 'dodecahedron'] completed_models = [] print_models(unprinted_designs, completed_models) show_completed_models(completed_models) unprinted_designs # → [] — permanently emptied! unprinted_designs = ['ferrari', 'honda', 'ford'] completed_models = [] print_models(unprinted_designs[:], completed_models) # passing a copy of the original list show_completed_models(completed_models) unprinted_designs # → ['ferrari', 'honda', 'ford'] — still intact! returns Lecture 28 · return values grad-text Lecture 27 taught functions to take; this lecture teaches them to give back. A function can process data internally and return the result — to be stored, reused, or passed on. This is where functions stop being shortcuts and start being building blocks. 1 return, not print print() is a dead end; return is a doorway card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm font-mono text-[.84rem] font-bold text-[#b45309] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 names.py — return, don't print Agastya Gupta The function combines the names, converts to title case and returns the result. The caller stores the return value in a variable — here, developer. grid content-start gap-3 insight return vs print store it developer = get_formatted_name('agastya', 'gupta') — provide a variable to catch what comes back. simplify the main body of the program shrinks — the heavy lifting lives inside the function. 2 Making an argument optional Empty-string default + one if — one function, both scenarios card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 grid content-start gap-5 v1 — middle name required Lana Del Rey Traceback ... missing 1 required positional argument: 'last_name' warn The problem v2 — middle name optional Arijit Singh Lana Del Rey The empty-string default is falsy — if middle_name: only builds the three-part name when one exists. Your Pizza is ready." import pizza pizza.make_pizza(16, 'pepperoni') print(pizza.greet("Aditya")) pizza.make_pizza(12, 'mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese') pizza.greet('Utkarsh') from pizza import make_pizza, greet make_pizza(16, 'pepperoni') print(greet('Aditya')) from pizza import make_pizza as mp mp(16, 'pepperoni') mp(12, 'mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese') import pizza as p p.make_pizza(16, 'pepperoni') p.greet('Aditya') def greet(name): # different greet function in the main file return f"Welcome home, {name}!" from pizza import * # This silently OVERWRITES your local greet()! greet("Neha") # Outputs: "Hello, Neha! Your Pizza is ready." #pizza.greet("Neha") # ← the dot would have kept yours safe funcs3 Lecture 30 · arbitrary arguments & modules grad-text The power moves: when you can't know in advance how many arguments will arrive, *toppings packs every one into a tuple and **user_info builds a dictionary from whatever key-value pairs show up — then the whole toolbox moves into pizza.py and imports itself back, five ways. 1 Passing an arbitrary number of arguments The asterisk makes an empty tuple and packs whatever the call sends — even a single value card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #f5c889 text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 pizzas.py — the asterisk packs a tuple ('pepperoni',) ('mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese') The asterisk tells Python: make an empty tuple called toppings and pack whatever values arrive into it. chapters.label: Classes I
chapters.text: Lecture 31 · Classes I. Dog class · instances · self · methods. class Dog(): """A simple attempt to model a dog.""" def __init__(self, name, age): # Initializing values """Initialize name and age attributes.""" self.name = name self.age = age # __init__() has no explicit return — Python # automatically returns an instance representing this dog. def sit(self): """Simulate a dog sitting in response to a command.""" print(self.name.title() + " is now sitting.") def roll_over(self): """Simulate rolling over in response to a command.""" print(self.name.title() + " rolled over!") my_dog = Dog('willie', 6) # Python reads this line → calls __init__() in Dog # with arguments 'willie' and 6 → sets name and age # → automatically RETURNS an instance → stored in my_dog # Accessing instance attributes print("My dog's name is " + my_dog.name.title() + ".") print("My dog is " + str(my_dog.age) + " years old. \\n") # Calling instance methods my_dog.sit() my_dog.roll_over() my_dog = Dog('willie', 6) your_dog = Dog('lucy', 3) t_dog = Dog('willie', 6) # same values as my_dog! print("My dog's name is " + my_dog.name.title() + ".") print("My dog is " + str(my_dog.age) + " years old.") my_dog.sit() print("\\nYour dog's name is " + your_dog.name.title() + ".") print("Your dog is " + str(your_dog.age) + " years old.") your_dog.sit() your_dog.roll_over() t_dog.sit() class Car(): """A simple attempt to represent a car.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """Initialize attributes to describe a car.""" self.make = make self.model = model self.year = year def get_descriptive_name(self): """Return a neatly formatted descriptive name.""" long_name = str(self.year) + ' ' + self.make + ' ' + self.model return long_name.title() my_new_car = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016) # creating an instance print(my_new_car.get_descriptive_name()) oop-intro Lecture 31 · classes & objects grad-text Object-oriented programming is one of the most effective approaches to writing software — and it starts with one image: a class is an architectural blueprint, an instance is the actual house built from it, with its own paint, occupants and address. One blueprint, many houses. Attributes · inheritance · composition. class Car(): def __init__(self, make, model, year): """Initialize attributes to describe a car.""" self.make = make self.model = model self.year = year self.odometer_reading = 0 # default, not a parameter def read_odometer(self): """Print a statement showing the car's mileage.""" print("This car has " + str(self.odometer_reading) + " miles on it.") my_new_car = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016) print(my_new_car.get_descriptive_name() + '\\n') my_new_car.read_odometer() def update_odometer(self, mileage): """ Set the odometer reading to the given value. Reject the change if it attempts to roll the odometer back. """ if mileage >= self.odometer_reading: self.odometer_reading = mileage else: print("You can't roll back an odometer!") # --- driving it --- my_new_car1 = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016) my_new_car1.update_odometer(20) # set to 20 my_new_car1.read_odometer() my_new_car1.update_odometer(18) # 18 < 20 → rejected! my_new_car1.read_odometer() my_new_car1.update_odometer(25) # 25 >= 20 → accepted my_new_car1.read_odometer() def increment_odometer(self, miles): """Add the given amount to the odometer reading.""" self.odometer_reading += miles # --- the used-car story --- my_used_car = Car('subaru', 'outback', 2013) print(my_used_car.get_descriptive_name()) my_used_car.update_odometer(23500) my_used_car.read_odometer() # We buy it and put 100 miles on it # between buying and registering: my_used_car.increment_odometer(100) my_used_car.read_odometer() class ElectricCar(Car): """Represent aspects of a car, specific to electric vehicles.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """Initialize attributes of the parent class.""" super().__init__(make, model, year) my_tesla = ElectricCar('tesla', 'model s', 2016) print(my_tesla.get_descriptive_name()) class ElectricCar(Car): """Represent aspects of a car, specific to electric vehicles.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """ Initialize attributes of the parent class. Then initialize attributes specific to an electric car. """ super().__init__(make, model, year) self.battery_size = 70 # child-only attribute def describe_battery(self): # child-only method """Print a statement describing the battery size.""" print("This car has a " + str(self.battery_size) + "-kWh battery.") my_tesla = ElectricCar('tesla', 'model s', 2016) print(my_tesla.get_descriptive_name()) # from Car ✓ my_tesla.describe_battery() # from ElectricCar ✓ my_maruti = Car('swift', 'XLI', 2018) print(my_maruti.get_descriptive_name()) # my_maruti.describe_battery() # ← Car has no battery! AttributeError # In Car: def fill_gas_tank(self): """Filling the gas tank of a car""" print("Filling the gas tank!") # In ElectricCar — same name, new behavior: def fill_gas_tank(self): """Electric cars don't have gas tanks.""" print("This car doesn't need a gas tank!") my_byd = ElectricCar('BYD', 'Seal', 2026) my_byd.fill_gas_tank() class Battery(): """A simple attempt to model a battery for an electric car.""" def __init__(self, battery_size=70): """Initialize the battery's attributes.""" self.battery_size = battery_size def describe_battery(self): """Print a statement describing the battery size.""" print("This car has a " + str(self.battery_size) + "-kWh battery.") def get_range(self): """Print a statement about the range this battery provides.""" if self.battery_size == 70: range = 240 elif self.battery_size == 85: range = 270 message = "This car can go approximately " + str(range) message += " miles on a full charge." print(message) class ElectricCar(Car): """Represent aspects of a car, specific to electric vehicles.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """ Initialize attributes of the parent class. Then initialize attributes specific to an electric car.
